reference.text:
Mother of Bacchus, sonorous, divine,
And many-form’d, the parent of the vine.
Associate of the Seasons, essence bright,
All-ruling virgin, bearing heav’nly light.
With fruits abounding, of a bounteous mind,
Horn‘d, and alone desir’d by those of mortal kind.
O vernal queen, whom grassy plains delight,
Sweet to the smell, and pleasing to the sight:
Whose holy form in budding fruits we view,
Earth's vig’rous offspring of a various hue :
Espous’d in autumn, life and death alone
To wretched mortals from thy pow’r is known:
For thine the task, according to thy will,
Life to produce, and all that lives to kill,
Hear, blessed Goddess, send a rich increase
Of various fruits from earth,
[context] with lovely Peace :

<meta>This page continues the Orphic Hymn to Persephone (XXIX), picking up from verse 8. The previous page introduced Persephone as the daughter of Zeus and Demeter and the queen of the underworld; this page expands on her cosmic roles as a bringer of seasons and the duality of life and death.</meta>

<header>HYMNS XXIX</header>

<columns>2</columns>

->mother of the loud-thundering, multiform Eubuleus,<-
->playmate of the Seasons, Light-bringer, of glorious form;<-
->10 venerable, all-ruling, maiden abounding in fruits,<-
->bright-shining, horned, alone desired by mortals,<-
->vernal, rejoicing in meadow-breezes,<-
->revealing your sacred form in green-fruited sprouts,<-
->wedded in an autumnal abduction to the marriage bed;<-
->15 life and death alone for much-toiling mortals,<-
->Persephoneia; for you always bear all things and slay all things.<-
->Hear, O blessed goddess, and send up fruits from the<-
->earth,<-

---

<margin>9. *weaver-together* commonly. *playmate* <note>Original: *sympaikt.*</note> Heringa, Observations II p. 87; as in Hymn 42, 7. *Light-bringer* <note>Original: *Phaesphore*</note> commonly. 10. *maiden—abounding* Voss. 12. *breezes* <note>Original: *pnoiesin*</note> Aldine edition, Paris manuscripts α, β. Dinnerus p. 633, 648. *blasts* commonly. 13. *green-fruited* <note>Original: *chlook.*</note> Af. Voss. See the note on Hymn 18, 8. *flesh-fruited* <note>Original: *chrookarpois*</note> commonly. 14. *abduction—autumnal* Voss. *abduction, bride, autumnal* Aldine. *abduction, bride* Dinnerus p. 633, for whom this verse is placed before the preceding one. 16. *Persephone* Af.</margin>

Nevertheless, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and others have described the births. **gesner**

**XXIX. (28) 8.** It is probable that this Eubuleus <note>A name often associated with Dionysus/Bacchus or a chthonic deity in the Eleusinian mysteries.</note> is Bacchus. See the Index. **gesner**

**XXIX. (28) 9.** Most of what follows pertains to this: that the alternating stay of Proserpina <note>The Latin name for Persephone.</note> among the inhabitants of the underworld and the upper world is a symbol of seeds lying hidden and then coming forth. **gesner**

**XXIX. (28) 9.** It is perhaps difficult to say who the *weaver-together* <note>Original: *Symplekteira*</note> of the Seasons <note>Original: *Horon*</note> might be. Nor does *ripener-together* <note>Original: *sympepteira*</note>, which Scaliger interpreted, please me. The Seasons, being girls of a blooming age, are those with whom it is fitting for Proserpina to play. Therefore, the conjecture of the illustrious Heringa [suggesting *sympaikteira* or 'playmate'] greatly pleases me. **gesner**

<column-break/>

**XXIX. 9.** See Hymn XLIII. 7.

**XXIX. (28) 12.** Concerning the shortening of the first syllable in *pnoiesi* <note>Original: *πνοῇσι*, breezes</note>, and similar instances, this was discussed at *Argonautica* 163. **gesner**

**XXIX. (28) 13.** The illustrious Lennep in his notes on Coluthus p. 132 suspects that Scaliger read the line as: *Brightening her sacred form*. **gesner**

**XXIX. 13.** *Green-fruited* <note>Original: *Chlookarpois*</note> is also used by Lennep on Coluthus p. 132 and Dinnerus under the entry for *Persephone*. Verses 12, 13, and 14 can be illustrated from the *Homeric Hymn to Ceres* [Demeter] 445: "and he decreed that for her daughter, as the year revolves, one third part should be beneath the murky gloom, but two parts with her mother and the other immortals..." Here it is clear a verse has fallen out from v. 471, which was continued from v. 465. For v. 466–470 were wrongly repeated by some very easy—

HYMNS XXIX

->Mother of the loud-thundering, many-formed Eubuleus,<-
->Playmate of the Seasons, Light-bringer, of glorious form;<-
->10 Holy one, ruler of all, maiden teeming with fruits,<-
->Radiant, horned, alone desired by mortals,<-
->Spring-like, rejoicing in the breezes of the meadows,<-
->Revealing your sacred form with green-fruited shoots,<-
->You who were wed in a stolen autumn marriage;<-
->15 Life and death alone for toil-worn mortals,<-
->Persephone; for you always bring forth and destroy all things.<-
->Hear me, blessed goddess, and send up fruits from the<-
->earth,<-

<margin>9. <term>symplekteira</term> <gloss>companion/weaver</gloss> is the common reading. <term>sympaikteira</term> <gloss>playmate</gloss> is suggested by Heringa, Observations II, p. 87; as in Hymn 42, 7. <term>Phaesphore</term> <gloss>Light-bringer</gloss> is the common reading. 10. <term>kore — bryousa</term> <gloss>maiden — teeming</gloss> (Voss). 12. <term>pnoēsin</term> <gloss>breezes</gloss> (Aldine, Paris a. b., Dinn. p. 633, 648). <term>pnoiaisin</term> is the common reading. 13. <term>chlookarpois</term> <gloss>green-fruited</gloss> (Af., Voss, V. ad 18. 8). <term>chrookarpois</term> is the common reading. 14. <term>harpaginaia — metopor.</term> (Voss). <term>harpagimaia, lechoi, metoporina</term> (Aldine). <term>harpagimaia lechoi</term> (Dinnerus p. 633), for whom this verse precedes the former. 16. <term>Persephone</term> (Af.).</margin>

However, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and others have recounted the births. <note>Gesner</note>

XXIX. (28) 8. It is probable that Eubuleus is Bacchus. See Index. <note>Gesner</note>

XXIX. (28) 9. Most of what follows serves to indicate that the alternating stay of Proserpina among the infernal and celestial powers is a symbol of seeds lying dormant and then emerging. <note>Gesner</note>

XXIX. (28) 9. It is perhaps difficult to say who the <term>sympaikteira</term> <gloss>playmate</gloss> of the Seasons could be. Nor does <term>sympepteira</term> <gloss>co-ripener</gloss>, which Scaliger interpreted, please me. The Seasons are maidens of flowering age, with whom it is fitting for Proserpina to play. Therefore, the conjecture of the distinguished Heringa is very pleasing. <note>Gesner</note>

<column-break/>

XXIX. 9. See Hymn XLIII. 7.

XXIX. (28) 12. Regarding the shortened first syllable in <term>pnoēsi</term> <gloss>breezes</gloss> and similar cases, it has been discussed at Argonautica 163. <note>Gesner</note>

XXIX. (28) 13. The distinguished Lennep, in his notes on Coluthus p. 132, suspects that Scaliger read it as: "Revealing a sacred form." <note>Gesner</note>

XXIX. 13. <term>Chlookarpois</term> <gloss>green-fruited</gloss> is also used by Lennep in his notes on Coluthus p. 132, and by Dinnerus in his entry for Persephone. Verses 12, 13, and 14 can be illustrated by Homer's Hymn to Demeter 445: "The maiden gave her a third part of the revolving year to dwell under the misty gloom, but two parts she spent with her mother and the other immortals..." It is clear that a verse has fallen out here from verse 471, which was continued to verse 465. For verses 466–470 were poorly repeated.

<summary>This page contains the Greek text of the Orphic Hymn to Persephone (XXIX), accompanied by critical notes from Gesner regarding textual variants, mythological interpretations of the goddess's seasonal cycle, and scholarly emendations.</summary>

<meta>This page contains the conclusion of the Orphic Hymn to Persephone and scholarly apparatus by Gottfried Hermann and Johann Matthias Gesner.</meta>

# HYMNS XXIX

->Mother of the loud-thundering, many-formed Eubuleus <note>original: Εὐβουλῆος; a name for Dionysus as the "Good Counselor"</note>,<-
->Playmate of the Seasons <note>original: Ὡρῶν</note>, Light-bringer, of glorious form;<-
->10 August, all-ruling maiden, teeming with fruits,<-
->Bright-shining, horned one, desired by mortals alone,<-
->Vernal one, rejoicing in the meadow breezes,<-
->Revealing your sacred body in green-fruited sprouts,<-
->Wedded in an autumnal marriage-bed by abduction;<-
->15 You alone are life and death to toil-worn mortals,<-
->Persephone; for you always nourish and you kill all things.<-
->Hearken, blessed goddess, and send up fruits from the<-
->earth,<-

<column-break/>

<margin>9. "Weaver together" <note>original: συμπλέκτειρα</note> in the common editions. "Playmate" <note>original: συμπαίκτ.</note> according to Heringa's observations, book II, page 87; as in Hymn 42, line 7. "Light-bringer" <note>original: Φαεσφόρε</note> in the common editions. 10. "Maiden... teeming" according to Voss. 12. "Breezes" <note>original: πνοῇσιν</note> in the Aldine and Paris editions alpha and beta; Dinnerus page 633, 648. "Gales" <note>original: πνοιαῖσιν</note> in the common editions. 13. "Green-fruited" <note>original: χλοοκ.</note> according to Af. and Voss. See note on 18, 8. "Skin-fruited" <note>original: χροοκάρποις</note> in the common editions. 14. "Abduction... autumnal" according to Voss. "Abduction, in childbed, autumnal" in the Aldine. Dinnerus page 633 places this verse before the preceding one. 16. "Phersephone" <note>original: Φερσεφόνη</note> according to Af.</margin>

Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and others have nevertheless explained the "offspring" <note>original: γονὰς</note>. **Gesner.**

**XXIX.** (28) 8. It is probable that this Eubuleus is Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>. See the Index. **Gesner.**

**XXIX.** (28) 9. Most of what follows pertains to this: that the alternating stay of Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> among those below and those above is a symbol of seeds lying hidden and then coming forth. **Gesner.**

**XXIX.** (28) 9. It is perhaps difficult to say what a "weaver together of the seasons" <note>original: Συμπλέκτειρα ὡρῶν</note> could be. Nor does "ripener together" <note>original: συμπέπτειρα</note>, which Scaliger interpreted, please me. The Seasons <note>Horae</note> are girls of a blooming age, with whom it is fitting for Proserpina to play. Therefore, the conjecture of the illustrious Heringa greatly pleases me. **Gesner.**

<column-break/>

**XXIX.** 9. See Hymn XLIII, line 7.

**XXIX.** (28) 12. Regarding the shortening of the first syllable in "breezes" <note>original: πνοῇσι</note> and similar words, see the note on the Argonautica, line 163. **Gesner.**

**XXIX.** (28) 13. The illustrious Lennep, in his notes on Coluthus page 132, suspects that Scaliger read it thus: "Brightening her sacred body." **Gesner.**

**XXIX.** 13. "Green-fruited" <note>original: Χλοοκάρποις</note> is also used by Lennep on Coluthus page 132 and Dinnerus under the entry "Persephone." Verses 12, 13, and 14 can be illustrated from the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, line 445: "He ordained for her that when the year comes round, the daughter should spend one third part beneath the murky gloom, and the other two parts with her mother and the other immortals." It is clear a verse has fallen out here from line 471, which was continued from line 465. For lines 466 to 470 were poorly repeated...

reference.title: The Dissertations of Maximus Tyrius, vol. II, Dissertation XXIX: Whether poets have entertained better conceptions about the gods than philosophers
reference.located: Maximus of Tyre, Or. 4.1–3 (Hobein) = Davies/Taylor Dissertation XXIX, Taylor vol. II pp. 97–99
reference.edition_note: Taylor translates the printed vulgate (Davies/Markland); the page is a late manuscript with many scribal/OCR variants; Taylor joins the 'day/sun' simile and 'οὕτω τοι' sentence with a colon
reference.coverage_note: full (page begins at 'οὕτω τοι καὶ τὰ ποιητικῆς πρὸς φιλοσοφίαν ἔχει' and breaks off at 'σοφώτερον Ἀριστοτέλους'); preceding simile and the rest of the final sentence given as context
reference.text:
[context] Just as if some one should conceive that day is any thing else than the light of the sun falling on the earth, or that the sun running above the earth is any thing else than day :
for thus poetry subsists with respect to philosophy. For what else is poetry than philosophy, ancient by time, metrical from harmony, and mythological from design ? And what else is philosophy than poetry, more recent in time, more strenuous in harmony, and more clear in its intention ? Since these two things, therefore, differ from each other in time only and form, how shall any one judge what is the difference between them in fhose things in which both poets and philosophers assert something about divinity ?
Or may we not say that this enquiry is just as if some one, comparing the most ancient medicine with the new, and which is now applied to bodies, should consider the better and the worse in each of these ? For Esculapius would say in answer to him, " That times do not change other arts (for of things of which there is the same use, of these the works, likewise, are always similar) but thct medicine, following the temperament of the body, a thing neither stable nor definite, but easily changed by ordinary aliment, necessarily invented different modes of diet accommodated to the present nutriment. Do not think, therefore, that those my sons, Machaon and Podalirius, were less dexterous in the healing art than their successors who discovered these sage and all- various methods of eure. But then, indeed, the art being conversant with bodies, which were neither easily changed, nor various, nor perfectly dissolute, managed them without difficulty, and its employment was something simple,
" To cut out arrows, and by med'cines bland
The wound to heal.M
But now, at length, bodies falling from this art into a more various diet and a depraved temperament, the art itself became diversified, and passed from its former simplicity into an all-various form."
Come, then, let one, who is a poet, and at the same time a philosopher, judge of the pursuits of the two in the same manner as Ksculapius has judged of medicine. This man, therefore, will be very indignant, if any one should think that Homer and Hesiod, or by Jupiter Orpheus, or any other of the poets of that time, was less wise than Aristotle
[context] the Stagirite, or Chrysippus the Cilician, or Clitomachus the Libyan, or than others who were the authors of these many wise inventions ; and that these poets were not in like manner, if not even more, skilful in the same things.

text: So it is with poetry in relation to philosophy; for poetry is another philosophy. In time, it is ancient; in harmony, it is metrical; in thought, it is mythological. And philosophy is another, ethical; in time, it is newer; in harmony, it is more discordant; in thought, it is clearer. Why, then, if they are busy with time and are carried along together, how should one train the difference in those things which each says about the divine, both the diverse [poets] and the philosophers? Or let the examination be like this: just as someone who has considered medicine, which he has first now, in relation to the new one and the one directed at diseases, would examine which of the two is better or worse; for Asclepius would [not] say to him: "Those who do not change simple arts, the times do not change them." For of those things whose need is simple, the works are also simple. But the medical [art], if it were to follow the head of the body's affairs, would not exist; nor would it be consistent. But because of the change and shift of the food [the body] currently has, it finds healing things that are sufficient for it, others appropriate at different times for the current food. Do not, therefore, consider this: he who cuts the ulcers with a knife, and the one suffering from gout, it was not then necessary to heal them [in the same way] as the one who applied himself to the art later. And these wise and varied cures of the keen-witted; but when the art, communing with bodies, is not therapeutic nor varied, nor completely dissolved, it handles them easily. And for them, the work is simple. But now, healing bodies that are becoming more varied and have an evil temperament, [the art] became varied itself, and changed from its former simplicity to a varied one. Therefore, let both the poet and the philosopher answer about the practices of Asclepius. This one [the philosopher] even gets angry at the sufferers; if someone ignored Homer and Hesiod, or Orpheus, or another who said the same things, or [who claimed] to be wiser than Aristotle...

text:
In this way, poetry relates to philosophy. For poetry is a different kind of philosophy: in time it is ancient, in harmony it is metrical, and in its judgment it is mythological. Philosophy, on the other hand, is something else: it is ethical, in time it is more recent, in harmony it is less rhythmic, and in its judgment it is clearer. Therefore, when one considers the time and the way they are brought together, how might one practice distinguishing between them, especially in what each says about the divine, both the poets and the philosophers? Or, if we consider the inquiry itself, let us say it is like this: just as someone who considers medicine, which he possesses from the beginning, and compares it to the new medicine applied to current diseases, he might judge which of the two is better or worse. Asclepius <note>the Greek god of medicine</note> would say to him: time does not change simple arts. For those things whose need is constant, their works are also simple. But medicine, if it follows the nature of the body, is not a fixed thing, nor is it uniform. Instead, it changes and shifts according to the food currently consumed, finding remedies sufficient for the patient, at one time using one thing, at another time another, suitable for the current diet. Therefore, do not think that the one who cuts out ulcers with a knife, or the one who treats gout, is not using the same art as the one who applies later methods. These wise and varied remedies are sharp. But when the art deals with bodies that are not sickly, nor complex, nor entirely weakened, it handles them easily, and its work is simple, such as applying mild drugs. However, when it treats bodies that are now becoming more complex and of a poor constitution, the art itself becomes varied, and it changes from its former simplicity into something multifaceted. Let both the poet and the philosopher answer to another Asclepius regarding their practices. This one will be indignant if anyone ignores Homer, Hesiod, or Orpheus, or anyone else who speaks of the same things, or claims that Aristotle is wiser.

<summary>Maximus of Tyre compares poetry and philosophy, using the analogy of medicine to explain how both disciplines adapt their methods to the changing needs of their subjects.</summary>
<keywords>Poetry, Philosophy, Medicine, Asclepius, Homer, Hesiod, Orpheus, Aristotle, Methodology</keywords>

text:
In this way, the relationship of poetry to philosophy stands: for poetry is essentially philosophy of a different kind. In terms of time, it is ancient; in its harmony, it is metrical; and in its intent, it is mythological. Philosophy, on the other hand, is a different form of ethics: in time, it is more recent; in its harmony, it is more straightforward <note>original: "azunouetera," likely meaning less complex in meter or more prosaic</note>; and in its intent, it is clearer. Therefore, since time alone is the matter of concern and they are carried along together, how might one examine the difference? In these matters, both the poets <note>literally: "the varied ones"</note> and the philosophers say something concerning the divine. Or rather, let us consider the inquiry in this way: just as if someone, reflecting on the medical art as it first existed compared to the new art now applied to diseases, should look to declare which is better or worse. For Asclepius <note>the god of medicine</note> would say to him: times do not alter simple arts. For where the need is simple, the works are also most simple. But in medical matters, if one follows the primary concerns of bodies, it is not a simple or agreed-upon thing. Rather, as the nature of our nourishment changes and shifts, the healing arts find sufficient remedies for it, providing different treatments at different times suitable to the current diet. Do not think, then, that the one who treated wounds with a knife or the one who treated gout was less skilled than those who later applied themselves to the art and these wise, manifold remedies of sharp mixtures. Rather, when the art dealt with bodies that were not pampered or complex, nor entirely weakened, it handled them easily, and its work was simple, using mild medicines for those who were struck. But now, as the art treats bodies that have become more complex and of a poor constitution through luxury, it has itself become varied and has changed from its former simplicity into a multifaceted state. Let both the poet and the philosopher answer together, like another Asclepius, on behalf of their practices. This man would be pained by those suffering from diseases if he ignored Homer and Hesiod and Orpheus, or any other who spoke in the same way, or if he thought himself wiser than Aristotle.

<summary>Maximus of Tyre compares poetry and philosophy, arguing they are different historical stages of the same pursuit. He uses a medical analogy to show how wisdom must adapt its form to the changing needs and complexities of the human condition.</summary>
<keywords>poetry, philosophy, medicine, Asclepius, Homer, Hesiod, Orpheus, Aristotle, ethics, mythology</keywords>

text:
Thus, the relationship of poetry to philosophy is as follows: for what is poetry, if not philosophy, ancient in time, metrical in harmony, and mythological in its judgment? And what is philosophy, if not poetry, newer in time, more concise in its harmony, and clearer in its judgment? Since these two things differ from one another only in time and form, how might one judge the difference between them, especially regarding what each says about the divine, both the poets and the philosophers? Let us say that this inquiry resembles the following: if someone were to consider the original medicine of the past in comparison to the new medicine prescribed for the bodies of today, and were to examine which of the two is better or worse. <note>Asclepius, the god of medicine, is invoked here as the arbiter of this comparison.</note> Asclepius would answer him that time does not alter other arts, for those things whose need is always the same also have similar works. But medicine must follow the constitution of bodies, which is not a stable or consistent thing, but one that changes and shifts according to the foods in one's diet. Therefore, it must discover remedies and diets that are appropriate at different times for the current nourishment. Do not, therefore, consider my sons, that Machaon and Podalirius <note>The sons of Asclepius, mentioned in the Iliad as healers.</note> were any less skilled in healing than those who later applied themselves to the art and discovered those wise and varied remedies. Rather, at that time, the art dealt with bodies that were not delicate, nor complex, nor entirely weakened, and it handled them easily. Their task was simple: to cut out arrows and sprinkle soothing medicines upon them. But now, as bodies have slipped into a more complex diet and a poor constitution, the art itself has become complex and has changed from its former simplicity into a varied form. Come then, let both the poet and the philosopher answer together, in the manner of Asclepius, on behalf of their pursuits. The latter is greatly distressed if anyone should think that Homer and Hesiod, or by Zeus, Orpheus, or any other man of that time, was less wise than Aristotle.

<summary>Maximus of Tyre compares poetry and philosophy, arguing they are essentially the same pursuit differing only in form and time, and uses the analogy of the evolution of medicine to explain how these disciplines adapt to the changing nature of their subjects.</summary>
<keywords>Poetry, Philosophy, Asclepius, Medicine, Homer, Hesiod, Aristotle, Ancient Wisdom</keywords>

[context] or according to passion, as
love succeeds beauty, anger contumely, pleasure prosperity, and pain calamity ; or according to place, as
" Pharis and Sparta, Thisbe, nurse of doves
Or according to distribution ; as,
" The hardy warriors whom Bocotia bred,
Penelius, Leitus, Prothocnor, led :
With these Arcesilaus and Clonius stand."
Or according to power ; as,
" O father Jove ! this task let Ajax prove,
Or Tydeus' son, or rich Mycene's king
The senses, therefore, as being established in the vestibules of the soul, when they come into contact with a certain beginning, and deliver it to intellect; then intellect, adhering to this, perceives what remains, and proceeds to things consequent either by time or by nature, by distribution or by place, by honour or by power. For, as in long and thin spears, he who moves their extremities sends the motion through the whole spear as far as to the other end ; and as he who shakes the beginning of long and stretched ropes diffuses the motion which proceeds to the end through the whole ; in like manner a small beginning only is necessary to intellect, in order to its conception of the whole of thinp-s. A man, therefore, of a naturally good disposition, and who rapidly runs to virtue, receiving the beginning from himself, eagerly proceeds in his journey, and apprehends and remits to memory the spectacles of intellect. But he who is less skilful has need of Socrates, who, indeed, teaches him nothing, but by interrogation and enquiry causes him to answer the truth itself. Who then can answer that which he does not yet know ? Unless some one should say, that he who walks when another leads him by the hand does not himself walk. What then is the difference between him who leads another by the hand and him who interrogates, and between him who walks and him who answers ? For the one possesses energy from himself, but the other imparts security to that energy.

Desire arises; and anger follows insult; and pleasure, good fortune; and grief, misfortune. Or it occurs by place, as in "Pharis and Sparta and dove-haunted Thisbe" <note>A reference to the Catalogue of Ships in Homer's Iliad, 2.582.</note>. Or by law, as "Peneleos and Leitus commanded the Boeotians, and Arcesilaus and Prothoenor and Clonius" <note>Iliad, 2.494-495.</note>. Or by power, as "Father Zeus, let either Ajax be chosen, or the son of Tydeus, or the king himself of gold-rich Mycenae" <note>Iliad, 7.179-180.</note>.

Since the senses are established in the vestibule of the soul, whenever they grasp some starting point and hand it over to the <term>nous</term> <gloss>intellect/mind</gloss>, the intellect seizes it and perceives the rest. It proceeds to the consequences, whether by time, nature, law, place, rank, or power. For just as with long and slender spears, he who shakes the butt-end transmits the motion through the entire length of the spear to the point; and just as with long and stretched-out ropes, he who shakes the beginning transmits the motion to the whole, traveling to the end; so too the intellect requires a brief starting point for the comprehension of all things.

The man who is well-disposed by nature, and most swift toward virtue, takes the starting point from himself. He proceeds, he investigates, he grasps, and he reflects in his memory upon the visions of the intellect. But the man who is less capable needs Socrates, who teaches him nothing, but asks questions and inquires. The man then answers the truths themselves. Who, then, would answer what he does not yet know? Unless one would say that a man walking, while another leads him by the hand, is not walking himself. What, then, is the difference between the one leading by the hand and the one asking questions, and what is the difference between the one walking and the one answering? For the one provides the activity for himself, while the other provides it for him <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>.

<summary>This passage discusses how the intellect processes information through sensory starting points and compares the Socratic method of questioning to the act of guiding someone by the hand.</summary>

[context] For one thing dries, but another heats, and other things produce a change in a different way.
It is necesary therefore, that in the soul also one thing should be essence, another power, and another energy. And it is requisite that he who wishes to apprehend and survey the whole of the soul, should speak about all these. Of the generation of the soul therefore, there will in the first place be three heads; the first, concerning its essence; the second concerning its power; and the third concerning its energy. For this will be a perfect disquisition of the things proposed for consideration. We may perceive however, that the psychical essence is a certain threefold nature. For the hyparxis of it is one thing, and the harmony in it another, according to which its essential multitude is connected; since it is not one essence like intellect, nor divisible to infinity, like body which is posterior to it; but it is divisible into more essential parts than one, of which it consists, yet they are finite in number, there not being more parts of the soul than these, since these parts of it cannot be divided into others, as will be evident as we proceed. And the form which is effected from these is another thing; so that the essence of the soul is one and threefold. For the monad and the triad are adapted to it, since we divide the whole soul into three parts. Hence its essence is one and triple: for hyparxis is one thing, harmony another, and form another. And the first of these indeed, alone defines existence, the second harmonizes the essential multitude, but the third contains the peculiarity of the whole system. All these likewise, are in each other. For hyparxis has with itself an harmonized multitude; since it is not without multitude; nor is it multitude alone unharmonized. And harmony is itself essential, and is connective of essence, to which also it gives form. Hence likewise it is shown in what respect the soul is harmony, and in what respect it is not, and that Plato accords with himself in asserting here that the soul is harmony, but in the Phxdo confuting those who maintain that it is. For it is one thing to be the harmony of itself, and of others things, and a different thing to be the harmony of another thing alone. For the latter produces harmony in a subject, and a harmony inseparable from the things harmonized, and established in a foreign seat. But the former produces a separate harmony, subsisting from itself, and converted to itself. Form likewise, is comprehensive of harmonic reasons, contains the hyparxis of the soul, and is the one reason according to which the soul is that which it is. All these therefore are in each other, viz. hyparxis, harmony, and form, and the essence of the soul is one and triple; since it also consists of three genera, essence, same and different. And again, hyparxis indeed,
[context] is rather defined according to essence, but harmony according to sameness, and form according to difference, through which it is separated from all things.

others similarly. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul have one essence, another power, and another activity; and one who wishes to grasp and contemplate the whole of it must speak about all of these. There will be, then, three primary chapters regarding the <term>psychogonia</term> <gloss>generation of the soul</gloss>: one concerning its essence, one concerning its power, and one concerning its activity; for this is a complete examination of the subjects proposed. But we see the psychic essence as threefold. For its own <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence/existence</gloss> is one thing, and the harmony within it is another, according to which its essential multitude is held together—being neither a single essence, as is the Intellect, nor divided into infinites, as is the body that comes after it, but rather into essential parts that are more than one, yet finite in number. It is impossible for there to be more parts of the soul than these, as the parts themselves are not further divisible into others, as will be clear as we proceed. Another thing is its <term>eidos</term> <gloss>form/species</gloss>, which is perfected from these; so that the essence of the soul is both one and threefold. For it is fitting for it to have both the monad and the triad, since we also divide the entire soul into three. Therefore, the essence is both one and triple. For existence is one thing, harmony another, and form another; the first defining existence alone, the second harmonizing the essential multitude, and the third holding together the <margin>C</margin> <note>marginal note: C</note> identity of the whole system. And all these are within one another. For existence has the harmonized multitude with itself; for it is not without multitude, nor does it have only multitude without harmony. And this harmony is also essential, connective, and formative of the essence; from which it is also shown how the soul is harmony and how it is not, and that Plato is consistent with himself here in positing it as harmony, while in the <term>Phaedo</term> <gloss>a dialogue of Plato</gloss> he refutes those who say these things. For it was one thing for a harmony to be of itself and of others, and another to be of another alone. The latter creates harmony in a subject, inseparable from the things harmonized and based upon an alien seat, but the former is separable, existing of itself, and turned toward itself. And indeed, the form of the harmonic ratios is comprehensive and contains the existence of the soul; for according to this, the identity of the soul is most defined, and the single <term>logos</term> <gloss>ratio/principle</gloss> according to which it is what it is. All these things, therefore, are in one another (the existence, the harmony, the form), and the essence is one and threefold, since it consists of three genera: essence, the same, and the other. <margin>D</margin> <note>marginal note: D</note> And again, existence is according to...

ON TIMAEUS G. 421

and others likewise. It is necessary, therefore, that the essence of the soul be one thing, its power another, and its activity yet another; and whoever wishes to grasp and contemplate the whole of it must speak about all of these. There will be, therefore, three primary chapters regarding the generation of the soul <margin>B</margin>: the first concerning its essence, the second concerning its power, and the third concerning its activity; for this is the complete examination of the subjects proposed. But we see that the psychic essence is threefold. For its very existence is one thing, and the harmony within it is another, according to which its essential multitude is held together—being neither a single essence, like the intellect, nor divided into infinities, like the body that follows it, but into essential parts that are more than one, from which it consists, yet finite in number, beyond which it is impossible for there to be more parts of the soul, as these parts are not further divisible into others, as will be clear to those who proceed further; and its form, which is perfected from these, is another thing. Thus, the essence of the soul is both one and threefold. For both the monad and the triad are appropriate to it, since we also divide the entire soul into three. Therefore, the essence is both one and triple. For existence is one thing, harmony is another, and form is another; the first defines existence alone, the second harmonizes the essential multitude, and the third holds together the <margin>C</margin> property of the whole system; and all these are within one another. For existence possesses the harmonized multitude with itself; for it is not without multitude, nor does it possess only a multitude that is unharmonized; and this harmony is also essential, connective, and formative of the essence. For the latter makes the harmony in a subject, inseparable from the things harmonized and seated upon an alien foundation, while the former is separable, existing of itself and turned toward itself. And indeed, the form of the harmonic ratios is comprehensive and contains the existence of the soul; for according to this, the property of the soul is most defined, as is the single ratio according to which it is what it is. # ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK III. 421

as with others likewise. It is necessary, then, that for the soul also the essence <term>ousia</term> <gloss>substance or being</gloss> is one thing, the power <term>dynamis</term> <gloss>potentiality</gloss> another, and the activity <term>energeia</term> <gloss>actualization</gloss> another; and he who wishes to grasp and contemplate the soul in its entirety must speak concerning all of these. There will be, therefore, three primary chapters of the generation of the soul <term>psychogonia</term>: the first concerning its essence, the second concerning its power, and the third concerning its activity; for this is the complete investigation of the subjects proposed. But we see that the psychic essence is triple in nature <note>The manuscript A contains a diagram here arranging existence, harmony, and form in a stemmatic fashion.</note>. For its existence <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>essential being</gloss> is one thing, the harmony within it is another—according to which its essential multiplicity is held together, being neither a single essence like the Intellect, nor divided into infinites like the body which comes after it, but divided into more than one essential parts from which it is composed, yet limited in number, of which it is impossible for there to be more parts of the soul, since its parts are no longer divisible into others, as will be clear as we proceed—and its form <term>eidos</term> <gloss>specific character</gloss> resulting from these is yet another. Thus the essence of the soul is both one and triple in nature. For both the monad and the triad belong to it, since we also divide the whole soul into three. The essence is therefore both one and triple. For existence is one thing, harmony another, and form another; the first defining being alone, the second harmonizing the essential multiplicity, and the third containing the <margin>C</margin> particularity of the whole system; and all these are in one another. For existence has with itself the harmonized multiplicity; for it is not without plurality, nor does it possess plurality alone in a discordant way. And the harmony is itself essential, being connective and formalizing of the essence; from which it is also shown how the soul is a harmony and how it is not, and that Plato is consistent with himself here in establishing it as a harmony, while in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul, where he refutes the theory that the soul is merely a harmony of the body's physical parts.</note> he refutes those who say such things. For it was one thing to be a harmony of oneself and of others, and another to be a harmony of something else alone. For the latter makes harmony exist in a subject and inseparable from the things harmonized, established upon a foreign seat, but the former makes it separate, existing of itself and turned toward itself. And indeed, the form is comprehensive of the harmonic ratios and contains the existence of the soul; for according to this especially the particularity of the soul is defined, as is the single reason <term>logos</term> <gloss>rational principle</gloss> according to which it is what it is. All these things, then, are in one another—existence, harmony, form—and the essence is one and triple in nature, since it also subsists from three genera: Essence, Sameness, and Difference. <margin>D</margin> And again, existence is according to...

<summary>Proclus explains that the soul's essence is a triad consisting of existence, harmony, and form. He reconciles Plato's description of the soul as a harmony in the Timaeus with its apparent rejection in the Phaedo by distinguishing between self-subsistent harmony and dependent harmony.</summary>

[context] For we shall be able to survey its dignity, and its order in the world, which is of a ruling nature, if we perceive h ow by all the genera that are in it,
it contains mundane essences; how by its harmony, it coharmonizes the whole world; how by its own figure, it comprehends all mundane forms and figures; after what manner, by the powers that are in it, it is able to perfect all physical, and all rational, or artificial powers; and how by its own proper energies, it excites mundane productions.
Why, therefore, did not Plato say, that the soul is a medium between intellect and sense? Because he says, that intellect and sense, are certain gnostic powers. But his intention was to deliver the middle nature of it in essences, and not in powers. Why, however, did he not say, that the soul is a medium between idea and things which are invested with form? Because it was not now proposed by him to teach us what the quality is of its form, but what its essence is. But it is not the same thing to speak of the essence, as it is to speak of the form of a certain thing. For form exhibits an essence of a certain quality. Why then, did he not place the soul as a medium between intelligible and sensible numbers?
Because in the following part of the discussion, he assigns to it an harmony, according to which it ranks as a medium between separate numbers, and separate harmony, and sensible numbers, and the harmony which is inseparable from subjects. For according to the conception of Plato, the soul is neither harmony itself, nor the harmon y which is in things harmonized. Harmony itself, indeed, is uniform and separate, and is exempt from all harmonized natures, of whatever kind they may be; being that alone which is called harmony itself. But the harmony which is in things harmonized, pertains to other things, and is naturally adapted to be moved by others. And the middle of both, is the harmony of the soul. For this is that which is first harmonized. Hence also it imparts harmony to other things. For that which is able to impart something to another thing, is either the form itself [which is participated], or primarily participates of it. This harmony therefore of the soul, is inferior to intelligible harmony, and to intelligible numbers, but transcending sensible harmony, it likewise transcends sensible numbers. And if it be requisite to speak concisely about each of these, each of them is fourfold. For with respect to number, the first is divine, the second essential, the third psychical, and the last physical. And the first, indeed, has the form of unity, the second is immoveable, the third is selfmotive, and the fourth is altermotive. With respect to harmony, also, the first is in the Gods, the second is in trulyexisting beings, the third is in souls, and the last is in the natures which are harmonized by other things. If, therefore, it had been n ow proposed by Plato to speak concerning the psychical harmony, he would have said that it is a medium between impartible and partible harmony. But since the present discussion is concerning the essence of the soul, he says that itis a medium between same and different.
Here, likewise, it is necessary to observe, that Plato in what is now said, makes as it were a conversion of the progressions of the psychical essence to their principles. For since the form of the mixtures is twofold, the one subsisting according to the mixture of the extremes,
[context] which we have in the mixture of essence, sameness, and difference; but the other, according to again collecting the media into one whole;

text:
<meta>This page continues Proclus’s examination of how the Soul acts as a mediating force between the eternal Intellect and the physical world. While the previous page focused on whether Forms exist for base things, this section explores the mathematical "Harmony" and "Numbers" that structure the Soul, and how the Soul uses these to govern the "Vehicle" (ochêma) and the celestial bodies.</meta>

# Commentary on Plato's Timaeus
## Book II: The Harmony of the Soul and the Cosmic Order

<page-num>272</page-num>

...to hold together, for every imposition of form from Being, after it is self-sufficient, acts as a **holding force** <term>Holding force: 'Synektikên', the power that keeps the universe from dissolving into chaos.</term> for the entire cosmos. This is not even the case with the figure itself, for **Forms** and **figures** are partial. But certain cosmic things do not possess all these powers. Just as with natural powers, those beyond reason or technical skill; by art they have power, but the majority in the whole will make the stars that are being formed. Why does the unity of souls remain? Not even there is there a power of the whole, nor in those is there a certain active quality because they are active; but all contribute their own particular qualities, by virtue of having them uniquely; participating in these powers. He fashions them, but not into the same things. He studied something uniquely, even their own psychic strengths. They are not the cause of the body, as we previously assumed; thus also those things that come into being, though they are the same, lack offspring. And from that sacrifice of creation there, why is it that in this way especially the things of the heavens and the numbers of sensible things follow the **Harmony** <term>Harmony: 'Harmonia', here referring to the mathematical ratios used by the Demiurge to weave the soul.</term> which creates **Reason** <term>Reason: 'Logos', often meaning mathematical proportion or ratio in this context.</term> within them? And the greatest things in the middle, toward the center, choose both the harmony of the soul and the sensible number, which are the underlying subjects. For just as the same harmony exists in souls, it does not exist in things that have been harmonized. For indeed, in the greatest intervals, it possesses its own "self-harmony," which does not exist when the soul-elements are safely settled as things harmonized within these. 

This alone is the Reason which is Harmony, as if it had the Form of harmony within itself; from which its works are also beautiful. Just as both remain through the harmony of the soul, for the <unclear>alpha</unclear> itself is harmonized, for through these they transmit it. For they transmit the harmony to certain divisions; and this same thing is well-being. Especially within his sight, he did not weave his own harmony and number from that of beings, but rather showed the sensible harmonies of itself. But the sensible harmony, as they say, has its numbers from its own particular nature. But that which is according to actions—for it is not this one—where the soul possesses harmony; because it might be carried along, even though it stands apart from harmony and the underlying things. But the harmony in **Form** <note>original: "en eidei"</note> is not truly from itself, but rather the things of the soul's **vehicle** <term>Vehicle: 'Ochêma', the subtle, celestial "chariot" or body that the soul inhabits before and after physical incarnation.</term>. And through each, again, the things directed toward the works are brought into harmony with the soul. And because it is the middle, the greatest harmony of number—whether in the earth or the ether—altogether perhaps has straight causes. He says he calls it this; he says it is something evil; for where it is failed, it must be a path, or soul, or mind. For things do not instill Form; this is not the appearance of the Form, for it is either the middle or the extremes.

<column-break/>

<page-num>273</page-num>

...a storehouse it shall have, the last of the private, the most identical, and the first. The order of the **Intellect** <term>Intellect: 'Nous', the divine mind containing the eternal Forms.</term>, increasing within the whole, does not bar this one, but holds equal things from the **Essence** <note>original: 'ousia', the fundamental nature of the soul.</note>. And there is a correction if you should destroy anything in the mind; they are ready for the Forms by not being in the divisible things, the self-same without the essence. But that which is mixed according to each season leads the way according to desire; and again, a preparation for souls, that of the Intellect from the beginning. For when they were studying in that place—among which there is also a certain greater soul, analogous to that which is with the Intellect. Some would be greater, and others would exist from the cause of division; for being placed as the cause of the even, and when the work is in the generation of Being, their parts were composed. The tongue of the thought and the matters of the essence were a concern. For the particular things, all being divided, are active in the forms of the senses; calling those things seen in the multitude. To make the whole from an excess; for he himself is also a power of being, and to God he is harmonized. Indeed, these things do not come from the superior to be understood; for they are similar. This soul established the chance occurrence, holding it together by this cause; and being thus by nature, it rightly sings of both these powers. But the things directed toward the ends in their forms are toward the power; or even the noble mixture, because it holds the power of these. 

Whence follow the things of power. They might speak of the meeting of the extremes with hope, but not by any means; as if to say the same thing of the second life, which is the explanation for the ordering. The cosmic power uses division in that which becomes an attribute of the indivisible—just as with living. For they become greater and similar, so that they are also divisible as if in potential; making it so that the soul may receive the Form. Just as the choice of the superior; for the whole is of each form; so that they are psychic powers of the stronger. He himself made these things best according to the soul; through which they might hold power themselves; where again they might only hold power. But the essence is in this way; whence it indeed seems to set apart—when the Intellect stands still in the greater vision of life; by such causes which, even if one sees such things, they would hold power. Just as the soul of the universe holds power; likewise to make her subordinate to itself, and to be. Not at all, the soul of the universe is of a greater cause; as many as are in their souls. For some are from the soul. The generation of these is eternal; these choose to hold power over the essence—they come into being. For after the sowing or the **demiurgy** <term>Demiurgy: 'Demiorgia', the act of cosmic creation or craftsmanship.</term> itself, the things from it will be established. The soul will make it with that which is from the **Demiurgic Mind**; with the straight power, since that which holds power is the same as those who might hold power. To use the straight path with the powers, this is the honor; the poetic things use the straight path. For these names, the soul...

<summary>This page discusses how the Soul mediates between the eternal Intellect and the physical world through mathematical harmony and ratio. Proclus explores how the Soul governs its "vehicle" and the celestial bodies, maintaining order through its participation in the divine "storehouse" of Forms.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, Harmony, Demiurge, Intellect, Forms, Soul Vehicle, Mathematical Ratio, Cosmic Order, Essence</keywords>

for it holds together every production from Being, after it suffices for itself, being connective of the whole cosmos. This is something that not even the shape <note>referring to the geometric or formal structure</note> by itself possesses, for the forms and the shapes are partial. But the cosmic ones—some of these are not in all powers. Just as with natural powers, or those beyond reason or technical ones; by art they are in potentiality; but the majority in the whole will produce the stars that are brought into being. Why is it that the one remains in the things of the souls? Not even there is it of a power, not of the whole, nor are they active powers for those, because they are active; but it contributes to all their own, the very having of it specifically; participating in powers; it fashions, but not into the same ones. Studying specifically something, and the psychic ones for themselves remaining. They are not a cause of the body, as we presupposed; and thus also the things of becoming, the fact that being the same, it lacks generations. And of that sacrifice of the making, why is it that thus especially also the things of the heavens and the numbers of the sensible things, because the harmony follows them, the one that makes the reason. And the greatest things, at least according to the one in the mean towards the middles, and the harmony of the psychic, and the sensible number, and the harmony it chooses, of which they are the subjects. For just as the same harmony being in souls is not in the things that are harmonized. For even the things with the most intervals, itself of itself, not being a self-harmony; when also psychic and safely established as in these harmonized things. This very thing alone, the reason is harmony, as it were; if it has harmony in them; where also the works are good; just as remaining both because of the harmony of the psychic, for it itself is the <unclear>a''</unclear> harmonized, for through it they impart. to hold together every production from Being, after it has achieved self-sufficiency, as a cohesive force for the entire cosmos. This is not even achieved by its own shape, for forms and shapes are particular. But certain cosmic things do not possess all these powers. Just as there are natural powers, there are also those beyond the rational or technical; by art <note>original: τέχνῃ</note> they have power, but the majority of things in the whole will produce the stars that are implanted within. Why is it that the souls remain as one? Not even there is the power of the whole, nor are there certain active forces in those things because they are effective. But all things contribute their own proper qualities, namely the fact of having a unique character; they participate through their powers. He fashions them, but not into the same forms. He was practicing something unique, even their own psychic strengths. They are not the cause of the body as we previously assumed; and so also the things that come to be, because being the same, the generation is lacking. And of that sacrifice and production there, because in this way especially the things of the heavens and the numbers of sensible things follow, because the harmony within them produces reason. And the greatest things, at least those in the middle relative to the centers, choose both the harmony of the soul and the sensible number and the harmony of the underlying things. For it is as if the same harmony existing in souls is not in the things that have been harmonized. For even the things with the greatest intervals possess a self-harmony that is not itself; when both psychic things and those safely established are as if harmonized in these. This alone is the reason: harmony is like a form; he saw that he has harmonies within them, from which also the works are beautiful. Just as both remain through the harmony of the soul, for it is the <unclear>a''</unclear> harmonized, for through these they impart it. For they impart harmony to some as divisions; and the same is well-being. In him especially, not even his own harmony and number are visible, having woven the harmony of beings and intending to show the sensible harmonies of herself. But the sensible is sensible, as they say, having its own numbers of itself. But the actions according to it, being indeed not this one; by which the soul has harmony; because it might be carried along, although from harmony and from things that subsist, but harmony is that which is in form; not truly from itself, but the vehicles of the souls; and through each one again the things brought toward the works in the harmony of the soul. And because the greatest harmony is the middle of the number; whether in the earth or the ether, it perhaps has straight causes. He says he calls it this, but he says it is an evil being; for where it is a failure, it is necessary that it be either a path or a soul or an intellect. For he does not place the form in this part of the form, but it does not seem so, for the middle or the extremes are.

storehouse and will have, the last of the private and most identical and first. But the order upon the intellect, increasing in the whole, does not restrain this, having equal parts from the essence. And there is a correction if you should destroy anything in the mind; they prepare the forms by not being in the divisible things, the same in itself without the essence. But the mixture according to each season led the way according to the <note>desire</note> preparation again for souls, and that of the intellect from the beginning. For when they were practicing in that place, among which was a certain greater soul, analogous to that which is with the intellect. Some would be greater, others from the cause of existing by division; for having been placed as an even cause, and when the work is among those things, the generation of being; and their parts were composed. The tongue is of the thought, and the things of the essence were a concern. For the proper things, all having been divided, are active in forms and concerned with sensations; calling those things seen in the multitude. To make associations from excess of the whole; for he himself is also a power of being, harmonized to God. Indeed, these things do not happen to the superior to understand; for it is similar. This soul established the chance occurrence, holding together the cause; and as this is by nature, both of these correctly belong to the powers. But the things toward the ends in forms are toward the powers; or even the noble mixture because it holds power over these. Whence follow the things of power. One might speak of the meeting of the extremes with hope, not by any means; as if saying the same thing for the second life of the arrangement, if there is an explanation of this. The cosmic use of division in itself becomes a property of the indivisible; as also with living. For they become greater and likewise; so that they are also divisive as if in potential; making it so that the soul may receive the form. Just as the choice of the superior; for the whole of each is in forms; so that the psychic things are of the stronger. But he himself thus makes the best things according to the soul; through which they might rule themselves. But where again they might only rule; the essence is in this way. Whence indeed it seems that one part is the setting apart; when also the intellect, standing still in the greater contemplation, lives. By such causes which, even if it sees such a thing, they might rule. As the soul of the universe ruling; likewise to make it subordinate to itself; both to be and not to be, the soul of the universe of how great a cause. And those in their souls. For some are from the soul. Of the generation, alas, and eternal; these things <note>to be able to choose the greater essence</note> choose so that they might rule; they become. For after the sowing or the craftsmanship itself; the things from it will subsist. And the soul will make it with the, for it is from the demiurgic intellect; a straight line with the ruler, since the ruling one is as the same of the rulers. <summary>Proclus discusses the metaphysical structure of the soul and its relationship to cosmic harmony, number, and the demiurgic intellect. He explores how the soul acts as a mediating force that holds the cosmos together through its participation in both indivisible essence and divisible form.</summary>

κ’ αἰώνια· ταῦτ’ δὲ (τὸ τοῖ’ μεῖζ’ δύνασθ’ τὴν οὐσίαν) αἱρεῖσθαι μ’ τὰς

τὰ δὲ ἐξ α’ ὑποστήσ’· ψυχὴν δὲ τὰ ποιήσειν αὐτὴν μετὰ τοῦ, ἡ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ
δημιουργικοῦ ν’· μετ’ κράτορος εὐθεῖαν, ἐπεὶ ἡ κρατοῦσ’ ὡς τὴν αὐτὴν
τοῦ κρατοῖεν· ταῖς δυνάμεσιν εὐθεῖαν χρῆσθαι, τοῦτ’ ἢ ἡ τιμὴ’

it holds together all worldly substances; how it harmonizes the whole world with its own harmony; how it contains all forms and worldly shapes within its own shape; in what manner it is able to perfect all natural powers, as well as all logical or technical ones, through the faculties within it; and how it awakens worldly creations through its own proper activities. Why, then, did he not call the soul the midpoint between intellect and sensation? Because he says that intellect and sensation are certain cognitive powers; but he wishes to convey the mediation that exists in their substances, not that which exists in their powers. And why did he not call it the midpoint between the Idea and the things formed by the Idea? Because it was not his purpose now to teach what its form is, but its substance; and it is not the same thing to speak of the substance of something and its form; he is presenting such a substance. Why did he not place it as the midpoint between intelligible and sensible numbers? Because he will provide the harmony in the following arguments, according to which it holds the midpoint between the separate numbers and the separate harmony, and the sensible numbers and the inseparable harmony of the underlying things. For the soul is neither self-harmony itself, nor is it in the things that are harmonized, according to Plato's thought; rather, self-harmony is uniform, separate, and removed from all things that are harmonized in any way, being only this very thing which is called harmony; but that which is in the harmonized things belongs to others and is naturally moved by others; the harmony of the soul is the midpoint between both; for this is what is primarily harmonized; therefore, it also imparts harmony to others; for that which is able to impart something to another is either the form itself, or has participated in it primarily. It is therefore subordinate to the intelligible harmony, and subordinate to the intelligible numbers; and being superior to the sensible harmony, it is also superior to the sensible numbers. And if one must speak briefly about each of these, each of them is fourfold; for the number is first the divine, second the essential, third the psychic, and last the physical; the one is uniform, the next is unmoved, the next is self-moved, and the next is moved by another. And the harmony is first that which is in the gods, second that which is in the things that truly are, third that which is in the souls, and last that which is in the things harmonized by others. If, therefore, it had been Plato's purpose now to speak about the psychic harmony, he would have said that it is the midpoint between the indivisible and the divisible harmony; but since the discussion at present is about substance, he says that it has grasped the midpoint of the Same and the Other and substance. One must also observe that, just as he has made a return in these matters of the progressions of the psychic substance to the principles; for since the type of mixtures is twofold, one consisting in the mixture of the extremes, as we have in the case of substance, sameness, and otherness, and the other in the gathering of the means back into one whole, in the former he began from substance and ended at the other, but in the latter, conversely, he first harmonized the other with the same, then both with substance, and ended at the substance from which he set out in the progression; and everywhere he holds to the two principles after the One; for even when he was making the soul from the indivisible and the divisible, he placed the indivisible analogous to the limit, and the divisible to the infinite; <unclear>for the infinite is the cause of plurality</unclear>, and the limit of unification; and when he placed the other as in the genera of being, it was of the series of the infinite, and the same, of the limit; and when he mixed these with substance; for substance is uniform, but these are dual and opposed to each other; and he did not cease gathering the plurality until he made the whole one; for the One is superior even to substance itself and the two principles. Since the mixture is twofold, as we have said, one being the constitutive of the elements themselves, and the other of that which is from the elements, Porphyry rightly asked whether he made both of these in the mixing bowl, or one outside the bowl and the other within it; and he decided that he mixes the elements without the bowl <unclear>acting</unclear>; but since the generation of the means occurred according to the meeting of the extremes, the extremes could not at all come together into the same; but in producing that which is from all the middle elements, he uses the mixing bowl, casting the elements into it and mixing them, so that the soul might be one in all things, and of the same color as itself, and homogeneous, with all the genera having permeated through everything, and so that the soul might receive the form, and that which is from the mixing bowl; for the form of each is according to the whole, so that, being a soul-maker, the mixing bowl creates the totality of the soul within itself; therefore, the second mixture is in the mixing bowl alone. Our teacher also agreed with this distinction. Plato also seems, in the arguments concerning the partial souls, to indicate this by saying: and again, into the former mixing bowl, in which he was mixing the soul of the universe, he poured the remainders of the previous things, mixing them; into which he says the soul of the universe was also cast, but not its elements, and in the case of our own, the remainders of the previous things are mixed within it; and these were the means, clearly the second mixture occurring in the mixing bowl <unclear>after another</unclear> than the first according to the creative cause, and the second also according to the life-giving cause, already making the soul from the middle genera; for it was necessary for the creator to act both before the mixing bowl, and with the mixing bowl, just as also after the mixing bowl, using the creative divisions, and the other activities concerning the soul; for after the totality of the soul, the

συνέχει πάσας τὰς ἐγκοσμίους οὐσίας· ὅπως μὲν τῇ αὑτῆς ἁρμονίᾳ

πάσας δὲ λογικὰς ἢ τεχνικὰς τελειοῦν δύναται· πῶς δὲ ταῖς

μένων; ὅτι μὴ τὸ εἶδος αὐτῆς νῦν προὔκειτο διδάξαι ποῖόν ἐστιν,

Πλάτωνος διάνοιαν· ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν αὐτοαρμονία μονοειδής ἐστι καὶ

to hold together; for every implanting that comes from being, after sufficing for itself, is cohesive of the whole cosmos. This is not so even for the figure taken by itself, for the forms and the figures are partial. But the cosmic things, and some of these, not with all powers. Just as the natural powers, those beside the rational or technical ones; by art, in potency; and the greater number in the whole will make the stars that are implanted. Why does the one, the things of the souls, remain? Nor is there power there, not that of the whole, nor are there in those certain active ones, because they are efficacious; and it contributes to all their own proper ones, the very fact of having in a particular way, as they partake of powers; but it does not mould them into the same. Something in a particular way of the members, and the psychic ones for themselves, remaining. They are not of body, a cause such as we presupposed; so too those by coming to be, and because, being the same, offspring is lacking. And of that making of the sacrifice there, why? Because in this way most of all both the things of the heaven and the numbers of the sensible things, because the harmony follows for them, the one that produces ratio. And the very greatest things, at least according to that which is in the mean, toward the middle terms, and the harmony of the psychic, and the sensible number and the harmony, are chosen, these being the substrates. For it is as it were the same harmony, existing in souls, not in the things that are harmonized. For indeed the things with the most intervals, itself of itself, not being <term>autoharmonia</term> <gloss>harmony itself</gloss>; when also psychic things, and securely, as in these harmonized things. This alone itself the ratio is, as it were, harmony; it has a form of harmony in them; of which the works too are beautiful; just as remaining, both, through the harmony of the psychic; for itself, the <unclear>α''</unclear> harmonized, for through them they impart it. For they also impart the harmony, and to some, divisions; and the same is the fair course; and in it most of all, under sight, nor has it woven its own harmony and number, that of beings, and intending to show forth the sensible harmonies of itself; and the sensible one, as they say, has the numbers of itself as its own; and itself, that according to which, being actions; for not this; by which the soul has harmony; because it might be carried, although from harmony, from things that subsist, and the first harmony is that in form; from itself, not truly, and the vehicles of the souls; and the one through each, again, and the things relating to the works brought forward in the harmony of the soul; and because it is the middle of the number, the first, the greatest harmony; and form, for the earth or for the aether, perhaps altogether has straight causes; he says to call it so; and he says it is, being bad; for of which it is, it stumbles, necessarily, either a course or soul or intellect; for it does not put in the form, of the form, and the other does not seem so, for the middle is first, or being the extremes.

<column-break/>

a storehouse, and to lead, the last of the particular and of the most identical and of the first; and the order at the level of intellect, growing together in the whole, does not shut this out, but has equal shares from being. And a setting right, if you should destroy anything in the intellect; and a preparation for the forms, by not being in the divisible things, the same by itself without being; and the one blended at each season led the way according to (the longing); and again a preparation for souls, the one of intellect, the other from the beginning; for they, when in that place, of the members; in which also a certain greater soul, analogous to what comes with intellect. text:
<header>G. | 68 Prop. VI, theor. III. B. || 144 253</header>

In this way, the eighth theorem converts with the fourth. For the one states that equal sides and angles subtend equal bases, while the other states that equal sides lying on equal bases contain equal angles. Of these, the one regarding equal bases was the conclusion of the former, while the one regarding "equal sides lying" was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that same theorem. Since there are these two types of conversion, the primary one is uniform and defined, while the other is varied and proceeds into a large number of theorems, converting not in one case, but in many, due to the number of hypotheses in compound theorems. Often, we also perform a conversion with a theorem starting from two <note>or more</note> hypotheses, when the hypotheses are not all defined, but some are indefinite.

One must also observe in these cases that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions; for instance, "every hexagonal number is a triangular number," but it is no longer true that "every triangular number is a hexagonal number." The reason is that the one is more common, while the other is more particular, and it is only said of the one that it is the other. In cases where the attribute belongs primarily and is taken according to that which it is <note>the essential nature</note>, conversion also follows. This has not escaped the notice of the mathematicians around Menaechmus and Amphinomus.

<summary>Proclus explores the mechanics of geometric conversion, noting that false conversions often arise when one term is more general than the other, and asserts that valid conversion requires an essential relationship between the concepts.</summary>
<keywords>conversion, logic, hexagonal numbers, triangular numbers, Menaechmus, Amphinomus, mathematical definitions</keywords>

In this way, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the one states that equal bases subtend equal sides and angles, while the other states that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. The conclusion regarding equal bases was the result of the former, while the condition of equal sides being placed <note>as a premise</note> was one of the hypotheses assumed in that same theorem. Now, since there are two such conversions, the primary one is uniform and definite, while the other is varied and proceeds into a large number of theorems, not converting in one instance but in many, due to the multitude of hypotheses in composite theorems. Often, we also convert a theorem that begins from two <note>or more</note> hypotheses, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

One must also observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example, every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangle is a hexagonal. The reason is that the one is more general, while the other is more specific.

text:
In this manner, the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the fourth says that bases subtended by equal sides and angles are equal, while the eighth says that equal sides placed upon equal bases contain equal angles. In these, the statement regarding equal bases was the conclusion of the former theorem, while the statement regarding equal sides was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that same theorem. Since there are these two types of conversion, the first kind is simple and definite, while the second is varied and proceeds into a great number of theorems; it does not convert in a single instance but in many, owing to the multitude of hypotheses in complex theorems. Often, we also convert from a starting point of two <insert>or more</insert> hypotheses, whenever the hypotheses are not all definite but some are indefinite.

It is necessary to observe in these matters that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions. For example: every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is a hexagonal number. The reason for this is that one term is more general, while the other is more specific.

<margin>The editor notes that the phrase "or more" was added to the text so that the word "all" in the following clause would have a proper referent. He also notes that the passage seems somewhat corrupted because the singular "one" does not harmonize well with the plural "some."</margin>

<summary>Proclus discusses the logic of geometric conversion, distinguishing between simple conversions and complex ones involving multiple hypotheses. He warns that not all mathematical statements are reversible, using the relationship between hexagonal and triangular numbers as a counter-example.</summary>

The reason is that the one is more general, while the other is more specific.

<summary>Proclus discusses the logical nature of geometric conversion, distinguishing between definite and indefinite conversions and noting that not all reciprocal statements are valid conversions.</summary>

in this way the eighth theorem is the converse of the fourth. For the one says that equal bases subtend equal sides and angles, while the other says that equal sides lying upon equal bases contain equal angles. Of these, "upon equal bases" was the conclusion of the earlier theorem, and "equal sides lying" was one of the hypotheses assumed beforehand in it. There being, then, these two kinds of conversion <note>original: "ἀντιστροφαί"</note>, the leading one is of a single form and determinate, while the other is varied and runs out into a great number of theorems, converting not in one case but in many, because of the multitude of the hypotheses in composite theorems. Often, too, we give a single converse to a theorem that starts from two <insert>or more</insert> hypotheses, when the hypotheses are not all determinate but some are indefinite.

One must also take notice here that many conversions turn out false and are not conversions in the proper sense. For example, every hexagonal number is a triangular number, but it is no longer true that every triangular number is hexagonal. The reason is that the one is more general, the other more particular

Bs = M, G. 11 "because of"] "on account of", and in the margin "according to" B, "owing to" Z. 12-13 "Often ... hypotheses" omitted in G. 12 "and the" M. 13 "or more" I have added myself, so that there may be something of which "all" can be said. Yet the passage does not seem to be sound, since "one" does not at all agree with the word "some". || "starting" <note>genitive plural</note> Bs, G. || "being conversely converted" Bs, G; "being converted in one" M, but a later hand placed dots above the "ον". 19 "but it is no longer ... is" omitted in G, added in C. || "still holds true" M.

PROPOSITION LXXXVIII.
Every thing which is truly being, is either prior to eternity, or in eternity, or participates of eternity.
For that there is true being prior to eternity has been demonstrated. But true being is also in eternity. For eternity possesses the always in conjunction with being. And that which participates of eternity, has both the alwqys and being , according to participation. Eternity, however, possesses the always primarily, but being according to participation. But being itself is primarily being.
PROPOSITION LXXXIX.
Every thing which is primarily being consists of bound and infinity.
For if it possesses infinite power, it is evident that it is infinite, and on this account consists from the infinite. If also it is impartible, and has. the form of the one , through this, it participates of bound. For that which participates of unity is bounded. Moreover, it i? impartible, and therefore possesses infinite power. Hence every thing which is truly £or primarily] being consists of bound and infinity.
PROPOSITION XC.
The first bound, and the first infinity subsist by themselves prior to every thing which consists of bound and the infinite.
For if beiugs which subsist by themselves, are prior to those which are certain beings, as being common to all essences, and principal causes, and not the causes of certain, but in short of all beings,
[context] it is necessary that the first bound, and the first infinity should be prior to that which consists of both these.
