text:
->88.<-

Every thing that is truly <term>Being</term> is either before <term>Aevum</term>, or in <term>Aevum</term>, or is a participant in <term>Aevum</term>. That it is before <term>Aevum</term> has been demonstrated. But it is also in <term>Aevum</term>. For <term>Aevum</term> possesses the "always" together with <term>Being</term>, as does that which participates in <term>Aevum</term>. For every eternal thing participates in both the "always" and the "being." It possesses both of these by participation, both the "always" and the "being." But <term>Aevum</term> possesses the "always" primarily, and <term>Being</term> by participation; but <term>Being</term> itself is primarily <term>Being</term>.

->89.<-

Everything that is truly <term>Being</term> consists of limit and infinity. For if it is endowed with infinite power, it is clear that it is infinite, and in this way it subsists from the infinite. But if it is indivisible and uniform, in this way it participates in limit. For that which has participated in the One is limited. But it is at once indivisible and endowed with infinite power. Therefore, everything that is truly <term>Being</term> is from limit and infinity.

->90.<-

Before all things that consist of limit and infinity, and which subsist through these two, the first limit and the first infinity exist in themselves. For if those things that exist in themselves subsist before those things that belong to something else, as common and authoritative causes of all things—and not as causes of some things, but of all—then there must exist, before the mixture of both, the first limit and the first infinity.

<summary>Proclus defines the ontological composition of true Being as a synthesis of limit and infinity, asserting that these principles pre-exist as self-subsistent, primary causes.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Being, Limit, Infinity, Aevum, First Causes, Metaphysics</keywords>

text:
->88<-

Everything that is truly being is either before eternity, or in eternity, or participating in eternity. That it is before eternity has been demonstrated. But it is also in eternity. For eternity possesses the "always" together with being, and that which participates in eternity. For everything eternal will participate in both the "always" and in being. This <note>referring to the eternal</note> possesses both through participation, both the "always" and being. But eternity possesses the "always" primarily, and being through participation; while being itself is primarily being.

->89<-

Everything that is truly being consists of limit and the unlimited. For if it has unlimited power, it is clear that it is unlimited, and in this respect it subsists from the unlimited. But if it is partless and unified, in this respect it has participated in limit. For that which has participated in the one has been limited. But it is at once partless and possessed of unlimited power. Therefore, everything that is truly being consists of limit and the unlimited.

->90<-

The first limit and the first unlimited exist prior to all things that subsist from limit and unlimitedness, existing by themselves. For if the things that exist by themselves subsist prior to the things that are of a certain kind, as common and originating causes of all things, and not as causes of some things, but of all—

---

<note>The following notes are in Latin, referencing various codices (A.) and editions.</note>

(1) A. 89, and continues "everything that is truly" well. In the edition it was: "everything that is truly being."
(2) The word "the" is absent from codex A.
(3) In the edition, between "eternity" and "this," there is a sign of a lacuna: ***. I have filled the lacuna from codex A.
(4) A. "first." I prefer to inquire rather than decide whether the final words should be understood as: "But that which is being itself, is primarily being."
(5) A. 90.
(6) A. "truly" correctly, as at the end of the chapter. Schw. I restored it. In the edition it was: "everything that is primarily being."
(7) Thus codex A. The edition: "therefore partless and."
(8) "Is" is absent from codex A.
(9) A. 91.
(10) A. "by itself."
(11) Both codex A and the edition provide the reading of Proclus, but in different ways.

<summary>Proclus discusses the ontological status of being in relation to eternity, limit, and the unlimited, establishing the priority of first principles.</summary>
<keywords>Eternity, Being, Limit, Unlimited, Proclus, Metaphysics, Participation</keywords>

text:
->88<-

Every truly existing being is either before eternity, in eternity, or participating in eternity. It has already been demonstrated that there is something before eternity. Furthermore, there is also that which is in eternity. For eternity possesses "always" along with "being," and there is also that which participates in eternity. For everything eternal will participate in both "always" and "being." The latter <note>that which participates in eternity</note> possesses both "always" and "being" by participation. Eternity itself possesses "always" primarily, but "being" by participation. However, Being itself is primarily being.

->89<- <margin>5</margin>

Every truly <margin>6</margin> existing being is composed of limit and infinity. For if it is infinite in power, it is clear that it is infinite, and in this respect it subsists from the infinite. But if it is indivisible and uniform, in this respect it partakes of limit. For that which partakes of the One has been limited. Furthermore, it is simultaneously indivisible and <margin>7</margin> infinite in power. Therefore, every truly existing being is <margin>8</margin> composed of limit and infinity.

->90<- <margin>9</margin>

Before all things that have their subsistence from limit and infinity, there pre-exist in themselves <margin>10</margin> the first Limit and the first Infinity. For if the things that exist in themselves pre-exist those that belong to something else, as being common to all and as originating causes and not belonging to some <margin>11</margin> but to all—

<column-break/>

<note>
The following notes are translated from the original Latin apparatus criticus:
1. Codex A reads 89 and continues "every truly" correctly. In the previous Edition it was: "altogether the truly existing being."
2. The word "the" is absent from Codex A.
3. In the edition, there is a sign of a gap between "eternity" and "this indeed": ***. I have filled the gap from Codex A.
4. Codex A reads "first." I prefer to inquire rather than decide whether the final words should be understood as: "But that which is being itself, is being in the first degree."
5. Codex A and G.
6. Codex A correctly reads "truly," as at the end of the chapter. Schweighäuser. I have restored it. In the edition it was: "every primarily existing being."
7. Thus in Codex A. The Edition reads: "indivisible therefore and."
8. The word "is" is absent from Codex A.
9. Codex A reads 91.
10. Codex A reads "in itself" <note>singular</note>.
11. Both Codex A and the Edition preserve the hand of Proclus, but in different ways.
</note>

<summary>Proclus defines the relationship between truly existing beings and eternity, while establishing that all such beings are composed of the metaphysical principles of Limit and Infinity.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Elements of Theology, eternity, being, limit, infinity, infinite power, participation, metaphysics</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] Good demons permit us to survey, in conjunction with themselves, their own works, and the benefits which they impart;
but avenging demons exhibit the species of punishments [which they inflict]; and such other demons as are depraved are surrounded by certain noxious, blood-devouring, and fierce wild beasts. Archons [of the first rank] exhibit, together with themselves, certain portions of the world ; but other archons attract to themselves the inordination and confusion of matter. With respect to soul, if it ranks as a whole, and does not belong to any particular species, it presents to the view a formless fire, extended through the whole world, which is indicative of the total, one, indivisible, and formless soul of the universe ; but a purified soul exhibits a fiery form, and a pure and unmingled fire. Then, also, the most inward light of it is seen, and an undefiled and stable form, and it most willingly and joyfully follows its elevating leader, and unfolds, by its works, its own appropriate order. But the soul which verges downward draws along with it the signs of bonds and punishments, is heavy with material spirits, is detained by the anomalous tumults of matter, and exhibits before itself, genesiurgic presiding demons.

text:
# 2, 7

...the punishing <term>daimones</term> manifest the forms of their punishments, and the others—who are wicked in whatever way—are surrounded by certain harmful, bloodthirsty, and wild beasts. The <term>archontes</term> <gloss>rulers of the cosmos</gloss> display certain cosmic portions along with themselves, while the other <term>archontes</term> drag with them the disorder and confusion of matter. 

As for the soul: if it is a whole soul and not confined to any particular species, an unformed fire is seen around the whole world, indicating the soul of the cosmos which is whole, one, indivisible, and unformed. But if the soul that appears has been purified, a fiery form is seen, and the fire is pure and unmixed. Then its light at the heart, its pure form, and its steadfast seat are seen. Following its <term>anagogic</term> <gloss>upward-leading</gloss> leader, it rejoices in its own good will, and it reveals its own proper order through its deeds. But the soul that leans downward drags with it signs of bonds and punishments. It is heavy with the formations of material spirits and is held by the irregular disturbances of matter. It is seen having the <term>daimones</term> that preside over generation <note>the process of birth and embodiment</note> standing before it.

the avenging <term>daimones</term> <gloss>divine spirits/intermediary beings</gloss> reveal the forms of the punishments, while other spirits of any kind of wickedness are surrounded by harmful, bloodthirsty, and wild beasts. text:
The appearances of the punishing <term>daimones</term> <gloss>divine or semi-divine spirits</gloss> display the various forms of their punishments. Those of other <term>daimones</term> who are in any way evil are surrounded by certain harmful, bloodthirsty, and wild beasts. The <term>archons</term> <gloss>rulers or planetary governors</gloss> of the first rank display certain cosmic portions along with themselves, while the other <term>archons</term> drag along the disorder and discord of <term>hyle</term> <gloss>matter</gloss>.

Regarding the soul: when it is the universal soul and not confined to any particular form, it is seen as a formless fire distributed throughout the entire cosmos, manifesting the whole, single, indivisible, and formless soul of the universe. When it is a purified soul, its appearance is seen as fiery; the fire is stainless and unmixed. Then its inner light and its form are seen as pure and stable, and it follows its uplifting leader, rejoicing in its good will and manifesting its own proper order through its works. 

However, the soul that inclines downward drags with it the signs of bonds and punishments. It is weighed down by the compositions of material spirits and is gripped by the irregular disturbances of matter. It is seen placing the <term>daimones</term> who preside over <term>genesis</term> <gloss>the realm of generation and birth</gloss> as overseers before itself.

<note>The Greek text describes the visual manifestations or epiphanies of different spiritual entities during theurgic rites. The appearance of the entity reflects its ontological status and its relationship to the material world.</note>

<summary>Iamblichus describes the visual characteristics of various spirits and souls during their manifestation, contrasting the orderly appearance of purified souls with the chaotic or beast-like forms of lower spirits and unpurified souls.</summary>
<keywords>daimones, archons, universal soul, purified soul, matter, genesis, theurgy, spiritual manifestation</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] After this, wishing to prove that there is no difference between Jews and Christians, and those animals previously enumerated by him,
he asserts that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, who never performed anything worthy of note, and never were held in any reputation or account. Now, on the point of their not being fugitives, nor Egyptians, but Hebrews who settled in Egypt, we have spoken in the preceding pages. But if he thinks his statement, that they were never held in any reputation or account, to be proved, because no remarkable event in their history is found recorded by the Greeks, we would answer, that if one will examine their polity from its first beginning, and the arrangement of their laws, he will find that they were men who represented upon earth the shadow of a heavenly life, and that among them God is recognised as nothing else, save He who is over all things, and that among them no maker of images was permitted to enjoy the rights of citizenship. For neither painter nor image-maker existed in their state, the law expelling all such from it; that there might be no pretext for the construction of images — an art which attracts the attention of foolish men, and which drags down the eyes of the soul from God to earth. There was, accordingly, among them a law to the following effect: Do not transgress the law, and make to yourselves a graven image, any likeness of male or female; either a likeness of any one of the creatures that are upon the earth, or a likeness of any winged fowl that flies under the heaven, or a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, or a likeness of any of the fishes which are in the waters under the earth. The law, indeed, wished them to have regard to the truth of each individual thing, and not to form representations of things contrary to reality, feigning the appearance merely of what was really male or really female, or the nature of animals, or of birds, or of creeping things, or of fishes. Venerable, too, and grand was this prohibition of theirs: Lift not up your eyes unto heaven, lest, when you see the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and all the host of heaven, you should be led astray to worship them, and serve them. And what a régime was that under which the whole nation was placed, and which rendered it impossible for any effeminate person to appear in public; and worthy of admiration, too, was the arrangement by which harlots were removed out of the state, those incentives to the passions of the youth! Their courts of justice also were composed of men of the strictest integrity, who, after having for a lengthened period set the example of an unstained life,
[context] were entrusted with the duty of presiding over the tribunals, and who, on account of the superhuman purity of their character, were said to be gods, in conformity with an ancient Jewish usage of speech.

...regarding the fact that they were not runaway slaves, but were Hebrews who had sojourned in Egypt, has been said by us in the preceding pages. But if he thinks that their not being significant in speech or in number is to be established by the fact that the history concerning them is not found very much among the Greeks, we shall say that if one were to dwell on their constitution from the beginning and the arrangement of their laws, one would find that they have been people demonstrating a shadow of a heavenly life on earth; among whom nothing else was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who makes images held citizenship. For neither a painter nor a sculptor was in their commonwealth, the Law casting out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the making of statues, which draws and drags down the foolish among humans from God to the earth, the eyes of the soul. Therefore, there was among them a law of this kind: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, every image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any animal that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird which flies under the heaven, a likeness of any reptile which creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters under the earth." <note>Deuteronomy 4:16-18</note> And indeed the law wished that they, communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, falsifying the truly male or the truly female, or the nature of animals, or the race of birds, or reptiles, or fish. But also solemn and noble among them was the command, "Lest you look up to the heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and being led astray, worship them and serve them." <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note>

What kind of commonwealth was it, of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear. It is also wonderful that the enticements of the youth, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just people and much proof of a healthy life provided...

text:
AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

Celsus says that the Christians are fugitives from Egypt, who have never done anything noteworthy, and have never been of any account in speech or in number. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt, we have spoken in the preceding sections. If he thinks that their being of no account in speech or in number is established by the fact that their history is not particularly found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to dwell upon their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people who demonstrated a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth. Among them, nothing else was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held citizenship. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which draws the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters underneath the earth." And the law indeed intended that they, by communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, misrepresenting the truly male or the truly female or the nature of beasts or the race of birds or the kind of fish. It is also solemn and noble among them that one should not "look up to the heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and be led astray and worship them and serve them."

What kind of commonwealth was that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just, and they had given much proof of a healthy life.

<note>The footnotes provided in the source text are editorial references to biblical passages (Job 8:9, Hebrews 10:1, Deuteronomy 4:16-19, 23:1, 23:17, Exodus 18:21-22, Deuteronomy 1:15) and to Philo Judaeus, De gigantibus, Chapter XIII.</note>

<summary>Origen defends the historical significance and moral integrity of the Jewish people against Celsus's claims, highlighting the Mosaic prohibition of idolatry and the strict ethical standards of their commonwealth.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Celsus, Mosaic Law, Idolatry, Jewish Commonwealth, Deuteronomy, Ethics, Theology</keywords>

For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which draws the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters underneath the earth." And the law indeed intended that they, by communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, misrepresenting the truly male or the truly female or the nature of beasts or the race of birds or the kind of fish. It is also solemn and noble among them that one should not "look up to the heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and be led astray and worship them and serve them."

<meta>continues from previous page: Origen is responding to Celsus's claim that the Christians and Jews have no ancient or noble origin.</meta>

# Against Celsus Book IV, 30–31

<margin>5</margin> Celsus says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, and that they never performed any noteworthy deed, nor were they ever of any account in terms of fame or numbers. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt as sojourners, we have already spoken in the preceding sections <note>referring to Book III, chapters 5–8</note>. If he thinks he can prove they were of no account in fame or numbers because very little of their history is found among the Greeks, we shall say this: if anyone were to dwell upon their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were men who displayed a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth <note>referring to Job 8:9 and Hebrews 10:1</note>. Among them, no other was recognized as God except the One over all, and no maker of images was permitted to be a citizen. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in <margin>10</margin> their commonwealth, as the law expelled all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of images—an activity which attracts the attention of foolish men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, among them a law to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness of a form, male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, the likeness of any <margin>15</margin> winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish that is in the waters beneath the earth" <note>Deuteronomy 4:16–18</note>. And the law intended that, by conversing with the truth concerning each thing, they should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which would give a false representation of the truly male or the truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish.

<margin>20</margin> Noble and sublime among them was also this: "Lest you look up to heaven and, seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them and serve them" <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note>.

<margin>25</margin> What a constitution this was for an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for an effeminate man <term>thēlydrian</term> <gloss>a man who has been feminized or a male prostitute</gloss> to be seen! It is also wonderful that the fuel for the passions of the young—prostitutes—were removed from their commonwealth <note>Deuteronomy 23:17</note>. There were also courts of justice composed of the most righteous men, who had given long proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the Jewish nation against Celsus's insults by highlighting the moral and spiritual superiority of the Mosaic Law, specifically its strict prohibition of idolatry and immorality.</summary>

AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

Celsus says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, having never accomplished anything noteworthy, and that they were never held in any account or number. Now, regarding the fact that they were not fugitives and were not Egyptians, but Hebrews who had resided in Egypt, we have spoken in the preceding pages. If he thinks that their being held in no account or number is established by the fact that their history is not found at all among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to look closely at their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people who displayed a shadow of a heavenly life upon earth. Among them, nothing else was considered God except the One who is over all, and no one who made images held citizenship. For there was neither a painter nor a sculptor in their commonwealth, as the law cast out all such people from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of statues, which entices the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was, therefore, a law among them such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast that is on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under the heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth." And the law indeed intended that they, by communing with the truth regarding each thing, should not fashion things other than the truth, lying about what is truly male or what is truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or the kind of creeping things or fish. Solemn and noble among them also is the command: "Do not, having looked up to the heaven and seen the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them."

What kind of commonwealth was that of an entire nation, among whom it was not even possible for effeminacy to appear? It is also wonderful that the incitements of the young, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts of the most just judges, and they had given much proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the historical significance and moral integrity of the Jewish people against Celsus, arguing that their strict adherence to Mosaic Law and rejection of idolatry created a unique, virtuous society.</summary>

[context] It must, however, be noticed that Eusebius Pamphilus wrote three entire books against Marcellus, in which he quotes that author's own words
to prove that he asserts with Sabellius the Libyan, and Paul of Samosata, that the Lord [Jesus] was a mere man.
Chapter 21. Defense of Eusebius Pamphilus.
But since some have attempted to stigmatize even Eusebius Pamphilus himself as having favored the Arian views in his works, it may not be irrelevant here to make a few remarks respecting him. In the first place then he was both present at the council of Nicæa, which defined the doctrine of the homoousion and gave his assent to what was there determined. And in the third book of the Life of Constantine, he expressed himself in these words: 'The emperor incited all to unanimity, until he had rendered them united in judgment on those points on which they were previously at variance; so that they were quite agreed at Nicæa in matters of faith.' Since therefore Eusebius, in mentioning the Nicene Synod, says that all differences were removed, and that all came to unity of sentiment, what ground is there for assuming that he was himself an Arian? The Arians are also certainly deceived in supposing him to be a favorer of their tenets. But some one will perhaps say that in his discourses he seems to have adopted the opinions of Arius, because of his frequently saying through Christ, to whom we should answer that ecclesiastical writers often use this mode of expression and others of a similar kind denoting the economy of our Saviour's humanity: and that before all these the apostle made use of such expressions, and never has been accounted a teacher of false doctrine. Moreover, inasmuch as Arius has dared to say that the Son is a creature, as one of the others, observe what Eusebius says on this subject, in his first book against Marcellus: 'He alone, and no other, has been declared to be, and is the only-begotten Son of God; whence any one could justly censure those who have presumed to affirm that he is a Creature made of nothing, like the rest of the creatures; for how then would he be a Son? And how could he be God's only-begotten, were he assigned the same nature as the other creatures...and were he one of the many created things, seeing that he, like them, would in that case be partaker of a creation from nothing? But the Sacred Scriptures do not thus instruct us.'

text:
<header>II. 21.] Eusebius not an Arian.</header>

...and contends against them, claiming that Marcellus introduces the Lord as a mere human, just as Sabellius the Libyan and Paul of Samosata did.

### CAP. XXI.

->An Apology for Eusebius of Pamphilus.<-

Since some have also attempted to slander Eusebius of Pamphilus, saying that he was an Arian in the discourses he published, I believe it is not out of place to say a little about him as well. First, he was present at the Council of Nicaea, which defined the <term>homoousion</term> <gloss>of the same substance</gloss>, and he agreed to it. He himself says these very words in the third book of the Life of Constantine:

<margin>Eus. V. C. iii. 13.</margin>
**"The Emperor, driving all toward harmony, established them as like-minded and like-believing on all points of dispute, so that the faith (at Nicaea) prevailed in harmony."**

If Eusebius, in making mention of the council there, says that the then-disputed issues were resolved and that all were like-minded and like-believing, how do some suspect him of Arianism? The Arians are also mistaken in thinking that he held their views. But someone might say that he seems to Arianzie in his discourses by constantly saying "through Christ." To whom we reply that the teachers of the church frequently used this phrase, as they did others that signify the economy of the humanity of our Savior. And above all these, the Apostle used these words; and he was never considered a teacher of heresy. Furthermore, when Arius dared to say that the Son was a creature like one of the others, listen to what Eusebius says about this in the first book of his work against Marcellus:

<margin>Eus. de Eccl. Theol. i. 8, 9.</margin>
**"The only-begotten Son of God is proclaimed as, and is, he alone and no other. Therefore, one could rightly blame those who have dared to say that he is a creature, made from nothing, like the other creatures. For how could he still be the Son, or the only-begotten of God, if he is ascribed the same nature as other creatures? ... He would be one of the many generated things, sharing in the communion of a creation made from nothing; but the divine oracles do not teach this about him."**

<summary>Socrates defends Eusebius of Caesarea against charges of Arianism, citing his support for the Nicene Creed and his writings against the view that the Son is a mere creature.</summary>
<keywords>Eusebius of Caesarea, Arianism, Council of Nicaea, Homoousion, Marcellus of Ancyra, Christology</keywords>

πρὸς αὐτὰ δὲ διαγωνίζεται, ὡς ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν Κύριον, καθὰ Σαβέλλιος ὁ Λίβυς καὶ Παῦλος ὁ Σαμοσατεὺς, τοῦ Μαρκέλλου εἰσάγοντος.

### CAP. XXI.

->’Απολογία ὑπὲρ Εὐσεβίου τοῦ Παμφίλου.<-

’Επειδὴ δέ τινες ἐπεχείρησαν καὶ αὐτὸν λοιδορῆσαι, φημὶ δὴ τὸν Παμφίλου Εὐσέβιον, ὡς ’Αρειανίζοντα ἐν οἷς λόγοις ἐξέδωκε, μικρὰ καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰπεῖν οὐκ ἄκαιρον ἡγοῦμαι. Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδῳ τὸ ‘ὁμοούσιον’ ὁριζούσῃ καὶ παρῆν καὶ συνέθετο· λέγει δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ βιβλίῳ τῷ εἰς τὸν βίον Κωνσταντίνου κατὰ λέξιν ταῦτα·

<margin>Eus. V. C. iii. 13.</margin>
**Πάντας δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς εἰς ὁμόνοιαν ἐλαύνων, εἰς ὅτε ὁμογνώμονας καὶ ὁμοδόξους αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀμφισβητουμένοις ἅπασι τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κατέστησεν· ὡς ὁμόφωνον κρατῆσαι τὴν (ἐν Νικαίᾳ, Soc.) πίστιν.**

Εἰ τοίνυν Εὐσέβιος, τῆς ἐκεῖσε συνόδου μνήμην ποιούμενος, λελύσθαι μὲν τὰ τότε ἀμφισβητούμενα λέγει, πάντας δὲ ὁμοφρονῆσαι καὶ ὁμοδοξῆσαι, πῶς ’Αρειανίζειν αὐτόν τινες ὑπολαμβάνουσιν ; πλανῶνται δὲ καὶ ’Αρειανοὶ φρονεῖν αὐτὸν νομίζοντες τὰ αὐτῶν. ’Αλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις ὡς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ ’Αρειανίζειν δοκεῖ τῷ συνεχῶς λέγειν ‘διὰ Χριστοῦ.’ Πρὸς ὃν ἀποκρινούμεθα, ὅτι τῇ λέξει ταύτῃ πολλάκις καὶ οἱ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐχρήσαντο, καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις ταῖς μηνυούσαις τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν. Καὶ πρό γε ἁπάντων τούτων ὁ ἀπόστολος ταῖς λέξεσι <margin>E. g. Eph. iii. 9.</margin> ταύταις ἐχρήσατο· καὶ οὐδὲ πώποτε ὡς κακοδοξίας διδάσκαλος ἐνομίσθη. Ἔτι μὴν καὶ ’Αρείου κτίσμα τὸν Υἱὸν ὡς ἓν τῶν ἄλλων τολμήσαντος εἰπεῖν, ἐπάκουσον οἷα Εὐσέβιος περὶ τούτου ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ βιβλίῳ τῷ πρὸς Μάρκελλον κατὰ λέξιν φησίν·

<margin>Eus. de Eccl. Theol. i. 8, 9.</margin>
**‘Ὁ μονογενὴς Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ μόνος αὐτὸς, καὶ οὐ δὲ ἄλλος ἀνηγόρευταί τε καὶ ἔστιν· ὅθεν εἰκότως ἄν τις μέμψαιτο τοῖς κτίσμα αὐτὸν φᾶναι τετολμηκόσιν, ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ὅμοιαν τοῖς λοιποῖς κτίσμασι γενόμενον. Καὶ πῶς γὰρ ἔτι ἔσται Υἱὸς, πῶς δὲ μονογενὴς τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὁ τὴν αὐτὴν τοῖς λοιποῖς κτίσμασιν ἐπιγραφόμενος φύσιν ; . . . . τῶν τε πολλῶν γενητῶν ἔσται εἷς, ἅτε τῆς ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων κτίσεως ὁμοίως αὐτοῖς μετασχὼν κοινωνίας· ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὧδε περὶ αὐτοῦ τὰ θεῖα παιδεύει λόγια.**

->An Apology for Eusebius of Pamphilus.<-

<margin>Eus. V. C. iii. 13.</margin>
**The emperor urged everyone toward harmony, until he established them as like-minded and of the same opinion regarding all the disputed points, so that the faith (at Nicaea, Soc.) prevailed in unison.**

If, therefore, Eusebius, in making mention of the council there, says that the points then in dispute were resolved and that everyone became like-minded and of the same opinion, how do some suppose that he held Arian views? The Arians themselves are also mistaken in thinking that he held their opinions. But someone might say that he appears to hold Arian views in his writings because he frequently says "through Christ." And before all of these, the Apostle used these expressions; and he was never considered a teacher of heresy. Furthermore, since Arius dared to call the Son a creature like one of the others, listen to what Eusebius says about this in the first book of his work against Marcellus:

<margin>Eus. de Eccl. Theol. i. 8, 9.</margin>
**The only-begotten Son of God is alone, and no other has been proclaimed or is such. Hence, one might reasonably blame those who have dared to call him a creature, having come into being from non-existence like the rest of the creatures. For how could he still be the Son, and how the only-begotten of God, if he is inscribed with the same nature as the rest of the creatures? ... He would be one of the many created things, since he shares in the communion of creation from non-existence just as they do. But the divine oracles do not teach this about him.**

Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδῳ τὸ ‘ὁμοούσιον’ ὁριζούσῃ καὶ παρῆν καὶ συνέθετο· λέγει δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ βιβλίῳ τῷ εἰς τὸν βίον Κωνσταντίνου κατὰ λέξιν ταῦτα·

<margin>Eus. V. C. iii. 13.</margin>
**Πάντας δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς εἰς ὁμόνοιαν ἐλαύνων, εἰς ὅτε ὁμογνώμονας καὶ ὁμοδόξους αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀμφισβητουμένοις ἅπασι τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κατέστησεν· ὡς ὁμόφωνον κρατῆσαι τὴν (ἐν Νικαίᾳ, Soc.) πίστιν.**

Εἰ τοίνυν Εὐσέβιος, τῆς ἐκεῖσε συνόδου μνήμην ποιούμενος, λελύσθαι μὲν τὰ τότε ἀμφισβητούμενα λέγει, πάντας δὲ ὁμοφρονῆσαι καὶ ὁμοδοξῆσαι, πῶς ’Αρειανίζειν αὐτόν τινες ὑπολαμβάνουσιν ; πλανῶνται δὲ καὶ ’Αρειανοὶ φρονεῖν αὐτὸν νομίζοντες τὰ αὐτῶν. ’Αλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις ὡς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ ’Αρειανίζειν δοκεῖ τῷ συνεχῶς λέγειν ‘διὰ Χριστοῦ.’ Πρὸς ὃν ἀποκρινούμεθα, ὅτι τῇ λέξει ταύτῃ πολλάκις καὶ οἱ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐχρήσαντο, καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις ταῖς μηνυούσαις τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν. Ἔτι μὴν καὶ ’Αρείου κτίσμα τὸν Υἱὸν ὡς ἓν τῶν ἄλλων τολμήσαντος εἰπεῖν, ἐπάκουσον οἷα Εὐσέβιος περὶ τούτου ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ βιβλίῳ τῷ πρὸς Μάρκελλον κατὰ λέξιν φησίν·

<margin>Eus. de Eccl. Theol. i. 8, 9.</margin>

<meta>continues from previous page: Marcellus of Ancyra</meta> but he fights against these views, claiming that Marcellus introduces the idea of the Lord as a mere man, just as Sabellius the Libyan <note>Sabellius was a third-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different modes or faces of one God, rather than distinct persons</note> and Paul of Samosata <note>a third-century bishop of Antioch who taught that Jesus was a human who became divine through his excellence</note> did.

### CHAPTER XXI.

->Defense of Eusebius Pamphilus.<-

Since some have attempted to slander even him, I mean Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the famous church historian and close associate of Pamphilus of Caesarea</note>, claiming that he favored Arianism <note>the belief that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father</note> in the works he published, I consider it not untimely to say a few things about him. First, he was present at the Council of Nicaea which defined the <term>homoousion</term> <gloss>of the same substance</gloss> and he agreed to it. He himself says the following, word for word, in the third book of his Life of Constantine:

<margin>Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 3, chapter 13.</margin>
**The Emperor, driving everyone toward harmony, established them as being of one mind and one opinion on all the disputed matters, as far as it lay in his power; so that the faith (at Nicaea, according to Socrates) prevailed in one voice.**

If, therefore, Eusebius, in making mention of the council there, says that the disputes of that time were resolved and that everyone was of one mind and one opinion, how can some suppose that he favored Arianism? The Arians are also mistaken in thinking that he held their views. But someone will say that in his writings he seems to favor Arianism because he constantly uses the phrase "through Christ." To this person we shall reply that the church writers have often used this expression, as well as others that indicate the <term>oikonomia</term> <gloss>divine plan or stewardship</gloss> of the humanity of our Savior. And before all of these, the Apostle <note>referring to Saint Paul</note> used these expressions <margin>For example, Ephesians 3:9.</margin> and was never considered a teacher of false doctrine. Furthermore, since Arius dared to call the Son a creature like one of the others, listen to what Eusebius says about this, word for word, in the first book of his work against Marcellus:

<margin>Eusebius, On Ecclesiastical Theology, book 1, chapters 8 and 9.</margin>
**The only-begotten Son of God is himself alone, and no other is so proclaimed or exists; wherefore one might reasonably blame those who have dared to call him a creature, having come into being from nothing like the rest of the creatures. For how could he still be the Son, and how could he be the only-begotten of God, if he were assigned the same nature as the rest of the creatures? ... He would be one of the many created things, since he would have shared in a common origin from nothing just like them; but the divine oracles do not teach this about him.**

<summary>Socrates Scholasticus defends Eusebius of Caesarea against charges of Arianism by citing his subscription to the Nicene Creed and his own writings against the idea of Christ as a created being.</summary>

and he contends against these very views, on the ground that Marcellus was introducing the Lord as a mere man, just as Sabellius the Libyan and Paul of Samosata had done.

### CHAPTER 21

->A defence of Eusebius Pamphili.<-

But since some have attempted to revile him too, I mean Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, called "of Pamphilus" after his teacher</note>, as though he took the Arian side in the works he published, I consider it not out of place to say a few words about him as well. In the first place, he was both present at the council in Nicaea when it defined the <term>homoousion</term> <gloss>"of one substance", the Nicene term for the Son's relation to the Father</gloss>, and he gave his assent to it. He himself also says, in the third book of his work on the Life of Constantine, word for word, the following:

<margin>Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.13.</margin>
**"The emperor, urging all toward concord, at length brought them, so far as lay in him, to be of one mind and one opinion on all the points in dispute, so that the faith <note>Socrates adds: "at Nicaea"</note> prevailed with one voice."**

If, then, Eusebius, in making mention of the council held there, says that the matters then in dispute were resolved, and that all came to be of one mind and one opinion, how is it that some suppose him to take the Arian side? The Arians too are mistaken in thinking that he holds their views. But someone will say that in his writings he appears to Arianize by continually saying "through Christ". To him we shall reply that the men of the church also often used this expression, and the others that indicate the dispensation of our Saviour's humanity. And before all of these the apostle used these expressions, <margin>For example, Ephesians 3:9.</margin> and he was never at any time considered a teacher of false doctrine. Moreover, since Arius dared to call the Son a creature, as one of the others, listen to what Eusebius says about this, word for word, in the first book of his work against Marcellus:

<margin>Eusebius, On Ecclesiastical Theology 1.8, 9.</margin>
**"The only-begotten Son of God, he himself alone and no other, has both been proclaimed such and is such. Hence one might reasonably blame those who have dared to say that he is a creature, brought into being out of things that are not, like the rest of the creatures. For how will he still be Son, and how the only-begotten of God, he who is assigned the same nature as the rest of the creatures? . . . . and he will be one of the many things that have come to be, inasmuch as he shares, in the same way as they do, in the fellowship of creation out of things that are not. But this is not how the divine oracles teach concerning him.**

<summary>Socrates opens his defence of Eusebius of Caesarea against the charge of Arianism. He points to Eusebius's assent at Nicaea and his account of it in the Life of Constantine, explains the phrase "through Christ" as apostolic usage, and quotes Eusebius against Marcellus denying that the Son is a creature.</summary>

text:
<header>HOMILY ON PSALM XLIV.</header>

...who have accepted the solemn life, not out of grief or necessity, but those who rejoice in gladness and exultation over such an achievement <note>original: "κατορθώματι"</note>, these shall be brought to the King, and they shall be led not into an ordinary place, but into the temple of the King. For the priestly vessels, which human use has not defiled, shall be brought into the Holy of Holies, and they shall have the authority of access into the inner sanctuaries, where profane feet shall not walk. The Prophet shows how great a thing it is to be led into the temple of the King, praying for himself and saying: *One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord, and to visit His temple* <note>Psalm xxvi, 4</note>.

12. *Instead of thy fathers, sons are born to thee: thou shalt make them princes over all the earth*. Since she was commanded above to forget her people and her father's house, as a reward for her obedience she now receives sons in place of her fathers, who are distinguished by such great dignities that they are made princes over all the earth. Who, then, are the sons of the Church? They are the sons of the Gospel, who have ruled over the whole earth. For, he says, *Into all the earth their sound has gone out* <note>Psalm xviii, 5</note>; and, *They shall sit on twelve thrones, and shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel* <note>Matthew xix, 28</note>. If, however, one understands the patriarchs as the fathers of the bride, the word of the Apostles does not fail even then. For instead of those men, sons were born to her through Christ, who do the works of Abraham <note>John viii, 39</note>; and for this reason they are reckoned as equal in honor to them, because they did the same things as those men, for which the fathers were deemed worthy of great honors. Indeed, the saints are princes of the whole earth because of their intimacy with the Good, since the very nature of the Good confers primacy upon them, just as it conferred upon Jacob the authority over Esau. For He says, *Become lord of your brother* <note>Genesis xxvii, 29</note>. Therefore, those who have become equal in honor to the fathers, and who have obtained superiority over all through the exercise of virtue, are both sons of Christ's bride and are established by their own mother as princes over all the earth. And observe the authority of the queen, how great it is: to ordain princes over all the whole earth. *I will be mindful of thy name in every generation and generation*. *Therefore shall the peoples confess to thee forever and for ever and ever*. Regarding all this, the word is spoken as if from the person of the Church, that *I will be mindful of thy name in every generation and generation*. And what is this memory of the Church? The confession of the peoples.

<column-break/>

human use, they shall be brought into the Holy of Holies, and it will be lawful for them to enter the inner sanctuaries, where profane feet shall not walk. The Prophet himself shows how great a matter it is to be led into the King's temple, praying for himself and saying: *One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life; that I may see the delight of the Lord, and visit His temple*.

Since it was commanded above that she should forget her people and her father's house, in the reward of obedience she now receives sons instead of fathers, marked by such great dignities that they are constituted princes over all the earth. Who then are the sons of the Church? Naturally the sons of the Gospel, who have commanded the entire world. For, he says, *Into all the earth their sound has gone out*; and, *They shall sit upon twelve thrones, and shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel*. If, however, anyone understands the patriarchs to be the fathers of the bride, the meaning understood in this way is not alien to the Apostles. ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης καταδεξάμενα τὸν σεμνὸν βίον, ἀλλ’ αἱ ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ καὶ ἀγαλλιάσει ἐπὶ τῷ τοιούτῳ κατορθώματι χαίρουσαι (13), αὗται ἀπενεχθήσονται τῷ βασιλεῖ, καὶ ἀχθήσονται οὐκ εἰς τὸν τυχόντα τόπον, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ βασιλέως. Τὰ γὰρ ἱερατικὰ σκεύη, ἃ οὐκ ἐμόλυνεν ἀνθρωπίνη χρῆσις, εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων εἰσενεχθήσεται, καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἕξει τῆς εἰς τὰ ἄδυτα παρόδου, ὅπου βέβηλοι πόδες οὐ περιπατήσουσιν. Ἡλίκον δέ ἐστι τὸ ἀχθῆναι εἰς ναὸν βασιλέως, ὁ Προφήτης δείκνυσιν, ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ προσευχόμενος καὶ λέγων· Μίαν ᾐτησάμην παρὰ Κυρίου, ταύτην ζητήσω· τὸ κατοικεῖν με ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς μου, τοῦ θεωρεῖν με (14) τὴν τερπνότητα Κυρίου, καὶ ἐπισκέπτεσθαι τὸν ναὸν αὐτοῦ.

12. Ἀντὶ τῶν πατέρων σου ἐγεννήθησαν (15) οἱ υἱοί σου· καταστήσεις αὐτοὺς ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Ἐπειδὴ ἄνω προσετάχθη ἐπιλαθέσθαι τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρὸς, εἰς ἀντίδοσιν τῆς ὑπακοῆς νῦν ἀντὶ τῶν πατέρων λαμβάνει υἱούς, ἐν τηλικούτοις ἀξιώμασι διαπρέποντας, ὥστε καταστῆναι (16) αὐτοὺς ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Τίνες οὖν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας; Ἤτοι οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, οἱ πάσης τῆς γῆς ἄρξαντες. Εἰς πᾶσαν γάρ, φησί, τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν· καὶ, Καθεσθήσονται ἐπὶ δώδεκα θρόνους, καὶ κρινοῦσι τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ. Ἐὰν δέ εἰσι πατέρας τῆς νύμφης λάβῃ τοὺς πατριάρχας, καὶ οὕτως ὁ λόγος τῶν ἀποστόλων οὐ διαπίπτει. Ἀντὶ γὰρ ἐκείνων ἐγεννήθησαν αὐτῇ υἱοὶ διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰσότιμοι αὐτοῖς χρηματίζοντες (17), ἐκ τοῦ πεποιηκέναι τὰ αὐτὰ ἐκείνοις, ἀφ’ ὧν τῶν μεγάλων τιμῶν ἠξιώθησαν οἱ πατέρες. Ἄρχοντες μέντοι εἰσὶν ἁπάσης τῆς γῆς οἱ ἅγιοι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ καλὸν οἰκείωσιν, αὐτῆς τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ φύσεως περιτιθείσης αὐτοῖς τὸ πρωτεῖον, ὡς περιέθηκε τῷ Ἰακὼβ τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Ἠσαῦ ἐξουσίαν. Γί-νου γάρ, φησί, κύριος τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου. Οἱ τοίνυν ἰσότιμοι τοῖς πατράσι γενόμενοι (18), καὶ τὴν κατὰ πάντων ὑπεροχὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἄσκησιν προσλαβόντες, καὶ υἱοὶ τῆς Χριστοῦ νύμφης εἰσὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῆς ἰδίας μητρὸς καθίστανται ἄρχοντες ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Σκόπει δέ μοι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῆς βασιλίδος, ὅση τις ἐπ’ αὐτῆς ἐστι· χειροτονεῖν ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Διὰ τοῦτο λαοὶ ἐξομολογήσονται σοι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος. Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ὡς ἐκ προσώπου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὁ λόγος εἴρηται, ὅτι Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Τίς δέ ἐστιν ἡ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας μνήμη; Ἡ ἐξομολόγησις τῶν λαῶν.

<column-break/>

A humanus usus, in sancta sanctorum introducentur, eisque licebit ad adyta accedere, ubi profani pedes non ambulabunt. Quanta autem res sit in templum regis adduci, Propheta ipse ostendit, pro se ipso orans ac dicens 83: Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram: ut inhabitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitæ meæ; ut videam voluptatem Domini, et visitem templum ejus.

12. VERS. 17. Pro patribus tuis nati sunt filii tui: constitues eos principes super omnem terram. Quandoquidem supra præceptum est ei ut oblivisceretur populi et domus patris, in obedientiæ remuneratione nunc pro patribus accipit filios tantis dignitatibus insignitos, ut constituantur principes super omnem terram. Qui sunt igitur Ecclesiæ filii? Nimirum Evangelii filii, qui orbi universo imperarunt. In omnem enim, inquit, terram exivit sonus eorum 84; et, Sedebunt super duodecim thronos, et judicabunt duodecim tribus Israel 85. Si quis autem sponsæ patres intelligat patriarchas, ita quoque intellecta sententia ab apostolis aliena non est. Nam pro illis nati sunt ei filii per Christum, facientes opera Abrahæ 86, et ideo æque honorati ac ipsi, quod eadem egerunt quæ illi, ob quæ honoribus magnis dignati sunt patres. Principes vero universæ terræ sunt sancti, ob suam cum bono necessitudinem, cum ipsa boni natura eis principatum tribuat, sicut Jacobo potestatem in ipsum Esau præbuit. Fias enim, inquit, dominus fratris tui 87. Quicunque igitur ab patribus pares facti sunt, atque per virtutis exercitationem omnibus præstiterunt, et filii sponsæ Christi sunt, et a propria matre principes super omnem terram constituuntur. Velim autem consideres quanta sit reginæ potestas, sic ut creet ac præficiat principes super omnem terram. VERS. 18. Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Propterea populi confitebuntur tibi in sæculum et in sæculum sæculi. Post omnia tanquam ex Ecclesiæ persona dictum est illud, Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Quæ autem est hæc Ecclesiæ memoria? Confessio populorum.

(14) Sic editio Basil. et mss. quinque. Deest μs in editione Paris. Ibidem Reg. secundus τὸν ναὸν τὸν ἅγιον αὐτοῦ.
(15) Codices tres ἐγεννήθησαν, facti sunt.
(16) Sic mss. quinque. Editi ὡς καταστῆναι.
(17) Sic Regii secundus, tertius et quartus cum Colbertinis primo et sexto. Editi χρηματίζουσιν.
(18) Sic quatuor mss. At editi γινόμενοι.

not from sorrow or necessity having accepted the honorable life, but those who rejoice in gladness and exultation over such an achievement, these shall be brought to the King, and they shall be led not into an ordinary place, but into the temple of the King. For the priestly vessels, which no human use has defiled, shall be brought into the holy of holies, and shall have the authority of passage into the inner sanctuaries, where profane feet shall not walk. How great a thing it is to be led into the temple of the King, the Prophet shows, praying for himself and saying: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord, and to visit his temple.

12. Instead of your fathers, your sons are born; you shall make them princes over all the earth. Since it was commanded above to forget the people and the house of the father, in recompense for this obedience she now receives sons instead of fathers, excelling in such great dignities that they are made princes over all the earth. Who, then, are the sons of the Church? They are the sons of the Gospel, who have ruled over the whole earth. For into all the earth, he says, their sound has gone out; and, They shall sit upon twelve thrones, and shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel. But if one takes the patriarchs to be the fathers of the bride, even so the word of the apostles does not fail. For instead of those, sons were born to her through Christ, who do the works of Abraham; and for this reason, they are accounted equal in honor to them, because they have done the same things as those for which the fathers were deemed worthy of great honors. Indeed, the saints are princes of all the earth because of their kinship with the Good, with the very nature of the Good bestowing upon them the primacy, just as it bestowed upon Jacob the authority over Esau. For, he says, become lord of your brother. Those, therefore, who have become equal in honor to the fathers, and have taken on superiority over all through the exercise of virtue, are both sons of the bride of Christ, and are appointed by their own mother as princes over all the earth. And consider for me the power of the queen, how great it is in her: to appoint princes over all the earth. I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore, peoples shall confess to you forever and ever. Above all, the word is spoken as if from the person of the Church, that I will remember your name in every generation and generation. And what is the memory of the Church? The confession of the peoples.

Who, therefore, are the sons of the Church? Surely the sons of the Gospel, who have commanded the entire world. Si quis autem sponsæ patres intelligat patriarchas, ita quoque intellecta sententia ab apostolis aliena non est. Nam pro illis nati sunt ei filii per Christum, facientes opera Abrahæ 86, et ideo æque honorati ac ipsi, quod eadem egerunt quæ illi, ob quæ honoribus magnis dignati sunt patres. Principes vero universæ terræ sunt sancti, ob suam cum bono necessitudinem, cum ipsa boni natura eis principatum tribuat, sicut Jacobo potestatem in ipsum Esau præbuit. Fias enim, inquit, dominus fratris tui 87. Quicunque igitur ab patribus pares facti sunt, atque per virtutis exercitationem omnibus præstiterunt, et filii sponsæ Christi sunt, et a propria matre principes super omnem terram constituuntur. Velim autem consideres quanta sit reginæ potestas, sic ut creet ac præficiat principes super omnem terram. VERS. 18. Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Propterea populi confitebuntur tibi in sæculum et in sæculum sæculi. Post omnia tanquam ex Ecclesiæ persona dictum est illud, Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Quæ autem est hæc Ecclesiæ memoria? Confessio populorum.

not from sorrow or necessity having accepted the honorable life, but those who rejoice in gladness and exultation over such an achievement, these shall be brought to the King, and they shall be led not into an ordinary place, but into the temple of the King. For the priestly vessels, which no human use has defiled, shall be brought into the holy of holies, and shall have the authority of passage into the inner sanctuaries, where profane feet shall not walk. How great a thing it is to be led into the temple of the King, the Prophet shows, praying for himself and saying: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord, and to visit his temple.

12. Instead of your fathers, your sons are born; you shall make them princes over all the earth. Since it was commanded above to forget the people and the house of the father, in recompense for this obedience she now receives sons instead of fathers, excelling in such great dignities that they are made princes over all the earth. Who, then, are the sons of the Church? They are the sons of the Gospel, who have ruled over the whole earth. For into all the earth, he says, their sound has gone out; and, They shall sit upon twelve thrones, and shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel. But if one takes the patriarchs to be the fathers of the bride, even so the word of the apostles does not fail. For instead of those, sons were born to her through Christ, who do the works of Abraham; and for this reason, they are accounted equal in honor to them, because they have done the same things as those for which the fathers were deemed worthy of great honors. Indeed, the saints are princes of all the earth because of their kinship with the Good, with the very nature of the Good bestowing upon them the primacy, just as it bestowed upon Jacob the authority over Esau. For, he says, become lord of your brother. Those, therefore, who have become equal in honor to the fathers, and have taken on superiority over all through the exercise of virtue, are both sons of the bride of Christ, and are appointed by their own mother as princes over all the earth. And consider for me the power of the queen, how great it is in her: to appoint princes over all the earth. I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore, peoples shall confess to you forever and ever. Above all, the word is spoken as if from the person of the Church, that I will remember your name in every generation and generation. And what is the memory of the Church? The confession of the peoples.

<column-break/>

12. VERS. 17. Instead of your fathers, your sons are born: you shall make them princes over all the earth. Since it was commanded above to her that she should forget the people and the house of her father, in the remuneration of obedience she now receives sons instead of fathers, distinguished by such great dignities that they are constituted princes over all the earth. Who, therefore, are the sons of the Church? Surely the sons of the Gospel, who have commanded the entire world. For into all the earth, he says, their sound has gone out; and, They shall sit upon twelve thrones, and shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel. For, he says, become lord of your brother. Whoever, therefore, have been made equal to the fathers, and through the exercise of virtue have excelled all, are both sons of the bride of Christ, and are constituted by their own mother as princes over all the earth. I would have you consider how great is the power of the queen, such that she creates and appoints princes over all the earth. VERS. 18. I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore, peoples shall confess to you forever and ever. After all, it is said as if from the person of the Church, I will remember your name in every generation and generation. ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης καταδεξάμενα τὸν σεμνὸν βίον, ἀλλ’ αἱ ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ καὶ ἀγαλλιάσει ἐπὶ τῷ τοιούτῳ κατορθώματι χαίρουσαι (13), αὗται ἀπενεχθήσονται τῷ βασιλεῖ, καὶ ἀχθήσονται οὐκ εἰς τὸν τυχόντα τόπον, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ βασιλέως. Τὰ γὰρ ἱερατικὰ σκεύη, ἃ οὐκ ἐμόλυνεν ἀνθρωπίνη χρῆσις, εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων εἰσενεχθήσεται, καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἕξει τῆς εἰς τὰ ἄδυτα παρόδου, ὅπου βέβηλοι πόδες οὐ περιπατήσουσιν. Ἡλίκον δέ ἐστι τὸ ἀχθῆναι εἰς ναὸν βασιλέως, ὁ Προφήτης δείκνυσιν, ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ προσευχόμενος καὶ λέγων· Μίαν ᾐτησάμην παρὰ Κυρίου, ταύτην ζητήσω· τὸ κατοικεῖν με ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς μου, τοῦ θεωρεῖν με (14) τὴν τερπνότητα Κυρίου, καὶ ἐπισκέπτεσθαι τὸν ναὸν αὐτοῦ.

12. Ἀντὶ τῶν πατέρων σου ἐγεννήθησαν (15) οἱ υἱοί σου· καταστήσεις αὐτοὺς ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Ἐπειδὴ ἄνω προσετάχθη ἐπιλαθέσθαι τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρὸς, εἰς ἀντίδοσιν τῆς ὑπακοῆς νῦν ἀντὶ τῶν πατέρων λαμβάνει υἱούς, ἐν τηλικούτοις ἀξιώμασι διαπρέποντας, ὥστε καταστῆναι (16) αὐτοὺς ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Τίνες οὖν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας; Ἤτοι οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, οἱ πάσης τῆς γῆς ἄρξαντες. Εἰς πᾶσαν γάρ, φησί, τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν· καὶ, Καθεσθήσονται ἐπὶ δώδεκα θρόνους, καὶ κρινοῦσι τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ. Ἐὰν δέ εἰσι πατέρας τῆς νύμφης λάβῃ τοὺς πατριάρχας, καὶ οὕτως ὁ λόγος τῶν ἀποστόλων οὐ διαπίπτει. Ἀντὶ γὰρ ἐκείνων ἐγεννήθησαν αὐτῇ υἱοὶ διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰσότιμοι αὐτοῖς χρηματίζοντες (17), ἐκ τοῦ πεποιηκέναι τὰ αὐτὰ ἐκείνοις, ἀφ’ ὧν τῶν μεγάλων τιμῶν ἠξιώθησαν οἱ πατέρες. Ἄρχοντες μέντοι εἰσὶν ἁπάσης τῆς γῆς οἱ ἅγιοι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ καλὸν οἰκείωσιν, αὐτῆς τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ φύσεως περιτιθείσης αὐτοῖς τὸ πρωτεῖον, ὡς περιέθηκε τῷ Ἰακὼβ τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Ἠσαῦ ἐξουσίαν. Γί-νου γάρ, φησί, κύριος τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου. Οἱ τοίνυν ἰσότιμοι τοῖς πατράσι γενόμενοι (18), καὶ τὴν κατὰ πάντων ὑπεροχὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἄσκησιν προσλαβόντες, καὶ υἱοὶ τῆς Χριστοῦ νύμφης εἰσὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῆς ἰδίας μητρὸς καθίστανται ἄρχοντες ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Σκόπει δέ μοι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῆς βασιλίδος, ὅση τις ἐπ’ αὐτῆς ἐστι· χειροτονεῖν ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Διὰ τοῦτο λαοὶ ἐξομολογήσονται σοι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος. Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ὡς ἐκ προσώπου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὁ λόγος εἴρηται, ὅτι Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Τίς δέ ἐστιν ἡ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας μνήμη; Ἡ ἐξομολόγησις τῶν λαῶν.

<column-break/>

A humanus usus, in sancta sanctorum introducentur, eisque licebit ad adyta accedere, ubi profani pedes non ambulabunt. Quanta autem res sit in templum regis adduci, Propheta ipse ostendit, pro se ipso orans ac dicens 83: Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram: ut inhabitem in domo Domini omnibus diebus vitæ meæ; ut videam voluptatem Domini, et visitem templum ejus.

12. VERS. 17. Pro patribus tuis nati sunt filii tui: constitues eos principes super omnem terram. Quandoquidem supra præceptum est ei ut oblivisceretur populi et domus patris, in obedientiæ remuneratione nunc pro patribus accipit filios tantis dignitatibus insignitos, ut constituantur principes super omnem terram. Qui sunt igitur Ecclesiæ filii? Nimirum Evangelii filii, qui orbi universo imperarunt. In omnem enim, inquit, terram exivit sonus eorum 84; et, Sedebunt super duodecim thronos, et judicabunt duodecim tribus Israel 85. Si quis autem sponsæ patres intelligat patriarchas, ita quoque intellecta sententia ab apostolis aliena non est. Nam pro illis nati sunt ei filii per Christum, facientes opera Abrahæ 86, et ideo æque honorati ac ipsi, quod eadem egerunt quæ illi, ob quæ honoribus magnis dignati sunt patres. Principes vero universæ terræ sunt sancti, ob suam cum bono necessitudinem, cum ipsa boni natura eis principatum tribuat, sicut Jacobo potestatem in ipsum Esau præbuit. Fias enim, inquit, dominus fratris tui 87. Quicunque igitur ab patribus pares facti sunt, atque per virtutis exercitationem omnibus præstiterunt, et filii sponsæ Christi sunt, et a propria matre principes super omnem terram constituuntur. Velim autem consideres quanta sit reginæ potestas, sic ut creet ac præficiat principes super omnem terram. VERS. 18. Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Propterea populi confitebuntur tibi in sæculum et in sæculum sæculi. Post omnia tanquam ex Ecclesiæ persona dictum est illud, Memor ero nominis tui in omni generatione et generatione. Quæ autem est hæc Ecclesiæ memoria? Confessio populorum.

text:
HOMILY ON PSALM 44

<meta>continues from previous page: ...not those who have</meta> accepted the venerable life out of grief or necessity, but those who rejoice in gladness and exultation over such an achievement <note>original: κατορθώματι, a successful accomplishment or virtuous deed</note>; these shall be brought to the King. They shall be led not to any ordinary place, but into the temple of the King. For the priestly vessels, which human use has not defiled, shall be brought into the Holy of Holies, and they shall have the authority to enter the inner sanctuary where profane feet shall not walk. How great a thing it is to be led into the temple of the King, the Prophet shows when praying for himself and saying: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit His temple <note>Psalm 26:4</note>.

12. Instead of your fathers, sons were born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth. Since she was commanded above to forget her people and her father's house, in return for her obedience she now receives sons instead of fathers, distinguished by such great dignities that they are appointed princes over all the earth. Who then are the sons of the Church? Surely they are the sons of the Gospel, who have ruled over the whole world. For it says: Their voice has gone out into all the earth <note>Psalm 18:5</note>; and: They shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel <note>Matthew 19:28</note>. If one takes the patriarchs to be the fathers of the bride, the word concerning the apostles still does not fail. For instead of those, sons were born to her through Christ, those who do the works of Abraham <note>John 8:39</note>; and for this reason they are called equal in honor to them, because they have done the same things as those fathers who were deemed worthy of great honors. Indeed, the saints are princes of all the earth because of their kinship with what is good, as the very nature of the good bestows the primacy upon them, just as it bestowed upon Jacob authority over Esau. For it says: Become lord of your brother <note>Genesis 27:29</note>. Therefore, those who have become equal in honor to the fathers, and have taken on preeminence over all through the practice of virtue, are both sons of the bride of Christ and are appointed by their own mother as princes over all the earth. Consider for me the power of the Queen, how great it is: to ordain princes over all the earth. I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore peoples shall give thanks to you forever, and for ages of ages. Finally, the word is spoken as if from the person of the Church: I will remember your name in every generation and generation. And what is this memory of the Church? The confession <note>or "giving of thanks"</note> of the peoples.

<column-break/>

<meta>The Latin column provides a parallel translation of the Greek text above. Significant variations or notes are captured in the annotations below.</meta>

---

<note>83. Psalm 26:4. 84. Psalm 18:5. 85. Matthew 19:28. 86. John 8:39. 87. Genesis 27:29.</note>

<note>13. A very learned man, according to Ducaeus, conjectured that the text should be amended; but Ducaeus himself judged that the common reading "rejoicing in such an achievement" should be retained, using the evidence of the Olivetan manuscript to prove it, to which can be added the fourth Royal, the sixth Colbertine, and several others.</note>
<note>14. Thus the Basel edition and five manuscripts. The word "me" is missing in the Paris edition. In the same place, the second Royal manuscript reads "His holy temple."</note>
<note>15. Three manuscripts read "were born" or "became."</note>
<note>16. Thus five manuscripts. The printed editions read "so as to appoint."</note>
<note>17. Thus the second, third, and fourth Royal manuscripts with the first and sixth Colbertine. The printed editions read "they are called."</note>
<note>18. Thus four manuscripts. But the printed editions read "becoming."</note>

<summary>Basil concludes his commentary on Psalm 44, interpreting the "sons" of the Church as the Apostles and saints who replace the Old Testament patriarchs as rulers of the spiritual world. He emphasizes that the Church's authority and the "memory" of God's name are sustained through the collective confession and thanksgiving of all nations.</summary>

Εἰς πᾶσαν γάρ, φησί, τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν· καὶ, Καθεσθήσονται ἐπὶ δώδεκα θρόνους, καὶ κρινοῦσι τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ. Ἐὰν δέ εἰσι πατέρας τῆς νύμφης λάβῃ τοὺς πατριάρχας, καὶ οὕτως ὁ λόγος τῶν ἀποστόλων οὐ διαπίπτει. Ἀντὶ γὰρ ἐκείνων ἐγεννήθησαν αὐτῇ υἱοὶ διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἱ ποιοῦντες τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰσότιμοι αὐτοῖς χρηματίζοντες (17), ἐκ τοῦ πεποιηκέναι τὰ αὐτὰ ἐκείνοις, ἀφ’ ὧν τῶν μεγάλων τιμῶν ἠξιώθησαν οἱ πατέρες. Ἄρχοντες μέντοι εἰσὶν ἁπάσης τῆς γῆς οἱ ἅγιοι διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ καλὸν οἰκείωσιν, αὐτῆς τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ φύσεως περιτιθείσης αὐτοῖς τὸ πρωτεῖον, ὡς περιέθηκε τῷ Ἰακὼβ τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Ἠσαῦ ἐξουσίαν. Γί-νου γάρ, φησί, κύριος τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου. Οἱ τοίνυν ἰσότιμοι τοῖς πατράσι γενόμενοι (18), καὶ τὴν κατὰ πάντων ὑπεροχὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἄσκησιν προσλαβόντες, καὶ υἱοὶ τῆς Χριστοῦ νύμφης εἰσὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῆς ἰδίας μητρὸς καθίστανται ἄρχοντες ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Σκόπει δέ μοι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῆς βασιλίδος, ὅση τις ἐπ’ αὐτῆς ἐστι· χειροτονεῖν ἄρχοντας ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν. Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Διὰ τοῦτο λαοὶ ἐξομολογήσονται σοι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος. Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ὡς ἐκ προσώπου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὁ λόγος εἴρηται, ὅτι Μνησθήσομαι τοῦ ὀνόματός σου ἐν πάσῃ γενεᾷ καὶ γενεᾷ. Τίς δέ ἐστιν ἡ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας μνήμη; Ἡ ἐξομολόγησις τῶν λαῶν.

Quandoquidem supra præceptum est ei ut oblivisceretur populi et domus patris, in obedientiæ remuneratione nunc pro patribus accipit filios tantis dignitatibus insignitos, ut constituantur principes super omnem terram. # IN CANTICA CANTIC. HOMILIA IX.
<sig>31</sig>

[...with] nard, and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, and every kind of Lebanon, and myrrh, and aloes, and the finest spices. Since, therefore, according to the blessedness of the perception mentioned in the Psalm, she, relying on the help of God, has laid these beautiful ascents in her heart, always going from strength to strength, it is rightly said that the emissions of her mouth are a paradise of pomegranates <note>original: "ῥοῶν παράδεισος"</note> in her more perfect state. The word "emission" is aptly applied to the underlying thought. For that which is sent passes from the sender to the receiver. One may learn this from the customary use of the word, as the Gospel says that the Word called those who were sent out to preach the truth "Apostles" <term>apostolous</term> <gloss>those who are sent</gloss>. What, then, is it that the mouth of the bride sends forth? It is clearly the word of faith, which, when it enters those who receive it, becomes a paradise, being planted in their hearts through hearing. Habitually, a grove full of trees and thick with foliage is called a paradise. Therefore, so that we may learn the kind of plants that are cultivated by the Word in the souls of those who have believed, he names the trees that the Word—sent forth by the mouth of the bride—cultivates as "pomegranates." 

The pomegranate tree is difficult for a thief to approach, as it puts forth thorny branches and contains and nurtures its fruit within a husk that is bitter and acrid to the taste. At the proper time, after it has ripened, the husk breaks open and the fruit appears within; it is pleasing to the sight and pleasant, honey-like in taste, and causes no harm, sweetening the taste buds with its wine-like juice. For this reason, it seems to me that the word sent forth from the bride's mouth creates a paradise of pomegranates in the souls of the hearers, so that we may be taught by what is said not to be softened by any laxity or luxury in the present life, but to choose a life hardened by self-control <term>enkrateia</term> <gloss>self-mastery/continence</gloss>. In this way, the fruit of virtue will be inaccessible to thieves, hedged about by the bitter covering of self-control, and, through a dignified and unyielding state, it wounds those who approach with evil intent, as if by the points of thorns. But when the season provides the opportunity to enjoy the fruits, the pomegranate becomes a bounty of luxury from every kind of fruit; this enjoyment is not found in plums or acorns or other such things, but a varied and multifaceted nature of aromas is discovered within the fruits. For there is cyprus with nard—a beautiful union, one being warm and the other fragrant. For heat is not laudable in itself when it is a foul-smelling inflammation; rather, purity must testify to the heat through a good scent, so that he who is purified of foul heat may become fervent in the Spirit. In these fruits, one may find the other aromas—nard, he says, and saffron. But we have learned of the fragrance of nard in the words above; it remains...

<column-break/>

[...fruits:] fruits, cyprus with nard, and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, and every other species of Lebanon, and myrrh, and aloes, and the finest ointments. Since, therefore, she has appropriately arranged in her heart these beautiful ascents, following the blessedness mentioned in the Psalm, relying on the help of God, and always walking from strength to strength, the emissions of her mouth are beautifully called a paradise of pomegranates in her more perfect state. The term "emission" was aptly adapted to the subject thought. For that which is sent passes from the one who sends to the one who receives. This can be learned from the customary use of the word, for as the Gospel says, the Word called those who are sent to preach the truth "Apostles," that is, those sent. What, then, does the bride's mouth emit? The word of faith, certainly; when it is in those who receive it, it becomes a paradise planted in their hearts through hearing. Custom dictates that a grove planted with many trees is called a paradise. Therefore, so that we may learn the genus of the trees that are cultivated by the Word in the gardens of the souls of those who have believed, he names the trees that the Word plants and tends—which are emitted from the mouth of the bride—as pomegranates. 

The pomegranate tree is difficult to approach, for it produces thorny branches and contains and nourishes its fruit within a husk that is bitter and acrid to the taste. In its own time, after it has ripened, the husk breaks and the fruit appears inside, pleasant to the sight and well-disposed, honeyed to the taste, and bringing nothing of burden, affecting the organs of taste with a sweetness similar to wine. For this reason, it seems to me that the paradise of pomegranates—namely, the word emitted into the souls of the hearers from the bride's mouth—is intended to teach us not to be softened or enervated by any dissolution and luxury in this present life, but to choose a hard and rugged life through self-control. For in this way, the path to the fruit of virtue will not be open to thieves, being hedged about by the austere ambit of self-control, and by a severe and rigid constitution of life, it stings those who approach to do evil as if with certain thorns. But when the time provides the opportunity for the fruits, the pomegranate becomes the delight of all fruits from any kind of tree; not that one should enjoy damsons, or acorns, or other such things, but a varied and manifold nature of aromas is found in the pomegranates: for cyprus with nard is a beautiful union, the former being warm, the latter odoriferous. For heat is not laudable in itself, when it is a fetid inflammation; rather, purity must bear witness to the heat through a good odor, so that he who is purged of foul heat may be fervent in the Holy Spirit. In these pomegranates, one may also find other aromas: nard, he says, and saffron. μετὰ νάρδου, καὶ κρόκος, κάλαμος καὶ κιννάμωμον, καὶ πᾶν εἶδος τοῦ Λιβάνου, καὶ σμύρνα, καὶ ἀλόη, καὶ τὰ πρῶτα μύρα. Ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν κατὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ διαμακαρισμὸν τῆς ἀντιλήψεως αὐτῇ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ γινομένης, τὰς καλὰς ταύτας ἀναβάσεις ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ δίθετο, πάντοτε ἐκ δυνάμεως πορευομένη εἰς δύναμιν, καλῶς ἐπὶ τῆς τελειοτέρας καταστάσεως ῥοῶν παράδεισος αἱ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῆς ἀποστολαὶ ὀνομάζονται. Προσφυῶς δὲ τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ νοήματι ἡ λέξις τῆς ἀποστολῆς ἐφηρμόσθη. Τὸ γὰρ ἀποστελλόμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ πέμποντος εἰς τὸν ὑποδεχόμενον μεταβαίνει. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς συνήθους τοῦ ῥήματος καταχρήσεως, ἔστι μαθεῖν, ὡς καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον λέγει, ὅτι τοὺς μαθητὰς τοὺς πρὸς τὸ κήρυγμα τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκπεμπομένους, Ἀποστόλους ὁ Λόγος ὠνόμασε. Τί οὖν ἐστιν ὃ ἀποστέλλει τὸ στόμα τῆς νύμφης; Δῆλον ὅτι τὸν λόγον τῆς πίστεως, ὃς ἐν τοῖς ὑποδεχομένοις γενόμενος, παράδεισος γίνεται, διὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ταῖς καρδίαις ἐμφυτευόμενος. Τὸ δὲ κατάφυτον καὶ συνηρεφὲς τοῖς δένδροις ἄλσος, παράδεισον εἴωθε καλεῖν ἡ συνήθεια. Ὡς ἂν οὖν καὶ τὸ γένος μάθοιμεν τῶν φυτῶν, ὅπερ διὰ τοῦ Λόγου ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν πεπιστευκότων κηπεύεται, ῥόας ὀνομάζει τὰ δένδρα ἧς φυτηκομεῖ ὁ Λόγος, ὁ παρὰ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης ἀποστελλόμενος. Ἡ δὲ ῥόα δυσεπιχείρητός ἐστι τῷ κλέπτῃ ἀκανθώδεις προβαλλόμενη τοὺς ὄρπηκας, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐστηρῷ τινι καὶ πικραίνοντι κατὰ τὴν γεῦσιν τῷ καλύμματι περιέχουσά τε καὶ ὑποτρέφουσα· ὃς κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον καιρὸν μετὰ τὸ πεπανθῆναι, τοῦ ἐλύτρου περιῤῥαγέντος ἔνδοθεν διαφαίνεται, ἡδὺς μὲν τὴν ὄψιν καὶ εὐδιάθετος, μελιειδὴς δὲ τὴν γεῦσιν καὶ ἄλυπος, καὶ καταγλυκαίνων τῷ οἰνοειδεῖ χυμῷ τὰ γευστικὰ αἰσθητήρια. Διὰ τοῦτό μοι δοκεῖ ῥοῶν παραδείσεως ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἀκουόντων ψυχαῖς ὁ ἀποστελλόμενος ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης λόγος ἐργάζεσθαι, ἵνα διδαχθῶμεν διὰ τῶν λεγομένων, μὴ διά τινος ἐκλύσεως καὶ τρυφῆς κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ζωὴν μαλακίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ τὸν κατεσκληκότα διὰ τῆς ἐγκρατείας αἱρεῖσθαι βίον. Οὕτω γὰρ ἀπρόσιτος γένοιτο τοῖς κλέπταις ὁ τῆς ἀρετῆς καρπός, τῇ στυφῇ καὶ τῇ τῆς ἐγκρατείας περιβολῇ πεφραγμένος, καὶ διὰ τῆς σεμνῆς τε καὶ ἀμειδοῦς καταστάσεως, οἷον τισιν ἀκανθῶν ἀκμαῖς, ἀμύσσων τοὺς ἐπὶ κακῷ προσεγγίζοντας. Ἀλλ’ ὅταν ὁ καιρὸς παράσχῃ τῆς ἀπολαύσεως τῶν καρπῶν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον, παγκαρπία τῆς τρυφῆς ἐκ παντὸς γένους τῶν ἀκροδρύων ῥόα γίνεται, οὐκ ἐν βραβύλοις ἢ βαλάνοις, ἥ τισι τοῖς τοιούτοις τῆς τῶν καρπῶν ἀπολαύσεως γινομένης· ἀλλὰ ποικίλη τις καὶ πολυειδὴς ἀρωμάτων φύσις ἐκ τῶν ἀκροδρύων εὑρίσκεται. Κύπρος γάρ ἐστι μετὰ νάρδων ἡ καλὴ συζυγία, τὸ μὲν θερμὸν, τὸ δὲ εὐῶδες. Οὐ γὰρ ἀπαιμετὸν ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὸ θερμὸν, ὅταν δυσώδης πύρωσις ἡ θερμάσης· ἀλλὰ συμμαρτυρεῖσθαι χρὴ τῷ θερμῷ διὰ τῆς εὐπνοίας τὴν καθαρότητα, ἵνα γένηται τῷ Πνεύματι ξένον, ὁ τῆς ἀηδοῦς θερμάτης κεκαθαρμένος. Ἐν τούτοις ἐστιν εὑρεῖν τὰς ἀκροδρύους, καὶ τὰ ἀλλὰ ἀρώματα, νάρδον, φησὶ, καὶ κρόκον. Ἀλλὰ τῆς μὲν νάρδου τὴν εὐπνοιαν ἐν τοῖς ἄνω μεμαθήκαμεν λόγοις· λοι-
