fructuum : poma, cyprum cum nardo, et crocum, calamum et cinnamomum, et omnem aliam speciem Libani, et myrrham, et aloen, et prima unguenta. Postquam ergo convenienter ei quæ est in Psalmo beatitudinis, ipsa Dei freta auxilio, disposuit in corde has pulchras ascensiones, semper a virtute ambulans in virtutem, pulchre in statu perfectiori melorum punicorum paradisum nominantur oris ejus emissiones. Apposite autem subjectæ sententiæ adaptata fuit dictio emissionis. Nam quod emittitur, ab eo qui mittit, transit ad eum qui suscipit. Idque licet discere ex consueto usu verbi, quod, ut dicit Evangelium, eos qui mittuntur ad prædicandam veritatem, Verbum nominavit apostolos, id est missos. Quid est igitur quod emittit os sponsæ? verbum scilicet fidei; quod cum est in iis qui suscipiunt, fit paradisus qui plantatur per auditionem in cordibus. Nemus autem plantatum et frequens arboribus, paradisum solet vocare consuetudo. Ut ergo discamus etiam genus arborum, quæ per Verbum coluntur in hortis animarum eorum qui crediderunt, malos punicas nominat arbores, quas Verbum plantat et colit, quod emittitur ex ore sponsæ. Malum autem punicam difficiliter aggreditur, ut quæ spinosos proferat ramos, et quodam in gustu austero et amarescenti propugnaculo fructum contineat et nutriat: qui suo tempore, postquam matuerit, fracto cortice intus apparet, visu jucundus et bene affectus, gustui autem mellitus et nihil afferens molestiæ, qui sapore quodam vini simili gustus instrumenta afficit dulcedine. Propterea mihi videtur paradisus malorum punicarum, nempe sermo qui emittitur in animas auditorum ex ore sponsæ, efficere, ut doceamur per ea quæ dicuntur, non per dissolutionem aliquam et delicias in vita præsenti emolliri ac enervari, sed per continentiam, duram et asperam vitam eligere. Ita enim ad fructum virtutis furibus non patebit aditus, ut qui sit obseptus austero continentiæ ambitu, et per severam ac rigidam vitæ constitutionem, veluti per quasdam spinas, eos pungens, qui ut malo afficiant, accedunt propius. Sed quando tempus præbuerit opportunitatem fructibus, malus punica fit omnium fructuum deliciæ ex quovis genere malorum, non quod prunis Damascenis, aut glandibus, aut aliquibus aliis ojusmodi sit fruendum, sed varia et multiplex natura aromatum invenitur in malis: est enim cyprus cum nardis pulchrum conjugium, illa quidem calida, hæc vero odorifera. Non est enim calor per se laudabilis, quando calor est fetida inflammatio, sed oportet puritatem per bonum odorem ferre testimonium de calore, ut sit sancto Spiritu fervens, qui est a tetro calore expurgatus. In his malis invenire licet etiam alia aromata, nardum, inquit, et crocum. Sed nardi quidem suavem odorem dicimus in iis quæ supra dicta sunt; restat autem ut croci ostendamus ænigmata. with nard, and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, and every kind of Lebanon, and myrrh, and aloes, and the first of all spices. Since, therefore, according to the beatitude in the Psalm regarding the help that comes to her from God, she has set these beautiful ascents in her heart, always going from strength to strength, the emissions of her mouth are well called a paradise of pomegranates in the more perfect state. The word "emission" <note>original: "ἀποστολῆς"</note> has been aptly applied to the underlying meaning. For that which is sent proceeds from the sender to the receiver. And this can be learned from the customary use of the word, as the Gospel also says, that the Word called those who are sent out for the preaching of the truth "Apostles" <note>original: "Ἀποστόλους"</note>. What, then, is it that the mouth of the bride sends forth? It is clearly the word of faith, which, when it comes to those who receive it, becomes a paradise, being planted in their hearts through hearing. Custom is accustomed to call a grove that is planted and shaded with trees a "paradise." Therefore, so that we might also learn the kind of plants that are cultivated through the Word in the souls of those who have believed, he calls the trees that the Word—which is sent forth from the mouth of the bride—cultivates "pomegranates." The pomegranate is difficult for a thief to attack, as it puts forth thorny branches and contains and nourishes its fruit within a covering that is somewhat astringent and bitter to the taste. At its proper time, after it has ripened, the husk breaks and it appears from within, pleasant to the sight and well-disposed, honey-sweet to the taste and painless, sweetening the organs of taste with a wine-like juice. For this reason, it seems to me that the word sent forth from the mouth of the bride works a paradise of pomegranates in the souls of the hearers, so that we may be taught through what is said not to be softened by any kind of dissipation and luxury in the present life, but to choose a life hardened through self-control. For thus the fruit of virtue would become inaccessible to thieves, fenced in by the astringent covering of self-control, and through a solemn and unyielding state, like the points of thorns, pricking those who approach for evil. But when the season provides the opportunity for the enjoyment of the fruits, the pomegranate becomes a collection of all the delights of the fruits from every kind of tree, not by enjoying plums or acorns or other such things, but a varied and manifold nature of aromatics is found in the pomegranates. For the cypress with nard is a beautiful union, the one being warm, the other fragrant. For warmth is not praiseworthy in itself when the heat is a foul-smelling inflammation; but the warmth must be testified to by purity through a sweet scent, so that he who is cleansed of foul heat may become fervent in the Spirit. In these it is possible to find the fruits, and the other aromatics, "nard," he says, "and saffron." But we have learned of the fragrance of nard in the preceding discourses; it remains...

μετὰ νάρδου, καὶ κρόκος, κάλαμος καὶ κιννάμωμον, καὶ πᾶν εἶδος τοῦ Λιβάνου, καὶ σμύρνα, καὶ ἀλόη, καὶ τὰ πρῶτα μύρα. Ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν κατὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ διαμακαρισμὸν τῆς ἀντιλήψεως αὐτῇ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ γινομένης, τὰς καλὰς ταύτας ἀναβάσεις ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ δίθετο, πάντοτε ἐκ δυνάμεως πορευομένη εἰς δύναμιν, καλῶς ἐπὶ τῆς τελειοτέρας καταστάσεως ῥοῶν παράδεισος αἱ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῆς ἀποστολαὶ ὀνομάζονται. Προσφυῶς δὲ τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ νοήματι ἡ λέξις τῆς ἀποστολῆς ἐφηρμόσθη. Τὸ γὰρ ἀποστελλόμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ πέμποντος εἰς τὸν ὑποδεχόμενον μεταβαίνει. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς συνήθους τοῦ ῥήματος καταχρήσεως, ἔστι μαθεῖν, ὡς καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον λέγει, ὅτι τοὺς μαθητὰς τοὺς πρὸς τὸ κήρυγμα τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκπεμπομένους, Ἀποστόλους ὁ Λόγος ὠνόμασε. Τί οὖν ἐστιν ὃ ἀποστέλλει τὸ στόμα τῆς νύμφης; Δῆλον ὅτι τὸν λόγον τῆς πίστεως, ὃς ἐν τοῖς ὑποδεχομένοις γενόμενος, παράδεισος γίνεται, διὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ταῖς καρδίαις ἐμφυτευόμενος. Τὸ δὲ κατάφυτον καὶ συνηρεφὲς τοῖς δένδροις ἄλσος, παράδεισον εἴωθε καλεῖν ἡ συνήθεια. Ὡς ἂν οὖν καὶ τὸ γένος μάθοιμεν τῶν φυτῶν, ὅπερ διὰ τοῦ Λόγου ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν πεπιστευκότων κηπεύεται, ῥόας ὀνομάζει τὰ δένδρα ἧς φυτηκομεῖ ὁ Λόγος, ὁ παρὰ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης ἀποστελλόμενος. Ἡ δὲ ῥόα δυσεπιχείρητός ἐστι τῷ κλέπτῃ ἀκανθώδεις προβαλλόμενη τοὺς ὄρπηκας, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐστηρῷ τινι καὶ πικραίνοντι κατὰ τὴν γεῦσιν τῷ καλύμματι περιέχουσά τε καὶ ὑποτρέφουσα· ὃς κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον καιρὸν μετὰ τὸ πεπανθῆναι, τοῦ ἐλύτρου περιῤῥαγέντος ἔνδοθεν διαφαίνεται, ἡδὺς μὲν τὴν ὄψιν καὶ εὐδιάθετος, μελιειδὴς δὲ τὴν γεῦσιν καὶ ἄλυπος, καὶ καταγλυκαίνων τῷ οἰνοειδεῖ χυμῷ τὰ γευστικὰ αἰσθητήρια. Διὰ τοῦτό μοι δοκεῖ ῥοῶν παραδείσεως ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἀκουόντων ψυχαῖς ὁ ἀποστελλόμενος ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης λόγος ἐργάζεσθαι, ἵνα διδαχθῶμεν διὰ τῶν λεγομένων, μὴ διά τινος ἐκλύσεως καὶ τρυφῆς κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ζωὴν μαλακίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ τὸν κατεσκληκότα διὰ τῆς ἐγκρατείας αἱρεῖσθαι βίον. Οὕτω γὰρ ἀπρόσιτος γένοιτο τοῖς κλέπταις ὁ τῆς ἀρετῆς καρπός, τῇ στυφῇ καὶ τῇ τῆς ἐγκρατείας περιβολῇ πεφραγμένος, καὶ διὰ τῆς σεμνῆς τε καὶ ἀμειδοῦς καταστάσεως, οἷον τισιν ἀκανθῶν ἀκμαῖς, ἀμύσσων τοὺς ἐπὶ κακῷ προσεγγίζοντας. Ἀλλ’ ὅταν ὁ καιρὸς παράσχῃ τῆς ἀπολαύσεως τῶν καρπῶν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον, παγκαρπία τῆς τρυφῆς ἐκ παντὸς γένους τῶν ἀκροδρύων ῥόα γίνεται, οὐκ ἐν βραβύλοις ἢ βαλάνοις, ἥ τισι τοῖς τοιούτοις τῆς τῶν καρπῶν ἀπολαύσεως γινομένης· ἀλλὰ ποικίλη τις καὶ πολυειδὴς ἀρωμάτων φύσις ἐκ τῶν ἀκροδρύων εὑρίσκεται. Κύπρος γάρ ἐστι μετὰ νάρδων ἡ καλὴ συζυγία, τὸ μὲν θερμὸν, τὸ δὲ εὐῶδες. Οὐ γὰρ ἀπαιμετὸν ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὸ θερμὸν, ὅταν δυσώδης πύρωσις ἡ θερμάσης· ἀλλὰ συμμαρτυρεῖσθαι χρὴ τῷ θερμῷ διὰ τῆς εὐπνοίας τὴν καθαρότητα, ἵνα γένηται τῷ Πνεύματι ξένον, ὁ τῆς ἀηδοῦς θερμάτης κεκαθαρμένος. fructuum : poma, cyprum cum nardo, et crocum, calamum et cinnamomum, et omnem aliam speciem Libani, et myrrham, et aloen, et prima unguenta. Postquam ergo convenienter ei quæ est in Psalmo beatitudinis, ipsa Dei freta auxilio, disposuit in corde has pulchras ascensiones, semper a virtute ambulans in virtutem, pulchre in statu perfectiori melorum punicorum paradisum nominantur oris ejus emissiones. Apposite autem subjectæ sententiæ adaptata fuit dictio emissionis. Nam quod emittitur, ab eo qui mittit, transit ad eum qui suscipit. Idque licet discere ex consueto usu verbi, quod, ut dicit Evangelium, eos qui mittuntur ad prædicandam veritatem, Verbum nominavit apostolos, id est missos. Quid est igitur quod emittit os sponsæ? verbum scilicet fidei; quod cum est in iis qui suscipiunt, fit paradisus qui plantatur per auditionem in cordibus. Nemus autem plantatum et frequens arboribus, paradisum solet vocare consuetudo. Ut ergo discamus etiam genus arborum, quæ per Verbum coluntur in hortis animarum eorum qui crediderunt, malos punicas nominat arbores, quas Verbum plantat et colit, quod emittitur ex ore sponsæ. Malum autem punicam difficiliter aggreditur, ut quæ spinosos proferat ramos, et quodam in gustu austero et amarescenti propugnaculo fructum contineat et nutriat: qui suo tempore, postquam matuerit, fracto cortice intus apparet, visu jucundus et bene affectus, gustui autem mellitus et nihil afferens molestiæ, qui sapore quodam vini simili gustus instrumenta afficit dulcedine. Propterea mihi videtur paradisus malorum punicarum, nempe sermo qui emittitur in animas auditorum ex ore sponsæ, efficere, ut doceamur per ea quæ dicuntur, non per dissolutionem aliquam et delicias in vita præsenti emolliri ac enervari, sed per continentiam, duram et asperam vitam eligere. Ita enim ad fructum virtutis furibus non patebit aditus, ut qui sit obseptus austero continentiæ ambitu, et per severam ac rigidam vitæ constitutionem, veluti per quasdam spinas, eos pungens, qui ut malo afficiant, accedunt propius. Sed quando tempus præbuerit opportunitatem fructibus, malus punica fit omnium fructuum deliciæ ex quovis genere malorum, non quod prunis Damascenis, aut glandibus, aut aliquibus aliis ojusmodi sit fruendum, sed varia et multiplex natura aromatum invenitur in malis: est enim cyprus cum nardis pulchrum conjugium, illa quidem calida, hæc vero odorifera. Non est enim calor per se laudabilis, quando calor est fetida inflammatio, sed oportet puritatem per bonum odorem ferre testimonium de calore, ut sit sancto Spiritu fervens, qui est a tetro calore expurgatus. In his malis invenire licet etiam alia aromata, nardum, inquit, et crocum. Sed nardi quidem suavem odorem dicimus in iis quæ supra dicta sunt; restat autem ut croci ostendamus ænigmata. <meta>continues from previous page: ...with nard, and saffron, reed and cinnamon, and every kind of Lebanon-wood, and myrrh, and aloe, and the finest perfumes.</meta>

Since, therefore, according to the blessing in the Psalm <note>Psalm 84:5-7</note> regarding the assistance she receives from God, she has set these beautiful ascents in her heart, always proceeding from strength to strength, the emissions of her mouth are beautifully named a paradise of pomegranates in this more perfect state. The word "emission" <note>Greek: <term>apostole</term> <gloss>a sending forth or mission</gloss></note> was aptly applied to the underlying meaning. For that which is emitted passes from the sender to the receiver. This can be learned from the common usage of the word, as the Gospel also says, that the Word named those disciples sent out to preach the truth "Apostles" <note>Greek: <term>apostoloi</term> <gloss>those sent forth</gloss></note>. What is it, then, that the mouth of the bride emits? Clearly it is the word of faith, which, when it enters those who receive it, becomes a paradise, being planted in their hearts through hearing. Custom usually calls a grove planted and thick with trees a "paradise." So that we might also learn the genus of the plants which are cultivated through the Word in the souls of believers, he names the trees which the Word—emitted from the mouth of the bride—tends as pomegranates.

The pomegranate is difficult for a thief to attack, as it puts forward thorny shoots and contains and nourishes its fruit within a covering that is somewhat harsh and bitter to the taste. In its proper season, after it has ripened and the husk has burst open, the fruit appears from within, pleasant to the sight and well-arranged, honey-like to the taste and without any unpleasantness, sweetening the organs of taste with its wine-like juice. For this reason, it seems to me that the word emitted from the mouth of the bride produces a paradise of pomegranates in the souls of the listeners, so that we may be taught by these sayings not to be softened or weakened by any dissipation or luxury in the present life, but to choose a life hardened through self-control <note>Greek: <term>enkrateia</term> <gloss>temperance or continence</gloss></note>. For in this way the fruit of virtue would be inaccessible to thieves, being fenced in by the harsh covering of self-control, and through a serious and unsmiling disposition—like certain sharp thorns—pricking those who approach with evil intent. 

But when the season provides the opportunity for the enjoyment of the fruits, the pomegranate becomes a harvest of delights from every kind of orchard fruit; not that the enjoyment of fruits consists of plums or acorns or such things, but a varied and manifold nature of aromatics is found within the fruits. For henna with nard is a beautiful pairing, the one being warm and the other fragrant. For warmth is not desirable in itself when it is a foul-smelling inflammation; rather, purity must bear witness to the warmth through a sweet breath, so that one may be "fervent in the Spirit" <note>Romans 12:11</note>, having been cleansed of foul heat. Among these fruits one may find the other aromatics: nard, he says, and saffron. We have already learned the sweet fragrance of nard in the previous discourses; it remains

[context] so neither will those, who daily melt themselves down with innumerable anxieties, easily receive this thing.
Now as to the fact, that there are many who have attained unto this, we might show it even from those, who have practised this self-denial even in our generation. But for you, just now, it is enough to learn not to covet, and that almsgiving is a good thing; and to know that you must impart of what you have. For these things if you will duly perform, beloved, you will speedily proceed to those others also. 6. For the present therefore let us lay aside our excessive sumptuousness, and let us endure moderation, and learn to acquire by honest labor all that we are to have: since even the blessed John, when he was discoursing with those that were employed upon the tribute, and with the soldiery, enjoined them to be content with their wages.
Anxious though he were to lead them on to another, and a higher self-command, yet since they were still unfit for this, he speaks of the lesser things. Because, if he had mentioned what are higher than these, they would have failed to apply themselves to them, and would have fallen from the others. For this very reason we too are practising you in the inferior duties. Yes, because as yet, we know, the burden of voluntary poverty is too great for you, and the heaven is not more distant from the earth, than such self-denial from you. Let us then lay hold, if it be only of the lowest commandments, for even this is no small encouragement. And yet some among the heathens have achieved even this, though not in a proper spirit, and have stripped themselves of all their possessions. However, we are contented in your case, if alms are bestowed abundantly by you; for we shall soon arrive at those other duties too, if we advance in this way. But if we do not so much as this, of what favor shall we be worthy, who are bidden to surpass those under the old law, and yet show ourselves inferior to the philosophers among the heathens? What shall we say, who when we ought to be angels and sons of God, do not even quite maintain our being as men? For to spoil and to covet comes not of the gentleness of men, but of the fierceness of wild beasts; nay, worse than wild beasts are the assailers of their neighbor's goods. For to them this comes by nature, but we who are honored with reason, and yet are falling away unto that unnatural vileness, what indulgence shall we receive? Let us then, considering the measures of that discipline which is set before us, press on at least to the middle station, that we may both be delivered from the punishment which is to come, and proceeding regularly, may arrive at the very summit of all good things; unto which may we all attain, by the grace and love towards man of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
Homily 22 on Matthew
Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin. And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Having spoken of our necessary food, and having signified that not even for this should we take thought, He passes on in what follows to that which is more easy. For raiment is not so necessary as food. Why then did He not make use here also of the same example, that of the birds, neither mention to us the peacock, and the swan, and the sheep? For surely there were many such examples to take from thence. Because He would point out how very far the argument may be carried both ways: both from the vileness of the things that partake of such elegance, and from the munificence vouchsafed to the lilies, in respect of their adorning. For this cause, when He has decked them out, He does not so much as call them lilies any more, but grass of the field.
And He is not satisfied even with this name, but again adds another circumstance of vileness, saying, which today is. And He said not, and tomorrow is not, but what is much baser yet, is cast into the oven. And He said not, clothe, but so clothe. Do you see everywhere how He abounds in amplifications and intensities? And this He does, that He may touch them home: and therefore He has also added, shall He not much more clothe you? For this too has much emphasis: the force of the word, you, being no other than to indicate covertly the great value set upon our race, and the concern shown for it; as though He had said, you, to whom He gave a soul, for whom He fashioned a body, for whose sake He made all the things that are seen, for whose sake He sent prophets, and gave the law, and wrought those innumerable good works; for whose sake He gave up His only begotten Son. And not till He has made His proof clear, does He proceed also to rebuke them, say ing, O you of little faith. For this is the quality of an adviser: He does not admonish only, but reproves also, that He may awaken men the more to the persuasive power of His words. Hereby He teaches us not only to take no thought, but not even to be dazzled at the costliness of men's apparel. Why, such comeliness is of grass, such beauty of the green herb: or rather, the grass is even more precious than such apparelling. Why then pride yourself on things, whereof the prize rests with the mere plant, with a great balance in its favor? And see how from the beginning He signifies the injunction to be easy; by the contraries again, and by the things of which they were afraid, leading them away from these cares. Thus, when He had said, Consider the lilies of the field, He added, they toil not: so that in desire to set us free from toils, did He give these commands. In fact, the labor lies, not in taking no thought, but in taking thought for these things. And as in saying, they sow not, it was not the sowing that He did away with, but the anxious thought; so in saying, they toil not, neither do they spin, He put an end not to the work, but to the care. But if Solomon was surpassed by their beauty, and that not once nor twice, but throughout all his reign:— for neither can one say, that at one time He was clothed with such apparel, but after that He was so no more; rather not so much as on one day did He array Himself so beautifully: for this Christ declared by saying, in all his reign: and if it was not that He was surpassed by this flower, but vied with that, but He gave place to all alike (wherefore He also said, as one of these: for such as between the truth and the counterfeit, so great is the interval between those robes and these flowers):— if then he acknowledged his inferiority, who was more glorious than all kings that ever were: when will you be able to surpass, or rather to approach even faintly to such perfection of form? After this He instructs us, not to aim at all at such ornament. See at least the end thereof; after its triumph it is cast into the oven: and if of things mean, and worthless, and of no great use, God has displayed so great care, how shall He give up you, of all living creatures the most important? Wherefore then did He make them so beautiful? That He might display His own wisdom and the excellency of His power; that from everything we might learn His glory.
For not the Heavens only declare the glory of God,
[context] but the earth too; and this David declared when he said, Praise the Lord, you fruitful trees, and all cedars.

<column-break/>

others would receive them. That there are many who have reached this perfection, we can demonstrate from those very people who in our age have professed this philosophy. But for you, meanwhile, it will be sufficient if you learn not to covet, and that almsgiving is a good thing, and to know that you must share what you have. For if you carry this out, beloved, you will quickly arrive at those higher things. Meanwhile, therefore, let us put aside that superfluous pomp, let us be content with moderation, and let us learn that all things we are to have should be acquired from just labors; since the blessed John, when he was speaking to those who sat at the tax office and to the soldiers, commanded them to be content with their wages <note>Luke 3:14</note>. He indeed wished to lead them to a greater philosophy; but because they were not yet fit for it, he said lesser things, because if he had discoursed on higher things, they would not have listened to him, and would have fallen away from these lesser ones. Therefore we too train you in these inferior matters. And meanwhile we know that the burden of casting off wealth is too heavy for you to bear; and as far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far are you distant from that philosophy. Therefore, let us at least keep the final commandments; for this is no small consolation: even if among the Greeks some have carried out what we said, and have left all things behind, although not with the purpose with which one should. Nevertheless, it will be enough for us if you spread alms generously: for we will quickly arrive at those things later, if we proceed in this way. If we do not even do this, what pardon shall we be worthy of, we who, having been commanded to surpass the holy men of the Old Law, seem less than the philosophers among the Greeks? What could we say, when we are obligated to be angels and sons of God, yet do not even maintain our standing as men? For to plunder and to covet is not of human gentleness, but of the cruelty of beasts; or rather, those who attack the property of others are worse even than those beasts. For this quality is inherent in them by nature; but we, who have been honored with reason, and yet fall into a baseness contrary to nature, what pardon shall we enjoy? Thinking then on the measures of the philosophy set before us, let us reach at least the middle path, so that we may escape the coming punishment, and by proceeding on the way, may come to the very summit of all goods: which may we all attain, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

->HOMILY XXII<-

Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: and yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these <note>Matthew 6:28-29</note>.

1. Having spoken about necessary food, and having shown that one should not worry even about that, he passes on to the lighter topic. For clothing is not as necessary as food. Why then does he not use the same example here as he did with the birds, nor speak to us of the sheep? For there were many such examples to be taken from there. Because he wishes to show the excess from both sides: both from the cheapness of those that share in such beauty, and from the extravagance of the adornment given to the lilies. Therefore, when he constructed the comparison, he no longer calls them lilies, but grass of the field. And he is not content even with this name, but adds another instance of cheapness, saying, which today is. And he did not say, which is not tomorrow, but something far more inferior, into the oven is cast. And he did not say, it clothes, but, so it clothes. Do you see the many excesses and intensifications everywhere? He does this to strike at them: therefore he added, Shall he not much more clothe you? For this also has much emphasis. For the word "you" hints at nothing else than the precious and highly sought-after nature of the human race; as if he were saying, "You, to whom he gave a soul, whose body he fashioned, for whom he made all visible things, for whom he sent prophets, and gave the law, and worked ten thousand good deeds; for whom he gave up his only-begotten Son." And since he has demonstrated this clearly, then he also reproaches them, saying, O you of little faith. For such is the one who counsels; he does not merely exhort, but also strikes, in order to rouse them more toward the persuasion of what is said. From these things he teaches us not only not to worry, but not even to desire the luxury of garments. For the beauty of the grass, and the fairness of the herb; rather, the grass is more valuable than such attire. Why then do you pride yourself, when the victory belongs to the herb with such abundance? And see how from the prologue he shows the commandment to be light, again leading them away from the opposites, and from those things which they fear. For having said, Consider the lilies of the field, he added, They do not toil. So, wishing to relieve us of labors, he commanded these things. Therefore, not worrying is not a labor, but worrying is. And just as when he said, They do not sow, he did not overturn the sowing, but the anxiety; so when he said, They do not toil, nor spin, he did not abolish the work, but the worry. If Solomon was defeated by their beauty, and not once or twice, but throughout his entire reign (for no one could say that now he was arrayed in such a way, and after that no longer, but he was not even adorned this way for a single day; for this he made clear by saying, In all his kingdom); and he was not defeated by this flower, and then imitated the other, but yielded to them all together; (wherefore he also said, As one of these; for as much as truth is distant from falsehood, so much is the distance between those garments and these flowers;) if then he, who was more brilliant than all the kings who ever were, confessed his defeat, when will you be able to prevail, or rather, to come even a little near to such beauty? From here he teaches us not to desire such adornment at all. For its end is this: after the victory, it is cast into the oven. If God showed such providence for cheap things of no account, and which provide only for the passing need, how will he forsake you, the most necessary of all living beings? Why then did he make them so beautiful? To demonstrate his wisdom and the abundance of his power, so that we may learn of his glory from everywhere. For not only do the heavens declare the glory of God, but the earth also; and David, declaring this, said: Praise the Lord, fruitful trees and all cedars <note>Psalm 148:9</note>. For some send up praise to the Creator through their fruit, some through their size, and others through their beauty. For this too is a sign of great and overflowing wisdom, when he has given beauty even to the most cheap things (for what is more cheap than that which is today, and which the grass does not need; for what does its beauty contribute to the nourishment of the fire?), how will he not provide you with what you need? If he adorned the cheapest of all things out of abundance, and did this not for need but for the sake of splendor; much more will he honor you, the most precious of all, in matters regarding your needs.

<summary>Chrysostom argues that God provides for the lilies of the field and birds, and therefore believers should not suffer from anxiety over food and clothing, trusting in God's fatherly care.</summary>
<keywords>Providence, anxiety, lilies, Solomon, faith, God as Father</keywords>

δέξοιντο. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν πολλοὶ οἱ τοῦτο κατορθωκότες εἰσὶν, ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δυνατὸν ἡμῖν δεῖξαι τὴν ταῦτα φιλοσοφοῦνταν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας γενεᾶς. Ἀλλ’ ὑμῖν τέως ἀρκεῖ τὸ μὴ πλεονεκτεῖν μαθεῖν, καὶ ὅτι καλὸν ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη, καὶ τὸ εἰδέναι ὅτι χρὴ τῶν ὄντων μεταδιδόναι. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν κατορθώσῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ταχέως καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα βαδιεῖ. Τέως τοίνυν τὴν πολυτέλειαν ἀποθώμεθα τὴν περιττὴν, καὶ ἀνασχώμεθα τῆς συμμετρίας, καὶ μάθωμεν ἀπὸ δικαίων πόνων κτᾶσθαι ἅπαντα ἅπερ μέλλομεν ἔχειν: ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης, ὅτε διελέγετο τοῖς περὶ τὴν τελωνείαν ἐσχολακόσι καὶ τοῖς στρατευομένοις, ἀρκεῖσθαι τοῖς ὀψωνίοις προσέταττεν 74.75. Ἐδουλεῦτο μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἐφ’ ἑτέραν μείζονα αὐτοὺς ἀγαγεῖν φιλοσοφίαν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐδέπω πρὸς ταῦτα ἦσαν ἐπιτήδειοι, τὰ ἐλάττονα λέγει, ὡς εἰ τὰ ὑψηλότερα τούτων εἶπεν, οὔτ’ ἂν ἐκείνοις 76 προσέσχον, καὶ τούτων ἐξέπεσον ἄν. Διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς καταδεεστέροις ὑμᾶς γυμνάζομεν. Καὶ γὰρ τέως ἴσμεν, ὅτι μεῖζον ὑμῶν τῆς ἀκτημοσύνης τὸ φορτίον, καὶ ὅσον ἀφέστηκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς τῆς γῆς, τοσοῦτον ὑμῶν ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκείνη. Οὐκοῦν κἂν τῶν ἐσχάτων ἐπιλαβώμεθα ἐπιταγμάτων· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὕτη μικρὰ παραμυθία. Καίτοιγε παρ’ Ἕλλησι 74.75 ἐπέταττεν Ε. 76 ἐκεῖνοι C. E. 77 ποίωμεν B. C. E. 78 γὰρ] Add. θηρίοις Edd. τίνες καὶ τοῦτο κατώρθωσαν, εἰ καὶ μὴ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης γνώμης, καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἅπαντα ἀπεδύσαντο. Ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡμεῖς ἀρκούμεθα ἐφ’ ὑμῶν τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην δαψιλῆ παρέχεσθαι [274] παρ’ ὑμῶν· ταχέως γὰρ καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα ἥξομεν, ἂν οὕτω προβαίνωμεν. Εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦμεν 77, τίνας ἂν εἴημεν συγγνώμης ἄξιοι, οἱ τοὺς ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ ὑπερβῆναι κελευόμενοι, καὶ τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλοσόφων ἐλάττους φαινόμενοι; Τί ἂν εἴποιμεν, ὅταν ὀφείλοντες εἶναι ἄγγελοι καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ, μηδὲ τὸ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι διατηρῶμεν; Τὸ γὰρ ἁρπάζειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν οὐ τῆς ἀνθρώπων ἡμερότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶν θηρίων ὠμότητος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐκείνων χείρους οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπιτιθέμενοι. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ 78 ἀπὸ φύσεως τοῦτο πρόσεστιν· ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ λόγῳ τιμηθέντες, καὶ πρὸς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν καταπίπτοντες δυσγένειαν, τίνας ἀπολαυσόμεθα συγγνώμης; Ἐννοήσαντες τοίνυν τὰ μέτρα τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν φιλοσοφίας, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα φθάσωμεν, ἵνα καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀπαλλαγῶμεν κολάσεως, καὶ ὁδῷ προβαίνοντες ἐπ’ αὐτὴν ἔλθωμεν τὴν κορυφὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, πῶς αὐξάνει· οὐ κοπιᾷ, οὐδὲ νήθει· λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲ Σολομῶν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ περιεβάλετο 79.80 ὡς ἓν τούτων.

α’. Εἰπὼν περὶ τῆς ἀναγκαίας τροφῆς, καὶ δείξας ὅτι οὐδὲ 81 ὑπὲρ ταύτης χρὴ μεριμνᾶν, ἐπὶ τὸ κουφότερον μεταβαίνει λοιπόν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἔνδυμα, ὡς τροφή. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὐ κέχρηται καὶ ἐνταῦθα τῷ αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι τῷ τῶν ὀρνίθων, οὐδὲ λέγει τὸ, ταῦνα ἡμῖν, καὶ τὸν κύκνον, καὶ τὸ πρόβατον; καὶ γὰρ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα παραδείγματα ἦν ἐκεῖθεν λαβεῖν. Ὅτι βούλεται ἑκατέρωθεν δεῖξαι τὴν ὑπερβολὴν, ἀπό τε τῆς εὐτελείας τὴν τοιαύτης μετασχόντων εὐπρεπείας, ἀπό τε τῆς φιλοτιμίας τοῦ καλλωπισμοῦ τῆς δοθείσης τοῖς κρίνοις. Διὰ τοῦτο ὅτε αὐτὰ κατεσκεύασεν, οὐδὲ κρίνα αὐτὰ καλεῖ λοιπὸν, ἀλλὰ χόρτον ἀγροῦ. Καὶ οὐδὲ 82 τῷ ὀνόματι ἀρκεῖται τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ πάλιν ἑτέραν εὐτέλειαν προστίθησιν, εἰπὼν, σήμερον ὄντα. Καὶ οὐχ εἶπεν, αὔριον οὐκ ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολλῷ πάλιν καταδεέστερον, εἰς κλίβανον βαλλόμενον. Καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν 83, ἀμφιέννυσιν, ἀλλ’, οὕτως ἀμφιέννυσιν. Ὁρᾷς πανταχοῦ πολλὰς τὰς ὑπερβολὰς καὶ τὰς ἐπιτάσεις; Ποιεῖ δὲ τοῦτο, ἵνα αὐτῶν καθάψηται: διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἐπήγαγεν· Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς; Καὶ γὰρ πολλὴν ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο τὴν ἔμφασιν. Τὸ γὰρ, ὑμᾶς, οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν αἰνιττομένου, ἢ τὸ πολυτίμητον καὶ περισπούδαστον τοῦ γένους· ὡσανεὶ [275] ἔλεγεν, Ὑμᾶς, οἷς ψυχὴν ἔδωκεν, οἷς σῶμα διέπλασε, δι’ οὓς τὰ ὁρώμενα πάντα ἐποίησε, δι’ οὓς προφήτας ἔπεμψε, καὶ νόμον ἔδωκε, καὶ τὰ μυρία εἰργάσατο ἀγαθὰ· δι’ οὓς τὸν μονογενῆ παῖδα ἐξέδωκεν 84. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπέδειξε σαφῶς, τότε καὶ ἐπιπλήττει λέγων· Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Τοιοῦτον 85 γὰρ ὁ συμβουλεύων· οὐ παραινεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθάπτεται, ἵνα διεγείρῃ πλέον πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν λεγομένων. Ἀπὸ τούτων ἡμᾶς οὐχὶ μὴ μεριμνᾶν διδάσκει μόνον, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἐπποθῆσαι

πρὸς τὴν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἱματίων. Χλόης γὰρ ἡ εὐπρέπεια, καὶ πόας τὸ κάλλος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τιμιώτερος ὁ χόρτος τῆς τοιαύτης στολῆς. Τί τοίνυν μέγα φρονεῖς, ἐν οἷς τὰ νικητήρια παρὰ τῇ βοτάνῃ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας; Καὶ ὅρα πῶς ἀπὸ τῶν προοιμίων κοῦφον δείκνυσι τὸ ἐπίταγμα, πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἀφ’ ὧν δεδοίκασιν, ἀπὸ τούτων ἀπάγων. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, ἐπήγαγεν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν. Ὥστε κόπων ἡμᾶς ἀπαλλάξαι βουλόμενος, ταῦτα ἐκέλευσεν. Οὐ τοίνυν τὸ μὴ μεριμνᾶν ταῦτα πόνος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μεριμνᾶν. Καὶ καθάπερ εἰπὼν, Οὐ σπείρουσιν, οὐ τὸν σπόρον ἀνέτρεψεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν φροντίδα· οὕτως εἰπὼν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν, οὐδὲ 86 νήθουσιν, οὐ τὸ ἔργον ἀνεῖλεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέριμναν. Εἰ δὲ Σολομῶν ἡττήθη τοῦ κάλλους αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐχ ἅπαξ οὐδὲ δὶς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ· (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχοι 87 τις εἰπεῖν, ὅτι νῦν μὲν τοιαῦτα περιεβάλετο, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐκέτι, ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ οὕτως ἐκαλλωπίσατο· τοῦτο γὰρ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ)· καὶ οὐχ ὑπὸ τούτου μὲν ἡττήθη τοῦ ἄνθους, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον ἐμιμήσατο, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁμοῦ παρεχώρησε· (διὸ καὶ ἔλεγεν, Ὡς ἓν τούτων· ὅσον γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας πρὸς τὸ ψεῦδος, τοσοῦτον τῶν ἱματίων ἐκείνων καὶ τῶν ἀνθῶν τούτων τὸ μέσον·) εἰ τοίνυν ἐκεῖνος ὡμολόγησε τὴν ἧτταν, ὁ πάντων βασιλέων τῶν πώποτε γενομένων λαμπρότερος, πότε σὺ περιγενέσθαι δυνήσῃ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐγγὺς γενέσθαι κἂν μικρὸν τῆς τοιαύτης εὐμορφίας; Ἐντεῦθεν ἡμᾶς παιδεύει μηδ’ ὅλως ἐφίεσθαι τοῦ τοιούτου καλλωπισμοῦ. Ἵνα γοῦν αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος· μετὰ τὴν νίκην εἰς κλίβανον βάλλεται. Εἰ δὲ περὶ τὰ εὐτελῆ καὶ οὐδενὸς ἄξια λόγου, καὶ τὴν τυχούσαν παρεχόμενα χρείαν, τοσαύτην πρόνοιαν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεδείξατο, πῶς σὲ προήσεται τὸ πάντων ἀναγκαιότατον 88 ζῶον; Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὕτω καλὰ αὐτὰ ἐποίησεν; ἵνα αὐτοῦ σοφίαν ἐπιδείξηται καὶ τὴν περιουσίαν τῆς δυνάμεως, ἵνα πανταχόθεν αὐτοῦ τὴν δόξαν μάθωμεν. Οὐ γὰρ οἱ οὐρανοὶ μόνοι διηγοῦνται τὴν

<column-break/>

to receive them. That there are many who have achieved this is something we can demonstrate from those who have practiced this philosophy in our own generation. But for now, it is enough for you to learn not to be greedy, that almsgiving is a good thing, and to know that one must share what one has. For if you achieve these things, beloved, you will quickly advance to those others as well. For the present, then, let us put aside superfluous luxury, let us be content with moderation, and let us learn to acquire everything we intend to possess through honest labor. For even the blessed John, when he was speaking to those who were occupied with tax collecting and those who were serving in the military, commanded them to be content with their wages <note>Luke 3:14</note>. He indeed desired to lead them to a higher philosophy, but since they were not yet ready for such things, he speaks of the lesser, for if he had spoken of things higher than these, they would neither have paid attention to those, and they would have fallen away from these. For this reason, we also train you in the more modest things. For we know for the time being that the burden of poverty is greater for you, and that philosophy is as far from you as heaven is from the earth. Therefore, let us at least take hold of the final commands, for this is no small consolation. And yet, among the Greeks, some achieved even this, even if not with the proper intention, and stripped themselves of all their possessions. But we are content for you to provide alms generously; for we will quickly arrive at those other things if we proceed in this way. But if we do not even do this, what excuse would we deserve, we who are commanded to surpass those in the Old Testament, and yet appear inferior to the philosophers among the Greeks? What could we say, when we are obligated to be angels and sons of God, yet do not even maintain the status of being human? For to plunder and to be greedy is not of human gentleness, but of the cruelty of wild beasts; or rather, those who set upon the property of others are worse even than them. For this is natural to them, but we who have been honored with reason, and fall into a baseness contrary to nature, what excuse shall we enjoy? Having considered, therefore, the measures of the philosophy set before us, let us at least reach the middle ground, so that we may escape the coming punishment, and by proceeding on the path, arrive at the very summit of good things; which may we all attain, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

---

->HOMILY XXII<-

Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin; and I say to you, that not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these <note>Matthew 6:28-29</note>.

1. Having spoken about necessary food, and having shown that one should not even be anxious about this, he moves on to the lighter matter. For clothing is not as necessary as food. Why then does he not use the same example here as he did with the birds, and why does he not speak of the sheep, or the swan, or the wool? For there were many such examples to be taken from there. Because he wishes to show the excess from both sides, both from the insignificance of those who partake of such beauty, and from the extravagance of the adornment given to the lilies. For this reason, when he described them, he no longer calls them lilies, but "grass of the field." And he is not satisfied with this name, but again adds another insignificance, saying, "which is today." And he did not say, "not being tomorrow," but that which is much more inferior, "being cast into the oven." And he did not say, "he clothes," but, "so he clothes." Do you see everywhere the many exaggerations and intensifications? He does this so that he may strike at them; for this reason he also added: "Will he not much more clothe you?" For this also has great emphasis. For the word "you" is hinting at nothing other than the highly valued and much-sought-after nature of the human race; as if he were saying, "You, to whom he gave a soul, whom he fashioned with a body, for whose sake he made all visible things, for whose sake he sent prophets, and gave the law, and performed ten thousand good deeds; for whose sake he gave up his only-begotten Son." And since he demonstrated this clearly, then he also rebukes them, saying, "O you of little faith." For such is the one who counsels; he does not only exhort, but also strikes, so that he may stir them up more toward the persuasion of what is being said. From these things he teaches us not only not to be anxious, but not even to desire the luxury of garments. For the beauty of the grass and the splendor of the herb; or rather, the grass is even more precious than such a robe. Why then are you proud, in things where the victory belongs to the plant with much abundance? And see how from the beginning he shows the command to be light, again leading them away from the opposites, and from the things they fear. For having said, "Consider the lilies of the field," he added, "They do not toil." So, wishing to relieve us of labors, he commanded these things. Therefore, not being anxious is not labor, but being anxious is. And just as by saying, "They do not sow," he did not overturn the sowing, but the anxiety; so by saying, "They do not toil, nor do they spin," he did not abolish the work, but the anxiety. And if Solomon was defeated by their beauty, and not once or twice, but throughout his entire reign (for no one could say that he was arrayed like this at one time, but not after that, but he was not even adorned like this for a single day; for this he made clear by saying, "In all his glory"); and he was not defeated by this flower, but imitated the other, but yielded to all of them together (wherefore he also said, "Like one of these"; for as much as the truth is from the falsehood, so much is the difference between those garments and these flowers); if, therefore, he confessed his defeat, he who was the most brilliant of all kings who ever existed, when will you be able to prevail, or rather, to come even a little close to such beauty? From this he teaches us not to desire such adornment at all. For look at its end; after the victory, it is cast into the oven. And if God showed such providence for things that are cheap and worth nothing, and provide only the common need, how will he abandon you, the most necessary of all living creatures? Why then did he make them so beautiful? So that he might demonstrate his wisdom and the abundance of his power, so that we might learn of his glory from every side. δέξοιντο. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν πολλοὶ οἱ τοῦτο κατορθωκότες εἰσὶν, ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δυνατὸν ἡμῖν δεῖξαι τὴν ταῦτα φιλοσοφοῦνταν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας γενεᾶς. Ἀλλ’ ὑμῖν τέως ἀρκεῖ τὸ μὴ πλεονεκτεῖν μαθεῖν, καὶ ὅτι καλὸν ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη, καὶ τὸ εἰδέναι ὅτι χρὴ τῶν ὄντων μεταδιδόναι. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν κατορθώσῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ταχέως καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα βαδιεῖ. Τέως τοίνυν τὴν πολυτέλειαν ἀποθώμεθα τὴν περιττὴν, καὶ ἀνασχώμεθα τῆς συμμετρίας, καὶ μάθωμεν ἀπὸ δικαίων πόνων κτᾶσθαι ἅπαντα ἅπερ μέλλομεν ἔχειν: ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης, ὅτε διελέγετο τοῖς περὶ τὴν τελωνείαν ἐσχολακόσι καὶ τοῖς στρατευομένοις, ἀρκεῖσθαι τοῖς ὀψωνίοις προσέταττεν 74.75. Ἐδουλεῦτο μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἐφ’ ἑτέραν μείζονα αὐτοὺς ἀγαγεῖν φιλοσοφίαν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐδέπω πρὸς ταῦτα ἦσαν ἐπιτήδειοι, τὰ ἐλάττονα λέγει, ὡς εἰ τὰ ὑψηλότερα τούτων εἶπεν, οὔτ’ ἂν ἐκείνοις 76 προσέσχον, καὶ τούτων ἐξέπεσον ἄν. Διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς καταδεεστέροις ὑμᾶς γυμνάζομεν. Καὶ γὰρ τέως ἴσμεν, ὅτι μεῖζον ὑμῶν τῆς ἀκτημοσύνης τὸ φορτίον, καὶ ὅσον ἀφέστηκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς τῆς γῆς, τοσοῦτον ὑμῶν ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκείνη. Οὐκοῦν κἂν τῶν ἐσχάτων ἐπιλαβώμεθα ἐπιταγμάτων· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὕτη μικρὰ παραμυθία. Καίτοιγε παρ’ Ἕλλησι 74.75 ἐπέταττεν Ε. 76 ἐκεῖνοι C. E. 77 ποίωμεν B. C. E. 78 γὰρ] Add. θηρίοις Edd. Non habent Interpp.

τίνες καὶ τοῦτο κατώρθωσαν, εἰ καὶ μὴ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης γνώμης, καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἅπαντα ἀπεδύσαντο. Ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡμεῖς ἀρκούμεθα ἐφ’ ὑμῶν τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην δαψιλῆ παρέχεσθαι [274] παρ’ ὑμῶν· ταχέως γὰρ καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα ἥξομεν, ἂν οὕτω προβαίνωμεν. Εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦμεν 77, τίνας ἂν εἴημεν συγγνώμης ἄξιοι, οἱ τοὺς ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ ὑπερβῆναι κελευόμενοι, καὶ τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλοσόφων ἐλάττους φαινόμενοι; Τί ἂν εἴποιμεν, ὅταν ὀφείλοντες εἶναι ἄγγελοι καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ, μηδὲ τὸ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι διατηρῶμεν; Τὸ γὰρ ἁρπάζειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν οὐ τῆς ἀνθρώπων ἡμερότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶν θηρίων ὠμότητος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐκείνων χείρους οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπιτιθέμενοι. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ 78 ἀπὸ φύσεως τοῦτο πρόσεστιν· ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ λόγῳ τιμηθέντες, καὶ πρὸς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν καταπίπτοντες δυσγένειαν, τίνας ἀπολαυσόμεθα συγγνώμης; Ἐννοήσαντες τοίνυν τὰ μέτρα τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν φιλοσοφίας, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα φθάσωμεν, ἵνα καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀπαλλαγῶμεν κολάσεως, καὶ ὁδῷ προβαίνοντες ἐπ’ αὐτὴν ἔλθωμεν τὴν κορυφὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

->ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΚΒ’<-

Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, πῶς αὐξάνει· οὐ κοπιᾷ, οὐδὲ νήθει· λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲ Σολομῶν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ περιεβάλετο 79.80 ὡς ἓν τούτων.

α’. Εἰπὼν περὶ τῆς ἀναγκαίας τροφῆς, καὶ δείξας ὅτι οὐδὲ 81 ὑπὲρ ταύτης χρὴ μεριμνᾶν, ἐπὶ τὸ κουφότερον μεταβαίνει λοιπόν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἔνδυμα, ὡς τροφή. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὐ κέχρηται καὶ ἐνταῦθα τῷ αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι τῷ τῶν ὀρνίθων, οὐδὲ λέγει τὸ, ταῦνα ἡμῖν, καὶ τὸν κύκνον, καὶ τὸ πρόβατον; καὶ γὰρ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα παραδείγματα ἦν ἐκεῖθεν λαβεῖν. Ὅτι βούλεται ἑκατέρωθεν δεῖξαι τὴν ὑπερβολὴν, ἀπό τε τῆς εὐτελείας τὴν τοιαύτης μετασχόντων εὐπρεπείας, ἀπό τε τῆς φιλοτιμίας τοῦ καλλωπισμοῦ τῆς δοθείσης τοῖς κρίνοις. Διὰ τοῦτο ὅτε αὐτὰ κατεσκεύασεν, οὐδὲ κρίνα αὐτὰ καλεῖ λοιπὸν, ἀλλὰ χόρτον ἀγροῦ. Καὶ οὐδὲ 82 τῷ ὀνόματι ἀρκεῖται τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ πάλιν ἑτέραν εὐτέλειαν προστίθησιν, εἰπὼν, σήμερον ὄντα. Καὶ οὐχ εἶπεν, αὔριον οὐκ ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολλῷ πάλιν καταδεέστερον, εἰς κλίβανον βαλλόμενον. Καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν 83, ἀμφιέννυσιν, ἀλλ’, οὕτως ἀμφιέννυσιν. Ὁρᾷς πανταχοῦ πολλὰς τὰς ὑπερβολὰς καὶ τὰς ἐπιτάσεις; Ποιεῖ δὲ τοῦτο, ἵνα αὐτῶν καθάψηται: διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἐπήγαγεν· Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς; Καὶ γὰρ πολλὴν ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο τὴν ἔμφασιν. Τὸ γὰρ, ὑμᾶς, οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν αἰνιττομένου, ἢ τὸ πολυτίμητον καὶ περισπούδαστον τοῦ γένους· ὡσανεὶ [275] ἔλεγεν, Ὑμᾶς, οἷς ψυχὴν ἔδωκεν, οἷς σῶμα διέπλασε, δι’ οὓς τὰ ὁρώμενα πάντα ἐποίησε, δι’ οὓς προφήτας ἔπεμψε, καὶ νόμον ἔδωκε, καὶ τὰ μυρία εἰργάσατο ἀγαθὰ· δι’ οὓς τὸν μονογενῆ παῖδα ἐξέδωκεν 84. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπέδειξε σαφῶς, τότε καὶ ἐπιπλήττει λέγων· Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Τοιοῦτον 85 γὰρ ὁ συμβουλεύων· οὐ παραινεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθάπτεται, ἵνα διεγείρῃ πλέον πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν λεγομένων. Ἀπὸ τούτων ἡμᾶς οὐχὶ μὴ μεριμνᾶν διδάσκει μόνον, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἐπποθῆσαι

πρὸς τὴν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἱματίων. Χλόης γὰρ ἡ εὐπρέπεια, καὶ πόας τὸ κάλλος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τιμιώτερος ὁ χόρτος τῆς τοιαύτης στολῆς. Τί τοίνυν μέγα φρονεῖς, ἐν οἷς τὰ νικητήρια παρὰ τῇ βοτάνῃ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας; Καὶ ὅρα πῶς ἀπὸ τῶν προοιμίων κοῦφον δείκνυσι τὸ ἐπίταγμα, πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἀφ’ ὧν δεδοίκασιν, ἀπὸ τούτων ἀπάγων. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, ἐπήγαγεν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν. Ὥστε κόπων ἡμᾶς ἀπαλλάξαι βουλόμενος, ταῦτα ἐκέλευσεν. Οὐ τοίνυν τὸ μὴ μεριμνᾶν ταῦτα πόνος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μεριμνᾶν. Καὶ καθάπερ εἰπὼν, Οὐ σπείρουσιν, οὐ τὸν σπόρον ἀνέτρεψεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν φροντίδα· οὕτως εἰπὼν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν, οὐδὲ 86 νήθουσιν, οὐ τὸ ἔργον ἀνεῖλεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέριμναν. Εἰ δὲ Σολομῶν ἡττήθη τοῦ κάλλους αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐχ ἅπαξ οὐδὲ δὶς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ· (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχοι 87 τις εἰπεῖν, ὅτι νῦν μὲν τοιαῦτα περιεβάλετο, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐκέτι, ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ οὕτως ἐκαλλωπίσατο· τοῦτο γὰρ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ)· καὶ οὐχ ὑπὸ τούτου μὲν ἡττήθη τοῦ ἄνθους, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον ἐμιμήσατο, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁμοῦ παρεχώρησε· (διὸ καὶ ἔλεγεν, Ὡς ἓν τούτων· ὅσον γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας πρὸς τὸ ψεῦδος, τοσοῦτον τῶν ἱματίων ἐκείνων καὶ τῶν ἀνθῶν τούτων τὸ μέσον·) εἰ τοίνυν ἐκεῖνος ὡμολόγησε τὴν ἧτταν, ὁ πάντων βασιλέων τῶν πώποτε γενομένων λαμπρότερος, πότε σὺ περιγενέσθαι δυνήσῃ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐγγὺς γενέσθαι κἂν μικρὸν τῆς τοιαύτης εὐμορφίας; Ἐντεῦθεν ἡμᾶς παιδεύει μηδ’ ὅλως ἐφίεσθαι τοῦ τοιούτου καλλωπισμοῦ. Ἵνα γοῦν αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος· μετὰ τὴν νίκην εἰς κλίβανον βάλλεται. Εἰ δὲ περὶ τὰ εὐτελῆ καὶ οὐδενὸς ἄξια λόγου, καὶ τὴν τυχούσαν παρεχόμενα χρείαν, τοσαύτην πρόνοιαν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεδείξατο, πῶς σὲ προήσεται τὸ πάντων ἀναγκαιότατον 88 ζῶον; Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὕτω καλὰ αὐτὰ ἐποίησεν; ἵνα αὐτοῦ σοφίαν ἐπιδείξηται καὶ τὴν περιουσίαν τῆς δυνάμεως, ἵνα πανταχόθεν αὐτοῦ τὴν δόξαν μάθωμεν. Οὐ γὰρ οἱ οὐρανοὶ μόνοι διηγοῦνται τὴν

<header>ON MATTHEW HOMILY XXII. al. XXIII.</header>

<column-break/>

to receive them. That there are many who have achieved this is something we can demonstrate from those who have practiced this philosophy in our own generation. But for now, it is enough for you to learn not to be greedy, that almsgiving is a good thing, and to know that one must share what one has. For if you achieve these things, beloved, you will quickly advance to those others as well. For the present, then, let us put aside superfluous luxury, let us be content with moderation, and let us learn to acquire everything we intend to possess through honest labor. For even the blessed John, when he was speaking to those who were occupied with tax collecting and those who were serving in the military, commanded them to be content with their wages <note>Luke 3:14</note>. He indeed desired to lead them to a higher philosophy, but since they were not yet ready for such things, he speaks of the lesser, for if he had spoken of things higher than these, they would neither have paid attention to those, and they would have fallen away from these. For this reason, we also train you in the more modest things. For we know for the time being that the burden of poverty is greater for you, and that philosophy is as far from you as heaven is from the earth. Therefore, let us at least take hold of the final commands, for this is no small consolation. And yet, among the Greeks, some achieved even this, even if not with the proper intention, and stripped themselves of all their possessions. But we are content for you to provide alms generously; for we will quickly arrive at those other things if we proceed in this way. But if we do not even do this, what excuse would we deserve, we who are commanded to surpass those in the Old Testament, and yet appear inferior to the philosophers among the Greeks? What could we say, when we are obligated to be angels and sons of God, yet do not even maintain the status of being human? For to plunder and to be greedy is not of human gentleness, but of the cruelty of wild beasts; or rather, those who set upon the property of others are worse even than them. For this is natural to them, but we who have been honored with reason, and fall into a baseness contrary to nature, what excuse shall we enjoy? Having considered, therefore, the measures of the philosophy set before us, let us at least reach the middle ground, so that we may escape the coming punishment, and by proceeding on the path, arrive at the very summit of good things; which may we all attain, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

---

->HOMILY XXII<-

Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin; and I say to you, that not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these <note>Matthew 6:28-29</note>.

1. Having spoken about necessary food, and having shown that one should not even be anxious about this, he moves on to the lighter matter. For clothing is not as necessary as food. Why then does he not use the same example here as he did with the birds, and why does he not speak of the sheep, or the swan, or the wool? For there were many such examples to be taken from there. Because he wishes to show the excess from both sides, both from the insignificance of those who partake of such beauty, and from the extravagance of the adornment given to the lilies. For this reason, when he described them, he no longer calls them lilies, but "grass of the field." And he is not satisfied with this name, but again adds another insignificance, saying, "which is today." And he did not say, "not being tomorrow," but that which is much more inferior, "being cast into the oven." And he did not say, "he clothes," but, "so he clothes." Do you see everywhere the many exaggerations and intensifications? He does this so that he may strike at them; for this reason he also added: "Will he not much more clothe you?" For this also has great emphasis. For the word "you" is hinting at nothing other than the highly valued and much-sought-after nature of the human race; as if he were saying, "You, to whom he gave a soul, whom he fashioned with a body, for whose sake he made all visible things, for whose sake he sent prophets, and gave the law, and performed ten thousand good deeds; for whose sake he gave up his only-begotten Son." And since he demonstrated this clearly, then he also rebukes them, saying, "O you of little faith." For such is the one who counsels; he does not only exhort, but also strikes, so that he may stir them up more toward the persuasion of what is being said. From these things he teaches us not only not to be anxious, but not even to desire the luxury of garments. For the beauty of the grass and the splendor of the herb; or rather, the grass is even more precious than such a robe. Why then are you proud, in things where the victory belongs to the plant with much abundance? And see how from the beginning he shows the command to be light, again leading them away from the opposites, and from the things they fear. For having said, "Consider the lilies of the field," he added, "They do not toil." So, wishing to relieve us of labors, he commanded these things. Therefore, not being anxious is not labor, but being anxious is. And just as by saying, "They do not sow," he did not overturn the sowing, but the anxiety; so by saying, "They do not toil, nor do they spin," he did not abolish the work, but the anxiety. And if Solomon was defeated by their beauty, and not once or twice, but throughout his entire reign (for no one could say that he was arrayed like this at one time, but not after that, but he was not even adorned like this for a single day; for this he made clear by saying, "In all his glory"); and he was not defeated by this flower, but imitated the other, but yielded to all of them together (wherefore he also said, "Like one of these"; for as much as the truth is from the falsehood, so much is the difference between those garments and these flowers); if, therefore, he confessed his defeat, he who was the most brilliant of all kings who ever existed, when will you be able to prevail, or rather, to come even a little close to such beauty? From this he teaches us not to desire such adornment at all. For look at its end; after the victory, it is cast into the oven. And if God showed such providence for things that are cheap and worth nothing, and provide only the common need, how will he abandon you, the most necessary of all living creatures? Why then did he make them so beautiful? So that he might demonstrate his wisdom and the abundance of his power, so that we might learn of his glory from every side. δέξοιντο. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν πολλοὶ οἱ τοῦτο κατορθωκότες εἰσὶν, ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δυνατὸν ἡμῖν δεῖξαι τὴν ταῦτα φιλοσοφοῦνταν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας γενεᾶς. Ἀλλ’ ὑμῖν τέως ἀρκεῖ τὸ μὴ πλεονεκτεῖν μαθεῖν, καὶ ὅτι καλὸν ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη, καὶ τὸ εἰδέναι ὅτι χρὴ τῶν ὄντων μεταδιδόναι. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν κατορθώσῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ταχέως καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα βαδιεῖ. Τέως τοίνυν τὴν πολυτέλειαν ἀποθώμεθα τὴν περιττὴν, καὶ ἀνασχώμεθα τῆς συμμετρίας, καὶ μάθωμεν ἀπὸ δικαίων πόνων κτᾶσθαι ἅπαντα ἅπερ μέλλομεν ἔχειν: ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης, ὅτε διελέγετο τοῖς περὶ τὴν τελωνείαν ἐσχολακόσι καὶ τοῖς στρατευομένοις, ἀρκεῖσθαι τοῖς ὀψωνίοις προσέταττεν 74.75. Ἐδουλεῦτο μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἐφ’ ἑτέραν μείζονα αὐτοὺς ἀγαγεῖν φιλοσοφίαν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐδέπω πρὸς ταῦτα ἦσαν ἐπιτήδειοι, τὰ ἐλάττονα λέγει, ὡς εἰ τὰ ὑψηλότερα τούτων εἶπεν, οὔτ’ ἂν ἐκείνοις 76 προσέσχον, καὶ τούτων ἐξέπεσον ἄν. Διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς καταδεεστέροις ὑμᾶς γυμνάζομεν. Καὶ γὰρ τέως ἴσμεν, ὅτι μεῖζον ὑμῶν τῆς ἀκτημοσύνης τὸ φορτίον, καὶ ὅσον ἀφέστηκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς τῆς γῆς, τοσοῦτον ὑμῶν ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκείνη. Οὐκοῦν κἂν τῶν ἐσχάτων ἐπιλαβώμεθα ἐπιταγμάτων· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὕτη μικρὰ παραμυθία. Καίτοιγε παρ’ Ἕλλησι 74.75 ἐπέταττεν Ε. 76 ἐκεῖνοι C. E. 77 ποίωμεν B. C. E. 78 γὰρ] Add. θηρίοις Edd. Non habent Interpp.

τίνες καὶ τοῦτο κατώρθωσαν, εἰ καὶ μὴ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης γνώμης, καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἅπαντα ἀπεδύσαντο. Ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡμεῖς ἀρκούμεθα ἐφ’ ὑμῶν τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην δαψιλῆ παρέχεσθαι [274] παρ’ ὑμῶν· ταχέως γὰρ καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα ἥξομεν, ἂν οὕτω προβαίνωμεν. Εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦμεν 77, τίνας ἂν εἴημεν συγγνώμης ἄξιοι, οἱ τοὺς ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ ὑπερβῆναι κελευόμενοι, καὶ τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλοσόφων ἐλάττους φαινόμενοι; Τί ἂν εἴποιμεν, ὅταν ὀφείλοντες εἶναι ἄγγελοι καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ, μηδὲ τὸ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι διατηρῶμεν; Τὸ γὰρ ἁρπάζειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν οὐ τῆς ἀνθρώπων ἡμερότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶν θηρίων ὠμότητος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐκείνων χείρους οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπιτιθέμενοι. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ 78 ἀπὸ φύσεως τοῦτο πρόσεστιν· ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ λόγῳ τιμηθέντες, καὶ πρὸς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν καταπίπτοντες δυσγένειαν, τίνας ἀπολαυσόμεθα συγγνώμης; Ἐννοήσαντες τοίνυν τὰ μέτρα τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν φιλοσοφίας, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα φθάσωμεν, ἵνα καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀπαλλαγῶμεν κολάσεως, καὶ ὁδῷ προβαίνοντες ἐπ’ αὐτὴν ἔλθωμεν τὴν κορυφὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

->ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΚΒ’<-

Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, πῶς αὐξάνει· οὐ κοπιᾷ, οὐδὲ νήθει· λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲ Σολομῶν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ περιεβάλετο 79.80 ὡς ἓν τούτων.

α’. Εἰπὼν περὶ τῆς ἀναγκαίας τροφῆς, καὶ δείξας ὅτι οὐδὲ 81 ὑπὲρ ταύτης χρὴ μεριμνᾶν, ἐπὶ τὸ κουφότερον μεταβαίνει λοιπόν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἔνδυμα, ὡς τροφή. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὐ κέχρηται καὶ ἐνταῦθα τῷ αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι τῷ τῶν ὀρνίθων, οὐδὲ λέγει τὸ, ταῦνα ἡμῖν, καὶ τὸν κύκνον, καὶ τὸ πρόβατον; καὶ γὰρ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα παραδείγματα ἦν ἐκεῖθεν λαβεῖν. Ὅτι βούλεται ἑκατέρωθεν δεῖξαι τὴν ὑπερβολὴν, ἀπό τε τῆς εὐτελείας τὴν τοιαύτης μετασχόντων εὐπρεπείας, ἀπό τε τῆς φιλοτιμίας τοῦ καλλωπισμοῦ τῆς δοθείσης τοῖς κρίνοις. Διὰ τοῦτο ὅτε αὐτὰ κατεσκεύασεν, οὐδὲ κρίνα αὐτὰ καλεῖ λοιπὸν, ἀλλὰ χόρτον ἀγροῦ. Καὶ οὐδὲ 82 τῷ ὀνόματι ἀρκεῖται τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ πάλιν ἑτέραν εὐτέλειαν προστίθησιν, εἰπὼν, σήμερον ὄντα. Καὶ οὐχ εἶπεν, αὔριον οὐκ ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολλῷ πάλιν καταδεέστερον, εἰς κλίβανον βαλλόμενον. Καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν 83, ἀμφιέννυσιν, ἀλλ’, οὕτως ἀμφιέννυσιν. Ὁρᾷς πανταχοῦ πολλὰς τὰς ὑπερβολὰς καὶ τὰς ἐπιτάσεις; Ποιεῖ δὲ τοῦτο, ἵνα αὐτῶν καθάψηται: διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἐπήγαγεν· Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς; Καὶ γὰρ πολλὴν ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο τὴν ἔμφασιν. Τὸ γὰρ, ὑμᾶς, οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν αἰνιττομένου, ἢ τὸ πολυτίμητον καὶ περισπούδαστον τοῦ γένους· ὡσανεὶ [275] ἔλεγεν, Ὑμᾶς, οἷς ψυχὴν ἔδωκεν, οἷς σῶμα διέπλασε, δι’ οὓς τὰ ὁρώμενα πάντα ἐποίησε, δι’ οὓς προφήτας ἔπεμψε, καὶ νόμον ἔδωκε, καὶ τὰ μυρία εἰργάσατο ἀγαθὰ· δι’ οὓς τὸν μονογενῆ παῖδα ἐξέδωκεν 84. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπέδειξε σαφῶς, τότε καὶ ἐπιπλήττει λέγων· Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Τοιοῦτον 85 γὰρ ὁ συμβουλεύων· οὐ παραινεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθάπτεται, ἵνα διεγείρῃ πλέον πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν λεγομένων. Ἀπὸ τούτων ἡμᾶς οὐχὶ μὴ μεριμνᾶν διδάσκει μόνον, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἐπποθῆσαι

πρὸς τὴν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἱματίων. Χλόης γὰρ ἡ εὐπρέπεια, καὶ πόας τὸ κάλλος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τιμιώτερος ὁ χόρτος τῆς τοιαύτης στολῆς. Τί τοίνυν μέγα φρονεῖς, ἐν οἷς τὰ νικητήρια παρὰ τῇ βοτάνῃ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας; Καὶ ὅρα πῶς ἀπὸ τῶν προοιμίων κοῦφον δείκνυσι τὸ ἐπίταγμα, πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἀφ’ ὧν δεδοίκασιν, ἀπὸ τούτων ἀπάγων. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, ἐπήγαγεν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν. Ὥστε κόπων ἡμᾶς ἀπαλλάξαι βουλόμενος, ταῦτα ἐκέλευσεν. Οὐ τοίνυν τὸ μὴ μεριμνᾶν ταῦτα πόνος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μεριμνᾶν. Καὶ καθάπερ εἰπὼν, Οὐ σπείρουσιν, οὐ τὸν σπόρον ἀνέτρεψεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν φροντίδα· οὕτως εἰπὼν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν, οὐδὲ 86 νήθουσιν, οὐ τὸ ἔργον ἀνεῖλεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέριμναν. Εἰ δὲ Σολομῶν ἡττήθη τοῦ κάλλους αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐχ ἅπαξ οὐδὲ δὶς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ· (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχοι 87 τις εἰπεῖν, ὅτι νῦν μὲν τοιαῦτα περιεβάλετο, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐκέτι, ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ οὕτως ἐκαλλωπίσατο· τοῦτο γὰρ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ)· καὶ οὐχ ὑπὸ τούτου μὲν ἡττήθη τοῦ ἄνθους, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον ἐμιμήσατο, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁμοῦ παρεχώρησε· (διὸ καὶ ἔλεγεν, Ὡς ἓν τούτων· ὅσον γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας πρὸς τὸ ψεῦδος, τοσοῦτον τῶν ἱματίων ἐκείνων καὶ τῶν ἀνθῶν τούτων τὸ μέσον·) εἰ τοίνυν ἐκεῖνος ὡμολόγησε τὴν ἧτταν, ὁ πάντων βασιλέων τῶν πώποτε γενομένων λαμπρότερος, πότε σὺ περιγενέσθαι δυνήσῃ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐγγὺς γενέσθαι κἂν μικρὸν τῆς τοιαύτης εὐμορφίας; Ἐντεῦθεν ἡμᾶς παιδεύει μηδ’ ὅλως ἐφίεσθαι τοῦ τοιούτου καλλωπισμοῦ. Ἵνα γοῦν αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος· μετὰ τὴν νίκην εἰς κλίβανον βάλλεται. Εἰ δὲ περὶ τὰ εὐτελῆ καὶ οὐδενὸς ἄξια λόγου, καὶ τὴν τυχούσαν παρεχόμενα χρείαν, τοσαύτην πρόνοιαν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεδείξατο, πῶς σὲ προήσεται τὸ πάντων ἀναγκαιότατον 88 ζῶον; Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὕτω καλὰ αὐτὰ ἐποίησεν; ἵνα αὐτοῦ σοφίαν ἐπιδείξηται καὶ τὴν περιουσίαν τῆς δυνάμεως, ἵνα πανταχόθεν αὐτοῦ τὴν δόξαν μάθωμεν. Οὐ γὰρ οἱ οὐρανοὶ μόνοι διηγοῦνται τὴν

<meta>continues from previous page: Chrysostom is discussing the virtue of detachment from wealth and the practice of almsgiving as a step toward higher spiritual philosophy.</meta>

...might receive. That many have indeed achieved this <note>the renunciation of possessions</note> is something we can demonstrate from those who practice this philosophy even in our own generation. But for you, it is enough for now to learn not to be greedy, to know that almsgiving is good, and to understand that one must share what they have. For if you achieve these things, beloved, you will quickly advance to those higher goals. For the time being, then, let us lay aside unnecessary luxury, let us embrace moderation, and let us learn to acquire everything we possess through honest labor. Even the blessed John <note>John the Baptist</note>, when he spoke to those occupied with tax collecting and to those in military service, commanded them to be content with their wages. He certainly desired to lead them toward another, greater philosophy; but since they were not yet ready for such things, he spoke of lesser matters. If he had spoken of things higher than these, they would neither have paid attention to him nor succeeded in the lesser ones. For this reason, we also train you in the more modest duties. For we know that for now, the burden of total poverty is too great for you, and that higher philosophy is as far from you as the heaven is from the earth. Therefore, let us at least take hold of the final commands; for even this is no small consolation. And yet, among the Greeks <note>the pagans</note>,

<column-break/>

there were some who achieved even this, though not with the proper intent, and stripped themselves of all their possessions. Nevertheless, we are satisfied if you provide abundant alms; for we will quickly arrive at those higher states if we proceed in this way. But if we do not even do this, what forgiveness could we deserve—we who are commanded to surpass those under the Old Law, yet appear inferior even to the Greek philosophers? What can we say when, being called to be angels and sons of God, we do not even maintain our status as human beings? For seizing and being greedy does not belong to human gentleness, but to the cruelty of wild beasts; or rather, those who set upon the property of others are worse than beasts. For in beasts, this is a matter of nature; but we, who have been honored with reason and yet fall into a baseness that is against nature, what forgiveness shall we enjoy? Considering, then, the measures of the philosophy set before us, let us at least reach the middle ground, so that we may be delivered from future punishment and, advancing on the path, come to the very summit of all good things. May we all attain this by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

### HOMILY XXII
<note>Numbered as XXIII in some editions</note>

->Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not toil, nor do they spin; yet I say to you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.<-

1. Having spoken about necessary food, and having shown that one should not worry even for this, He moves on to a lighter matter. For clothing is not as necessary as food. Why then did He not use the same example of the birds here, and speak of the peacock, the swan, and the sheep? For many such examples could be taken from there. It is because He wishes to show the superiority from both sides: from the lowliness of those things that share in such beauty, and from the excellence of the splendor given to the lilies. For this reason, when He describes them, He no longer calls them lilies, but "grass of the field." And He is not satisfied with this name alone, but adds another mark of lowliness, saying, "which exists today." And He did not say, "and tomorrow is not," but something much more humble: "is thrown into the oven." And He did not simply say "He clothes," but "so clothes." Do you see the many exaggerations and intensifications everywhere? He does this to strike home to them; therefore He added: "Will He not much more clothe you?" This also carries great emphasis. For the word "you" hints at nothing other than the high value and preciousness of the human race; as if He were saying: "You, to whom He gave a soul, for whom He fashioned a body, for whose sake He made all visible things, for whom He sent prophets, gave the law, and worked ten thousand good deeds; for whose sake He gave up His only-begotten Son." Since He has demonstrated this clearly, He then rebukes them, saying: "O you of little faith." Such is the way of a counselor; he does not only exhort, but also reproves, so that he may stir them more toward obeying what is said. From these things He teaches us not only not to worry, but not even to long

<column-break/>

for the luxury of garments. For that beauty is of the grass, and that splendor is of the herb; or rather, the grass is more precious than such a robe. Why then do you think so highly of yourself for things in which the plant holds the prize with great abundance? And see how from the very beginning He shows the command is light, leading them away from the very things they fear. For having said, "Consider the lilies of the field," He added, "They do not toil." Thus, wishing to deliver us from toils, He gave these commands. Therefore, not worrying is not a labor, but worrying is. And just as when He said, "They do not sow," He did not forbid sowing, but anxiety; so by saying, "They do not toil, nor do they spin," He did not abolish the work, but the worry. If Solomon was surpassed by their beauty—and not once or twice, but throughout his entire reign (for one cannot say that he wore such things at one time but not later; he never adorned himself so on any single day, as indicated by the phrase "in all his glory")—and if he was not just surpassed by this flower while imitating another, but yielded to them all collectively (which is why He said, "as one of these"; for as much as truth differs from a lie, so much is the distance between those garments and these flowers); if then he confessed defeat, he who was more brilliant than all kings who ever lived, when will you be able to surpass them, or rather, to come even slightly near such beauty? From this He instructs us not to desire such adornment at all. Look at its end: after its victory, it is thrown into the oven. If God showed such providence for lowly things of no account, which serve only a passing need, how will He abandon you, the most necessary of all living beings? <summary>John Chrysostom concludes a discourse on almsgiving as a prerequisite for higher spiritual life and begins Homily 22 on Matthew 6:28-29. He explains that Christ uses the lilies of the field to shame human anxiety over clothing, noting that even Solomon's artificial glory cannot match the natural beauty God grants to temporary grass.</summary>

δέξοιντο. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν πολλοὶ οἱ τοῦτο κατορθωκότες εἰσὶν, ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δυνατὸν ἡμῖν δεῖξαι τὴν ταῦτα φιλοσοφοῦνταν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας γενεᾶς. Ἀλλ’ ὑμῖν τέως ἀρκεῖ τὸ μὴ πλεονεκτεῖν μαθεῖν, καὶ ὅτι καλὸν ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη, καὶ τὸ εἰδέναι ὅτι χρὴ τῶν ὄντων μεταδιδόναι. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν κατορθώσῃς, ἀγαπητὲ, ταχέως καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα βαδιεῖ. Τέως τοίνυν τὴν πολυτέλειαν ἀποθώμεθα τὴν περιττὴν, καὶ ἀνασχώμεθα τῆς συμμετρίας, καὶ μάθωμεν ἀπὸ δικαίων πόνων κτᾶσθαι ἅπαντα ἅπερ μέλλομεν ἔχειν: ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ μακάριος Ἰωάννης, ὅτε διελέγετο τοῖς περὶ τὴν τελωνείαν ἐσχολακόσι καὶ τοῖς στρατευομένοις, ἀρκεῖσθαι τοῖς ὀψωνίοις προσέταττεν 74.75. Ἐδουλεῦτο μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἐφ’ ἑτέραν μείζονα αὐτοὺς ἀγαγεῖν φιλοσοφίαν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐδέπω πρὸς ταῦτα ἦσαν ἐπιτήδειοι, τὰ ἐλάττονα λέγει, ὡς εἰ τὰ ὑψηλότερα τούτων εἶπεν, οὔτ’ ἂν ἐκείνοις 76 προσέσχον, καὶ τούτων ἐξέπεσον ἄν. Διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς καταδεεστέροις ὑμᾶς γυμνάζομεν. Καὶ γὰρ τέως ἴσμεν, ὅτι μεῖζον ὑμῶν τῆς ἀκτημοσύνης τὸ φορτίον, καὶ ὅσον ἀφέστηκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς τῆς γῆς, τοσοῦτον ὑμῶν ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκείνη. Οὐκοῦν κἂν τῶν ἐσχάτων ἐπιλαβώμεθα ἐπιταγμάτων· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὕτη μικρὰ παραμυθία. Καίτοιγε παρ’ Ἕλλησι 74.75 ἐπέταττεν Ε. 76 ἐκεῖνοι C. E. 77 ποίωμεν B. C. E. 78 γὰρ] Add. θηρίοις Edd. Non habent Interpp.

τίνες καὶ τοῦτο κατώρθωσαν, εἰ καὶ μὴ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης γνώμης, καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἅπαντα ἀπεδύσαντο. Ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἡμεῖς ἀρκούμεθα ἐφ’ ὑμῶν τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην δαψιλῆ παρέχεσθαι [274] παρ’ ὑμῶν· ταχέως γὰρ καὶ ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα ἥξομεν, ἂν οὕτω προβαίνωμεν. Εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦμεν 77, τίνας ἂν εἴημεν συγγνώμης ἄξιοι, οἱ τοὺς ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ ὑπερβῆναι κελευόμενοι, καὶ τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλοσόφων ἐλάττους φαινόμενοι; Τί ἂν εἴποιμεν, ὅταν ὀφείλοντες εἶναι ἄγγελοι καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ, μηδὲ τὸ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι διατηρῶμεν; Τὸ γὰρ ἁρπάζειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν οὐ τῆς ἀνθρώπων ἡμερότητος, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶν θηρίων ὠμότητος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐκείνων χείρους οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπιτιθέμενοι. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ 78 ἀπὸ φύσεως τοῦτο πρόσεστιν· ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ λόγῳ τιμηθέντες, καὶ πρὸς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν καταπίπτοντες δυσγένειαν, τίνας ἀπολαυσόμεθα συγγνώμης; Ἐννοήσαντες τοίνυν τὰ μέτρα τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν φιλοσοφίας, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα φθάσωμεν, ἵνα καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀπαλλαγῶμεν κολάσεως, καὶ ὁδῷ προβαίνοντες ἐπ’ αὐτὴν ἔλθωμεν τὴν κορυφὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, πῶς αὐξάνει· οὐ κοπιᾷ, οὐδὲ νήθει· λέγω δὲ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲ Σολομῶν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ περιεβάλετο 79.80 ὡς ἓν τούτων.

α’. Εἰπὼν περὶ τῆς ἀναγκαίας τροφῆς, καὶ δείξας ὅτι οὐδὲ 81 ὑπὲρ ταύτης χρὴ μεριμνᾶν, ἐπὶ τὸ κουφότερον μεταβαίνει λοιπόν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἔνδυμα, ὡς τροφή. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὐ κέχρηται καὶ ἐνταῦθα τῷ αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι τῷ τῶν ὀρνίθων, οὐδὲ λέγει τὸ, ταῦνα ἡμῖν, καὶ τὸν κύκνον, καὶ τὸ πρόβατον; καὶ γὰρ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα παραδείγματα ἦν ἐκεῖθεν λαβεῖν. Ὅτι βούλεται ἑκατέρωθεν δεῖξαι τὴν ὑπερβολὴν, ἀπό τε τῆς εὐτελείας τὴν τοιαύτης μετασχόντων εὐπρεπείας, ἀπό τε τῆς φιλοτιμίας τοῦ καλλωπισμοῦ τῆς δοθείσης τοῖς κρίνοις. Διὰ τοῦτο ὅτε αὐτὰ κατεσκεύασεν, οὐδὲ κρίνα αὐτὰ καλεῖ λοιπὸν, ἀλλὰ χόρτον ἀγροῦ. Καὶ οὐδὲ 82 τῷ ὀνόματι ἀρκεῖται τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ πάλιν ἑτέραν εὐτέλειαν προστίθησιν, εἰπὼν, σήμερον ὄντα. Καὶ οὐχ εἶπεν, αὔριον οὐκ ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολλῷ πάλιν καταδεέστερον, εἰς κλίβανον βαλλόμενον. Καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν 83, ἀμφιέννυσιν, ἀλλ’, οὕτως ἀμφιέννυσιν. Ὁρᾷς πανταχοῦ πολλὰς τὰς ὑπερβολὰς καὶ τὰς ἐπιτάσεις; Ποιεῖ δὲ τοῦτο, ἵνα αὐτῶν καθάψηται: διὰ δὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἐπήγαγεν· Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς; Καὶ γὰρ πολλὴν ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο τὴν ἔμφασιν. Τὸ γὰρ, ὑμᾶς, οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν αἰνιττομένου, ἢ τὸ πολυτίμητον καὶ περισπούδαστον τοῦ γένους· ὡσανεὶ [275] ἔλεγεν, Ὑμᾶς, οἷς ψυχὴν ἔδωκεν, οἷς σῶμα διέπλασε, δι’ οὓς τὰ ὁρώμενα πάντα ἐποίησε, δι’ οὓς προφήτας ἔπεμψε, καὶ νόμον ἔδωκε, καὶ τὰ μυρία εἰργάσατο ἀγαθὰ· δι’ οὓς τὸν μονογενῆ παῖδα ἐξέδωκεν 84. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπέδειξε σαφῶς, τότε καὶ ἐπιπλήττει λέγων· Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Τοιοῦτον 85 γὰρ ὁ συμβουλεύων· οὐ παραινεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθάπτεται, ἵνα διεγείρῃ πλέον πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν λεγομένων. Ἀπὸ τούτων ἡμᾶς οὐχὶ μὴ μεριμνᾶν διδάσκει μόνον, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἐπποθῆσαι

πρὸς τὴν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἱματίων. Χλόης γὰρ ἡ εὐπρέπεια, καὶ πόας τὸ κάλλος· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τιμιώτερος ὁ χόρτος τῆς τοιαύτης στολῆς. Τί τοίνυν μέγα φρονεῖς, ἐν οἷς τὰ νικητήρια παρὰ τῇ βοτάνῃ μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας; Καὶ ὅρα πῶς ἀπὸ τῶν προοιμίων κοῦφον δείκνυσι τὸ ἐπίταγμα, πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἀφ’ ὧν δεδοίκασιν, ἀπὸ τούτων ἀπάγων. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ, ἐπήγαγεν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν. Ὥστε κόπων ἡμᾶς ἀπαλλάξαι βουλόμενος, ταῦτα ἐκέλευσεν. Οὐ τοίνυν τὸ μὴ μεριμνᾶν ταῦτα πόνος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μεριμνᾶν. Καὶ καθάπερ εἰπὼν, Οὐ σπείρουσιν, οὐ τὸν σπόρον ἀνέτρεψεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν φροντίδα· οὕτως εἰπὼν, Οὐ κοπιῶσιν, οὐδὲ 86 νήθουσιν, οὐ τὸ ἔργον ἀνεῖλεν, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέριμναν. Εἰ δὲ Σολομῶν ἡττήθη τοῦ κάλλους αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐχ ἅπαξ οὐδὲ δὶς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ· (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχοι 87 τις εἰπεῖν, ὅτι νῦν μὲν τοιαῦτα περιεβάλετο, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐκέτι, ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ οὕτως ἐκαλλωπίσατο· τοῦτο γὰρ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ)· καὶ οὐχ ὑπὸ τούτου μὲν ἡττήθη τοῦ ἄνθους, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον ἐμιμήσατο, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁμοῦ παρεχώρησε· (διὸ καὶ ἔλεγεν, Ὡς ἓν τούτων· ὅσον γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας πρὸς τὸ ψεῦδος, τοσοῦτον τῶν ἱματίων ἐκείνων καὶ τῶν ἀνθῶν τούτων τὸ μέσον·) εἰ τοίνυν ἐκεῖνος ὡμολόγησε τὴν ἧτταν, ὁ πάντων βασιλέων τῶν πώποτε γενομένων λαμπρότερος, πότε σὺ περιγενέσθαι δυνήσῃ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐγγὺς γενέσθαι κἂν μικρὸν τῆς τοιαύτης εὐμορφίας; Ἐντεῦθεν ἡμᾶς παιδεύει μηδ’ ὅλως ἐφίεσθαι τοῦ τοιούτου καλλωπισμοῦ. Ἵνα γοῦν αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος· μετὰ τὴν νίκην εἰς κλίβανον βάλλεται. Εἰ δὲ περὶ τὰ εὐτελῆ καὶ οὐδενὸς ἄξια λόγου, καὶ τὴν τυχούσαν παρεχόμενα χρείαν, τοσαύτην πρόνοιαν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεδείξατο, πῶς σὲ προήσεται τὸ πάντων ἀναγκαιότατον 88 ζῶον; Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν οὕτω καλὰ αὐτὰ ἐποίησεν; ἵνα αὐτοῦ σοφίαν ἐπιδείξηται καὶ τὴν περιουσίαν τῆς δυνάμεως, ἵνα πανταχόθεν αὐτοῦ τὴν δόξαν μάθωμεν. Οὐ γὰρ οἱ οὐρανοὶ μόνοι διηγοῦνται τὴν

For those that do all that is lawful, quickly fall into doing what is unlawful. And just as righteousness is not attained by avarice, nor temperance by excess; so neither is the regimen of a Christian formed by indulgence; for the table of truth is far from lascivious dainties. For though it was chiefly for men's sake that all things were made, yet it is not good to use all things, nor at all times. For the occasion, and the time, and the mode, and the intention, materially turn the balance with reference to what is useful, in the view of one who is rightly instructed; and this is suitable, and has influence in putting a stop to a life of gluttony, which wealth is prone to choose, not that wealth which sees clearly, but that abundance which makes a man blind with reference to gluttony. No one is poor as regards necessaries, and a man is never overlooked. For there is one God who feeds the fowls and the fishes, and, in a word, the irrational creatures; and not one thing whatever is wanting to them, though they take no thought for their food.
And we are better than they, being their lords, and more closely allied to God, as being wiser; and we were made, not that we might eat and drink, but that we might devote ourselves to the knowledge of God. For the just man who eats is satisfied in his soul, but the belly of the wicked shall want,
filled with the appetites of insatiable gluttony. Now lavish expense is adapted not for enjoyment alone, but also for social communication. Wherefore we must guard against those articles of food which persuade us to eat when we are not hungry, bewitching the appetite. For is there not within a temperate simplicity a wholesome variety of eatables? Bulbs, olives, certain herbs, milk, cheese, fruits, all kinds of cooked food without sauces; and if flesh is wanted, let roast rather than boiled be set down. Have you anything to eat here? Said the Lord
to the disciples after the resurrection; and they, as taught by Him to practice frugality, gave Him a piece of broiled fish; and having eaten before them, says Luke, He spoke to them what He spoke. And in addition to these, it is not to be overlooked that those who feed according to the Word are not debarred from dainties in the shape of honey-combs. For of articles of food, those are the most suitable which are fit for immediate use without fire, since they are readiest; and second to these are those which are simplest, as we said before. But those who bend around inflammatory tables, nourishing their own diseases, are ruled by a most lickerish demon, whom I shall not blush to call the Belly-demon, and the worst and most abandoned of demons. He is therefore exactly like the one who is called the Ventriloquist-demon. It is far better to be happy than to have a demon dwelling with us. And happiness is found in the practice of virtue. Accordingly, the apostle Matthew partook of seeds, and nuts, and vegetables, without flesh. And John, who carried temperance to the extreme, ate locusts and wild honey. Peter abstained from swine; but a trance fell on him, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, and he saw heaven opened, and a vessel let down on the earth by the four corners,
[context] and all the four-looted beasts and creeping things of the earth and the fowls of heaven in it; and there came a voice to him, Rise, and slay, and eat.
