<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Clement’s discourse on Christian moderation at the table. Having previously warned against the "belly-madness" of gluttony, he now contrasts the "Table of Truth" with the luxurious habits of the wealthy, concluding with the ascetic examples of the Apostles.</meta>

-># THE INSTRUCTOR, BOOK II<-

<page-num>109</page-num>

...those who do everything that is permitted, swallow down what is forbidden. Just as justice is not demonstrated through greed, nor temperance through intemperance, so too the Christian way of life is not acquired through luxury. For the Table of Truth is far from rich and fatty foods <note>original Greek: παχυκνίκων (pachyknikōn), referring to foods heavy with the smell of fat or rich seasonings</note>. For even if all things were created for the sake of man, it is not good to use all things, nor to use them always. Indeed, the occasion, the time, the manner, and the purpose provide no small instruction to the Tutor <note>The "Tutor" or "Instructor" refers to the Logos/Christ, the title of this work</note> regarding what is profitable. This fitness of purpose has the power to nullify the prevailing force of luxury. Wealth is inclined to be sluggish, yet it sees sharply—but that "persuasion" which surrounds gluttony is blind. No one is poor regarding the necessities of life, nor is any man ever truly overlooked. For there is one God who feeds the birds, the fish, and, to put it simply, the irrational animals. They lack for nothing, even though they take no care for their food. We are better than they, in as much as we are their masters and more closely related to God, being more temperate. We were created not so that we might eat and drink, but that we might come to the knowledge of God. "The righteous man," it says, "eats and satisfies his soul, but the bellies of the ungodly are wanting," <margin>Proverbs 13</margin> reaching out with a greed that never ceases. Magnificence is not suited for empty enjoyment, but for social sharing. Therefore, we must be on guard against those foods that persuade us to eat when we are not hungry, bewitching our appetites. For is there not a healthy variety of simple foods within a temperate frugality? There are bulbs <note>likely referring to edible hyacinth or muscari bulbs, common in ancient diets</note>, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, and fruits, as well as all kinds of cooked dishes prepared without rich sauces. And if there is a need for meat, whether roasted or boiled, it should be shared. "Have you anything here to eat?" <margin>Luke 24</margin> the Lord said to the disciples after the resurrection. And they, having been taught to practice frugality by Him, gave Him a piece of broiled fish; and having eaten before them, as Luke says, He spoke to them. Furthermore, those who dine according to reason should not be without a share of the earthy products of the honeycomb. For of foods, those that can be used as they are, without fire, are the most suitable, since they are more easily prepared; second to these are the simpler foods, as we said before. But for those who hover around inflamed tables, nursing their own diseases, a most gluttonous demon leads the way; I would not be ashamed to call him a "belly-demon" <note>original Greek: κοιλιοδαίμονα (koiliodaimona). Clement is punning on the word "eudaimonia" (happiness/blessedness), suggesting gluttons have a "demon" in their gut rather than "good spirits" in their soul.</note>, the worst and most destructive of all demons. He is exactly like the one who is called a "belly-speaker" <note>original Greek: ἐγγαστριμύθῳ (engastrimythō), a term for a ventriloquist or a soothsayer who spoke from the stomach</note>. It is much better to be happy <note>original: εὐδαίμονα (eudaimona), literally "having a good spirit"</note> than to have a demon as a roommate. Happiness is found in the practice of virtue. Thus, Matthew the Apostle partook of seeds, nuts, and vegetables, without meat. And John, extending his self-restraint to the utmost, ate locusts and wild honey. Likewise, Peter also abstained <margin>Matthew 3</margin> from [certain foods]; but a trance fell upon him, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, and he beheld heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending like a sheet bound at the four corners upon the earth...

καταπίνουσιν ἀντὶ τοῦ δρᾶν τὸ μὴ ἐξὸν, οἱ πάντα δρῶντες ἃ ἐξόν. ὡς δὴ δικαιοσύνη διὰ πλεονεξίας, οὐ δείκνυται, οὐδὲ ἡ σωφροσύνη δι’ ἀκολασίας· οὕτως οὐδὲ ἡ Χριστιανοῦ δίαιτα, ἡδυπαθείᾳ περικτᾶται· πόῤῥω γάρ ἐστι τῶν παχυκνίκων ἐδεσμάτων, ἡ τράπεζα τῆς ἀληθείας. εἰ γὰρ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα ἕνεκεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐγένετο τὰ πάντα, ἀλλ’ οὐ πᾶσι χρῆσθαι καλὸν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἀεί. καὶ γὰρ καὶ ὁ καιρὸς, καὶ ὁ χρόνος, καὶ ὁ τρόπος, καὶ τὸ πρὸς τί, οὐκ ὀλίγην τῷ παιδαγωγῷ δίδωσι πρὸς τὸ λυσιτελὲς ἐνδιδασκαλίαν· καὶ τὸ γέ ἐστιν ἐπιτήδειον, καὶ ἰσχὺν ἔχει καταργῆσαι τὴν ἐπιπροθέουσαν βίαν· ὁ πλοῦτος ἔστιν ὀκνητικὸς, καὶ βλέπων ὀξὺ, ἀλλ’ ἡ τυφλώττουσα περὶ τὴν γαστριμαργίαν πειθοῖα. οὐδεὶς δέ ἐστι πένης εἰς τὰ ἀναγκαῖα· οὐδὲ περιορᾶταί ποτε ἄνθρωπος· ὁ γὰρ καὶ τὰ πτηνὰ, καὶ τὰ νηκτὰ, καὶ, συνελόντι εἰπεῖν, τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα διατρέφων, εἷς ἔστιν ὁ θεός. λείπει δὲ αὐτοῖς οὐδὲ ἓν ὁπόθεν μὴ μεριμνῶσι τροφῆς, ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ τούτων ἀμείνους, ὅσῳ καὶ κύριοι, καὶ θεῷ οἰκειότεροι, ὅσῳ σωφρονέστεροι, γεγόναμεν δὲ, οὐχ ἵνα ἐσθίωμεν καὶ πίνωμεν, ἀλλ’ ἵνα ὦμεν εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν γεγονότες τοῦ θεοῦ. Δίκαιος γάρ, φησὶν, ἐσθίων, ἐμπίμπλαται τῇ ψυχῇ· κοιλίαι δὲ ἀσεβῶν ἐνδεεῖς, ἀκαταπαύστῳ λιχνείᾳ ὀρεγόμεναι. πολυτέλεια δὲ οὐκ εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν ἔρημον, ἀλλ’ εἰς μετάδοσιν κοινωνικὴν ἐπιτήδειος· διὸ παραφυλακτέον τῶν βρωμάτων ἃ μὴ πεινῶντας ἡμᾶς ἐσθίειν ἀναπείθει, γοητεύοντα τὰς ὀρέξεις. μὴ γὰρ οὐκ ἔνεστι καὶ ἐν εὐτελείᾳ σώφρονι πολυειδία ἐδεσμάτων ὑγιεινή; βολβοὶ, ἐλαῖαι, λαχάνων ἔνια, γάλα, τυρὸς, τά τε ὡραῖα ἑψήματά τε παντοδαπὰ, ζωμῶν αὐτά. κἂν ἀποδέῃ κρέως, ἢ ἑφθοῦ, μεταδοτέον. Ἔχετέ τι βρώσιμον ἐνθάδε; εἶπεν ὁ κύριος πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν. οἱ δὲ, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτοῦ εὐτελείας ἀσκεῖν δεδιδαγμένοι, ἐπέδωκαν αὐτῷ ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος· καὶ φαγὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν, εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, φησὶν ὁ Λουκᾶς, ὅσα εἶπεν. πρὸς τούτοις οὐδὲ τὰ γήϊνα τῶν κηρίων ἀμοίρους περιορᾶτέον τοὺς δειπνοῦντας κατὰ λόγον. τῶν γὰρ τοι βρωμάτων διττὴ δειότης τε, οἷς αὐτόθεν χρῆσθαι ὑπάρχει δίχα πυρὸς, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἑτοιμότερα· δεύτερα δὲ, τὰ εὐτελέστερα, ὡς προειρήκαμεν. τῶν δὲ ἀμφὶ τὰς φλεγμαινούσας κυπαζόντων τραπέζας, τῷ σφετέρῳ ἐκθεσμωμένων πάθει, δαίμων καθηγεῖται λιχνότατος· ὃν ἔγωγε οὐκ ἂν αἰσχυνθείην κοιλιοδαίμονα προσειπεῖν, ὃς δαιμόνων κάκιστος, καὶ ἐξώλιστος. τὸν δὲ πλησίον ἐν αὐτῷ ἀτεχνῶς τῷ ἐγγαστριμύθῳ καλοῦμεν. ἄμεινον δὲ πολλῷ, ὦ δαίμονα ἔχειν σύνοικον, εὐδαίμονα γίνεσθαι. εὐδαιμονία δὲ ἐν χρήσει ἀρετῆς ἐξετάζεται. Ματθαῖος μὲν οὖν ὁ ἀπόστολος, σπερμάτων καὶ ἀκροδρύων καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρεῶν, μετελάμβανεν· Ἰωάννης δὲ, ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον. ὡσαύτως ἀπείχετο καὶ Πέτρος· ἀλλ’ ἔπεσεν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ἔκστασις, ὡς ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων γέγραπται· καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον, καὶ τὸ σκεῦος τι παρὸν ἀρχαῖς ἐκδεδεμένον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς·

modum autem non aduenit iustitia per auaritiam & plura habendi cupiditatem, neque temperantia per intemperantiam: ita nec victus Cristiani ratio lautitijs paratur & delitijs. A cibis enim titillantibus & ad venerem incitantibus, procul est mensa veritatis. Etsi enim maxime propter homines omnia facta sunt, non tamen omnibus vti bonum est, sed neque semper: nam tempus, occasio, modus, & respectus rei alicuius, non paruum ei qui instituitur momentum afferunt ad id, quod sibi est vtile. Atque hoc quidem aptum est, & magnam vim habet ad abolendam vitam quæ est ventri dedita, ad quam quidem diuitiæ incitant, non eæ quæ acute vident, sed nimiæ quæ circa gulæ insaniam cæcutiunt copiæ. Nemo autem ad res necessarias pauper est, neque homo vnquam despicitur. Qui enim & pennata & natatilia, & vt semel dicam, à ratione aliena nutrit animantia, vnus est Deus. eis autem nihil deest, etsi nullam de victu curam gerant. Nos autem eis fumo eo præstantiores, quod & Domini: & Deo eo familiariores, quo & temperantiores. Facti autem sumus non vt comedamus & bibamus, sed facti sumus vt essemus ad Dei agnitionem: Iustus enim, inquit, comedens, impletur animo: ventres autem impiorum egent, vt qui nunquam cessaturas cupiditas appetant. Magnificentia autem non ad solum vsum, sed etiam ad socialem communicationem apta est: quocirca ij cibi cauendi sunt, qui non esurientes nos cogunt comedere, appetitiones nostras veluti quibusdam præstigijs fallentes. An non est enim etiam in moderata frugalitate multiplex ciborum varietas? bulbi, oliuæ, quædam olera, lac, caseus, fructus, & quæcunque absque iure coquuntur: & si assa carne vel elixa opus fuerit, ea est quoque impertienda. Habetis hic aliquid quod edi possit? dixit Dominus discipulis post resurrectionem. illi vero, vt qui frugalitatem exercere ab eo didicerant, ei assi piscis partem dederunt. Et cum coram eis comedisset, dixit eis, inquit Lucas, quæcunque dixit. Ad hæc autem nabellariorum quidem, nempe fauorum, expertes esse oportet eos qui rationi conuenienter cœnant. Ex cibis enim ij sunt aptissimi, quibus ex se vti licet absque igne, quoniam sunt paratiores: secundi autem, qui sunt frugaliores ac viliores, vt ante diximus. Iis autem qui ad luxum mensarum propensi sunt, & suos sibi morbos enutriunt, præest dæmon helluo maximus, quem ego non verebor appellare Ventridæmonem, dæmonum omnium pessimum & perniciosissimum. Is autem est reuera similis ei qui dicitur ventriloquus. Melius est autem esse felicem, quam habere cohabitantem dæmonem. In vsu autem virtutis esse censetur felicitas. Matthæus itaque Apostolus seminibus, baccis & oleribus absque carnibus vtebatur. Ioannes autem continentiam vlterius extendens, locustas & mel agreste comedebat. Porro autem Petrus quoque abstinebat à suibus. Sed ei persuasit quæ in eum cecidit ecstasis, vt in Actibus Apostolorum scriptum est: Et videt cælum apertum, & vas quoddam quatuor initijs alligatum super

<header>PÆDAGOGVS, LIB. II.</header>
<sig>K</sig>
<meta>continues from previous page: catchword "πάντα" (all things)</meta>

all things, those who do all things that are permitted, swallow up what is not permitted instead of acting. Just as justice is not demonstrated through greed, nor temperance through intemperance, so too the diet of a Christian is not acquired through self-indulgence. For the table of truth is far removed from rich and heavy foods. Even if all things were created for the sake of humanity, it is not good to use all of them, nor even to use them always. For the occasion, the time, the manner, and the purpose provide no small amount of instruction to the <term>paidagogos</term> <gloss>tutor/instructor</gloss> regarding what is beneficial. This is appropriate and has the power to abolish the violence that rushes forward. Wealth is sluggish and sharp-sighted, but it is the persuasion that blinds one regarding gluttony. No one is poor regarding necessities, nor is a human ever overlooked. For there is one God who feeds the winged creatures, the swimming creatures, and, to put it briefly, the irrational animals. They lack nothing, even though they do not worry about food. We are better than these, inasmuch as we are masters and more familiar with God, to the extent that we are more temperate. We were made not to eat and drink, but we were made to exist for the knowledge of God. For it says, "The righteous man, eating, is filled in his soul; but the bellies of the ungodly are needy, reaching out with unceasing greed." Luxury is not suitable for solitary enjoyment, but for social sharing. Therefore, one must be on guard against foods that persuade us to eat when we are not hungry, bewitching our appetites. For is it not possible to have a healthy variety of foods even in temperate frugality? Bulbs, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, seasonal fruits, and all kinds of boiled dishes, including those made with broths. And if there is a need for meat or boiled food, it should be shared. "Do you have anything edible here?" the Lord said to the disciples after the resurrection. And they, having been taught to practice his frugality, gave him a piece of broiled fish. And having eaten in their presence, he said to them, says Luke, whatever he said. In addition to these, those who dine according to reason should not overlook the fruits of the earth that are free from honeycomb. For there is a twofold quality of foods: those that can be used directly without fire, since they are more readily available; and second, the more frugal ones, as we have said before. A most gluttonous demon leads those who are inclined toward inflammatory tables and who are abandoned to their own passion. I would not be ashamed to call him a "belly-demon," who is the worst and most destructive of demons. We call the neighbor of such a person, quite simply, a ventriloquist. It is much better to be happy than to have a demon as a housemate. Happiness is examined in the use of virtue. Matthew the apostle partook of seeds, nuts, and vegetables, without meat. John, extending his self-control further, ate locusts and wild honey. Peter likewise abstained from pork; but a trance fell upon him, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles; and he sees heaven opened, and a certain vessel bound by four corners upon the earth;

<column-break/>

but justice does not arrive through avarice and the desire to have more, nor does temperance arrive through intemperance. Thus, the manner of a Christian's diet is not prepared through luxuries and delights. For the table of truth is far from foods that tickle the palate and incite lust. Even if all things were made for the sake of humans, it is not good to use all of them, nor even to use them always. For the time, the occasion, the manner, and the respect for a thing provide no small momentum to the one being instructed toward what is useful to him. And this is indeed appropriate, and has great power to abolish the life that is dedicated to the belly, to which riches incite—not those that see sharply, but the excessive riches that are blind regarding the madness of gluttony. No one is poor regarding necessary things, nor is a human ever despised. For there is one God who nourishes the winged, the swimming, and, to speak once, the irrational animals. They lack nothing, even if they take no care regarding their diet. We are more excellent than them, inasmuch as we are masters, and more familiar with God, to the extent that we are more temperate. We were made not so that we might eat and drink, but we were made so that we might exist for the knowledge of God. For the righteous man, he says, eating, is filled in his soul; but the bellies of the impious are needy, as they desire what is a never-ending greed. Magnificence is not suitable for solitary use, but also for social communication. Therefore, those foods are to be avoided which force us to eat when we are not hungry, deceiving our appetites as if by certain tricks. For is there not a manifold variety of foods even in moderate frugality? Bulbs, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, fruits, and whatever is cooked without sauce; and if there is a need for roasted or boiled meat, it is also to be shared. "Do you have anything here that can be eaten?" said the Lord to the disciples after the resurrection. They, indeed, as those who had learned to practice frugality from him, gave him a part of a broiled fish. And when he had eaten in their presence, he said to them, says Luke, whatever he said. In addition to these, those who dine according to reason should be free from the products of bees, namely honeycombs. For of foods, those are most suitable which it is permitted to use by themselves without fire, since they are more ready; second are those which are more frugal and cheaper, as we said before. To those who are inclined toward the luxury of tables and who nourish their own diseases, a most gluttonous demon presides, whom I will not be ashamed to call the "Belly-demon," the worst and most pernicious of all demons. He is truly similar to the one who is called a ventriloquist. It is better to be happy than to have a demon as a cohabitant. Happiness is considered to be in the use of virtue. Matthew the Apostle, therefore, used seeds, berries, and vegetables without meats. John, however, extending his continence further, ate locusts and wild honey. Furthermore, Peter also abstained from pork. But the trance that fell upon him persuaded him, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "And he sees heaven opened, and a certain vessel bound by four corners upon the earth."

<summary>Clement of Alexandria discusses the Christian approach to diet, emphasizing temperance, frugality, and the avoidance of gluttony as a form of spiritual discipline. He contrasts the simple, natural diet of the apostles with the excessive, demon-influenced luxury of the gluttonous.</summary>

Ἔχετέ τι βρώσιμον ἐνθάδε; εἶπεν ὁ κύριος πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν. οἱ δὲ, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτοῦ εὐτελείας ἀσκεῖν δεδιδαγμένοι, ἐπέδωκαν αὐτῷ ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος· καὶ φαγὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν, εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, φησὶν ὁ Λουκᾶς, ὅσα εἶπεν. πρὸς τούτοις οὐδὲ τὰ γήϊνα τῶν κηρίων ἀμοίρους περιορᾶτέον τοὺς δειπνοῦντας κατὰ λόγον. τῶν γὰρ τοι βρωμάτων διττὴ δειότης τε, οἷς αὐτόθεν χρῆσθαι ὑπάρχει δίχα πυρὸς, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἑτοιμότερα· δεύτερα δὲ, τὰ εὐτελέστερα, ὡς προειρήκαμεν. τῶν δὲ ἀμφὶ τὰς φλεγμαινούσας κυπαζόντων τραπέζας, τῷ σφετέρῳ ἐκθεσμωμένων πάθει, δαίμων καθηγεῖται λιχνότατος· ὃν ἔγωγε οὐκ ἂν αἰσχυνθείην κοιλιοδαίμονα προσειπεῖν, ὃς δαιμόνων κάκιστος, καὶ ἐξώλιστος. τὸν δὲ πλησίον ἐν αὐτῷ ἀτεχνῶς τῷ ἐγγαστριμύθῳ καλοῦμεν. ἄμεινον δὲ πολλῷ, ὦ δαίμονα ἔχειν σύνοικον, εὐδαίμονα γίνεσθαι. εὐδαιμονία δὲ ἐν χρήσει ἀρετῆς ἐξετάζεται. Ματθαῖος μὲν οὖν ὁ ἀπόστολος, σπερμάτων καὶ ἀκροδρύων καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρεῶν, μετελάμβανεν· Ἰωάννης δὲ, ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον. ὡσαύτως ἀπείχετο καὶ Πέτρος· ἀλλ’ ἔπεσεν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ἔκστασις, ὡς ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων γέγραπται· καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον, καὶ τὸ σκεῦος τι παρὸν ἀρχαῖς ἐκδεδεμένον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς·

<column-break/>

<language>Latin</language>
modum autem non aduenit iustitia per auaritiam & plura habendi cupiditatem, neque temperantia per intemperantiam: ita nec victus Cristiani ratio lautitijs paratur & delitijs. A cibis enim titillantibus & ad venerem incitantibus, procul est mensa veritatis. Etsi enim maxime propter homines omnia facta sunt, non tamen omnibus vti bonum est, sed neque semper: nam tempus, occasio, modus, & respectus rei alicuius, non paruum ei qui instituitur momentum afferunt ad id, quod sibi est vtile. Atque hoc quidem aptum est, & magnam vim habet ad abolendam vitam quæ est ventri dedita, ad quam quidem diuitiæ incitant, non eæ quæ acute vident, sed nimiæ quæ circa gulæ insaniam cæcutiunt copiæ. Nemo autem ad res necessarias pauper est, neque homo vnquam despicitur. Qui enim & pennata & natatilia, & vt semel dicam, à ratione aliena nutrit animantia, vnus est Deus. eis autem nihil deest, etsi nullam de victu curam gerant. Nos autem eis fumo eo præstantiores, quod & Domini: & Deo eo familiariores, quo & temperantiores. Facti autem sumus non vt comedamus & bibamus, sed facti sumus vt essemus ad Dei agnitionem: Iustus enim, inquit, comedens, impletur animo: ventres autem impiorum egent, vt qui nunquam cessaturas cupiditas appetant. Magnificentia autem non ad solum vsum, sed etiam ad socialem communicationem apta est: quocirca ij cibi cauendi sunt, qui non esurientes nos cogunt comedere, appetitiones nostras veluti quibusdam præstigijs fallentes. An non est enim etiam in moderata frugalitate multiplex ciborum varietas? bulbi, oliuæ, quædam olera, lac, caseus, fructus, & quæcunque absque iure coquuntur: & si assa carne vel elixa opus fuerit, ea est quoque impertienda. Habetis hic aliquid quod edi possit? dixit Dominus discipulis post resurrectionem. illi vero, vt qui frugalitatem exercere ab eo didicerant, ei assi piscis partem dederunt. Et cum coram eis comedisset, dixit eis, inquit Lucas, quæcunque dixit. Ad hæc autem nabellariorum quidem, nempe fauorum, expertes esse oportet eos qui rationi conuenienter cœnant. Ex cibis enim ij sunt aptissimi, quibus ex se vti licet absque igne, quoniam sunt paratiores: secundi autem, qui sunt frugaliores ac viliores, vt ante diximus. Iis autem qui ad luxum mensarum propensi sunt, & suos sibi morbos enutriunt, præest dæmon helluo maximus, quem ego non verebor appellare Ventridæmonem, dæmonum omnium pessimum & perniciosissimum. Is autem est reuera similis ei qui dicitur ventriloquus. Melius est autem esse felicem, quam habere cohabitantem dæmonem. In vsu autem virtutis esse censetur felicitas. Matthæus itaque Apostolus seminibus, baccis & oleribus absque carnibus vtebatur. Ioannes autem continentiam vlterius extendens, locustas & mel agreste comedebat. Porro autem Petrus quoque abstinebat à suibus. Sed ei persuasit quæ in eum cecidit ecstasis, vt in Actibus Apostolorum scriptum est: Et videt cælum apertum, & vas quoddam quatuor initijs alligatum super

<header>PÆDAGOGVS, LIB. II.</header>
<sig>K</sig>
<meta>continues from previous page: catchword "πάντα" (all things)</meta>

all things, those who do all things that are permitted, swallow up what is not permitted instead of acting. Just as justice is not demonstrated through greed, nor temperance through intemperance, so too the diet of a Christian is not acquired through self-indulgence. For the table of truth is far removed from rich and heavy foods. Even if all things were created for the sake of humanity, it is not good to use all of them, nor even to use them always. For the occasion, the time, the manner, and the purpose provide no small amount of instruction to the <term>paidagogos</term> <gloss>tutor/instructor</gloss> regarding what is beneficial. This is appropriate and has the power to abolish the violence that rushes forward. Wealth is sluggish and sharp-sighted, but it is the persuasion that blinds one regarding gluttony. No one is poor regarding necessities, nor is a human ever overlooked. For there is one God who feeds the winged creatures, the swimming creatures, and, to put it briefly, the irrational animals. They lack nothing, even though they do not worry about food. We are better than these, inasmuch as we are masters and more familiar with God, to the extent that we are more temperate. We were made not to eat and drink, but we were made to exist for the knowledge of God. For it says, "The righteous man, eating, is filled in his soul; but the bellies of the ungodly are needy, reaching out with unceasing greed." Luxury is not suitable for solitary enjoyment, but for social sharing. Therefore, one must be on guard against foods that persuade us to eat when we are not hungry, bewitching our appetites. For is it not possible to have a healthy variety of foods even in temperate frugality? Bulbs, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, seasonal fruits, and all kinds of boiled dishes, including those made with broths. And if there is a need for meat or boiled food, it should be shared. "Do you have anything edible here?" the Lord said to the disciples after the resurrection. And they, having been taught to practice his frugality, gave him a piece of broiled fish. And having eaten in their presence, he said to them, says Luke, whatever he said. In addition to these, those who dine according to reason should not overlook the fruits of the earth that are free from honeycomb. For there is a twofold quality of foods: those that can be used directly without fire, since they are more readily available; and second, the more frugal ones, as we have said before. A most gluttonous demon leads those who are inclined toward inflammatory tables and who are abandoned to their own passion. I would not be ashamed to call him a "belly-demon," who is the worst and most destructive of demons. We call the neighbor of such a person, quite simply, a ventriloquist. It is much better to be happy than to have a demon as a housemate. Happiness is examined in the use of virtue. Matthew the apostle partook of seeds, nuts, and vegetables, without meat. John, extending his self-control further, ate locusts and wild honey. Peter likewise abstained from pork; but a trance fell upon him, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles; and he sees heaven opened, and a certain vessel bound by four corners upon the earth;

<column-break/>

but justice does not arrive through avarice and the desire to have more, nor does temperance arrive through intemperance. Thus, the manner of a Christian's diet is not prepared through luxuries and delights. For the table of truth is far from foods that tickle the palate and incite lust. Even if all things were made for the sake of humans, it is not good to use all of them, nor even to use them always. For the time, the occasion, the manner, and the respect for a thing provide no small momentum to the one being instructed toward what is useful to him. And this is indeed appropriate, and has great power to abolish the life that is dedicated to the belly, to which riches incite—not those that see sharply, but the excessive riches that are blind regarding the madness of gluttony. No one is poor regarding necessary things, nor is a human ever despised. For there is one God who nourishes the winged, the swimming, and, to speak once, the irrational animals. They lack nothing, even if they take no care regarding their diet. We are more excellent than them, inasmuch as we are masters, and more familiar with God, to the extent that we are more temperate. We were made not so that we might eat and drink, but we were made so that we might exist for the knowledge of God. For the righteous man, he says, eating, is filled in his soul; but the bellies of the impious are needy, as they desire what is a never-ending greed. Magnificence is not suitable for solitary use, but also for social communication. Therefore, those foods are to be avoided which force us to eat when we are not hungry, deceiving our appetites as if by certain tricks. For is there not a manifold variety of foods even in moderate frugality? Bulbs, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, fruits, and whatever is cooked without sauce; and if there is a need for roasted or boiled meat, it is also to be shared. "Do you have anything here that can be eaten?" said the Lord to the disciples after the resurrection. They, indeed, as those who had learned to practice frugality from him, gave him a part of a broiled fish. And when he had eaten in their presence, he said to them, says Luke, whatever he said. In addition to these, those who dine according to reason should be free from the products of bees, namely honeycombs. For of foods, those are most suitable which it is permitted to use by themselves without fire, since they are more ready; second are those which are more frugal and cheaper, as we said before. To those who are inclined toward the luxury of tables and who nourish their own diseases, a most gluttonous demon presides, whom I will not be ashamed to call the "Belly-demon," the worst and most pernicious of all demons. He is truly similar to the one who is called a ventriloquist. It is better to be happy than to have a demon as a cohabitant. Happiness is considered to be in the use of virtue. Matthew the Apostle, therefore, used seeds, berries, and vegetables without meats. John, however, extending his continence further, ate locusts and wild honey. Furthermore, Peter also abstained from pork. But the trance that fell upon him persuaded him, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "And he sees heaven opened, and a certain vessel bound by four corners upon the earth."

<margin>Prov. 13.</margin>
<margin>Luke 24.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 5.</margin>
<margin>Acts 10.</margin>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria discusses the Christian approach to diet, emphasizing temperance, frugality, and the avoidance of gluttony as a form of spiritual discipline. He contrasts the simple, natural diet of the apostles with the excessive, demon-influenced luxury of the gluttonous.</summary>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: those who do everything that is permitted</meta> swallow down what is forbidden instead of doing what is right. Just as justice is not demonstrated through greed, nor temperance through excess, so the Christian way of life is not acquired through luxury. For the table of truth is far removed from pungent and fatty foods. Even if all things were created primarily for the sake of humans, it is not good to use all things, nor to use them always. Indeed, the right moment, the time, the manner, and the purpose provide no small instruction to the <term>Paedagogus</term> <gloss>Tutor/Instructor</gloss> regarding what is beneficial. This sense of fitness has the power to nullify the violence of rushing desires. Wealth is prone to hesitation and is sharp-sighted, but the persuasion that surrounds gluttony is blind. No one is poor in regards to necessities, nor is any human ever overlooked. For the one who nourishes the birds, the swimming creatures, and, to put it briefly, the irrational animals, is the one God. They lack nothing, though they do not worry about food; and we are better than they, inasmuch as we are their masters and more closely related to God, being more temperate. We were created not so that we might eat and drink, but so that we might come to the knowledge of God. For the righteous man, it says, eats and is satisfied in his soul, but the bellies of the impious are in want <margin>Proverbs 13</margin>, reaching out with unceasing greed. Magnificence is not suited for solitary enjoyment, but for social sharing. Therefore, we must guard against those foods that persuade us to eat when we are not hungry, bewitching our appetites. Is there not a healthy variety of foods even in moderate frugality? Bulbs, olives, certain vegetables, milk, cheese, fruits, and all kinds of cooked dishes without rich sauces. And if there is a need for meat, whether roasted or boiled, it should be shared. Have you anything to eat here? <margin>Luke 24</margin> the Lord said to the disciples after the resurrection. And they, having been taught by Him to practice frugality, gave Him a piece of broiled fish; and having eaten in their presence, as Luke says, He spoke to them. In addition to these, those who dine according to reason should not be deprived of the earthly produce of honeycombs. For there are two kinds of suitable foods: first, those which can be used as they are without fire, since they are more readily available; and second, those that are simpler, as we said before. But over those who hover around inflamed tables, enslaved to their own lawless passions, a most gluttonous demon presides. I would not be ashamed to call him a belly-demon, the worst and most destructive of demons. He is exactly like the one we call a ventriloquist <note>original: "engastrimythos", literally "belly-speaker"</note>. It is much better to be happy <note>original: "eudaimona", literally "having a good spirit"</note> than to have a demon <note>original: "daimona"</note> as a housemate. Happiness is found in the practice of virtue. Now Matthew the Apostle partook of seeds, nuts, and vegetables without meat; and John, extending his self-control to the limit, ate locusts and wild honey. Likewise, Peter abstained <note>The Latin margin notes Matthew 5, but the text refers to Peter's vision in Acts</note>; but a trance fell upon him, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles <margin>Acts 10</margin>, and he saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending, bound by its four corners to the earth.

καταπίνουσιν ἀντὶ τοῦ δρᾶν τὸ μὴ ἐξὸν, οἱ πάντα δρῶντες ἃ ἐξόν. ὡς δὴ δικαιοσύνη διὰ πλεονεξίας, οὐ δείκνυται, οὐδὲ ἡ σωφροσύνη δι’ ἀκολασίας· οὕτως οὐδὲ ἡ Χριστιανοῦ δίαιτα, ἡδυπαθείᾳ περικτᾶται· πόῤῥω γάρ ἐστι τῶν παχυκνίκων ἐδεσμάτων, ἡ τράπεζα τῆς ἀληθείας. εἰ γὰρ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα ἕνεκεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐγένετο τὰ πάντα, ἀλλ’ οὐ πᾶσι χρῆσθαι καλὸν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἀεί. καὶ γὰρ καὶ ὁ καιρὸς, καὶ ὁ χρόνος, καὶ ὁ τρόπος, καὶ τὸ πρὸς τί, οὐκ ὀλίγην τῷ παιδαγωγῷ δίδωσι πρὸς τὸ λυσιτελὲς ἐνδιδασκαλίαν· καὶ τὸ γέ ἐστιν ἐπιτήδειον, καὶ ἰσχὺν ἔχει καταργῆσαι τὴν ἐπιπροθέουσαν βίαν· ὁ πλοῦτος ἔστιν ὀκνητικὸς, καὶ βλέπων ὀξὺ, ἀλλ’ ἡ τυφλώττουσα περὶ τὴν γαστριμαργίαν πειθοῖα. οὐδεὶς δέ ἐστι πένης εἰς τὰ ἀναγκαῖα· οὐδὲ περιορᾶταί ποτε ἄνθρωπος· ὁ γὰρ καὶ τὰ πτηνὰ, καὶ τὰ νηκτὰ, καὶ, συνελόντι εἰπεῖν, τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα διατρέφων, εἷς ἔστιν ὁ θεός. λείπει δὲ αὐτοῖς οὐδὲ ἓν ὁπόθεν μὴ μεριμνῶσι τροφῆς, ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ τούτων ἀμείνους, ὅσῳ καὶ κύριοι, καὶ θεῷ οἰκειότεροι, ὅσῳ σωφρονέστεροι, γεγόναμεν δὲ, οὐχ ἵνα ἐσθίωμεν καὶ πίνωμεν, ἀλλ’ ἵνα ὦμεν εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν γεγονότες τοῦ θεοῦ. Δίκαιος γάρ, φησὶν, ἐσθίων, ἐμπίμπλαται τῇ ψυχῇ· κοιλίαι δὲ ἀσεβῶν ἐνδεεῖς, ἀκαταπαύστῳ λιχνείᾳ ὀρεγόμεναι. πολυτέλεια δὲ οὐκ εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν ἔρημον, ἀλλ’ εἰς μετάδοσιν κοινωνικὴν ἐπιτήδειος· διὸ παραφυλακτέον τῶν βρωμάτων ἃ μὴ πεινῶντας ἡμᾶς ἐσθίειν ἀναπείθει, γοητεύοντα τὰς ὀρέξεις. μὴ γὰρ οὐκ ἔνεστι καὶ ἐν εὐτελείᾳ σώφρονι πολυειδία ἐδεσμάτων ὑγιεινή; βολβοὶ, ἐλαῖαι, λαχάνων ἔνια, γάλα, τυρὸς, τά τε ὡραῖα ἑψήματά τε παντοδαπὰ, ζωμῶν αὐτά. κἂν ἀποδέῃ κρέως, ἢ ἑφθοῦ, μεταδοτέον. Ἔχετέ τι βρώσιμον ἐνθάδε; εἶπεν ὁ κύριος πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν. οἱ δὲ, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτοῦ εὐτελείας ἀσκεῖν δεδιδαγμένοι, ἐπέδωκαν αὐτῷ ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος· καὶ φαγὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν, εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, φησὶν ὁ Λουκᾶς, ὅσα εἶπεν. πρὸς τούτοις οὐδὲ τὰ γήϊνα τῶν κηρίων ἀμοίρους περιορᾶτέον τοὺς δειπνοῦντας κατὰ λόγον. τῶν γὰρ τοι βρωμάτων διττὴ δειότης τε, οἷς αὐτόθεν χρῆσθαι ὑπάρχει δίχα πυρὸς, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἑτοιμότερα· δεύτερα δὲ, τὰ εὐτελέστερα, ὡς προειρήκαμεν. τῶν δὲ ἀμφὶ τὰς φλεγμαινούσας κυπαζόντων τραπέζας, τῷ σφετέρῳ ἐκθεσμωμένων πάθει, δαίμων καθηγεῖται λιχνότατος· ὃν ἔγωγε οὐκ ἂν αἰσχυνθείην κοιλιοδαίμονα προσειπεῖν, ὃς δαιμόνων κάκιστος, καὶ ἐξώλιστος. τὸν δὲ πλησίον ἐν αὐτῷ ἀτεχνῶς τῷ ἐγγαστριμύθῳ καλοῦμεν. ἄμεινον δὲ πολλῷ, ὦ δαίμονα ἔχειν σύνοικον, εὐδαίμονα γίνεσθαι. εὐδαιμονία δὲ ἐν χρήσει ἀρετῆς ἐξετάζεται. Ματθαῖος μὲν οὖν ὁ ἀπόστολος, σπερμάτων καὶ ἀκροδρύων καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρεῶν, μετελάμβανεν· Ἰωάννης δὲ, ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον. ὡσαύτως ἀπείχετο καὶ Πέτρος· ἀλλ’ ἔπεσεν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ἔκστασις, ὡς ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων γέγραπται· καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον, καὶ τὸ σκεῦος τι παρὸν ἀρχαῖς ἐκδεδεμένον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς·

modum autem non aduenit iustitia per auaritiam & plura habendi cupiditatem, neque temperantia per intemperantiam: ita nec victus Cristiani ratio lautitijs paratur & delitijs. A cibis enim titillantibus & ad venerem incitantibus, procul est mensa veritatis. Etsi enim maxime propter homines omnia facta sunt, non tamen omnibus vti bonum est, sed neque semper: nam tempus, occasio, modus, & respectus rei alicuius, non paruum ei qui instituitur momentum afferunt ad id, quod sibi est vtile. Atque hoc quidem aptum est, & magnam vim habet ad abolendam vitam quæ est ventri dedita, ad quam quidem diuitiæ incitant, non eæ quæ acute vident, sed nimiæ quæ circa gulæ insaniam cæcutiunt copiæ. Nemo autem ad res necessarias pauper est, neque homo vnquam despicitur. Qui enim & pennata & natatilia, & vt semel dicam, à ratione aliena nutrit animantia, vnus est Deus. eis autem nihil deest, etsi nullam de victu curam gerant. Nos autem eis fumo eo præstantiores, quod & Domini: & Deo eo familiariores, quo & temperantiores. [context] For since to be utterly sinless belongs to God, and to the first and uncompounded nature (for simplicity is peaceful, and not subject to dissension), and I venture to say also that it belongs to the Angelic nature too; or at least, I would affirm that nature to be very nearly sinless, because of its nearness to God; but to sin is human and belongs to the Compound on earth (for composition is the beginning of separation); therefore the master did not think it right to leave His creature unaided, or to neglect its danger of separation from Himself; but on the contrary, just as He gave existence to that which did not exist,
so He gave new creation to that which did exist, a diviner creation and a loftier than the first, which is to those who are beginning life a Seal, and to those who are more mature in age both a gift and a restoration of the image which had fallen through sin, that we may not, by becoming worse through despair, and ever being borne downward to that which is more evil, fall altogether from good and from virtue, through despondency; and having fallen into a depth of evil (as it is said) despise Him; but that like those who in the course of a long journey make a brief rest from labour at an inn, we should be enabled to accomplish the rest of the road fresh and full of courage. Such is the grace and power of baptism; not an overwhelming of the world as of old, but a purification of the sins of each individual, and a complete cleansing from all the bruises and stains of sin. VIII. And since we are double-made, I mean of body and soul, and the one part is visible, the other invisible, so the cleansing also is twofold, by water and the spirit; the one received visibly in the body, the other concurring with it invisibly and apart from the body; the one typical, the other real and cleansing the depths.
And this which comes to the aid of our first birth,
[context] makes us new instead of old, and like God instead of what we now are; recasting us without fire, and creating us anew without breaking us up.

->To the Holy.<-

<margin>...so He re-formed those who had been saved. [A] re-forming more divine and higher than the first; which for those who are beginning is a seal, but for those who are more perfect [it is] maturity, and a gift, and a correction of the image that has suffered because of wickedness. [This is] so that we might not become worse through ignorance and, always being carried toward the worse, fall completely away from the good and from virtue through despair; nor, having fallen into the depth of evils, should we grow to despise [goodness]. But as travelers cutting a long road, having rested [from] their labors at an inn, so we may finish the rest of the road young and eager. This is the grace and power of baptism, not having a flood of the world as of old, but the cleansing of the sin of each person and the complete washing away of the obstacles or pollutions that have entered from wickedness. And since we are twofold, I speak of soul and body, and of the visible and the invisible nature, the cleansing is also twofold, I say: by water and by spirit. The one [is] received contemplatively and bodily, the other runs alongside incorporeally and unobservably; the one [is] typical, the other true and cleansing the depths. If [this is] the assistance of the first birth...</margin>

text:
<header>On the Holy [Baptism].</header>

<margin>Common grace instead of the [grace] of withdrawal. If indeed toward [the] purity of baptism, one must consider whether he has a soul [that is] appearing [to be] hindered. The danger [is] to make a covenant, and not [only] to [keep it], but also [to live] in the truth itself. [Of] regeneration, [the] ancient [is] not [what I] seek, but the divine [is] what [I] seek. [It is] with difficulty [that one] comes [to]... [he] cast many [things]... he himself [needs]... [the] leaders... [of] the [first]...</margin>

Thus, He refashioned those who had been saved. A refashioning more divine and higher than the first. To those who are beginning, it is a seal; to those who are more perfect, it is maturity, a gift, and a restoration of the image that suffered because of wickedness. This is so that we do not become worse through ignorance, and by being constantly carried toward what is worse, fall completely away from the good and from virtue through despair. Nor, having fallen into the depth of evils, should we become contemptuous, as it is said. But as travelers cutting through a long road, having rested our labors at an inn, let us thus finish the rest of the road fresh and eager. This is the grace and power of baptism. It does not contain a flood of the world as of old, but a cleansing of the sin of each individual, and a complete washing away of the obstructions or pollutions that have entered from wickedness. Since we are twofold, I mean of soul and body, and of visible and invisible nature, the cleansing is also twofold, I say, through water and spirit. The one is received theoretically and bodily, while the other runs along with it incorporeally and invisibly. The one is typical, while the other is true and cleanses the depths. If the assistance of the first birth happens...

<summary>This passage discusses the theological significance of baptism as a divine refashioning of the human person, serving as both a seal for beginners and a means of restoration for the mature, cleansing the individual of sin through both water and spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Baptism, Grace, Cleansing, Spirit, Water, Regeneration, Sin, Virtue</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] But when He sees a question that calls for reasoning, then He does not deem His questioners unworthy of prudent answers.
The question which you have put seems to me to do honour to chastity, and to demand a kind reply. Chastity, in respect of which I see that the majority of men are ill-disposed, and that their laws are unequal and irregular. For what was the reason why they restrained the woman, but indulged the man, and that a woman who practises evil against her husband's bed is an adulteress, and the penalties of the law for this are very severe; but if the husband commits fornication against his wife, he has no account to give? I do not accept this legislation; I do not approve this custom. They who made the Law were men, and therefore their legislation is hard on women, since they have placed children also under the authority of their fathers, while leaving the weaker sex uncared for. God does not so; but says Honour your father and your mother, which is the first commandment with promise; that it may be well with you; and, He that curses father or mother, let him die the death. Similarly He gave honour to good and punishment to evil. And, The blessing of a father strengthens the houses of children, but the curse of a mother uproots the foundations.
See the equality of the legislation. There is one Maker of man and woman; one debt is owed by children
[context] to both their parents.

of the response; it seems to me that we should look toward what is right in this matter, and honor it with wisdom. And there are responses regarding the love of beauty and with self-control <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note>. Regarding those who see their equals and are not left behind, and that which is of the same nature as himself, struggling equally and suffering the same things. For it is not the case that the middle path is a punishment. That which flows through is spoken as one; and a mind with a lightened spirit of a man is favored. And how could one be loved with passion? On the one hand, I desire the same thing; but on the other hand, they lay waste to it. Being long-suffering and dulling the edge, I do not accept this legislation; I do not accept the making of this covenant. These legislators were but men. From the point of understanding

<column-break/>

the legislation; as many things as give authority to fathers over their female servants. But the weaker part belongs to humanity. As for the things that are not so, why rather do they act for the day? Or how could the present situation be? It is not a matter of scripture, but of violence. And they are reckoned by days. Often indeed it comes to an end; likewise also the good or the half. And that which is not from God; and a blessing toward the root, such as the work is. And the things of the easy path do not take root. You see the laws of this place; how a man is the maker of a woman. Both are practicing; the village is a blame to so many. At the same time, in the same way, a man belongs to a woman in the scriptures, though in time there is lawlessness.

<summary>Gregory of Nazianzus critiques human legislation regarding marriage and gender, arguing that laws often favor men unfairly while ignoring the spiritual equality of both sexes before God.</summary>

of responses: the question which you asked is this. It seems to me that one should honor temperance. And to demand a response that is humane: temperance. Regarding which I see many people poorly disposed, and their law is unequal and uneven. For why on earth did they punish the female, but permit the male? And a woman, having plotted poorly regarding the marriage bed of her husband, commits adultery, and bitter from this are the penalties of the laws. But a man, whoring against his wife, is unaccountable. I do not accept this legislation. I do not praise the custom. Men were the ones who were legislating. Because of this, the legislation is against women.

<column-break/>

Since they have also given children into the authority of their fathers, but they left the weaker one unhealed. But God is not so. Rather, "Honor your father and your mother," which is the first commandment, so that it may go well with you, being set among promises. And he who speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death. Likewise, He honored the good and punished the evil. And the blessing of a father establishes the houses of children, but the curse of a mother uproots foundations. Do you see the equality of the legislation? One creator of man and woman. One dust for both. One image. One law. One death. One resurrection. Likewise, we have been born from man and woman. One debt from children

reference.text:
[context] Secondly, among those who admit that there is an art of divination through birds, it is not agreed as to why the divination takes that form ; for some say that it is from demons or gods of divination that the animals receive their impulses,
the birds to different flights and cries, the other animals to such and such movements ; while others hold that the souls of these animals are more
divine than others, and are adapted to the purpose ; which is most improbable.
If Celsus wished to prove by the foregoing that the irrational creatures have a Divine nature and are wiser than man, he ought to have fully shown that there is such an art as divination ; then, he should have more clearly shown how it can be defended ; then have given clear grounds for rejecting the arguments of those who would do away with such arts ; and, lastly, should have decisively upset the arguments of those who say that it is from demons or gods the animals derive their divination impulses. Then would be the time for dealing with the question, whether the soul of irrational creatures is more Divine than that of men. If he had thus shown a philosophic spirit in treating such important matters, we would have withstood his plausible assertions to the best of our power ; we would have upset his statement that the irrational creatures are wiser than men, and we would have proved how false it is that they have more sacred conceptions of God
[context] than we have, and that they hold certain sacred assemblies.

text:
<header>PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.</header>

<column-break/>
...into different flights and different cries, and for the rest, into these or those movements. Others say their souls are more divine and better suited for this, which is most implausible. Celsus therefore, wishing to prove from the proposed subjects that irrational animals are more divine and wiser than humans, should have established through many arguments that such divination exists. After this, he should have more effectively and demonstrably rejected the arguments of those who abolish such divinations. He should also have demonstrably refuted the arguments of those who say that these movements in animals are caused by gods or demons for the purpose of divination. Finally, he should have established that the soul of irrational animals is more divine than the human soul. For in this way, we have stood against the persuasive arguments of one who acts as a philosopher on such matters, as far as we were able. We refute the claim that irrational animals are wiser than humans, and we demonstrate as false the claim that they possess thoughts regarding the divine...

<column-break/>
...into different flights and different cries, and for the rest into these or those movements: others [claim] their souls are more divine and more suited to divination, which is least of all credible. It was necessary, therefore, for Celsus, who wanted to show from the proposed matters that brute animals are more divine and wiser than humans, to show and prove through many [arguments] that such divination exists. Then, afterward, to reject more strongly and with demonstration the statements of those who remove such prophecies, and to pull down with firm arguments the discourses of those who said that such movements for the purpose of divination are excited in animals by gods or demons; then, finally, to prove that the soul of the brutes is more divine than the human. Thus, indeed, against his disputation—he who plays the philosopher in such matters—we have set ourselves up as far as we were able. We overturn that [claim] that brutes are wiser than humans; [and] that other [claim], that they have thoughts about God, [we refute].

<summary>This page contains a portion of Origen's critique of Celsus regarding the alleged wisdom and divinity of animals, specifically challenging the idea that animal behavior serves as a valid source of divine divination.</summary>
<keywords>Celsus, Origen, divination, irrational animals, soul, theology, philosophy</keywords>

reasons.j1: [served] renders both the Greek and the Latin column completely; the list of what Celsus 'ought' to have done (ἐχρῆν ... κατασκευάσαι ... ἀποδοκιμάσαι ... ἀνατρέψαι) is intact; only the closing 'ἂν ... ἐνέστημεν' is turned from a hypothetical into a statement of fact in the Greek half, and '[we refute]' supplies the verb that stands on the next page (mendacij conuicimus).
reasons.j2: Both columns rendered in full and accurately up to the last sentence; there the Greek 'ἂν ... ἐνέστημεν' is an unreal condition (reference: 'we would have withstood'), which [served] turns into fact, following the Latin column's indicative 'instituimus ... subvertimus'; '[we refute]' is supplied from the next page's 'conuicimus'.

served.note: Clear argumentative prose, though the page is rendered twice (Greek and Latin columns) which a lay reader may find repetitive; key terms steady (irrational animals, divination, demons); ambiguity n/a; brackets and ellipses mark supplements and page edges.

into various flights and various cries, and for the rest into such and such movements. Others say that their souls are more divine and naturally suited for this purpose, which is highly improbable. It was necessary, therefore, for Celsus, wishing by these arguments to show that irrational animals are more divine and wiser than men, to establish through more extensive proofs that they possess this kind of divination. After this, he should have more effectively and demonstratively rejected the arguments of those who do away with such forms of prophecy. He ought to have overturned with proof the words of those who say that these movements are produced in animals by gods or demons for the sake of foretelling the future. Finally, he should have established that the soul of irrational animals is more divine than the human soul. For if he had presented his case with such plausibility, we would have opposed him to the best of our ability, as one who maintains a philosophical habit regarding such great matters. We would have overturned the claim that irrational creatures are wiser than men, and exposed as false the idea that they even possess sacred conceptions of the divine

<column-break/>

into various flights and various cries, and for the rest into these or those movements. Others say that their souls are more divine and more fit for divination, which is not at all credible. It was necessary, therefore, for Celsus, who wished to show from the matters proposed that irrational animals are more divine and wiser than men, to demonstrate and prove with more evidence this kind of divination. Then, afterwards, he should have more strongly and with demonstration disapproved of the sayings of those who take away such prophecies, and with firm arguments torn down the speeches of those who said that such movements for divining are excited in animals by gods or demons. Then, finally, he should have proved that the soul of brutes is more divine than the human soul. For thus, against the disputation of one who acts the philosopher in such matters, we would have proceeded as far as we were able. We would have subverted that claim that brutes are wiser than men, and also that they have thoughts concerning God

reference.text:
[context] It is only to one who can turn to either side that a law is given —
one who is at liberty to do battle with the adverse power. No law is laid down for a nature that is under necessity. The sun, the heaven and the earth, call for no legislation ; such creatures are of a nature governed by necessity, and for this reason they are not liable to reward or punishment. Reward and glory are prepared for him who turns to the good ; hell and punishment are prepared for this convertible nature, capable of fleeing from the evil and throwing its weight upon the right-hand side, the side of good. If you say that he is not of an alterable nature, you make the good man undeserving of praise. For one who is good and kind by nature does not deserve praise for it, though he may be very desirable. What is not good by choice is not praiseworthy, however desirable it may be. Praise is only deserved by one who by his personal resolution with effort and struggle makes the good his own through free-will and choice.
As if when
[context] the Persians have a camp on one side and the Romans a camp on the other, two winged youths of equal powers should come forth from them and engage in a struggle, so the opposing force and the mind are in equipoise.

For to a bound nature, law is not given; for neither the sun, nor the heaven and the earth are placed under law, because they are creatures of a bound nature; whence they are not subject to either honor or punishment. For honor and glory are prepared for that which is turned to the good. But again, hell and punishment are prepared for this changeable nature, which is able to avoid evil and to incline to the good and to the right side. See, you say he is of a bound nature; therefore, you do not make the good man worthy of praise. For he who is virtuous and good by nature is not worthy of praise, even if he is desirable. For that which is not good by choice is not praiseworthy, even if it is desirable. For that person is worthy of praise who, by his own diligence, not without struggle and wrestling, has embraced the good by the free authority of his choice.

authority to wage war against the contrary power. For law is not imposed upon a bound nature; for neither the sun, nor the heaven or the earth are held by law; because they are creatures of a bound nature; whence they are subject neither to reward nor to punishment. For honor and glory are prepared for that which can be turned toward the good; on the contrary, however, hell and punishment are prepared for the same changeable nature which, indeed, is able to avoid evil and to incline to the good and right side. ἐξουσίαν ποιῆσαι πόλεμον πρὸς τὴν ἐναντίαν δύναμιν· δετῇ γὰρ φύσει νόμος οὐ κεῖται· οὔτε γὰρ ὁ ἥλιος, οὔτε ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ νενομοθέτηται· ἐπειδὴ τὰ κτίσματα δετῆς εἰσι φύσεως· ὅθεν οὔτε τιμῇ, οὔτε κολάσει ὑπόκεινται· ἡ γὰρ τιμὴ καὶ ἡ δόξα ἡτοίμασται τῷ τρεπτομένῳ εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν· πάλιν δὲ ἡ γέεννα καὶ ἡ κόλασις ταύτῃ τῇ τρεπτῇ φύσει ἡτοίμασται, τῇ δυναμένῃ ἀποφυγεῖν τὸ κακὸν, καὶ ῥέψαι εἰς τὸ ἀγαθὸν, καὶ δεξιὸν μέρος. ἰδὲ λέγεις αὐτὸν δετῆς φύσεως· λοιπὸν, τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνθρωπον οὐ ποιεῖς ἄξιον ἐπαίνου· ὁ γὰρ ἀπὸ φύσεως χρηστὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς, οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπαίνου ἄξιος, εἰ καὶ ἐπιθυμητός ἐστιν· οὐ γὰρ ἐπαινετὸν, εἰ καὶ ἐπιθυμητὸν, τὸ μὴ προαιρετικὸν ἀγαθόν· ἐκεῖνος γάρ ἐστιν ἐπαίνου ἄξιος, ὁ ἰδίᾳ σπουδῇ μὴ ἀγῶνος καὶ πάλης ἐπανελόμενος τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτεξουσίῳ προαιρέσεως·

§. XXII. Ὥσπερ ὅταν ᾖ

<column-break/>

[context] But he had particularly cultivated logic, and was profoundly skilled in the interpretation of the holy Scriptures;
insomuch that the heretic Eunomius often shrank from the acumen which his reasoning displayed. As regards his diet he was not simple; for although he practised the strictest moderation, yet his table was always sumptuously furnished. He was also accustomed to indulge himself by wearing white garments, and bathing twice a day in the public baths. And when some one asked him 'why he, a bishop, bathed himself twice a day?' he replied, 'Because it is inconvenient to bathe thrice.' Going one day from courtesy to visit the bishop Arsacius, he was asked by one of the friends of that bishop, 'why he wore a garment so unsuitable for a bishop? And where it was written that an ecclesiastic should be clothed in white?' 'Do you tell me first,' said he, 'where it is written that a bishop should wear black?' When he that made the inquiry knew not what to reply to this counter-question: 'You cannot show,' rejoined Sisinnius, 'that a priest should be clothed in black. But Solomon is my authority, whose exhortation is, Let your garments be white.
And our Saviour in the Gospels appears clothed in white raiment: moreover he showed Moses and Elias to the apostles, clad in white garments.' His prompt reply to these and other questions called forth the admiration of those present. Again when Leontius bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, who had taken away a church from the Novatians, was on a visit to Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him, and begged him to restore the church. But he received him rudely, saying, 'You Novatians ought not to have churches; for you take away repentance, and shut out Divine mercy.' As Leontius gave utterance to these and many other such revilings against the Novatians, Sisinnius replied: 'No one repents more heartily than I do.' And when Leontius asked him 'Why do you repent?' 'That I came to see you,' said he. On one occasion John the bishop having a contest with him, said, 'The city cannot have two bishops.' 'Nor has it,' said Sisinnius. John being irritated at this response, said, 'You see you pretend that you alone are the bishop.' 'I do not say that,' rejoined Sisinnius; 'but that I am not bishop in your estimation only, who am such to others.' John being still more chafed at this reply, said, 'I will stop your preaching; for you are a heretic.' To which Sisinnius good-humoredly replied, 'I will give you a reward, if you will relieve me from so arduous a duty.' John being softened a little by this answer, said, 'I will not make you cease to preach, if you find speaking so troublesome.' So facetious was Sisinnius, and so ready at repartee: but it would be tedious to dwell further on his witticisms. Wherefore by means of a few specimens we have illustrated what sort of a person he was, deeming these as sufficient. I will merely add that he was celebrated for erudition, and on account of it all the bishops who succeeded him loved and honored him; and not only they but all the leading members of the senate also esteemed and admired him. He is the author of many works: but they are characterized by too great an affectation of elegance of diction, and a lavish intermingling of poetic expressions. On which account he was more admired as a speaker than as a writer; for there was dignity in his countenance and voice, as well as in his form and aspect, and every movement of his person was graceful. On account of these features he was loved by all the sects, and he was in special favor with Atticus the bishop. But I must conclude this brief notice of Sisinnius.
Not long after the death of John, the Emperor Arcadius died also.
[context] This prince was of a mild and gentle disposition, and toward the close of his life was esteemed to be greatly beloved of God, from the following circumstance.

text:
<meta>This page continues the biography of Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop of Constantinople, known for his wit and urbanity. It follows the discussion of the omens and political shifts following the exile of John Chrysostom.</meta>

### SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS, BOOK VI

...it frequently happened that he avoided the [trap of] cleverness in debate. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple <note>original: "λιτός" — referring to an ascetic or plain way of living</note>, but he practiced luxury with extreme self-control. He delighted in wearing **white clothing**, and he continued the habit of bathing twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, as a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time for a third."

On another occasion, while seeing **Sergius** the bishop <note>likely the Novatian bishop of another see</note>, he was asked by one of those in the circle of **Arsacius** <note>The bishop who replaced John Chrysostom</note> why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss for an answer, **Sisinnius** followed up his counter-question: "You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But **Solomon** advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed **Moses** and **Elijah** to the Apostles wearing white." Having said these things and many others quite readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When **Leontius**, the bishop of **Ancyra** in **Galatia**, was seizing a church from the **Novatians** <note>The Novatians were a rigorist Christian sect who believed those who fell into serious sin after baptism could not be readmitted to communion</note> and happened to be visiting **Constantinople**, **Sisinnius** went to him and urged him to return the church. **Leontius** answered him warmly <note>meaning with heat or anger</note> and said to him, "You **Novatians** ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the mercy of God." As **Leontius** said these things and more against the **Novatians**, **Sisinnius** replied, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When **Leontius** asked him again, "How have you repented?" **Sisinnius** replied, "That I ever came to see you!"

On another occasion, when **John** <note>John Chrysostom</note> the bishop was accusing him of something and saying that a city could not have two bishops, **Sisinnius** said, "It does not." When **John** grew angry and said, "Do you see that you admit I am the only bishop in your opinion?" **Sisinnius** replied, "I do not say that; rather, I mean that I am not a bishop to you alone, though I am a bishop to the ears [of my own people]." **John**, becoming indignant at this remark, said, "I will stop you from speaking, for you are a heretic." To this, **Sisinnius** wittily replied, "I would even pay you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor!" **John**, softened by this response, said, "I will not stop you from your freedom of speech if speaking is so painful to you." 

Such was the readiness and wit of **Sisinnius** in his replies. To write down and record all the things he said would be a long task. Therefore, through these few examples, I have shown what kind of man he was when he took up leadership. I say this: everyone knows him for his education, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Not only that, but all the distinguished members of the Senate loved and admired him. Many books have been written by him, but he uses a specific style in them, mixing in poetic vocabulary. He was admired more when speaking than when being read, for there was such grace in him—in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all religions, and especially by Bishop **Atticus**. These are the matters concerning **Sisinnius**.

Not long after the death of **John**, the Emperor **Arcadius** died, a man of...

text:
SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS BOOK 6

He often avoided the cleverness required for debate, yet his lifestyle was not simple. Rather, he used luxury with great temperance. He delighted in white clothing and bathed in public baths twice a day. When someone once asked him why, as a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time for a third." Once, when he saw Sergius the bishop at that time, he was asked by one of those around Arsatius why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a clergyman should dress in white. He replied, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop should wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question by saying, "You would not be able to show that a clergyman must wear black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having readily said these things and many others, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of the Novatians in Galatia Minor, was in Constantinople and was taking away a church, Sisinnius came to him and urged him to return the church. Leontius responded heatedly and said to him, "You Novatians do not deserve to have churches, you who abolish repentance and shut out the philanthropy of God." As Leontius said these and many other such things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one has repented as much as I have." When Leontius asked again, "How have you repented?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

When John <note>John Chrysostom</note> once complained to the bishop and said that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "It does not have two." When John became angry and said, "You see that you are the only one who thinks you are a bishop," Sisinnius replied, "I do not say that, but rather that I am not a bishop to you alone, as I am to those who hear me." John, indignant at what was said, replied, "But I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic." To this, Sisinnius replied wittily, "But I will even pay you a reward if you relieve me of such great labor." Softened by this reply, John said, "But I will not stop you from speaking freely, if speaking causes you such grief."

Thus, Sisinnius was ready with his replies and witty. It would be a long task to write down and record everything he said. Therefore, I have shown in a few words what he was like, having decided to do so. I will say this: everyone knew him for his learning, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate loved and admired him. He wrote many books, using a refined style and mixing in poetic expressions. He was admired more when speaking than when being read. For he possessed such grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his gaze, and the entire movement of his body. He was therefore loved for these reasons by all religious groups, and especially by Bishop Atticus. These are the things concerning Sisinnius.

ἐσθῆτι λευκῇ, καὶ δὶς τῆς ἡμέρας ἐν λουτροῖς δημοσίοις λουόμενος διετέλει. καὶ πο-
τέ ἐρομένου αὐτόν τινὸς, τίνος χάριν ἐπίσκοπος ὢν, δὶς λούοιτο τῆς ἡμέρας, ὅτι τὸ τρί-
τον οὐ φθάνω, ἀπεκρίνατο. δήποτε δὲ Σεργίον τὸν ἐπίσκοπον κατ' ἐκεῖνο ὁρῶν, ἠρω-
τήθη ὑπό τινος τῶν περὶ Ἀρσάκιον, διὰ τί ἀνοίκειον ἐπισκόπῳ ἐσθῆτα φορείη,
καὶ ποῦ γέγραπται λευκὰ τὸν ἱερωμένον ἀμφιέννυσθαι. ὁ δὲ, σὺ πρότερον, ἔφη,
εἰπὲ, ποῦ γέγραπται μέλαιναν ἐσθῆτα φορεῖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον. τοῦ δὲ ἐρωτήσαντος ἐν
ἀπορίᾳ γενομένου, πρὸς τὴν ἀντερώτησιν ἐπήγαγεν ὁ Σισίνιος. ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν οὐκ
ἂν, ἔφη, δεῖξαι δυνηθείης, ὡς δεῖ τὸν ἱερωμένον μέλανα ἀμφιέννυσθαι. ἐμοὶ δὲ καὶ Σο-
λομῶν παρήνεσε λέγων, ἔστωσάν σου ἱμάτια λευκά. καὶ ὁ Σωτὴρ ἐν ταῖς εὐαγγε-
λίοις, λευκῇ φαίνεται ἐσθῆτι χρησάμενος. οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ Μωσῆν καὶ Ἡλίαν, λευ-
κοφοροῦντας τοῖς ἀποστόλοις ἔδειξεν. ταῦτα δὴ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ ἑτοίμως εἰπὼν, τὰ μέ-
γιστα ὑπὸ τῶν παρόντων ἐθαυμάσθη. Λεοντίου δὲ τοῦ Ἀγκύρας ἐν τῇ μικρᾷ Γα-
λατίᾳ ἐπισκόπου Ναυατιανῶν ἐκκλησίαν ἀφαιρουμένου, ἐν τῇ Κωνσταντίνου πό-
λει ἐπιδημοῦντος, ὁ Σισίνιος ἥξων παρ' αὐτὸν, παρεκάλει ἀποδοῦναι τὴν ἐκκλη-
σίαν. ὁ δὲ θερμῶς ἀπήντησε, καὶ φησὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν, ὑμεῖς, φησὶν, οἱ Ναυατιανοὶ, οὐκ
ὀφείλετε ἐκκλησίας ἔχειν, οἳ τὴν μετάνοιαν ἀναιρεῖτε, καὶ τὴν φιλανθρωπίαν
τοῦ θεοῦ ἀποκλείοντες. ταῦτα καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα πλείονα τοῦ Λεοντίου κακῶς τοῖς Ναυα-
τιανοῖς λέγοντος, ἔφη ὁ Σισίνιος, καὶ μὲν οὐδεὶς οὕτω μετανόησεν ὡς ἐγώ. τοῦ δὲ πά-
λιν ἐπάγοντος, πῶς μετανόης, ἔφη ὁ Σισίνιος, ὅτι σε εἶδον, ἀπεκρίνατο. Ἰωάννου δὲ
ποτὲ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ἐγκαλοῦντός τι, καὶ λέγοντος ὅτι οὐ δύναται ἡ πόλις δύο ἐ-
πισκόπους ἔχειν, ὁ Σισίνιος ἔφη, οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχει. τοῦ δὲ Ἰωάννου χαλεπήναντος, καὶ φή-
σαντος, ὁρᾷς ὅτι μόνος εἶ βουλῇ ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ Σισίνιος οὐ τοῦτο, ἔφη, λέγω, ἀλλ' ὅτι
ἐγὼ παρά σοι μόνῳ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐπίσκοπος, ὡς ταῖς ἀκοαῖς εἰμί. ὁ δὲ Ἰωάννης πρὸς τὸ
λεχθὲν ἀγανακτήσας, ἀλλ' ἐγώ, ἔφη, παύσω σε τῆς ὁμιλίας· αἱρετικὸς γὰρ ὑπάρχεις.
πρὸς δὴ τοῦτο χαριέντως ὁ Σισίνιος ὑπήντησεν. ἀλλ' ἐγώ, ἔφη, καὶ μισθὸν παρέξω,
εἴ με τηλικούτου καμάτου ἀπαλλάξας. ἅμα μαλαχθεὶς δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἀποκρίσεως ὁ
Ἰωάννης, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄν σε, ἔφη, παύσω τῆς παρρησίας ἐγὼ, εἴ σε ὅλως τὸ λέγειν λυ-
πεῖ. οὕτω μὲν οὖν ἕτοιμος πρὸς τὰς ἀποκρίσεις καὶ χαρίεις ἦν ὁ Σισίνιος. γράφειν
δὲ ταῦτα καὶ ἀπομνημονεύειν τὰ εἰρημένα αὐτῷ, μακρὸν ἂν εἴη. διὸ δὲ δι' ὀλίγων
ἀπέδειξα οἷος ἦν ἄρχειν ἡγησάμενος. ἐκεῖνο δὲ φημι, ὅτι διὰ παιδείαν πάν-
τες ἴσασι· καὶ διὰ ταύτην, πάντες ἐφεξῆς οἱ ἐπίσκοποι ἠγάπων τε καὶ ἐτίμων
αὐτόν. οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντες οἱ τῆς συγκλήτου περιφανεῖς ἔστεργον αὐτὸν καὶ ἐ-
θαύμαζον. καὶ πολλὰ μὲν αὐτῷ βιβλία συνγέγραπται· λέξει χρησάμενος αὐτοῖς, καὶ ποιη-
τικὰς παραμίγνυσι λέξεις. λέγων δὲ μᾶλλον, ἢ ἀναγινωσκόμενος ἐθαυμάζετο. τοσαύ-
τη γὰρ αὐτῷ χάρις, τῷ τε προσώπῳ καὶ τῇ φωνῇ, καὶ τῷ σχήματι, καὶ τῷ βλέμμα-
τι, καὶ τῇ ὅλῃ κινήσει τοῦ σώματος. ἠγαπᾶτο οὖν καὶ διὰ ταῦτα παρὰ πασῶν τε
τῶν θρησκειῶν, καὶ μάλιστα παρὰ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου Ἀττικοῦ. καὶ τὰ μὲν περὶ Σισι-
νίου, ταῦτα.

Τελευτᾷ δὲ οὐ πολὺ μετὰ τὴν Ἰωάννου τελευτὴν, ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἀρκάδιος, ἀνὴρ κρᾶ-

# SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS BOOK 6

<meta>continues from previous page: describing the character and wit of Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop</meta>

It often happened that his skill in debate escaped him <note>meaning his wit was so natural it seemed effortless</note>. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple, yet he practiced great moderation within a luxurious manner of living. He delighted in wearing white clothing and continued to bathe in the public baths twice a day. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I cannot manage a third time." On another occasion, while visiting the bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of the associates of Arsacius why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said, "You first tell me where it is written that a bishop should wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question by saying, "You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>modern-day Ankara, Turkey</note>, took away a church from the <term>Novatians</term> <gloss>a rigorist Christian sect</gloss> while he was visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and urged him to restore the church. Leontius answered warmly <note>here meaning with heat or anger</note> and said to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, you who do away with repentance and shut out the loving-kindness of God." When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When the other asked again, "How have you repented?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom</note> was accusing the bishop of something and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "Indeed it does not." When John became angry and said, "You see that you alone are a bishop by your own will," Sisinnius said, "I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, though I am one to the ears of others." John, being provoked by what was said, cried, "I will stop you from speaking, for you are a heretic!" To this Sisinnius wittily replied, "I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor." John, softened by the response, said, "I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking is truly a burden to you."

Such was the readiness and grace of Sisinnius in his replies. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown through a few examples what kind of man he was, having been considered worthy to lead. I say this: everyone knew him for his learning, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. He composed many books, using a refined style in them, and he mixed in poetic expressions. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For there was such grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all the religious sects, and especially by the bishop Atticus. And such are the matters concerning Sisinnius.

Not long after the death of John, the Emperor Arcadius died, a man of <unclear>gentle</unclear>...

SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS BOOK VI

He often avoided the sharpness of his opponents in debate. His lifestyle was not austere, but he lived in great moderation and luxury. He delighted in white clothing and bathed twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why, as a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time to bathe a third time." On another occasion, seeing Arsacius the bishop being honored, he was asked by one of Arsacius's associates why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a clergyman should dress in white. He replied, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop should wear black clothing." When the questioner was left at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question by saying, "You will not be able to show that a clergyman must wear black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having readily said these things and many others, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was taking away a church from the Novatians <note>a Christian sect considered heretical by the state church</note> while visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius came to him and urged him to return the church. Leontius responded heatedly, saying to him, "You Novatians ought not to have churches, since you reject repentance and exclude the philanthropy of God." When Leontius said these and many other such things, speaking ill of the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, no one repents as much as I do." When Leontius asked again, "How do you repent?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

When John <note>John Chrysostom</note> the bishop once reproached him, saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "It does not have two." When John became angry and said, "You see that you wish to be the only bishop," Sisinnius replied, "I do not say that, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, though I am to others." John, indignant at what was said, replied, "I will stop speaking with you, for you are a heretic." To this, Sisinnius wittily replied, "And I will even pay you, if you would relieve me of such great labor." Softened by this reply, John said, "I will not stop speaking with you, if the mere act of speaking causes you such pain."

Thus, Sisinnius was ready with his replies and witty. It would be a long task to write down and record everything he said. Therefore, I have shown in a few words what he was like, considering it sufficient. I will say this, however: he was famous for his learning. Because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate loved and admired him. He wrote many books, in which he hunted for rare words and mixed in poetic expressions. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For he possessed grace in his face, his voice, his manner, his gaze, and the entire movement of his body. He was therefore loved for these reasons by all religious groups, and especially by the bishop Atticus. These are the things concerning Sisinnius.
