6. And it shall be that the child who is born shall be established by the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be blotted out from Israel.
7. But if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, the woman shall go up to the gate to the elders and say: My husband's brother refuses to raise up the name of his brother in Israel; my husband's brother has refused.
8. And the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and he shall stand and say: I do not wish to take her.
9. And the wife of his brother shall approach before the elders, and she shall loosen his one sandal from his foot, and she shall spit in his face, and answering she shall say: Thus shall they do to the man who will not build the house of his brother in Israel,
10. and his name shall be called in Israel, the house of him whose sandal was loosened.
11. If men fight together, a man with his brother, and the wife of one of them approaches to rescue her husband from the hand of the one striking him, and she stretches out her hand and seizes his private parts,
12. you shall cut off her hand; your eye shall not spare her.
13. There shall not be in your pouch a weight and a weight, large or small.
14. There shall not be in your house a measure and a measure, large or small.
15. A true and just weight shall be yours, and a true and just measure shall be yours, so that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance.
16. For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination to the Lord your God.
17. Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you were coming out of the land of Egypt,
18. how he stood against you on the way and struck your rear guard, those who were weary behind you, while you were hungry and exhausted, and he did not fear God.
19. And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest from all your enemies around you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven, and you shall not forget.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

1. And it shall be, when you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, and you possess it and dwell in it,
2. that you shall take from the first fruits of the produce of your land which the Lord your God gives you, and you shall put them into a basket, and you shall go to the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called there.
3. And you shall come to the priest who is in those days, and you shall say to him: I declare today to the Lord my God that I have entered into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give to us.

<column-break/>

6. And the child who is born shall be established by the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be blotted out from Israel.
7. But if a man does not wish to take his brother's wife, the woman shall go up to the gate to the senate <note>original: "senatum"</note>, and shall say: My husband's brother does not wish to raise up the name of his brother in Israel; my husband's brother has refused.
8. And the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and he shall stand and say: I do not wish to take her.
9. And the brother's wife shall approach before the elders, and she shall loosen his one sandal from his foot, and she shall spit in his face, and answering she shall say: Thus shall they do to the man who will not build the house of his brother in Israel,
10. and his name shall be called in Israel, the house of the discalced <note>original: "discalceati"</note> (the one whose sandal was loosened).
11. But if men have fought together, a man with his brother, and the wife of one of them has approached to rescue her husband from the hand of the one striking him, and stretching out her hand she has seized his testicles,
12. you shall cut off her hand; your eye shall not spare her.
13. There shall not be in your purse a weight and a weight, large or small.
14. There shall not be in your house a measure and a measure, large or small.
15. A true and just weight shall be yours, and a true and just measure shall be yours, that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you as a portion.
16. For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination to the Lord your God.
17. Remember whatever Amalek did to you on the way, when you were coming out of the land of Egypt,
18. how he stood against you on the way, and struck the tail of your column, the weary ones behind you, while you were hungry and laboring, and he did not fear God.
19. And it shall be, after the Lord your God has made you rest from all your enemies who are around you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven, and you shall not forget.

1. And it shall be, if you have entered into the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, and you have inherited it, and have dwelt in it,
2. and you shall take from the first fruits of the produce of your land which the Lord your God gives you, and you shall put them into a basket, and you shall go to the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be invoked there.
3. And you shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and you shall say to him: I announce today to the Lord my God that I have entered into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give to us.

13. Οὐκ ἔσται ἐν τῷ μαρσίππῳ σου στάθμιον καὶ στάθμιον, μέγα ἢ μικρόν.

6. And it shall be that the firstborn child she bears shall be established in the name of the deceased, so that his name shall not be blotted out from Israel.
7. But if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, the woman shall go up to the gate to the elders <note>original Greek: "gerousian", Latin: "senatum"</note> and say: My husband's brother refuses to raise up a name for his brother in Israel; my husband's brother was not willing.
8. Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he stands and says: I do not wish to take her;
9. then his brother's wife shall come before the elders and loosen one of his sandals from his foot, and spit in his face, and answering she shall say: So shall they do to the man who will not build up his brother's house in Israel.
10. And his name shall be called in Israel: The house of him whose sandal was loosened.
11. If men fight together, a man with his brother, and the wife of one of them approaches to rescue her husband from the hand of the one striking him, and reaching out her hand she seizes his private parts <note>original Greek: "didymon", Latin: "testes"</note>,
12. you shall cut off her hand; your eye shall not pity her.
13. You shall not have in your bag diverse weights <note>literally: "a weight and a weight"</note>, a large and a small.
14. You shall not have in your house diverse measures, a large and a small.
15. You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, so that you may live many days upon the land which the Lord your God gives to you as an inheritance.
16. For everyone who does these things, everyone who acts unjustly, is an abomination to the Lord your God.
17. Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, as you were coming out of the land of Egypt,
18. how he resisted you on the way and cut off your rear guard, those who were weary behind you, while you were hungry and tired; and he did not fear God.
19. And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest from all your enemies around you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

### CAPUT XXVI.

2. et sumes de primitiis fructuum terræ tuæ quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, et mittes in cartallum , et ibis in locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus ut invocetur nomen suum ibi.

text:
<meta>This page continues the sixteenth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew. The previous page ended with Jesus rebuking the religious leaders for being able to predict the weather but failing to interpret the "signs of the times." This page records his refusal to give a sign other than that of Jonah and his warning to the disciples regarding the teachings of the Pharisees and Sadducees.</meta>

<page-num>93</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 16, 9. 93</header>

<margin>12, 39</margin>
4 <sup>163. 6</sup> An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of Jonah. And leaving them, he departed.

<margin>5—12 Mark 8, 14—21</margin>
5 And when the disciples came to the other side, they forgot to take bread. 6 <sup>164. 2</sup> But Jesus said to them: “See and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” 7 <sup>165. 6</sup> And they were reasoning among themselves, saying: “It is because we took no bread.” 8 But knowing this, Jesus said: “Why are you reasoning among yourselves, <term>you of little faith</term> <note>original: "oligopistoi"; a term Jesus often uses for his disciples when they lack spiritual perception</note>, because you took no bread? 9 Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five...”

<margin>Luke 12, 1</margin>

---

<note>The following notes are the critical apparatus, documenting variations in ancient manuscripts. Abbreviations like "al" mean "others," "pler" means "most manuscripts," and letters like א, B, and D refer to specific famous codices (ancient books).</note>

**3.** **The sky is red:** <note>original: "pyrrazel"</note> Supported by most manuscripts, including the Old Latin **b, e, f, g1, ff1**, the Syriac, and Coptic versions. | **Can you not:** <note>original: "dynasthe"</note> Found in **Codices C, D, E, F, H, K, M, Π** and many others. Some manuscripts read "cannot *judge*" <note>original: "dokimazein"</note> (as in Luke), while others (the Vulgate and some Old Latin) read "cannot *know*" <note>original: "scire" or "cognoscere"</note>. A few manuscripts read "you do not understand" <note>original: "syniete"</note> or "you do not know."

**4.** **And adulterous:** <note>original: "kai moichalis"</note> Supported by the Vulgate, but omitted by **Codex Bezae (D)** and some Old Latin versions. | **Seeks a sign:** <note>original: "sēmeion epizētei"</note> **Codex Vaticanus (B)** uses a different verb for "asks" <note>original: "aitēei"</note>, while **Codex Bezae (D)** simply uses "seeks" <note>original: "zētei"</note>. | **Jonah:** The majority of later manuscripts add **"the prophet"** <note>original: "tou prophētou"</note> to harmonize with Matthew 12:39, but the earliest witnesses (**א, B, D, L**) omit it.

**5.** **When they came:** The Old Latin and Hilary translate this as "when he had come." | **The disciples:** Most manuscripts (**א, B, C, D**) say "the disciples," while others add "**his** disciples." | **Take bread:** <note>original: "artous labein"</note> The order of words varies; some Latin manuscripts suggest "to buy" <note>original: "emere"</note> or "to put in" <note>original: "inponere"</note> bread.

**6.** **Jesus:** Omitted in some Latin and Syriac versions. | **See and:** Omitted in some Old Latin versions. | **And Sadducees:** Omitted by some manuscripts and early church fathers. <note>Manuscript "k" (Codex Bobiensis) is damaged here, but its surviving text reads: "and they forgot to put in loaves and when they had only one loaf in the ship he broke [it] for them saying beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the leaven of the Herodians."</note>

**7.** **And they:** Some versions read "Then they." | **Saying:** Omitted in the Old Latin "k" and some Syriac versions. | **We took:** Some Syriac versions read "they took."

**8.** **Said:** Most manuscripts include "to them," though early ones (**א, B, D, K**) omit it. | **You took:** <note>original: "elabete"</note> The earliest manuscripts (**א, B, D**) read "**you have**" <note>original: "echete"</note> instead of "you took," likely to match the wording in the Gospel of Mark.

**9.** **Do you not:** A few manuscripts omit "nor remember." | **The five thousand:** Some manuscripts (like **D**) add "who were among" or "those five thousand."

<summary>Jesus refuses to provide a miraculous sign to the Pharisees and Sadducees, pointing instead to the "sign of Jonah," and later warns his disciples to beware of the corrupting influence ("leaven") of these leaders.</summary>
<keywords>Sign of Jonah, Pharisees, Sadducees, Leaven, little faith, bread, manuscript variants, Codex Bobiensis, Herodians</keywords>

ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 16, 9. 93

<margin>12, 39</margin>
4 An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of Jonah. And leaving them, he departed.

<margin>5—12 Mark 8, 14—21</margin>
5 And when the disciples reached the other side, they forgot to take bread. 6 Jesus said to them: "Watch out and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." 7 They began to discuss among themselves, saying, "It is because we took no bread." 8 But Jesus, knowing this, said: "Why are you discussing among yourselves, you of little faith, that you have no bread? 9 Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five <note>The sentence continues on the next page, referring to the five loaves of the five thousand.</note>

<margin>Luke 12, 1</margin>

***

<note>The following section is the critical apparatus, a scholarly record of variations found in different ancient manuscripts of the New Testament.</note>

<note>Notes on verse 3</note> ... <term>sun</term> <gloss>the sun</gloss> in most manuscripts including b, e, f, g1, ff1, the Syriac Peshitta, Coptic, and others; compare Luke | <term>dunasthe</term> <gloss>you are able</gloss> in manuscripts C, D, E, F, H, K, M, Pi, and many others; manuscripts G, M, U read "you are able to discern"; others read "you are able to know" (manuscripts c, e, ff1, and the Vulgate use the Latin *scire* or *nosse*; b and ff2 use *cognoscere*); manuscript L reads "you discern" (as in Luke); others read "you understand" or "you know."

4. **and adulterous** (also in b, c, f, q, and the Vulgate; Origen): omitted in D, a, e, ff1, ff2, and Prosper | **seeks a sign** (Manuscript B reads "asks for") ... Manuscript D reads "seeks a sign"; manuscripts b, c, e read "seeks a sign" (as in Mark) | **Jonah**: found in manuscripts Sinaiticus, B, D, L, and others; the received text adds "the prophet" following manuscripts C, E, F, G, H, K, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Delta, Pi, most Latin versions, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Origen; compare Matthew 12, 39. | Manuscripts E, F, H, X, Gamma, Delta read "leaving" with a slight spelling variation.

5. **when they reached**: manuscripts a, b, c, ff2, g1, and Hilary read "when he had come" | **the disciples**: found in Sinaiticus, B, C, D, and others; the received text reads "his disciples" following E, F, G, H, K, L, M, S, U, V, X, Gamma, Pi; omitted in Delta. Furthermore, D and most Old Latin versions place this after "forgot"; similarly the Coptic places it after "to the other side" | **to take bread**: found in most Latin and the Vulgate; manuscripts B, K, Pi read "to take bread" in a different word order (as in Mark).

6. **Jesus**: omitted in ff1, g2, k, the Vulgate, and Syriac Peshitta | **Watch out and**: omitted in a, b, e, ff2, q | **and Sadducees**: omitted in U and some others. In manuscript k, much of the text between 16:1 and 16:5 is lost; it then continues: "and they forgot to put in bread, and since they had only one loaf in the boat, he broke it for them saying, 'beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of the Herodians.'"

7. **they**: manuscripts D, a, b, c, e, ff2 read "then" | Manuscript L reads "among them" | **saying**: omitted in k and the Curetonian Syriac | **we took**: the Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac read "they took."

8. **said**: found in Sinaiticus, B, D, K, L, M, S, X, Delta, Pi, most Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, Origen, and others; the received text adds "to them" following C, E, F, G, H, U, V, Gamma, and others | **among yourselves**: manuscript L reads "among them" | **you took**: found in most manuscripts; however, Sinaiticus, B, D, and others read "you have" (as in Mark).

9. The first hand of Sinaiticus omits "nor remember" | Manuscripts D and Delta read "remember when" | Manuscript D reads "to the five thousand."

# TESTAMENT OF NAPHTALI IX. 1

IX. And having commanded them in many <note>original: "πολλὰ"</note> such things, he exhorted them to carry up his bones and bury him with his fathers. 2. And having eaten and drunk in gladness of soul, he covered his face and died. 3. And his sons did according to all that Naphtali their father commanded them.

### Testament of Gad, the ninth son of Jacob and Zilpah.

I. Copy of the testament of Gad, which he spoke to his sons in the hundred and twenty-fifth year of his life, saying to them: 2. Hear, my children; I was the ninth son born to Jacob, and I was brave in tending the flocks. 3. I therefore kept watch by night over the flock, and whenever the lion, or the wolf, or any wild beast came upon the flock, I would pursue it, and reaching it, I would seize its foot with my hand and hurl it as if a stone’s throw, and I would kill it. 4. So Joseph, my brother, pastured with us for thirty days, and being young, he was sickened by the heat. 5. And he returned to Hebron to our father, and he laid him down beside him, because he loved him very much. 6. And Joseph told our father that the sons of Zilpah and Bilhah were slaughtering the choice beasts and eating them against the will of Reuben and Judah. 7. For he had seen that I had snatched a lamb from the mouth of the bear, and that one...

### Testament of Gad, the ninth son of Jacob and Zilpah.

I. Copy of the testament of Gad, which he spoke to his sons in the one hundred and twenty-fifth year of his life, saying to them. 2. Hear, my children; I was the ninth son born to Jacob, and I was brave in the keeping of the flocks. 3. I therefore kept in the

<header>ΔΙΑΘΗΚΗ ΝΕΦΘΑΛΕΙΜ [IX. 1</header>

IX. \*Καὶ πολλὰ$^1$ τοιαῦτα ἐντειλάμενος$^2$ αὐτοῖς παρεκάλεσεν ἵνα μετακομίσωσι$^3$ τὰ ὀστᾶ αὐτοῦ$^4$ \* ἐν Χεβρών, καὶ θάψωσι αὐτὸν$^5$ μετὰ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ$^6$. 2. Καὶ$^7$ φαγὼν \* καὶ πιὼν$^8$ ἐν ἱλαρότητι ψυχῆς$^9$ συνεκάλυψε$^{10}$ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπέθανε. 3. Καὶ ἐποίησαν \* οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ$^{11}$ \* κατὰ πάντα$^{12}$ ὅσα$^{13}$ ἐνετείλατο αὐτοῖς$^{11}$ Νεφθαλείμ$^{14}$ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῶν$^{15}$.

### Διαθήκη Γὰδ τοῦ ἐννάτου υἱοῦ Ἰακὼβ καὶ Ζέλφας$^1$.

I. Ἀντίγραφον διαθήκης Γὰδ$^2$, ἃ$^3$ ἐλάλησε$^4$ τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτοῦ$^5$ ἐν \* τῷ ἑκατοστῷ εἰκοστῷ πέμπτῳ ἔτει τῆς ζωῆς$^6$ αὐτοῦ, \* λέγων αὐτοῖς$^7$. 2. \* Γ' Ἀκούσατε, τέκνα μου$^7$· ἐγὼ ἐγενόμην ἔννατος υἱὸς$^8$ τῷ Ἰακὼβ$^9$, καὶ$^{10}$ ἤμην$^{11}$ ἀνδρεῖος ἐπὶ τῶν ποιμνίων$^{12}$. 3. \* Ἐγὼ οὖν$^{13}$ ἐφύλαττον ἐν τῇ$^{14}$

<margin>
β, A, S
ἔννατος
υἱὸς ἐγεν-
νήθην.
</margin>

---

IX. $^1$ **A** = πολλὰ οὖν. For καὶ πολλὰ . . . παρεκάλεσεν **d** reads ταῦτα ἐντειλάμενος Ν. τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τοιαῦτα διετάξατο αὐτοῖς. $^2$ **A$^a$** = ἐνετείλατο. **A$^{bcd}$** διηγησάμενος (through an internal corruption). $^3$ **deg** read μετακομίσουσιν. **g** adds αὐτοῦ. $^4$ **g** om. $^5$ **adef** (save that **ae** read εἰς and **de** θάψουσιν). **bg, A, S$^1$** read εἰς (g ἐν) Χ. καὶ θάψωσι (g θάψουσι). **α** om. through hmt. (?). $^6$ **g** adds ὁ καὶ ἐποίησαν. $^7$ **A$^{abb*cd}$** according to printed text om. but not **A$^{e}$**. $^8$ **f** om. **d** adds καὶ πάντα. **g** σὺν αὐτοῖς. $^9$ **d** adds πράξας. $^{10}$ **e** reads συνεκάλυψατο. $^{11}$ **g** om. $^{12}$ **β-g, A, S$^1$, hi** read πάντα. **c, g** om. $^{13}$ **d** reads ἅ. **g** adds εἶπεν καί. $^{14}$ **d** om. $^{15}$ **d** adds τῷ δὲ Θεῷ ἡμῶν κ. τ. λ. **f, S$^1$** adds Νεφθαλείμ υἱὸς Ἰακὼβ η', υἱὸς Βάλλας β' (**S$^1$** reads καὶ Λείας for η' υἱ. Βάλλας)· ἔζησεν ἔτη ρλβ'. **g** οὕτως. Ἀμήν.

$^1$ Title. **α** as in text. **β-ad, S** read Διαθήκη Γὰδ θ' (bef, som. **g** trs. before Διαθήκη) περὶ μίσους (+ Γὰδ ἑρμηνεύεται πειρατήριον **f**). **a** Γάδ. **d** Γ. υἱὸς Ἰ. θ' υἱὸς Ζ. α' περὶ μίσους πειρατήριον. **A** = Δ. Γ. περὶ ὁράσεως, but <unclear>...</unclear> is corrupt for <unclear>...</unclear> = μίσους. $^2$ **hi** add τοῦ ἐννάτου υἱοῦ Ι. **A$^{b*}$** adds υἱοῦ Ἰακώβ. $^3$ **dg** read ὅσα. **α** adds ἐποίησε καί. This may have arisen through <term>ידבר</term> being repeated in the MS. as <term>יעבד</term>. $^4$ **β-dg, S** add αὐτοῖς. $^5$ **d** adds πρὸ τοῦ ἀποθανεῖν αὐτόν. $^6$ **α, A** (save that **h** om. εἰκοστῷ). **bf, S** read ἔτει ἑκατοστῷ εἰκοστῷ πέμπτῳ (**b** ἑβδόμῳ) ζωῆς. **aeg** ἔτει ρκε' (+ τῆς **ag**) ζωῆς. **d** ρκε' ἔτει τῆς ζωῆς. $^7$ **α, A$^{abcd}$** = καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς. **b** reads λέγων. **dg** καλέσας γὰρ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς (**g** αὐτοὺς εἶπεν). **aef, S$^1$** om. **A$^{b*}$** = συνήγαγε τοὺς υἱοὺς αὐτοῦ καὶ θυγατέρας καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς. **S$^2$** ἐκαλέσατο γὰρ τοὺς υἱοὺς αὐτοῦ καὶ εἶπεν. Here **S$^2$** agrees closely with **dg, A$^{b*}$**. $^8$ **α, β, A, S** read as in margin (save that **d** prefixes ἐγώ, τέκνα μου, **b** reads ἕβδομος for ἔννατος, and **bg** ἐγενόμην for ἐγεννήθην). $^9$ **d** adds ἡ δὲ μήτηρ μου Ζέλφας παιδίσκη Λείας. $^{10}$ **d** reads ἐγώ. $^{11}$ **A$^{abcdef}$** om. $^{12}$ **d** adds σφόδρα. **A$^{ab}$** om. next eight words through hmt. $^{13}$ **α, A$^{b*cdef}$** = καὶ ἐγώ. **β, S** read ἐγώ.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: the final instructions of Naphtali to his children.</meta>

IX. And after giving them many such commands, he exhorted them to carry his bones to Hebron and bury him with his fathers. 2. And after eating and drinking in gladness of soul, he covered his face and died. 3. And his sons did according to all that Naphtali their father had commanded them.

### The Testament of Gad, the ninth son of Jacob and Zilpah.

I. A copy of the testament of Gad, the things which he spoke to his sons in the one hundred and twenty-fifth year of his life, saying to them: 2. Listen, my children; I was born the ninth son to Jacob, and I was courageous in tending the flocks. 3. I, therefore, used to guard in the <margin>Manuscripts β, A, S: I was born the ninth son.</margin>

---

<note>The following section contains the critical apparatus, noting variations between different Greek manuscripts of the text.</note>

IX. 1. **A** reads "many things therefore." For "And many... he exhorted," manuscript **d** reads "Having commanded these things, Naphtali appointed for his sons many other such things." 2. **A$^a$** reads "he commanded." **A$^{bcd}$** read "having related" <note>likely due to an internal scribal error</note>. 3. **deg** read "they shall carry." **g** adds "his." 4. **g** omits. 5. **adef** <note>except **ae** read "into" and **de** "they shall bury"</note>. **bg, A, S$^1$** read "into (g: in) Hebron and they shall bury." **α** omits due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <gloss>a scribal error where the eye skips between similar word endings</gloss>. 6. **g** adds "which they also did." 7. **A$^{abb*cd}$** according to the printed text omits, but not **A$^{e}$**. 8. **f** omits. **d** adds "and all." **g** "with them." 9. **d** adds "having done." 10. **e** reads "he covered himself." 11. **g** omits. 12. **β-g, A, S$^1$, hi** read "all things." **c, g** omit. 13. **d** reads "which." **g** adds "he said and." 14. **d** omits. 15. **d** adds "but to our God etc." **f, S$^1$** add "Naphtali, son of Jacob the 8th, son of Bilhah the 2nd; he lived 132 years." **g** "thus. Amen."

1. Title. **α** as in the main text. **β-ad, S** read "Testament of Gad 9th (bef, s omit; **g** transposes before 'Testament') concerning hatred (+ Gad is interpreted as 'pirate-stronghold' **f**)." **a** "Gad." **d** "Gad, son of Jacob the 9th, son of Zilpah the 1st, concerning hatred, a pirate-stronghold." **A** = "Testament of Gad concerning the vision," but <unclear>the Armenian text</unclear> is corrupt for <unclear>the word</unclear> meaning "hatred." 2. **hi** add "the ninth son of Jacob." **A$^{b*}$** adds "son of Jacob." 3. **dg** read "as many as." **α** adds "he did and." This may have arisen through the Hebrew <term>yadabber</term> <gloss>he spoke</gloss> being repeated in the manuscript as <term>ya'abod</term> <gloss>he did/served</gloss>. 4. **β-dg, S** add "to them." 5. **d** adds "before he died." 6. **α, A** <note>except **h** omits "twentieth"</note>. **bf, S** read "in the year one hundred twenty-fifth (**b** seventh) of life." **aeg** "in the 125th year (+ of **ag**) life." **d** "in the 125th year of life." 7. **α, A$^{abcd}$** = "and he said to them." **b** reads "saying." **dg** "for having called them he said to them (**g** he said to them)." **aef, S$^1$** omit. **A$^{b*}$** = "he gathered his sons and daughters and said to them." **S$^2$** "for he called his sons and said." Here **S$^2$** agrees closely with **dg, A$^{b*}$**. 8. **α, β, A, S** read as in the margin <note>except **d** prefixes "I, my children," **b** reads "seventh" for "ninth," and **bg** "I became" for "I was born"</note>. 9. **d** adds "and my mother was Zilpah, the handmaid of Leah." 10. **d** reads "I." 11. **A$^{abcdef}$** omit. 12. **d** adds "exceedingly." **A$^{ab}$** omit the next eight words through <term>homoeoteleuton</term>. 13. **α, A$^{b*cdef}$** = "And I." **β, S** read "I."

<summary>This page concludes the Testament of Naphtali with his death and burial in Hebron, and begins the Testament of Gad, where Gad introduces himself as Jacob's ninth son and a courageous shepherd.</summary>
<keywords>Naphtali, Gad, Jacob, Zilpah, Hebron, Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, Greek manuscripts, textual criticism</keywords>

TESTAMENT OF NAPHTALI [IX. 1

IX. And having commanded them many things, he exhorted them to carry his bones to Hebron, and to bury him with his fathers. 2. And having eaten and drunk in gladness of soul, he covered his face and died. 3. And his sons did according to all that Naphtali their father commanded them.

### Testament of Gad, the ninth son of Jacob and Zilpah.

I. Copy of the testament of Gad, which he spoke to his sons in the one hundred and twenty-fifth year of his life, saying to them. 2. Hear, my children; I was the ninth son born to Jacob, and I was brave in the keeping of the flocks. 3. I, therefore, was keeping in the <margin>B, A, S: I was born the ninth son.</margin>

<note>The critical apparatus below details the textual variations found in the manuscripts of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, noting differences in phrasing, omissions, and additions across various codices (identified by letters such as A, B, S, etc.).</note>

---

IX. 1. **A** = and therefore many. For "And having commanded... he exhorted," **d** reads: "Having commanded these things to his sons, he ordered them many other such things." 2. **A$^a$** = he commanded. **A$^{b*d}$** having related (through an internal corruption). 3. **deg** read "they shall carry." **g** adds "his." 4. **g** omits. 5. **adef** (except that **ae** read "into" and **de** "they shall bury"). **bg, A, S$^1$** read "into" (g "in") Hebron, and "they shall bury" (g "they shall bury"). **α** omits through homoeoteleuton. 6. **g** adds "which they also did." 7. **A$^{abb*cd}$** according to the printed text omits, but not **A$^{ef}$**. 8. **f** omits. **d** adds "and all things." **g** "with them." 9. **d** adds "having done." 10. **e** reads "he covered himself." 11. **g** omits. 12. **β-g, A, S$^1$, hi** read "all things." **c, g** omit. 13. **d** reads "which." **g** adds "he said and." 14. **d** omits. 15. **d** adds "to our God, etc." **f, S$^1$** adds "Naphtali, son of Jacob, eighth son of Bilhah" (**S$^1$** reads "and of Leah" for "eighth son of Bilhah"); "he lived 132 years." **g** "thus. Amen."

1. Title. **α** as in text. **β-ad, S** read "Testament of Gad, the ninth" (bef, S omit; **g** transposes before "Testament") "concerning hatred" (+ "Gad is interpreted as a pirate" **f**). **a** Gad. **d** "Gad, son of Jacob, ninth son of Zilpah, first concerning hatred, a pirate." **A** = "Testament of Gad concerning a vision," but <unclear>...</unclear> is corrupt for <unclear>...</unclear> = "hatred." 2. **hi** add "the ninth son of Jacob." **A$^{b*}$** adds "son of Jacob." 3. **dg** read "all things." **α** adds "he did and." This may have arisen through the Hebrew term <term>ידבר</term> <gloss>he will speak</gloss> being repeated in the manuscript as <term>יעבד</term> <gloss>he will do</gloss>. 4. **β-dg, S** add "to them." 5. **d** adds "before he died." 6. **α, A** (except that **h** omits "twentieth"). **bf, S** read "in the one hundred and twenty-fifth year" (**b** "seventh") "of his life." **aeg** "in the 125th year" (+ "of" **ag**) "of his life." **d** "in the 125th year of his life." 7. **α, A$^{abcd}$** = "and he said to them." **b** reads "saying." **dg** "having called, he said to them" (**g** "he said to them"). **aef, S$^1$** omit. **A$^{b*}$** = "he gathered his sons and daughters and said to them." **S$^2$** "he called his sons and said." Here **S$^2$** agrees closely with **dg, A$^{b*}$**. 8. **α**. **β, A, S** read as in margin (except that **d** prefixes "I," "my children," **b** reads "seventh" for "ninth," and **bg** "I was" for "I was born"). 9. **d** adds "and my mother was Zilpah, the handmaid of Leah." 10. **d** reads "I." 11. **A$^{ab*def}$** omit. 12. **d** adds "exceedingly." **A$^{ab}$** omit the next eight words through homoeoteleuton. 13. **α, A$^{b*cdef}$** = "and I." **β, S** read "I."

[context] And, as Asenath was fleeing before, lo ! Pharaoh's son met her and fifty horsemen with him :
and Asenath, when she saw him, was seized with very great fear and was trembling, and she called upon the name of the Lord her God.
And Benjamin was sitting with her on the chariot on the right side ;
and Benjamin was a strong
lad of about nineteen years, and upon him was ineffable beauty and might as of a lion's whelp, and he was also one who feared God exceedingly. Then Benjamin leaped down from the chariot, and took a round stone from the ravine and filled his hand and hurled at Pharaoh's son and smote his left temple, and wounded him with a grievous wound, and he fell from his horse upon
the earth half-dead.
And thereupon Benjamin, having run up on to a rock, saith to Asenath's chariot-man : " Give me stones from the ravine." And he gave him fifty
stones. And Benjamin hurled the stones and slew the fifty
men who were with Pharaoh's son, all the stones sinking in through their temples. Then the sons of Leah, Reuben and Simeon, Levi and Judah, Issachar and Zebulon, pursued after the men who had lain in wait against Asenath and fell upon them unawares and cut them all down ; and the six men slew two thousand and seventy-six men. And the sons of Balla and Zelpha fled from their face and said : " We have perished at the hands of our brethren, and Pharaoh's son hath also died by the hand of Benjamin the lad,
[context] and all who were with him perished by the hand of the boy Benjamin.

him, Aseneth was very afraid, and she trembled, and she called upon the name of the Lord her God.

[XXVII.] Benjamin was sitting with her on the chariot on the right side. Benjamin was a strong young man, about nineteen years old, and he possessed an indescribable beauty and power like a lion's whelp; he was also a man who feared God greatly. Then Benjamin leaped down from the chariot and took a round stone from the ravine. Filling his hand, he threw it at the son of Pharaoh and struck his left temple, wounding him with a severe wound. He fell from his horse, appearing half-dead. And then, running up to the rocks, Benjamin said to the charioteer of Aseneth, "Give me stones from the ravine." He gave him fifty stones, and Benjamin threw the stones and killed the fifty men who were with the son of Pharaoh, the stones piercing through their temples. Then the sons of Leah—Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun—pursued the men who had set the ambush for Aseneth. They fell upon them suddenly and cut them all down; the six men killed two thousand and seventy-six. The sons of Bilhah and Zilpah fled from their presence and said, "We have perished because of our brothers, and the son of Pharaoh is dead by the hand of Benjamin, the child..."

Τότε κατεπήδησε Βενιαμὶν ἐκ τοῦ ὀχήματος, καὶ ἔλαβε λίθον ἐκ τοῦ χειμάρρου στρογγύλον, καὶ πλήσας τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἠκόντισε κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ Φαραώ, καὶ ἐπάταξε τὸν κρόταφον αὐτοῦ τὸν εὐώνυμον, καὶ ἐτραυμάτισεν αὐτὸν τραύματι βαρεῖ. Aseneth saw him and was greatly afraid, and she trembled, and she called upon the name of the Lord her God.

### XXVII.

Now Benjamin was sitting with her in the chariot on the right side. Benjamin was a strong youth of about nineteen years, and upon him was an inexpressible beauty and strength like that of a lion's cub, and he was also one who feared God greatly. Then Benjamin leaped down from the chariot and took a round stone from the torrent-bed, and filling his hand, he hurled it at the son of Pharaoh and struck his left temple, wounding him with a severe wound. And he fell from his horse to the ground, being half-dead. And then, having run up onto a rock, Benjamin said to Aseneth's charioteer: "Give me stones from the torrent-bed." And he gave him fifty stones. And Benjamin, hurling the stones, killed the fifty men who were with the son of Pharaoh, all the stones sinking through their temples. Then the sons of Leah—Reuben and Simeon, Levi and Judah, Issachar and Zebulun—pursued after the men who had ambushed Aseneth, and they fell upon them suddenly and cut them all down. These six men killed two thousand and seventy-six. reference.text:
[context] And the space between has a breadth of not less than fifty feet; in that place the citizens of Daras are accustomed to put their cattle and other animals when an enemy assails them.
At first then Chosroes made an assault on the fortifications toward the west, and forcing back his opponents by overwhelming numbers of missiles, he set fire to the gates of the small wall. However no one of the barbarians dared to get inside. Next he decided to make a tunnel secretly at the eastern side of the city. For at this point alone can the earth be dug, since the other parts of the fortifications were set upon rock by the builders. So the Persians began to dig, beginning from their trench. And since this was very deep, they were neither observed by the enemy nor did they afford them any means of discovering what was being done. So they had already gone under the foundations of the outer wall, and were about to reach the space between the two walls and soon after to pass also the great wall and take the city by force; but since it was not fated to be captured by the Persians, someone from the camp of Chosroes came alone about midday close to the fortifications, whether a man or something else greater than man, and he made it appear to those who saw him that he was collecting the weapons which the Romans had a little before discharged from the wall against the barbarians who were assailing them. And while doing this and holding his shield before him, he seemed to be bantering those who were on the parapet and taunting them with laughter. Then he told them of everything and commanded them all to be on the watch and to take all possible care for their safety. After revealing these things he was off, while the Romans with much shouting and confusion were ordering men to dig the ground between the two walls.
The Persians, on the other hand, not knowing what was being
[context] done, were pushing on the work no less than before.

## PROCOPIUS ON THE WARS II. 14.

<margin>19</margin> ...waiting to be thrown in. At first, then, Khosrow <note>Khosrow I, the Sasanian King of Persia.</note> made an assault against the western side of the circuit wall; forcing his way with a multitude of missiles, he set fire to the gates of the short wall <margin>20</margin> <note>The *proteichisma*, or outer defensive wall, which was lower than the main inner wall.</note>. However, none of the barbarians <note>A standard term used by Byzantine writers for non-Romans, in this case, the Persians.</note> dared to go inside. After this, he decided to secretly construct an underground tunnel toward the eastern parts of the city. <margin>5</margin> For only in this area was the earth of such a nature that it could be dug, since the rest of the circuit wall had been built upon rock by its original builders. <margin>21</margin> B 213 The Persians, therefore, began digging from the trench <note>The moat or ditch surrounding the city.</note>. Because this was quite deep, they were neither <margin>10</margin> seen by the enemy, nor did they provide the Romans with any perception of what was being done. <margin>22</margin> They had already undermined the foundations of the outer wall and were shortly about to reach the space between the two circuit walls; after passing the great wall <note>The massive inner main wall of the fortress.</note>, they would have taken the city <margin>15</margin> by force. But (for it was not destined for the city to be captured by the Persians) a certain individual from Khosrow’s camp arrived alone around midday very near the circuit wall. Whether he was a man or something greater than a man <note>Procopius frequently suggests divine or supernatural intervention in his histories when events take a miraculous turn.</note>, he gave the impression to those watching <margin>20</margin> that he was collecting the arrows which the Romans had shot a little earlier from the wall against the harassing barbarians. <margin>23</margin> While doing this and holding his shield before him, he seemed to mock those on the battlements and taunt them with laughter. Then, having told them the whole story, he ordered them all to be awake <margin>25</margin> and to care for their safety as much as possible. <margin>24</margin> Having signaled these things, he departed and was gone; the Romans, with much shouting and confusion, ordered digging to begin in the space between the two walls. <margin>25</margin> And the Persians, however, not knowing the things...

text:
PROCOPIUS ON THE WARS II. 14.

<margin>19</margin> <note>The Persian King Chosroes I continues his siege of the city of Daras.</note> Chosroes first launched an assault against the western side of the fortifications. By overwhelming the defenders with a great number of missiles, he succeeded in burning the gates of the outer wall <note>literally: the short wall</note>. <margin>20</margin> However, none of the barbarians <note>the Persians</note> dared to venture inside. He then decided to secretly construct a mine <note>a subterranean tunnel used in siege warfare</note> toward the eastern side of the city. This was the only area where the earth was suitable for digging, as the rest of the circuit wall had been built upon rock by its founders. <margin>21</margin> The Persians therefore began digging from the trench. Since this trench was quite deep, they were not seen by the enemy, nor did they give any indication to the Romans of what was being done. <margin>22</margin> They had already undermined the foundations of the outer wall and were about to pass through the space between the two walls. A little later, after bypassing the great wall, they would have taken the city by force. But it was not destined for the city to be captured by the Persians. Around midday, a single figure came very close to the fortifications from the camp of Chosroes. Whether he was a man or something greater than a man, he gave the impression to those watching that he was collecting the arrows which the Romans had recently shot from the wall at the harassing barbarians. <margin>23</note> While doing this and holding his shield before him, he appeared to mock those on the battlements and taunt them with laughter. Then, revealing the whole plan to them, he commanded them all to stay awake and to take the greatest possible care for their safety. <margin>24</margin> Having signaled this, he departed and was gone. The Romans, with much noise and commotion, ordered digging to begin in the space between the two walls. <margin>25</margin> The Persians, however, were unaware of these developments.

[context] With these words Cabades dismissed the ambassador, dropping the hint that he was willing to take money from the Romans
and have done with the causes of the war.
This was reported to the emperor by Rufinus when he came to Byzantium.
Hermogenes also came thither not long afterwards, and the winter came to a close; thus ended the fourth year of the reign of the Emperor Justinian.
At the opening of spring a Persian army under the leadership of Azarethes invaded the Roman territory. They were fifteen thousand strong, all horsemen. With them was Alamoundaras, son of Saccice, with a very large body of Saracens. But this invasion was not made by the Persians in the customary manner; for they did not invade Mesopotamia, as formerly, but the country called Commagene of old, but now Euphratesia, a point from which, as far as we know, the Persians never before conducted a campaign against the Romans. But why the land was called Mesopotamia and why the Persians refrained from making their attack at this point is what I now propose to relate.
There is a mountain in Armenia which is not especially precipitous, two-and-forty stades removed from Theodosiopolis and lying toward the north from it. From this mountain issue two springs, forming immediately two rivers, the one on the right called the Euphrates, and the other the Tigris.
One of these, the Tigris, descends, with no deviations and with no tributaries except small ones
[context] emptying into it, straight toward the city of Amida.

text:
These things Rufinus reported to the Emperor when he came to Byzantium. Not long after him, Hermogenes also arrived, the winter was ending, and the fourth year was ending for Emperor Justinian holding the imperial rule.

<margin>17</margin>. At the beginning of spring, an army of Persians, led by <term>Azarethes</term>, invaded the land of the Romans. There were fifteen thousand of them, all cavalry. Alamoundaros, the son of Sakkikes, was with them, having a very large multitude of Saracens. <margin>2</margin> This Persian incursion did not happen as was usual; for they did not invade Mesopotamia, as they had before, but into what was formerly <term>Commagene</term>, but now called <term>Euphratesia</term>, from which, as far as we know, the Persians had never previously campaigned against the Romans. <margin>3</margin> I shall now proceed to tell why the region was called Mesopotamia and why the Persians refrained from invading it.

<margin>4</margin> There is a mountain not very steep in Armenia, located forty-two <term>stadia</term> <gloss>units of distance, approx. 185-192 meters each</gloss> from Theodosiopolis, turned toward the north wind. Two springs issue from there, immediately forming two rivers: the one on the right, the <term>Euphrates</term>, and the other, the <term>Tigris</term>. <margin>5</margin> One of these, the Tigris, does not wind its course, nor does it gather many waters...

# PROCOPIUS ON THE WARS I. 17.

<margin>10</margin> and to do away with the causes of the war. Rufinus, having arrived in Byzantium <note>modern Istanbul</note>, reported these matters to the Emperor. Not long after him, Hermogenes also arrived, and the winter was ending; thus the fourth year of the reign of the Emperor Justinian as absolute ruler came to a close. <margin>5</margin>

17. At the beginning of spring, a Persian army led by Azarethes invaded the land of the Romans. They numbered fifteen thousand, all of whom were horsemen. Alamoundaros <note>Al-Mundhir III</note>, the leader of the <term>Sakkike</term> <gloss>likely a reference to the Lakhmid Arabs</gloss>, accompanied them with a very large host of Saracens. This invasion by the Persians did not happen in the usual manner; for they did not invade Mesopotamia as they had in former times, but rather into what was anciently called Commagene, but is now called <margin>B 82</margin> Euphratesia. From that direction, as far as we know, the Persians had never before campaigned against the Romans. I shall now explain why the region was named Mesopotamia and why the Persians refrained from their usual route of attack through it.

<margin>4</margin> There is a mountain in Armenia, not very steep, located forty-two <term>stadia</term> <gloss>about 5 miles</gloss> from Theodosiopolis, situated toward the north wind. Two springs issue from there, immediately forming two rivers: the one on the right is the Euphrates, while the other is named the Tigris. One of these, the Tigris, neither follows a winding course nor contains anything but a small amount of water <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence</note>.

reference.text:
[context] On learning that he had collected a large sum from certain taxes and was conveying it to the treasury, he urged him
to halt for the night with him, promising that at daybreak he should go off where he liked. At the other's refusing and getting angry, the Emperor insisted all the more and finally persuaded him - for he was marvellously glib of speech and quick in thought, and persuasion sat on his tongue as if he were a second Aeschines or Demosthenes. So he took him with him and turned in at an inn, where he detained him by looking after him kindly in all ways, making him share his table and seeing that he could rest comfortably. But at dawn just when the sun was climbing up the eastern horizon, the Byzantine spread the cloths on the horses and was for hurrying off to ride at full speed to Byzantium. The Emperor seeing this called: "Stop and travel with us," but the other not knowing where he was going and being moreover quite in the dark about the reason which made him the object of so much solicitude, became vexed and suspicious again of the Emperor
and his friendly ways. But the Emperor insisted and began pulling at him, and as the other still did not yield, he changed his manner and spoke more roughly and threatened him if he would not do as he was ordered. As the other still did not obey he ordered all the stranger's possessions to be packed with his own on his beasts and started on his journey, giving the other permission to go where he liked. Then the man abandoned his intention of going to the Palace from fear of being imprisoned if the Treasury-officials saw him come with empty hands; again he was not anxious to return home because of the unsettled and confused state of the country resultant upon the rebellion of the Comneni which had emerged, and so against his will he followed the Emperor. And next the following incident took place. As he was starting, the Emperor fell in with some Turks who had just crossed the river Eurus.
So drawing reign, he enquired whence and whither they were going, and straightway promised them much money and all kinds of rewards
[context] if they would accompany him to the Comneni - and so they consented.

text:
promising to depart with him at daybreak, wherever he might wish to go. As the man hesitated and took this <note>the prospect of departing</note> heavily, the Caesar pressed him more strongly and persuaded him, being as he was quick in speech and formidable in thought, and carrying persuasion on his tongue like another Aeschines or Demosthenes. Having therefore taken such a man along, he lodged in a certain room, and having treated him with every kind of hospitality, having deemed him worthy of his table, and having refreshed him well, he kept the man there. When it was already the break of dawn, when the sun is hastening to reach the eastern horizon, the Byzantine began to urge that the saddles be placed on the horses, eager to drive straight for Byzantium. 

But the Caesar, observing this, said, "Stay, and travel with us." The man, not knowing where he was going, and being entirely ignorant of the reason for which he had been deemed worthy of such hospitality, was again uneasy and held suspicions regarding the Caesar and the Caesar's acts of hospitality. But the Caesar persisted in drawing him along. When he would not comply, the Caesar changed his tone and used harsher words toward him, threatening what would happen if he did not do as ordered. Since he still would not comply, the Caesar ordered all the man's possessions to be loaded onto his own pack animals and to follow the route ahead, while giving the man freedom to go wherever he wished. But he, having entirely abandoned the entry into the palace—fearing that he might be placed under guard because he appeared to those around the royal bedchamber with empty hands—and not wishing to turn back due to the instability and confusion that had fallen upon affairs from the rebellion of the Komnenos that had already arisen, chose not to, and followed the Caesar. 

And something like this happened by chance. As the Caesar was departing, he encountered Turks who were just crossing the river called the Evros. He therefore pulled on the reins and asked whence they came and whither they were going, at the same time promising to give them much money and to deem them worthy of every kind of favor if they would journey with him to the Komnenos. They agreed then and there. And he demanded an oath from their leaders, wishing to confirm the agreements through this. And they immediately fulfilled the oath according to their custom, assuring him most eagerly that they would fight as allies for the Komnenos.

<summary>Caesar John Doukas detains a traveler to accompany him and recruits Turkish mercenaries to join the forces of the Komnenoi.</summary>
<keywords>John Doukas, Turks, Evros River, rebellion, alliance</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: the Caesar Nikephoros Melissenos was attempting to delay the official messenger from the capital.</meta>

The Caesar promised to lodge him for the night, assuring him that at daybreak he would travel wherever he wished. When the man resisted and took this delay poorly, the Caesar pressed him more vehemently and persuaded him; for he was a man swift in speech and clever in thought, carrying a persuasion on his tongue like another Aeschines or Demosthenes <note>Aeschines and Demosthenes were the most famous rival orators of ancient Athens, known for their supreme rhetorical skill.</note>. Taking the man with him, he lodged him in a certain room, and after showing him every kind of hospitality, honoring him with a table and giving him good rest, he detained the man. 

At the break of dawn, when the sun was already hastening to reach the eastern horizon, the Byzantine <note>The messenger from Constantinople, referred to here by his city of origin.</note>, having placed the saddle-cloths upon his horses, was eager to ride straight for Byzantium <note>Constantinople.</note>. Seeing this, the Caesar said, "Stay, and travel with us." The man, knowing neither where he was going nor the reason why he had been deemed worthy of such hospitality, was again distressed and grew suspicious of the Caesar and the Caesar's friendly overtures. 

The Caesar continued to urge him, drawing him along; but when he would not comply, the Caesar changed his tone and used harsher words, threatening what would happen if he did not do as commanded. When the man still did not obey, the Caesar ordered that all the man's belongings be merged with his own baggage train and proceed on the intended journey, while giving the man leave to go wherever he wished. 

The man, having completely renounced his entry into the palace—as he feared he might be imprisoned for appearing before those of the royal bedchamber empty-handed—and yet unwilling to turn back because of the instability and confusion that had fallen upon affairs due to the already emerging rebellion of Komnenos <note>Alexios Komnenos, the future Emperor Alexios I.</note>, followed the Caesar against his will. 

Then, a certain event occurred by chance. As the Caesar was departing, he encountered some Turks who were just then crossing the river called Evros <note>The Maritsa River in the Balkans.</note>. Drawing back his reins, he inquired where they had come from and where they were going, while at the same time promising to give them much money and to treat them with every kind of care.

<summary>The Caesar Nikephoros Melissenos uses rhetoric and then force to detain a royal messenger during the confusion of the Komnenos rebellion. While traveling, the Caesar encounters a group of Turks at the Evros river and begins negotiations.</summary>
<keywords>Nikephoros Melissenos, Alexios Komnenos, Byzantine diplomacy, Evros River, Turks, oratory, rebellion</keywords>

[context] The Egyptians therefore sent out eighty galleys,
the Phoenicians an equal number, the Ionians and Dorians of Asia sixty, the Cyprians thirty, the Carians twenty, the Bithynians thirty, and the Africans fifty. His foot-soldiers amounted to nearly a hundred and fifty thousand, but his horse only to fifteen thousand, which were sent to him from Phrygia and Cappadocia. Constantine's navy lay at Piraeus, that of Licinius in the Hellespont. When they had thus established their naval and military forces, Licinius encamped at Adrianople in Thrace, whilst Constantine sent for his navy from Piraeus, which was built and manned chiefly in. Greece. Advancing with his infantry from Thessalonica, he encamped on the bank of the river Hebrus, which runs to the left of Adrianople. At the same time, Licinius drew up his army in order of battle, extending from a mountain which is above the town two hundred stadia, as far as the junction of another river with the Hebrus; thus the armies continued opposite to each other for several days. Constantine. observing where the river was least broad, concerted this plan. He ordered his men to bring trees from the mountain, and to tie ropes around them, as if he intended to throw a bridge over the river for the passage of his army. By this stratagem he deluded the enemy, and, ascending a hill on which were thick woods sufficient to conceal any that were in them, he planted there five thousand archers and eight hundred horse.
[context] Having done this, he crossed the Hebrus at the narrowest place, and so surprised the enemy that many fled with all their speed, while others, who were amazed at his unexpected approach, were struck with wonder at his coming over so suddenly.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the escalating conflict between Constantine and Licinius. After Constantine's victory over the Sarmatians and his arrival in Thessalonica mentioned on the previous page, the text now details the massive military and naval mobilizations on both sides as they prepare for a decisive confrontation near Adrianople.</meta>

thirty, and the **Libyans** fifty. The land-based army

cavalry; these were provided by **Phrygia** and **Cappadocia**.
The ships of **Constantine** were moored in the **Piraeus** <note>The famous port of Athens.</note>,
<margin>3</margin> while those belonging to **Licinius** were stationed at the **Hellespont**. With both
the naval and land forces thus organized, Licinius
had his camp at **Adrianople** <note>Modern Edirne, Turkey; a strategic city in Thrace.</note> in Thrace, while Constan-

were from **Greece**—and having set out from **Thessalonica** with
his infantry, he marched along the bank of the **Hebrus River** <note>The Maritsa River, which flows through the Balkans.</note>,
<margin>4</margin> passing **Adrianople** on his left, and there established his camp. When

<note>Critical notes on the Greek text:
1. "Dorians" spelled as "Dorieis" instead of "Dories" in Manuscript V.
4. "Cavalry" (hippeis) has various spellings in the manuscripts.
5. The word "and" (de) was added based on Manuscript V.
7. "Hellespont" (elesponton) has various corrections in the spelling of the 'e' and 't' in Manuscript V.
9. "In" (en) was added by a second hand in Manuscript V. The spelling of "Adrianople" varies between manuscripts and early printed editions (Sylburg).
10. "Piraeus" (peirai os) shows word-spacing corrections in Manuscript V.
11. "Thessalonica" (thesalonikes) is spelled with a single 's' by the first scribe.
12. "Bank" (iona) and "Hebrus" (ebrou) lack proper accents in the manuscript; a letter 'm' was erased before "Hebrus".
13. "Passing on his left" (en aristera iontos) is written as a continuous phrase.
15. "At which" (katho) lacks accents in the manuscript.
16. "Tonoszeios": This is undoubtedly the Tundzha River (referencing C. Mueller's Ptolemy commentary). It is unlikely to be the Erkene River (as P. Meyer suggested) due to the distance. However, the exact form of the name used by Zosimus cannot be guessed with certainty. 
18. "Narrowest" (stenotatos) was corrected by the editor from "narrower" (stenoteros) in the manuscript.
19. "Ordered" (epetatte) has a slight variation in ending.
20. "Camp" (stratopaidoi) is misspelled in Manuscript V.
21. "In that way": Sylburg suggests "by that reasoning"; Manuscript V has a corrupted "kan", while Reitemeier suggests "there".
23. "Continuous" (synechis) lacks accents in the manuscript.
24. "Stationed" (enkatesstesen) is written as two words in Manuscript V.
25. "Eighty": A conjecture suggests "eight hundred".</note>

The Phoenicians provided an equal number, the Ionians and Dorians in Asia sixty, the Cypriots thirty, the Carians twenty, the Bithynians thirty, and the Libyans fifty. The infantry army was about one hundred and fifty thousand, and the cavalry fifteen thousand; Phrygia and Cappadocia provided these. The ships of Constantine were anchored at the Piraeus, while those of Licinius were at the Hellespont. With the naval and infantry forces thus arranged for each side, Licinius held his camp at Adrianople in Thrace, while Constantine summoned his ships from the Piraeus, as they were mostly from Greece, and advancing from Thessalonica with his infantry along the bank of the Hebrus River, which flows to the left of Adrianople, he set up camp. Licinius also drew up his forces from the mountain overlooking the city for a distance of two hundred <term>stadia</term> <gloss>an ancient unit of distance, approximately 185 meters</gloss>, to the point where the Tonoszeios River joins the Hebrus. The armies sat opposite each other for many days. Constantine, having observed where the river was narrowest, devised the following plan. He ordered his army to bring down timber from the mountain and to weave ropes, as if he intended to bridge the river and lead his army across at that point. Having deceived the enemy with this, he went up to a hill covered with dense woods, capable of concealing those within them, and stationed there five thousand infantry archers and eighty cavalrymen. cause.diagnosis: The hand is clear but the OCR misread about a third of the words, including two negations that are not on the page (ἐδίδου read as οὐδ’ οὖν, δὲ καὶ διάδοχον read as οὐ καὶ διάδοχον) and the contraction π(ατ)ρικῶς left as πρικῶς, so every major fault in the English - the invented drugs, Clearchus, "bitterly", "not as a successor", the lost 65/7 years - starts in the OCR and the translator smoothed the garble into fluent sentences.

causes.ocr_has: καὶ νέωμα φάρμακα ἐρύθωνος τε καὶ ὀσμέου ἀποφυγὴν
causes.english_says: and with new drugs of the red and of the bone to ward off [the decay]

causes.ocr_has: ἐξ ὧν ἀβυρτανίας τε καὶ τας μοῖς ἐξεδίδοτο
causes.english_says: from which he was given over to madness and rage
causes.note: Sleeplessness and spasms misread into non-words; English guessed.

causes.note: ἐδίδου read as οὐδ’ οὖν (a negation that is not on the page), ὥσπερ καὶ split, τελευτῶν and ἀπαιτεῖσθαι misread: "like Clearchus, he too" became "not even Clearchus".

causes.image_reads: τὸν θάνατον ἐπελθεῖν αὐτῷ κατευχόμενον μὴ τυχεῖν· ἀλλὰ συχναῖς ἡμέραις
causes.ocr_has: τὸν θάνατον ἐπῆλθον ἐπαπελθὼν μηδὲν· ἀλλὰ σγναῖς ἡμέραις
causes.english_says: death came upon him, but it did not, and for seven days he was consumed
causes.note: The praying (κατευχόμενον) and not obtaining (μὴ τυχεῖν) are lost in the OCR; "seven" is the translator's fill for the garbled συχναῖς ("many").

text: and with new drugs of the red <note>a type of medicinal plant or mineral</note> and of the bone <note>likely referring to bone-marrow or similar substance</note> to ward off [the decay], he surrendered to the corruption within, more bitterly. When his flesh rotted, an enemy to his own enemy, it flowed out heavily and in great quantity, so that neither the discharge nor the audacity of the physician could hide the sickly, swirling corruption. Constantly slipping and rushing, it consumed his whole body, from which he was given over to madness and rage, until the spirit, up to the very vitals, was torn apart by the spreading of the disease. Not even thus was Clearchus <note>referring to the previous tyrant</note> cleared of the punishments he was perceived by those who saw him to be announcing, which he had lawlessly inflicted upon the citizens. For they often say that in his sickness, death came upon him, but it did not, and for seven days he was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus, the curse slipped away, and the six years which the tyranny held passed. Agesilaus was king of the Lacedaemonians at that time. This Timotheus, having received the rule, adjusted it toward a gentler and more democratic form, so that he was no longer called a tyrant, but a benefactor by those things he did. He resolved the debts for the men, and for those who needed [funds] for trade and other life, he assisted without hesitation. And he was not only a deliverer of those in prison, but also an accurate judge for those who were unworthy <note>of their status or legal standing</note>, and he was kind. In other matters, he was useful and did not turn away from petitions. He treated his brother Dionysius <note>also referred to as Dionusios</note> in these matters bitterly, but he held him as a partner in the rule, though not as a successor. But he also acted bravely toward the military affairs, and being self-controlled in body and soul, he was also grateful and not useless toward the dissolutions of battles.

text:
And new medicines, both of erythron <note>a plant, likely a type of dogtooth violet or similar medicinal herb</note> and osmeos <note>a fragrant plant</note>, were administered to prevent the inward spread, though they proved more bitter. As the flesh became hostile to the enemy <note>referring to the disease</note>, a heavy and diseased discharge flowed out in great quantity, so that neither the discharge nor the putrefaction caused by the physician’s daring could be seen as anything but a diseased agitation, constantly slipping and rushing, consuming the whole body. From this, a state of confusion and distress was produced, until the spirits, through the spread of the affliction, broke away even to the very entrails. Nor was Clearchus <note>a historical tyrant of Heraclea Pontica</note> even then exposed to those who saw him, intending to announce judgments which they had lawlessly imposed upon the citizens. For they themselves often say that in the sickness, death approached, yet it did not come; but for six days, the body was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus, the ruin having slipped away, he lived for six years, and for six years the tyranny lasted. Agesilaus was king of the Lacedaemonians at that time. This Timotheus, having taken up the rule, so transformed it toward a milder and more democratic state that he was no longer called a tyrant, but a benefactor by those who observed his actions. He settled the debts of the men for himself, and for those in need of trade and other necessities of life, he provided without interest. He opened the prisons, not only for those who were worthy, but also for those who were undeserving, acting as a precise and humane judge. He was good in other respects and did not turn away from legal cases. He treated his brother Dionysius with kindness in these matters, and immediately made him a partner in the rule, not merely a successor. Furthermore, he conducted himself bravely in military affairs, being temperate in both body and soul, and was also grateful and capable in the resolution of battles.

<summary>This passage describes the physical suffering caused by a severe illness and transitions into a historical account of the transition of power from the tyrant Clearchus to Timotheus, who reformed the government into a more democratic and benevolent administration.</summary>

text:
And new medicines, both of erythron <note>a plant, likely a type of dogtooth violet or similar medicinal herb</note> and osmeos <note>a fragrant plant</note>, were administered to prevent the inward spread, though they proved more bitter. As the flesh became hostile to the enemy <note>referring to the disease</note>, a heavy and diseased discharge flowed out in great quantity, so that neither the discharge nor the putrefaction caused by the physician’s daring could be seen as anything but a diseased agitation, constantly slipping and rushing, consuming the whole body. From this, a state of confusion and distress was produced, until the spirits, through the spread of the affliction, broke away even to the very entrails. Nor was Clearchus <note>a historical tyrant of Heraclea Pontica</note> even then exposed to those who saw him, intending to announce judgments which they had lawlessly imposed upon the citizens. For they themselves often say that in the sickness, death approached, yet it did not come; but for six days, the body was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus, the ruin having slipped away, he lived for six years, and for six years the tyranny lasted. Agesilaus was king of the Lacedaemonians at that time. This Timotheus, having taken up the rule, so transformed it toward a milder and more democratic state that he was no longer called a tyrant, but a benefactor by those who observed his actions. He settled the debts of the men for himself, and for those in need of trade and other necessities of life, he provided without interest. He opened the prisons, not only for those who were worthy, but also for those who were undeserving, acting as a precise and humane judge. He was good in other respects and did not turn away from legal cases. He treated his brother Dionysius with kindness in these matters, and immediately made him a partner in the rule, not merely a successor. Furthermore, he conducted himself bravely in military affairs, being temperate in both body and soul, and was also grateful and capable in the resolution of battles.

<summary>This passage describes the physical suffering caused by a severe illness and transitions into a historical account of the transition of power from the tyrant Clearchus to Timotheus, who reformed the government into a more democratic and benevolent administration.</summary>
<keywords>Timotheus, Clearchus, Agesilaus, Dionysius, tyranny, democracy, medical symptoms, political reform, Lacedaemonians</keywords>

And new medicines of <term>erythron</term> <gloss>a red plant-based remedy</gloss> and <term>osmeon</term> <gloss>fragrant ointment</gloss> were applied, but as they reached the internal parts, they produced a more bitter result. As the flesh opened up, an enemy to an enemy, there flowed out a heavy and diseased mass in great quantity. Consequently, neither the discharge nor the physician's daring could withstand the surge of the rot, which appeared diseased and continuous. Constant slippages and eruptions consumed the entire body, from which <term>abyrtaniai</term> <gloss>pungent, acidic discharges</gloss> and twitching were given off, until the spirits of the disease, by the spreading of the flow, tore apart his very vitals.

Even so, Clearchus <note>Clearchus of Heraclea, a notorious tyrant known for his cruelty</note> did not fail to suggest to those watching him that he was paying the penalty for the lawless and cruel way he had treated the citizens. For they say that many times during the illness he sought death, but it did not come. Instead, for many days, he was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus, having lived a life of ruin, he slipped away after a reign of twelve years <note>literally: six and six</note>, during which time Agesilaus was king of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>.

When Timotheus <note>the son of Clearchus</note> took over the rule, he transformed it into something so much milder and more democratic that he was no longer called a tyrant, but was named a benefactor by his actions. He settled the debts of the men from his own resources and provided what was lacking to those in need for trade and their general livelihood. He did not only open the doors of the prisons, but also acted as a precise and philanthropic judge for those treated unworthily. In all other respects he was excellent and did not turn away from his responsibilities. Among these, he treated his brother Dionysius with great affection, immediately making him a partner in the government and later his successor. Furthermore, he engaged bravely in military actions, being temperate in both body and soul, and was sensible and effective in resolving conflicts of battle.

<summary>This page describes the gruesome death of the tyrant Clearchus of Heraclea from a wasting disease and the subsequent benevolent reign of his son Timotheus, who restored justice and financial stability.</summary>
<keywords>Clearchus of Heraclea, Timotheus, Agesilaus, tyranny, medical treatment, democratic reform, succession, Heraclea Pontica</keywords>

text:
For a carcinoma had grown between the groin and the scrotum, and as it developed inward, it became more severe. From this, fluids flowed out through the opened flesh, emitting a heavy and unbearable stench, such that neither the attendants nor the physicians could endure the intolerable foulness of the decay. Constant and sharp pains racked the entire body, by which he was surrendered to sleeplessness and spasms, until the spread of the disease reached the very internal organs and severed his life. Like Clearchus, he gave those who saw him at his end cause to believe that he was paying the penalty for the cruel and lawless way he had treated his citizens. Indeed, they say that during his illness he often prayed for death to come to him, but did not obtain it; instead, he was consumed for many days by the bitter and heavy disease, thus paying his debt. He lived for sixty-five years, of which his tyranny occupied seven. At that time, Agesilaus reigned over the Lacedaemonians.

Timotheus, having taken up the rule, transformed it toward a milder and more democratic form, so that he was no longer called a tyrant, but a benefactor and savior for his actions. For he paid off the debts to the creditors from his own funds, and he provided for those in need of capital for trade and other aspects of life without interest. He released from the prisons not only those who were unaccountable, but also those who were under accusation. He was a precise and at the same time humane judge, and in other matters he was upright and trusted in his dealings. Among these, he treated his brother Dionysius with paternal care in all things, and he immediately made him a partner in the government, and subsequently his successor. Furthermore, he conducted himself bravely in military affairs, being high-minded and noble in body and soul, yet he was also grateful and not ungracious regarding the resolution of battles.

<summary>This passage describes the agonizing death of a tyrant from a malignant tumor, interpreting his suffering as divine retribution for his past cruelty, and contrasts this with the subsequent, benevolent rule of Timotheus.</summary>
<keywords>Timotheus, tyranny, democracy, carcinoma, Agesilaus, Dionysius, Clearchus, historical ethics</keywords>

# Διοκλητιανός — Διονύσιος α

discovered the harmony used in bowls, in earthen vessels, which he struck with a stick. *The Sea* is the name of a hetaira <note>courtesan</note>, as Athenaeus says (p. 567).

**Diocletian**: Emperor of the Romans. Under him and his son-in-law Maximian, a most horrifying persecution against the Christians was stirred up. For they ordered that the churches of Christ be destroyed in every land and city and their divine scriptures be burned, and that the Christians who were found be compelled to sacrifice to the demons. Defeated by the multitude of the Christians being destroyed, they issued an edict that the Christians who were found should have their right eye gouged out, not only because of the pain, but also because of the disgrace, and that it was clear and alien to the Roman polity. Divine justice, pursuing them righteously, justly struck them down; one was slaughtered by the senate, and the other hanged himself.

This senseless and Christ-hating man, because of the memory and rage regarding the rebellions around the beginning of his reign in Egypt, did not use his power with moderation or kindness. Instead, he traversed Egypt, staining it with proscriptions and the murders of prominent men. At that time, he searched out and burned the books written by their ancient predecessors concerning the chemistry of silver and gold, so that wealth might no longer accrue to the Egyptians from such an art, and so that they, trusting in an abundance of money, might not rise up against the Romans hereafter. He was varied and cunning in character, but by his extreme intelligence and sharpness of mind, he often concealed the flaws of his own nature, attributing every cruel act to others. Yet he was diligent and swift in the application of what needed to be done. And he changed many of the imperial customs into a more arrogant style, contrary to the traditions established for the Romans. Io. Antioch. p. 834.

Diocletian and Maximian, having abandoned the imperial power, pursued the life of a private citizen. One arrived in the Illyrian city of Salona, and the other in the land of the Lucanians. Maximian, out of a longing for power, came to repentance, but Diocletian grew old in peace for three years, showing outstanding virtue, yet not departing at all from the Greek religion.

**diokōchē**: A delay of time; "Having defeated them in certain battles, he granted them a delay when they asked for it."

**diolisthainō**: To slip away. And *diolistheîn* <gloss>to escape</gloss>: "So as to escape the creditors" (*Clouds* 433), that is, to escape the money lenders.

**diolkē**: A hauling across <note>specifically of ships across an isthmus</note>.

**diólou**: Adverb, throughout the whole time.

**Diomeis**: A deme of the Aegeid tribe, from Diomus, the beloved of Heracles. Aristophanes (*Frogs* 663): "I thought about when the Heraclea in Diomeis takes place." The Heracleum is the temple of Heracles. And he speaks of the "Diomeian braggarts" (*Acharnians* 606), from the deme of Diomeis, which was named in this way from a certain Diomus.

**Diomedeia**: The island.

**Diomedeian epic**: A style of poetry.

**Diomedeian necessity**: A proverb, from Tydeus, or from the Thracian <note>King Diomedes of Thrace</note>, who compelled strangers to have intercourse with his daughters, whom he also allegorizes as horses, and then destroyed them. Others say that Diomedes and Odysseus, having stolen the Palladium, were returning at night, and Odysseus, following behind, wished to kill Diomedes. Seeing the shadow of the sword in the moonlight, Diomedes, fearing Odysseus, made him move forward, striking his back with his sword. It is applied to those doing something out of necessity. For this reason, he says (Eccl. 1021?) that Diomedes had man-eating horses.

**diómnutai**: Swears.

**diomologô**: With the accusative case <note>to agree upon something</note>.

**dîon**: Famous, noble.

**Dionysia**: A festival among the Athenians. And the proverb "From it, almost as much as from the Dionysia" (*Thesmophoriazusae* 754). It was the custom for the Attics to count the years and the remaining number from the Dionysia. And again (*Acharnians* 194): "O Dionysia, these smell of ambrosia and nectar." It is said of things worthy of acceptance.

**Dionysiades** of Mallus, son of Phylarchides, a tragic poet. He was one of the Pleiad, and among other things, he wrote *Characters* or *Comedy-lovers*, in which he announces the characters of the poets.

**Dionysius** of Alexandria, whose commentary on Solomon's *Ecclesiastes* I found, which is very eloquent.

<summary>This page details the reign of Diocletian, the etymology of Diomeis, the proverb of Diomedeian necessity, and the Dionysian festivals, concluding with a mention of the writer Dionysius of Alexandria.</summary>
