[context] Onesicritus, for example, says of Taprobane, that its magnitude is 5000 stadia,
without distinction of length or breadth, and that it is distant twenty days’ sail from the continent, but that it was a voyage performed with difficulty and danger by vessels with sails ill constructed, and built with prows at each end, but without holds and keels; that there are other islands between this and India, but that Taprobane lies farthest to the south; that there are found in the sea, about the island, animals of the cetaceous kind, in form like oxen, horses, and other land-animals.
The bosmorum, according to Onesicritus, is a kind of corn smaller than wheat, and grows in places situated between rivers. After it is threshed out, it is roasted; the threshers being previously bound by an oath not to carry it away unroasted from the threshing floor; a precaution to prevent the exportation of the seed.
India produces many singular trees. There is one whose branches incline downwards, and whose leaves are not less in size than a shield. Onesicritus, describing minutely the country of Musicanus, which he says is the most southerly part of India, relates, that there are some large trees the branches of which extend to the length even of twelve cubits. They then grow downwards, as though bent (by force), till they touch the earth, where they penetrate and take root like layers. They next shoot upwards and form a trunk. They again grow as we have described, bending downwards, and implanting one layer after another, and in the above order, so that one tree forms a long shady roof, like a tent, supported by many pillars. In speaking of the size of the trees, he says their trunks could scarcely be clasped by five men.
The account of Onesicritus confirms the facts of the rising of the rivers and of the absence of land breezes. He says that the sea-shore is swampy, particularly near the mouths of rivers, on account of the mud, tides, and the force of the winds blowing from the sea.
This would not be admitted by the followers of Aristobulus, who say that the plains are not watered by rain. Onesicritus, however, thinks that rain-water is the cause of the peculiar properties of animals, and alleges in proof, that the colour of foreign herds which drink of it is changed to that of the native animals.
This is a just remark; but it is not proper to attribute to the power of the water merely the cause of the black complexion and the woolly hair of the Ethiopians,
[context] and yet he censures Theodectes, who refers these peculiarities to the effects of the sun, in these words,

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: Nearchus says a four-month voyage</meta> stadia, not defining length or width, but saying it is a voyage of twenty days from the mainland. He says the ships sail poorly because they are badly equipped with sails and are constructed without <term>en koiliois metron</term> <gloss>rib-frames</gloss> or keels. There are other islands between it and India, though it is the furthest south. He claims amphibious sea monsters live around it, some resembling oxen, some horses, and some other land animals. Regarding Taprobane <gloss>Sri Lanka</gloss>, see von Bohlen, page 29 and following.

### 14.

Strabo, Book 15, page 692: Concerning <term>bosmoron</term> <gloss>a type of grain</gloss>, which Onesicritus says is a grain smaller than wheat and grows in the lands between rivers. It is roasted when it is threshed, and the people take an oath not to carry it away from the threshing floor unroasted, so that the seed cannot be exported.
Compare Diodorus, Book 2, chapter 36, where the books show the spelling "bosporon." See Stephanus's Thesaurus under "bosmoron." — "grain": so says the author of the Epitome; the manuscripts of Strabo say "septos."

### 15.

Strabo, Book 15, page 694: India produces many remarkable trees, among which is one with branches that lean downward, and leaves no smaller than a shield. Onesicritus, going into more detail about the territory of <term>Musicanus</term> <gloss>a ruler in the Indus valley</gloss>, which he says is the southernmost part of India, describes certain large trees whose branches grow upward for twelve cubits, then take the rest of their growth downward, as if bent, until they touch the ground. Then, spreading through the earth, they take root like layers, and then rising up, they form a trunk. From this, they bend down again in the same manner of growth, making another layer, and then another, and so on in succession, so that from a single tree a long sunshade is formed,

<column-break/>

resembling a tent with many pillars. He also mentions the size of the trees, saying the trunks are so large that five men can hardly embrace them.
Compare Aristobulus, Fragment 30, where it is said that Aristobulus described trees of such magnitude that fifty horsemen could rest under the shade of one; Strabo adds: "but this man (Onesicritus) says four hundred." Nearchus, Fragment 40; Diodorus, Book 17, chapter 90.

### 16.

Strabo, Book 15, page 693: The fact that the rivers overflow and the land winds do not blow is confirmed by what was said by Onesicritus. For he says the coastline of India is swampy, especially at the mouths of the rivers, because of the silt, the floods, and the dominance of the sea winds.
"The argument of this fragment confirms what was narrated by Aristobulus regarding the flooding of Indian rivers in Fragment 29." — GEIER. See below, Fragment 20.

### 17.

Strabo, Book 15, page 695: Regarding this (the idea that water from the clouds is already decocted when it is poured out), those around Aristobulus would not agree, as they claim it does not rain on the plains. But to Onesicritus, it seems that this water is the cause of the physical peculiarities in animals. He offers as evidence that the colors of foreign livestock change to the local color when they drink it. This point is well made; but he is no longer correct when he places the cause of the Ethiopians being black and curly-haired simply in the water, and

<column-break/>

reproaches Theodectes for attributing the cause to the sun itself, as that author says:

<note>original: 
"Whose sun at the near-border changing
a dark flower of soot leaped forth
into men's bodies and curled their hair
with the contracts of fire that stunted their forms."</note>

Yet Onesicritus might have some reasoning; for he says the sun is no closer to the Ethiopians than to others, but is rather more directly overhead <term>kata katheton</term> and for this reason burns more. Thus, he says it is not well said that the sun is "near-bordering" to them, since it is at an equal distance from everyone. He also argues that heat is not the cause of such a condition, since it is not so for those in the womb, whom the sun does not touch.

<note>continues from previous page</note> of the islands, without specifying length or breadth, but stating the voyage from the mainland takes twenty days, and that the ships sail poorly, being badly rigged and constructed without <term>engoilion metron</term> <gloss>internal ribs/frames</gloss>. He says there are other islands between it and India, and that this one is the southernmost. Amphibious sea-monsters are found around it, some resembling oxen, others horses, and others other land animals. <note>original: "De Taprobane v. Bohlen. l. l. p. 29 sqq."</note>

14.

Strabo XV, p. 692: Regarding the <term>bosmoron</term>, which Onesicritus says is a type of grain smaller than wheat, it grows in the lands between the rivers. It is roasted when threshed, and the people swear not to carry it away from the threshing floor unheated, so that the seed may not be exported.
<note>Cf. Diodor. II, 36, where the manuscripts present "bosporon." See Steph. Thes. v. "bosmoron." — "sitos" <gloss>grain</gloss> is the reading of the author of the Epitome; the manuscripts of Strabo read "septos."</note>

15.

Strabo XV, p. 694: India indeed nurtures many paradoxical trees, among which is one that has its branches pointing downward, with leaves no smaller than a shield. Onesicritus, describing more curiously the things in the land of Musicanus, which he says is the southernmost part of India, relates that there are certain large trees whose branches grow to twelve cubits, and then take a downward direction, as if bending until they touch the ground. Then, spreading along the ground, they take root like layers, and then rising up, they form a trunk. From this, again, bending down in the same manner as they grew, they make another layer, and then another, and so on in succession, so that from a single tree a long shade is formed, similar to a tent with many columns. He also speaks of the size of the trees, such that the trunks are difficult for five men to encompass.
<note>Cf. Aristobul. fr. 30, where, when Aristobulus is said to have narrated that there are trees of such magnitude that 50 horsemen can rest under the shade of one, Strabo adds: "This man (i.e., Onesicritus, who was spoken of in the preceding) says four hundred." Nearch. fr. 40; Diodor. XVII, 90.</note>

16.

Strabo XV, p. 693: That the rivers overflow and that the winds from the land do not blow is also agreed upon by what was said by Onesicritus. For he says that the coastline (of India) is marshy, especially at the mouths of the rivers, because of the silt, the tides, and the prevalence of sea winds.
<note>"The arguments of this fragment confirm what was narrated by Aristobulus regarding the inundations of the Indian rivers, fr. 29." GEIER. Cf. infra fr. 20.</note>

17.

Strabo XV, p. 695: This (i.e., that water is already poured down from the clouds) those around Aristobulus (fr. 29) would not concede, claiming that the plains do not receive rain. But to Onesicritus, this water seems to be the cause of the peculiarities in animals, and he brings as evidence that the colors of foreign livestock that drink it change to the local color. This, then, is well said; but he is no longer correct in attributing the cause of the Ethiopians being black and curly-haired to the waters alone.

He says there are other islands between it and India, and that this one is the southernmost. Amphibious sea-monsters are found around it, some resembling oxen, others horses, and others other land animals. <note>original: "De Taprobane v. Bohlen. l. l. p. 29 sqq."</note>

14.

Strabo XV, p. 692: Regarding the <term>bosmoron</term>, which Onesicritus says is a type of grain smaller than wheat, it grows in the lands between the rivers. It is roasted when threshed, and the people swear not to carry it away from the threshing floor unheated, so that the seed may not be exported.
<note>Cf. Diodor. II, 36, where the manuscripts present "bosporon." See Steph. Thes. v. "bosmoron." — "sitos" <gloss>grain</gloss> is the reading of the author of the Epitome; the manuscripts of Strabo read "septos."</note>

15.

Strabo XV, p. 694: India indeed nurtures many paradoxical trees, among which is one that has its branches pointing downward, with leaves no smaller than a shield. Onesicritus, describing more curiously the things in the land of Musicanus, which he says is the southernmost part of India, relates that there are certain large trees whose branches grow to twelve cubits, and then take a downward direction, as if bending until they touch the ground. Then, spreading along the ground, they take root like layers, and then rising up, they form a trunk. From this, again, bending down in the same manner as they grew, they make another layer, and then another, and so on in succession, so that from a single tree a long shade is formed, similar to a tent with many columns. He also speaks of the size of the trees, such that the trunks are difficult for five men to encompass.
<note>Cf. Aristobul. fr. 30, where, when Aristobulus is said to have narrated that there are trees of such magnitude that 50 horsemen can rest under the shade of one, Strabo adds: "This man (i.e., Onesicritus, who was spoken of in the preceding) says four hundred." Nearch. fr. 40; Diodor. XVII, 90.</note>

16.

Strabo XV, p. 693: That the rivers overflow and that the winds from the land do not blow is also agreed upon by what was said by Onesicritus. For he says that the coastline (of India) is marshy, especially at the mouths of the rivers, because of the silt, the tides, and the prevalence of sea winds.
<note>"The arguments of this fragment confirm what was narrated by Aristobulus regarding the inundations of the Indian rivers, fr. 29." GEIER. Cf. infra fr. 20.</note>

17.

Strabo XV, p. 695: This (i.e., that water is already poured down from the clouds) those around Aristobulus (fr. 29) would not concede, claiming that the plains do not receive rain. But to Onesicritus, this water seems to be the cause of the peculiarities in animals, and he brings as evidence that the colors of foreign livestock that drink it change to the local color. This, then, is well said; but he is no longer correct in attributing the cause of the Ethiopians being black and curly-haired to the waters alone.

stades, without defining its length or width, and that it is a twenty-day voyage from the mainland. However, he says the ships sail poorly because they are badly fitted with sails and are constructed without <term>belly-ribs</term> <gloss>internal structural frames or keels</gloss> to support them. He also states there are other islands between it and India, but that this one lies furthest to the south. He claims amphibious sea monsters live around it, some resembling oxen, others horses, and others various land animals. <note>Regarding Taprobane, see Bohlen, in the place cited, page 29 and following.</note>

14.

Strabo, Book 15, page 692: Concerning <term>bosmorum</term> <gloss>a type of Indian grain, perhaps millet or a variety of wheat</gloss>, which Onesicritus says is a grain smaller than wheat and grows in the lands between rivers. It is roasted after being threshed, and the people take an oath not to carry it away from the threshing floor unroasted, so that the seed cannot be exported.
<note>Compare Diodorus, Book 2, Chapter 36, where the manuscripts show the word as "bosporon." See Stephanus's Thesaurus under the entry "bosmoron." The word "grain" is used by the author of the Epitome; the manuscripts of Strabo read "septos."</note>

15.

Strabo, Book 15, page 694: India nourishes many wonderful trees, among which is one that has branches leaning downwards, with leaves no smaller than a shield. Onesicritus, describing in greater detail the things in the land of Musicanus <note>a ruler in Upper Sindh</note>, which he says are the southernmost parts of India, relates that there are certain great trees whose branches grow to twelve cubits <note>about 18 feet</note>. Then the rest of their growth takes a downward turn, bending until they touch the ground. Then, spreading out under the earth, they take root like layers <note>cuttings used for propagation</note>, and then rising up, they form a trunk. From this, after growing, they bend down again in the same way to make another layer, and then another, and so on, so that from a single tree a long shaded area is formed, like a tent with many pillars. He also mentions the sizes of the trees, saying the trunks are so large that five men can hardly reach around them.
<note>Compare Aristobulus, fragment 30, where Aristobulus is said to have related that trees are of such magnitude that 50 horsemen can rest under the shade of one; Strabo adds: "but this man (Onesicritus) says four hundred." See also Nearchus, fragment 40; Diodorus, Book 17, Chapter 90.</note>

<column-break/>

16.

Strabo, Book 15, page 693: The flooding of the rivers and the fact that the land-winds do not blow is also confirmed by what was said by Onesicritus. For he says the coastline of India is marshy and shallow, especially at the mouths of the rivers, because of the silt, the tides, and the prevalence of winds from the sea.
<note>Geier remarks: "The subject of this fragment confirms what was narrated by Aristobulus concerning the floods of the Indian rivers in fragment 29." See also fragment 20 below.</note>

17.

Strabo, Book 15, page 695: Regarding this (that is, that water already "cooked" <note>warmed or processed by the sun</note> falls from the clouds), Aristobulus and his followers would not agree, as they claim the plains do not receive rain. But to Onesicritus, it seems that this water is the cause of the physical peculiarities in animals. He offers as proof that the color of foreign livestock changes to the local color when they drink it. This point is well made; however, he is no longer correct when he places the cause of the Ethiopians being black and curly-haired solely in the water.

The Phocian Medeon is on the Crisaean Gulf, at a distance of one hundred and sixty stadia from Boeotia, whereas the Boeotian Medeon, which was named after it, is near Onchestus at the base of the mountain Phoenicius; and from this fact its name has been changed to Phoenicis. This mountain is also called a part of the Theban territory; but by some both Medeon and Ocalea are called a part of the territory of Haliartus.
Homer then goes on to say: “Copae, and Eutresis, and Thisbe abounding in doves.” Concerning Copae I have already spoken. It lies towards the north on Lake Copais; and the others around the lake are these: Acraephiae, Phoenicis, Onchestus, Haliartus, Ocalea, Alalcomenae, Tilphusium, Coroneia. In early times, at least, the lake had no common name, but was called by different names corresponding to the several settlements lying on it, as, for instance, Copais from Copae, Haliartis from Haliartus, and so in the case of the rest of the settlements; but later the whole lake was called Copais, this name prevailing over all others; for the region of Copae forms the deepest recess of the lake. Pindar calls this lake Cephissis; at any rate, he places near it the spring Tilphossa, which flows at the foot of Mount Tilphossius near Haliartus and Alalcomenae, near which latter is the tomb of Teiresias; and here, too, is the temple of the Tilphossian Apollo.
Next in order after Copae Homer names Eutresis, a small village of the Thespians, where Zethus and Amphion are said to have lived before they reigned over Thebes. Thisbe is now called Thisbae; the place is inhabited and is situated slightly above the sea, bordering on the territory of the Thespians and on that of Coroneia; and it, too, lies at the foot of Helicon on the south; and it has a seaport situated on a rocky place, which abounds in doves, in reference to which the poet says, “Thisbe abounding in doves.” From here to Sicyon is a voyage of one hundred and sixty stadia.
Next Homer names Coroneia, Haliartus,
[context] Plataeae, and Glissas.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>The Phocian <note>original: Phokikos</note> is in the Crissaean Gulf, at a distance of one hundred and sixty stadia from Boeotia. The Boeotian <note>original: Boiotiakos</note> is named after it, and is near Onchestus, situated below Mount Phoenicium, from which it has also been renamed Phoenicis. This area is also said to belong to the territory of Thebes, though <unclear>by some</unclear> it is assigned to Haliartus, as are Medeon and Ocalea.

<margin>27</margin> Next, the poet <note>Homer, in the Catalogue of Ships</note> says: "Copae, and Eutresis, and Thisbe, the haunt of many doves." Regarding Copae, it has already been mentioned; it lies to the north on Lake Copais. The other settlements around the lake are these: Acraephiae, Phoenicis, Onchestus, Haliartus, Ocalea, Alalcomenae, Tilphossium, and Coroneia. In <margin>C. 411</margin> ancient times, the lake did not have a single common name, but was named after each individual settlement situated by it: it was called Copais after Copae, Haliartis after Haliartus, and so on for the others. Later, the whole was called Copais, which became the dominant name because that location is the deepest part of the basin. Pindar calls this lake Cephissis. At any rate, he places the Tilphossa spring flowing beneath Mount Tilphossium near Haliartus and Alalcomenae, where the monument of Tiresias <note>the famous blind seer of Thebes</note> is located; there also is the temple of <unclear>Tilphossian Apollo</unclear>.

<margin>28</margin> Following Copae, the poet places Eutresis, a small village of the Thespians. They say that Zethus and Amphion <note>the twin founders of Thebes</note> lived here before they became kings of Thebes. Thisbe is now called Thisbae; the place is inhabited slightly above the sea, bordering the territory of Thespiae and Coroneia, and it also lies at the southern foot of Mount Helicon. It has a rocky harbor full of doves, which is why the poet calls it "Thisbe, the haunt of many doves." The voyage from there to Sicyon is one hundred and sixty stadia.

and the Phocian one is on the Crisaean Gulf, one hundred and sixty stadia distant from Boeotia, while the Boeotian one has been named after it. It is near Onchestus, below Mount Phoenicius, from which its name has also been changed to Phoenicis. This place too is said to belong to the Theban territory, but by some both Medeon and Ocalea are said to belong to the territory of Haliartus.

<margin>27</margin> Next he says: "Copae and Eutresis and Thisbe, abounding in doves." <note>Homer, Iliad 2.502, from the Catalogue of Ships</note> Now Copae has already been discussed. It lies toward the north, on Lake Copais. The other towns around the lake are these: Acraephiae, Phoenicis, Onchestus, Haliartus, Ocalea, Alalcomenae, Tilphusium, Coroneia. And in ancient times, at least, <margin>C. 411</margin> there was no common name for the lake, but it was called by a different name after each settlement beside it: Copais from Copae, Haliartis from Haliartus, and so on for the others. Later the whole was called Copais, the name that prevailed, for this district is the deepest hollow. Pindar calls this lake Cephissis as well. At any rate he sets beside it the spring Tilphossa, which flows below Mount Tilphossius near Haliartus and Alalcomenae, and at which is the tomb of Teiresias. In the same place is also the sanctuary of the Tilphossian Apollo.

<margin>28</margin> The poet <note>Homer</note> places Eutresis, a small village of the Thespians, next after Copae. Here they say Zethus and Amphion lived before they became kings of Thebes. As for Thisbe, it is now called Thisbae. The place is inhabited a little above the sea, bordering on the Thespians and on the territory of Coroneia, and it too lies at the foot of Helicon on its southern side. It has a rocky seaport full of doves, on account of which the poet says "and Thisbe, abounding in doves." From here the voyage to Sicyon is one hundred and sixty stadia.

reference.located: Pausanias 4.9.4 (oracle) – 4.10.4 (Euphaes wounded)
reference.edition_note: the reference translates the Spiro/Loeb text; the page is the 1583 Sylburg-era printing, which gives the oracle as five iambic lines (modern text: hexameter/iambic mix) and reads ἔτει ἕκτῳ (Jones: 'five years after')
reference.coverage_note: full; the oracle's opening words may stand on the preceding page (page opens mid-oracle with Κόρῳ ἄχραντον), but the English oracle is given whole; page ends on λιποψυχήσαντα
reference.text:
Ye shall sacrifice a pure maiden to the gods below, appointed by lot of the blood of the sons of Aepytus, and slay her by night. But if that ye cannot do, offer a maiden from another house, if the father gives her freely for the slaughter.
When the god declared this, all the maidens of the house of the Aepytidae forthwith cast lots, and the lot fell on the daughter of Lyciscus. But Epebolus the seer forbade them to offer her, for she was not the daughter of Lyciscus, but the woman who was married to Lyciscus being unable to bear a child had palmed off the girl as hers. While Epebolus was making this declaration, Lyciscus took the girl away and deserted to Sparta. The Messenians were in despair when they saw that Lyciscus had fled; thereupon Aristodemus, a son of the house of the Aepytidae, of higher standing than Lyciscus both in reputation and in war, freely offered his daughter for the sacrifice. But human affairs and human purpose above all are obscured by fate, just as the mud of a river hides a pebble; for when Aristodemus was striving his utmost to save Messene, fate set this obstacle in his path. A Messenian, whose name is not recorded, was in love with the daughter of' Aristodemus, and was already about to make her his wife. He at first disputed the rights of Aristodemus over the girl for Aristodemus, since he had betrothed her to himself had no further rights over the girl, but he to whom she was betrothed had greater rights than the father. Next, when he saw that this was of no avail, he had recourse to a shameless plea, that the girl was with child by him. At last he drove Aristodemus to such a fury of passion that lie killed his daughter; then cutting her open he showed that she was not pregnant. Epebolus, who was present, ordered another man to come forward and offer his daughter, for the daughter of Aristodemus was of no avail to them dead; for the father had murdered her, not offered her to the gods whom the Pythia ordained. When the seer said this, the multitude of the Messenians rushed on the girl's lover to kill him, since he had fixed the guilt of bloodshed on Aristodemus to no purpose, and had made their hopes of safety doubtful. But as he was a close friend of Euphaes, Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle was fulfilled by the death of the girl and that the deed done by Aristodemus sufficed for them. When he said this, all the members of the house of the Aepytidae said that he spoke truth, for each was eager to be rid of the terror threatening his daughter. The people took the advice of' the king and broke up the assembly and thereupon turned to sacrifices to the gods and feasting. But the Lacedaemonians, when they heard the oracle given to the Messenians, were in despair, both they and their kings, and for the future shrank from offering battle.But five years after the escape of Lyciscus from Ithome, the victims being auspicious, the Lacedaemonians marched against Ithome. The Cretans were no longer with them. The allies of the Messenians also were late, for the Spartans had now incurred the suspicion of others of the Peloponnesians, especially of the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to come without the knowledge of the Lacedaemonians, and by private enterprise rather than by public declaration. The expedition was openly proclaimed among the Arcadians, but they did not arrive either. For the Messenians were induced by the credit placed in the oracle to face the risk without allies. This engagement did not differ in most points from the first, as on this occasion too daylight failed the combatants, but they record that on neither side was a wing or division broken, as they did not maintain the formation in which they were originally posted, champions on either side meeting in the middle, and there supporting the whole combat. Euphaes, who showed more eagerness than a king should and recklessly attacked Theopompus' bodyguard, received a number of mortal wounds.
When he swooned and fell,
[context] the Lacedaemonians did their utmost to drag him into their own ranks, as he still breathed.

<header>PAUSANIAS</header>
<meta>catchword: santa</meta>

> To the gods below, a pure maiden,
> Chosen by lot from the blood of the Aepytidae,
> Sacrifice in the slaughters of the night.
> But if she fail the slaughter, then from another,
> Sacrifice one given voluntarily to the death.

After the god had revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the virgins who were of the race of the Aepytidae; and the lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Epebolus the seer forbade her to be sacrificed, saying it was not right, for she was not the daughter of Lyciscus; rather, the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had substituted the child as her own. While he was explaining the circumstances regarding her, Lyciscus took the girl and deserted to Sparta. When the Messenians were disheartened upon learning that Lyciscus had fled, Aristodemus—a man of the Aepytid line, more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and especially in matters of war—offered his own daughter to be sacrificed voluntarily. But fate often conceals human eagerness in such matters, much like the mud of a river catching a voting-pebble; and so, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, fate brought the following obstacle upon him. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus, and was then on the point of taking her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that since the girl had been betrothed to him, Aristodemus was no longer her master, and that he, as her betrothed, had more authority over her than the father. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless story: that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterwards, he cut her open and showed that she was not with child. 

Epebolus, being present, ordered that someone else should give a daughter; for he said that the death of Aristodemus's daughter had profited them nothing, because her father had murdered her, but had not sacrificed her to the gods whom the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of the Messenians rushed to kill the girl's suitor, on the grounds that he had brought a needless pollution upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of safety uncertain. But this man was a very close friend of Euphaës. Euphaës persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had its fulfillment in the girl's death, and that what had been done by Aristodemus was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those who were of the Aepytid race said that he spoke the truth; for the fear concerning their own daughters was ended, and each man was eager for it to be so. The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly, and from there they turned to sacrifices and a festival to the gods. 

The Lacedaemonians, hearing of the oracle that had come to the Messenians, were also disheartened—both they and their kings—being hesitant for the future and reluctant to begin a battle. In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (as the sacrifices had become favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them, and the allies of the Messenians also arrived too late. For the Spartans were already held in suspicion by others of the Peloponnesians, and especially by the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and by private arrangement rather than by public decree; as for the Arcadians, the expedition had been openly forbidden to them, yet they were not present either. For the expectation of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. For the most part, the battle was not much different from the previous one; the day failed them while they were still fighting. They do not record that either wing or any company was forced back, for they say that the ranks did not remain as they had been stationed at the beginning; rather, the best men from both sides came together in the center, and there the whole weight of the labor fell. For Euphaës, showing more spirit than was expected even of a king, and pressing unsparingly upon those around Theopompus, received many incurable wounds. Having fainted...

<language>Ancient Greek</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>ΠΑΥΣΑΝΙΟΥ</header>
<meta>catchword: σαντα</meta>

> Κόρῳ ἄχραντον νερτέροισι δαίμοσι,
> Κλήρῳ λαχοῦσαν Αἰπυτιδῶν ἀφ’ αἵματος,
> Θυηπολεῖτε νυκτέροισιν ἐν σφαγαῖς.
> Ἢν δ’ σφαγῇ τε, καὶ παρ’ ἀλλοίῳ, τότε
> Θύειν, διδόντας ἐς σφαγὴν ἑκουσίως.

Ταῦτα τοῦ θεοῦ δηλώσαντος, αὐτίκα ἐκληροῦντο ὅσαι παρθένοι τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν γένους ἦσαν. καὶ ἐπελάμβανε γὰρ Λυκίσκου θυγατέρα ὁ κλῆρος. Ταύτην Ἐπήβολος ὁ μάντις ἀπηγόρευεν ὡς οὐ δέοι θύειν· οὐ γὰρ εἴη Λυκίσκου· τὴν δὲ γυναῖκα ἣ Λυκίσκῳ συνῴκησεν, ὡς τεκεῖν οὐκ οἵα τε ἦν, ἐν τούτῳ τὴν παῖδα ὑποβαλέσθαι. ἐν ὅσῳ δὲ οὗτος διεδίδασκε τὰ ἐς αὐτὴν, ἐν τοσῷδε ὁ Λυκίσκος ἐπαγόμενος ἅμα καὶ τὴν παρθένον ηὐτομόλησεν ἐς Σπάρτην. ἐχόντων δὲ ἀθύμως τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὡς Λυκίσκον ἀποδράντα ᾔσθοντο, ἐνταῦθα σφίσιν Ἀριστόδημος ἀνὴρ καὶ γένος τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν, καὶ Λυκίσκου τῇ τε ἄλλῃ δόξῃ, καὶ τὰ ἐς πόλεμον ἐπιφανέστερος, ἐδίδου τὴν θυγατέρα ἑκὼν θῦσαι. τὰ δὲ ἀνθρώπων οὐχ ἥκιστα τὸ πρόθυμον πεπρωμένη κατὰ ταῦτα ἐπικρύπτει, καὶ ἡ ψηφίδα ἐπιλαβοῦσα ἰλὺς ποταμοῦ. ὅπου καὶ τότε Ἀριστοδήμῳ διασῶσαι Μεσσηνίους ἀγώνισμα ποιουμένῳ, τὸ ἐμπόδιον ἐπήγαγε τοιόνδε. ἀνὴρ τῶν Μεσσηνίων (τὸ δὲ ὄνομα οὐ λέγουσιν) ἐρῶν ἔτυχε τῆς Ἀριστοδήμου θυγατρός. τότε δὲ ἤδη ἔμελλε γυναῖκα ἄξεσθαι. οὗτος κατ’ ἀρχὰς ἐς ἀμφισβήτησιν Ἀριστοδήμῳ καθίστατο, ἐκεῖνον μὲν ἐγγυήσαντά οἱ μηκέτι εἶναι κύριον τῆς παιδός, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγγυησάμενος κυριώτερος ἐκείνου γίνεσθαι. δεύτερα δὲ ὡς τοῦτο οὐχ ἑώρα οἱ κατορθούμενον, ἐπ’ ἀναίσχυντον τρέπεται λόγον, συγγενέσθαι τε τῇ παιδί, καὶ τεκύειν ἐξ αὐτῆς. τέλος δὲ ἐς τοσοῦτον Ἀριστόδημον προήγαγεν, ὡς ἐκμανέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ θυμοῦ τὴν θυγατέρα ἀποκτεῖναι. μετὰ δὲ ἀνέτεμνε, καὶ ἐπεδείκνυεν αὐτὴν οὐκ ἔχουσαν ἐν γαστρί. παρὼν δὲ Ἐπήβολος, ἐκέλευεν ἄλλον τινὰ τὴν θυγατέρα ἐπιδώσοντα γενέσθαι· τῆς γὰρ τοῦ Ἀριστοδήμου, πλέον αὖ σφισιν ἀποθανόσης οὐδέν· φονεῦσαι γὰρ τὸν πατέρα αὐτὴν, θεοῖς δὲ οἷς ἡ Πυθία προσέταξεν, οὐ θῦσαι. τοιαῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ μάντεως, τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὥρμησεν ἀποκτενοῦντες τὸν μνηστῆρα τῆς παιδός, ὡς Ἀριστοδήμῳ τε μίασμα εἰκαῖον προσάψαντα, καὶ σφίσι τῆς σωτηρίας τὴν ἐλπίδα ἀμφίβολον πεποιηκότα. ἦν δὲ ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος ἐς τὰ μάλιστα τῷ Εὐφάῃ φίλος. πείθει τοὺς Μεσσηνίους Εὐφάης, τόν τε χρησμὸν ἔχειν τέλος ἀποθανούσης τῆς παιδός, καὶ σφίσιν ἀποχρᾶν τὸ ὑπὸ Ἀριστοδήμου πεποιημένον. λέγοντος δὲ ταῦτα, ἔφασαν τὰ ὄντα λέγειν ὅσοι τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν γένους ἦσαν· ἀπεπαύετο γὰρ σφίσι ὁ δέος ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ θυγατρί, ἕκαστός τε ἔσπευδε, καὶ οἱ μὲν τῶν βασιλέων τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι, τὴν ἐκκλησίαν διαλύουσιν· καὶ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς πρός τε θυσίας καὶ θεῶν ἑορτὴν τρέπονται. Λακεδαιμόνιοι δὲ ἀκούσαντες τὸν γενόμενον Μεσσηνίοις χρησμόν, ἀθύμως διέκειντο καὶ αὐτοί, καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς, ἔς τε τὰ λοιπὰ καὶ ἀρχὴν ὀκνοῦντες μάχης. Ἔτει δὲ ἕκτῳ μετὰ τὸν ἐξ Ἰθώμης Λυκίσκου δρασμὸν οἱ Λακεδαιμόνιοι (τὰ γὰρ ἱερὰ ἐγίνετο αὐτοῖς αἴσια) στρατεύουσιν ἐπὶ τὴν Ἰθώμην. οἱ δὲ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι παρόντες σφίσιν ἔτυχον. ὑστέρησαν δὲ καὶ οἱ τῶν Μεσσηνίων σύμμαχοι. δι’ ὑποψίας γὰρ οἱ Σπαρτιᾶται καὶ ἄλλοις ἤδη Πελοποννησίων, καὶ Ἀρκάσιν ἦσαν καὶ Ἀργείοις μάλιστα. καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἀργεῖοι κρύφα ἔμελλον τῶν Λακεδαιμονίων ἀφίξεσθαι, καὶ ἰδίᾳ δὴ μᾶλλον μετὰ δόγματος κοινοῦ. τοῖς δὲ Ἀρκάσιν ἡ στρατεία μὲν ἀπείρητο ἐκ τοῦ φανεροῦ. παρέτυχον δὲ οὐδ’ οὗτοι. τοὺς γὰρ Μεσσηνίους καὶ ἄνευ συμμάχων κινδυνεῦσαι προήγαγεν ἡ δόξα τοῦ χρησμοῦ. τὰ μὲν οὖν πολλὰ οὐδέν τι ἐγένετο διάφορα, ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς προτέρας μάχης· ἥ τε ἡμέρα καὶ τότε μαχομένους προαπέλιπεν. οὐ μὲν τοι βιασθῆναί γε οὐδέτερον κέρας, ἢ καὶ λόχον μνημονεύουσιν. ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τῷ τάξιν ὡς ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἐτάχθησαν, συμμεῖναί φασιν· ἀλλ’ ἀφ’ ἑκατέρων τοὺς ἀρίστους συνελθόντας ἐς μέσον, ταύτῃ τὸν πάντα ἔχειν πόνον. ὁ γὰρ Εὐφάης πλέον τι ἢ βασιλέα εἰκὸς ἦν, προθυμούμενος, καὶ ἀφειδῶς τοῖς περὶ τὸν Θεόπομπον ἐγκείμενος, θαύματά τε καὶ πολλά τε οὐκ ἰάσιμα λαμβάνει. λιποψυχήσαντα

defects.detail: 'The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly' for 'οἱ μὲν τοῦ βασιλέως τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι' (they, persuaded by the king's advice)
'The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly' for 'οἱ μὲν τῶν βασιλέων τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι' (they, obeying the king's advice)
'But if she fail the slaughter, then from another' for 'Ἢν δ’ σφαγῇ τε [σφαλῆτε], καὶ παρ’ ἀλλοίῳ' (if you fail, from another house)
'The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly' for 'οἱ μὲν τῶν βασιλέων τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι' (they, obeying the king's advice)
'But if she fail the slaughter, then from another' for garbled 'Ἢν δ’ σφαγῇ τε, καὶ παρ’ ἀλλοίῳ' (ref: if you cannot, a maiden from another house)
'the mud of a river catching a voting-pebble' for 'ψηφίδα ἐπιλαβοῦσα ἰλὺς ποταμοῦ' (mud hiding a pebble)

reasons.j1: [served] follows the page sentence by sentence from the oracle to 'λιποψυχήσαντα' with nothing dropped. 'sixth year' matches the source's 'Ἔτει δὲ ἕκτῳ' (reference has five years) and 'openly forbidden' matches the source's 'ἀπείρητο' (reference 'proclaimed' reflects another reading), so neither is charged. Slips: the subject of the assembly's dissolution (kings instead of the people heeding the king) and the oracle's fourth line.
reasons.j2: [served] renders the whole page in order, 'sixth year' = Ἔτει ἕκτῳ, ends on 'Having fainted' = λιποψυχήσαντα; 'openly forbidden' to the Arcadians follows the OCR's ἀπείρητο (the reference's edition has 'proclaimed'), so not charged; slips are the kings made subject of πειθόμενοι and the oracle's fourth line.

served.note: Clear modern narrative prose, oracle set as verse lines; ambiguity n/a; no notes or brackets, proverb and garbled oracle line smoothed without flag, ends on an ellipsis.

reference.note: Fluent, slightly archaic historiographic voice with oracle in 'Ye shall' prose; scan typos ('lie killed'); miasma flattened to guilt; ambiguity n/a; nothing flagged.

six_dimensions.choice: The oracle is kept as lineated verse in A ("Sacrifice in the slaughters of the night") but recast as archaic prose in B ("and slay her by night").

reference.edition_note: the reference translates the Spiro/Loeb text; the page is the 1583 Sylburg-era printing, which gives the oracle as five iambic lines (modern text: hexameter/iambic mix) and reads ἔτει ἕκτῳ (Jones: 'five years after')

text:
PAUSANIAS

> To the nether gods, a maiden undefiled,
> Chosen by lot from the Aepytid blood,
> Sacrifice in the slaughter of the night.
> But if this fails, and another be slain,
> Then offer those who give themselves to die.

When the god had declared these things, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens of the Aepytid line. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Ephebolus the seer forbade this, claiming she ought not to be sacrificed, for she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; rather, the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had passed the girl off as her own. While he was explaining these matters, Lyciscus took the maiden and deserted to Sparta. The Messenians were disheartened when they learned of Lyciscus’s flight. At this point, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage and more distinguished than Lyciscus in reputation and military matters, voluntarily offered his own daughter for the sacrifice. Human affairs are often obscured by fate, and the lot was covered by river mud. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, an obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name is not recorded) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. He was about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus no longer had authority over the girl, and that by betrothing her himself, he had become more authoritative than the father. When he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. In the end, he drove Aristodemus to such a state of madness and rage that he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and showed that she was not pregnant. Ephebolus, who was present, ordered that someone else be provided to be sacrificed; for the death of Aristodemus’s daughter had gained them nothing, as the father had killed her, but they had not sacrificed her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unholy stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man had been a very close friend of Euphais. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl’s death, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the Aepytid line agreed that he spoke the truth. The fear they felt regarding the daughter ceased, and everyone hastened to act. The kings, persuaded by this advice, dismissed the assembly, and from that point, they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves disheartened, and the kings hesitated to begin the battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens were favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to be no longer present with them. The allies of the Messenians also arrived late. The Spartans were already suspicious of other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly, without the knowledge of the Lacedaemonians, and more privately by a common decree. The campaign had been forbidden to the Arcadians openly. They did not appear either. The reputation of the oracle had encouraged the Messenians to take the risk even without allies. For the most part, nothing happened that was different from the previous battle; the day ended while they were still fighting. They do not record that either wing was forced back, nor do they mention any ambush. They say that they did not remain in the formation in which they were originally drawn up, but that the best men from both sides met in the middle, and the entire struggle took place there. Euphais, showing more zeal than was expected of a king, attacked Theopompus and his men without restraint, and he received many wounds that could not be healed. Having fainted

<summary>This passage recounts the tragic sacrifice of Aristodemus's daughter to fulfill a Delphic oracle, the subsequent internal strife among the Messenians, and the renewal of hostilities between the Messenians and the Lacedaemonians at Ithome.</summary>

PAUSANIAS

> To the nether gods, a maiden undefiled,
> Chosen by lot from the Aepytid blood,
> Sacrifice in the slaughter of the night.
> But if this fails, and another be slain,
> Then offer those who give themselves to die.

When the god had declared these things, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens of the Aepytid line. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Ephebolus the seer forbade this, claiming she ought not to be sacrificed, for she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; rather, the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had passed the girl off as her own. While he was explaining these matters, Lyciscus took the maiden and deserted to Sparta. The Messenians were disheartened when they learned of Lyciscus’s flight. At this point, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage and more distinguished than Lyciscus in reputation and military matters, voluntarily offered his own daughter for the sacrifice. Human affairs are often obscured by fate, and the lot was covered by river mud. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, an obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name is not recorded) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. He was about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus no longer had authority over the girl, and that by betrothing her himself, he had become more authoritative than the father. When he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. In the end, he drove Aristodemus to such a state of madness and rage that he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and showed that she was not pregnant. Ephebolus, who was present, ordered that someone else be provided to be sacrificed; for the death of Aristodemus’s daughter had gained them nothing, as the father had killed her, but they had not sacrificed her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unholy stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man had been a very close friend of Euphais. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl’s death, and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the Aepytid line agreed that he spoke the truth. The fear they felt regarding the daughter ceased, and everyone hastened to act. The kings, persuaded by this advice, dismissed the assembly, and from that point, they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves disheartened, and the kings hesitated to begin the battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens were favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to be no longer present with them. The allies of the Messenians also arrived late. The Spartans were already suspicious of other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly, without the knowledge of the Lacedaemonians, and more privately by a common decree. The campaign had been forbidden to the Arcadians openly. They did not appear either. The reputation of the oracle had encouraged the Messenians to take the risk even without allies. For the most part, nothing happened that was different from the previous battle; the day ended while they were still fighting. They do not record that either wing was forced back, nor do they mention any ambush. They say that they did not remain in the formation in which they were originally drawn up, but that the best men from both sides met in the middle, and the entire struggle took place there. ἀποθανόσης οὐδέν· φονεῦσαι γὰρ τὸν πατέρα αὐτὴν, θεοῖς δὲ οἷς ἡ Πυθία προσέταξεν, οὐ θῦσαι. τοιαῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ μάντεως, τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὥρμησεν ἀποκτενοῦντες τὸν μνηστῆρα τῆς παιδός, ὡς Αἰπυτιδῶν, καὶ Λυκίσκου τῇ τε ἄλλῃ δόξῃ, καὶ τὰ ἐς πόλεμον ἐπιφανέστερος, ἐδίδου τὴν θυγατέρα ἑκὼν θῦσαι. τὰ δὲ ἀνθρώπων οὐχ ἥκιστα τὸ πρόθυμον πεπρωμένη κατὰ ταῦτα ἐπικρύπτει, καὶ ἡ ψηφίδα ἐπιλαβοῦσα ἰλὺς ποταμοῦ. ὅπου καὶ τότε Ἀριστοδήμῳ διασῶσαι Μεσσηνίους ἀγώνισμα ποιουμένῳ, τὸ ἐμπόδιον ἐπήγαγε τοιόνδε. ἀνὴρ τῶν Μεσσηνίων (τὸ δὲ ὄνομα οὐ λέγουσιν) ἐρῶν ἔτυχε τῆς Ἀριστοδήμου θυγατρός. τότε δὲ ἤδη ἔμελλε γυναῖκα ἄξεσθαι. οὗτος κατ’ ἀρχὰς ἐς ἀμφισβήτησιν Ἀριστοδήμῳ καθίστατο, ἐκεῖνον μὲν ἐγγυήσαντά οἱ μηκέτι εἶναι κύριον τῆς παιδός, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγγυησάμενος κυριώτερος ἐκείνου γίνεσθαι. δεύτερα δὲ ὡς τοῦτο οὐχ ἑώρα οἱ κατορθούμενον, ἐπ’ ἀναίσχυντον τρέπεται λόγον, συγγενέσθαι τε τῇ παιδί, καὶ τεκύειν ἐξ αὐτῆς. τέλος δὲ ἐς τοσοῦτον Ἀριστόδημον προήγαγεν, ὡς ἐκμανέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ θυμοῦ τὴν θυγατέρα ἀποκτεῖναι. μετὰ δὲ ἀνέτεμνε, καὶ ἐπεδείκνυεν αὐτὴν οὐκ ἔχουσαν ἐν γαστρί. παρὼν δὲ Ἐπήβολος, ἐκέλευεν ἄλλον τινὰ τὴν θυγατέρα ἐπιδώσοντα γενέσθαι· τῆς γὰρ τοῦ Ἀριστοδήμου, πλέον αὖ σφισιν ἀποθανόσης οὐδέν· φονεῦσαι γὰρ τὸν πατέρα αὐτὴν, θεοῖς δὲ οἷς ἡ Πυθία προσέταξεν, οὐ θῦσαι. τοιαῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ μάντεως, τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὥρμησεν ἀποκτενοῦντες τὸν μνηστῆρα τῆς παιδός, ὡς Ἀριστοδήμῳ τε μίασμα εἰκαῖον προσάψαντα, καὶ σφίσι τῆς σωτηρίας τὴν ἐλπίδα ἀμφίβολον πεποιηκότα. ἦν δὲ ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος ἐς τὰ μάλιστα τῷ Εὐφάῃ φίλος. πείθει τοὺς Μεσσηνίους Εὐφάης, τόν τε χρησμὸν ἔχειν τέλος ἀποθανούσης τῆς παιδός, καὶ σφίσιν ἀποχρᾶν τὸ ὑπὸ Ἀριστοδήμου πεποιημένον. λέγοντος δὲ ταῦτα, ἔφασαν τὰ ὄντα λέγειν ὅσοι τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν γένους ἦσαν· ἀπεπαύετο γὰρ σφίσι ὁ δέος ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ θυγατρί, ἕκαστός τε ἔσπευδε, καὶ οἱ μὲν τῶν βασιλέων τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι, τὴν ἐκκλησίαν διαλύουσιν· καὶ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς πρός τε θυσίας καὶ θεῶν ἑορτὴν τρέπονται. Λακεδαιμόνιοι δὲ ἀκούσαντες τὸν γενόμενον Μεσσηνίοις χρησμόν, ἀθύμως διέκειντο καὶ αὐτοί, καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς, ἔς τε τὰ λοιπὰ καὶ ἀρχὴν ὀκνοῦντες μάχης. Ἔτει δὲ ἕκτῳ μετὰ τὸν ἐξ Ἰθώμης Λυκίσκου δρασμὸν οἱ Λακεδαιμόνιοι (τὰ γὰρ ἱερὰ ἐγίνετο αὐτοῖς αἴσια) στρατεύουσιν ἐπὶ τὴν Ἰθώμην. οἱ δὲ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι παρόντες σφίσιν ἔτυχον. ὑστέρησαν δὲ καὶ οἱ τῶν Μεσσηνίων σύμμαχοι. δι’ ὑποψίας γὰρ οἱ Σπαρτιᾶται καὶ ἄλλοις ἤδη Πελοποννησίων, καὶ Ἀρκάσιν ἦσαν καὶ Ἀργείοις μάλιστα. καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἀργεῖοι κρύφα ἔμελλον τῶν Λακεδαιμονίων ἀφίξεσθαι, καὶ ἰδίᾳ δὴ μᾶλλον μετὰ δόγματος κοινοῦ. τοῖς δὲ Ἀρκάσιν ἡ στρατεία μὲν ἀπείρητο ἐκ τοῦ φανεροῦ. παρέτυχον δὲ οὐδ’ οὗτοι. τοὺς γὰρ Μεσσηνίους καὶ ἄνευ συμμάχων κινδυνεῦσαι προήγαγεν ἡ δόξα τοῦ χρησμοῦ. τὰ μὲν οὖν πολλὰ οὐδέν τι ἐγένετο διάφορα, ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς προτέρας μάχης· ἥ τε ἡμέρα καὶ τότε μαχομένους προαπέλιπεν. οὐ μὲν τοι βιασθῆναί γε οὐδέτερον κέρας, ἢ καὶ λόχον μνημονεύουσιν. ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τῷ τάξιν ὡς ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἐτάχθησαν, συμμεῖναί φασιν· ἀλλ’ ἀφ’ ἑκατέρων τοὺς ἀρίστους συνελθόντας ἐς μέσον, ταύτῃ τὸν πάντα ἔχειν πόνον. ὁ γὰρ Εὐφάης πλέον τι ἢ βασιλέα εἰκὸς ἦν, προθυμούμενος, καὶ ἀφειδῶς τοῖς περὶ τὸν Θεόπομπον ἐγκείμενος, θαύματά τε καὶ πολλά τε οὐκ ἰάσιμα λαμβάνει. λιποψυχήσαντα

PAUSANIAS

> A maiden undefiled for the nether gods,
> Chosen by lot from the blood of the Aepytidae,
> You shall sacrifice in nocturnal slaughter.
> But if you are slaughtered, and by another, then
> Sacrifice, giving them up to the slaughter willingly.

When the god had declared these things, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens who were of the Aepytidae lineage. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. The seer Epibolus forbade this, saying that she ought not to be sacrificed; for she was not the daughter of Lyciscus, but the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had substituted the girl in that time. While he was explaining these matters regarding her, Lyciscus, taking the maiden with him, deserted to Sparta. When the Messenians were despondent upon learning that Lyciscus had fled, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytidae lineage and, in general reputation and military matters, more distinguished than Lyciscus, offered his own daughter willingly to be sacrificed. Fate, however, often conceals the eagerness of men, and in this case, it obscured the lot with river mud. Even then, when Aristodemus was making an effort to save the Messenians, it brought about the following obstacle. A man of the Messenians (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already about to take her as his wife. Initially, he came forward to dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, having betrothed her, had become more authoritative than him. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding for him, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, maddened by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and showed that she was not pregnant. Epibolus, who was present, ordered that someone else be provided to be sacrificed; for the death of Aristodemus’ daughter was of no benefit to them, as the father had killed her, but they had not sacrificed her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said these things, the multitude of the Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unmerited stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man was a very close friend of Euphais. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had reached its fulfillment with the death of the girl, and that what had been done by Aristodemus was sufficient for them. When he said these things, all those of the Aepytidae lineage said he spoke the truth; for the fear regarding the daughter was removed from them, and each person hastened, and those who were persuaded by the king’s exhortation dissolved the assembly; and from that point, they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard of the oracle that had come to the Messenians, were themselves despondent, and the kings were hesitant regarding the rest and the beginning of the battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens were favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened not to be present with them. The allies of the Messenians also arrived late. For the Spartans were already suspicious of other Peloponnesians, and especially of the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and indeed more privately, following a common decree. For the Arcadians, the campaign had been forbidden openly. Neither did they arrive. For the reputation of the oracle had led the Messenians to risk the battle even without allies. In most respects, nothing happened differently than in the previous battle; the day left them while they were still fighting. However, they do not record that either wing was forced back, or even a company. For they say that the formation did not remain as they were originally drawn up; but the best men from each side came together in the middle, and there the entire struggle took place. For Euphais, showing more zeal than was expected of a king, and attacking those around Theopompus without restraint, received many wounds that were incurable. Fainting

text:
# HERODOTUS IV 288

These are the things the cities report, but I know what happened to the Metapontines in Italy four hundred and forty years after the second disappearance of Aristeas, as I discovered by comparing accounts in Proconnesus and Metapontum. The Metapontines say that Aristeas appeared to them in their land and commanded them to set up an altar to Apollo and to place beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas the Proconnesian. They claim that Apollo had come to them, the only Italians to be visited by him, and that the current Aristeas was following him; at that time, when he followed the god, he was a raven. The <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> told them to obey the phantom, for if they obeyed, it would go better for them. They accepted this advice and carried out the instructions. Even now, a statue bearing the name of Aristeas stands next to the image of Apollo itself, and laurel trees stand around it; the image is set up in the marketplace. Let this much be said concerning Aristeas.

As for the land concerning which this discussion was started, no one knows for certain what lies beyond it. I have not been able to learn from anyone who claims to have seen it with his own eyes. Even Aristeas, whom I mentioned just a moment ago, did not claim in his poems to have gone further than the Issedones. Instead, he spoke of the regions beyond by hearsay, stating that it was the Issedones who told these things. However, everything that we have been able to reach as far as possible by hearsay with certainty shall be told.

From the trading post of the Borysthenites <note>The Borysthenites were Greek colonists living near the mouth of the Dnieper River</note> (for this is the most central point of the coastal regions of all Scythia), from <margin>30</margin>

reference.text:
[context] After a number of different conferences held during the summer she succeeded in persuading Athens to withdraw from Pylos the Messenians and
the rest of the Helots and deserters from Laconia, who were accordingly settled by her at Cranii in Cephallenia.
Thus during this summer there was peace and intercourse between the two peoples. Next winter, however, the Ephors under whom the treaty had been made were no longer in office, and some of their successors were directly opposed to it. Embassies now arrived from the Lacedaemonian confederacy, and the Athenians, Boeotians, and Corinthians also presented themselves at Lacedaemon, and after much discussion and no agreement between them, separated for their several homes; when Cleobulus and Xenares, the two Ephors who were the most anxious to break off the treaty, took advantage of this opportunity to communicate privately with the Boeotians and Corinthians, and advising them to act as much as possible together, instructed the former first to enter into alliance with Argos, and then try and bring themselves and the Argives into alliance with Lacedaemon. The Boeotians would so be least likely to be compelled to come in to the Attic treaty; and the Lacedaemonians would prefer gaining the friendship and alliance of Argos even at the price of the hostility of Athens and the rupture of the treaty.

cause.diagnosis: The manuscript is a clear minuscule that reads Thucydides 5.35.7-36.1 line for line, but the OCR produced plausible-looking wrong Greek on nearly every line (ἐφόρων→φόρου, διαλῦσαι→ἀμῦναι, χειμῶνος→ἔχει μόνος, Βοιωτῶν καὶ Κορινθίων lost), and the English faithfully translates that garble.

text:
<margin>Megara</margin>
...and others different things. And those who are in danger regarding the city, especially to dissolve [the war] for them with the alliances and the fame—it was only for this summer that the advances were parallel. Those who were opposing [them] were the only ones holding it, for they had tributes... and the treaties were becoming nothing, already ruling [their] own [territory]. And the treaties that came were to act for themselves [regarding] the alliance, and the presence of the Athenians, and hating the Lacedaemonians. And many things to each other [when] the ones were gone... no alliances, as they were absent regarding those things that were, and to the Lacedaemonians, for whom [they were intended]. And <term>Xenares</term> <gloss>a Lacedaemonian ephor</gloss>, these were the ones who most wanted the tribute, [but] to defend the treaties, they make arguments. More of them [asked] that they especially understand these [matters] of the land, and to act to make the Argives who had come [into an alliance] with them [instead] make the Lacedaemonians allies to them. For in this way they would most likely dissolve the Athenians... [when] the messages of the treaties came... for the Lacedaemonians, before [the] hatred itself of their own [enemies] and to wash away the treaties [to make the] Argives friends to themselves.
<margin>of the Lacedaemonians</margin>

<margin>Megara</margin>
These things are different for different people; and as many as are in the greatest danger regarding the city, and to dissolve their alliances with the reputation <note>referring to the prestige or public standing of the parties involved</note> for this summer alone, these were also the parallel incursions. But those who were opposing them held them alone, for they had taxes <note>or tributes</note> gathered, and the treaties were becoming no taxes, already ruling both their own and those who had come through the treaties to act for themselves, both of the alliance and the present things of the Athenians and hating those of the Lacedaemonians, and many to one another while absent, with no allies, as they were away on those things that were present and for the Lacedaemonians for whatever reason, and Xenares <note>a Spartan ephor</note> and these men, at the time of the tribute, wished most of all to defend the treaties, they make speeches; more people requesting that they know these things of the land most of all, and to act for me, the Argives having become toward the allies themselves, rather the Argives to make the Lacedaemonians allies; for in this way they would most of all dissolve the Athenians to the messages of the treaties having come
<margin>of the Lacedaemonians</margin>
for the Lacedaemonians, before the enmity of them themselves and to dissolve the treaties with the Argives as friends to themselves.

<summary>This passage discusses the complex political maneuvering and shifting alliances between the Athenians, Lacedaemonians, and Argives, focusing on the desire to dissolve existing treaties and the strategic importance of Megara.</summary>

<margin>Megara</margin>
These things are different for different people; and as many as are in the greatest danger regarding the city, and to dissolve their alliances with the reputation <note>referring to the prestige or public standing of the parties involved</note> for this summer alone, these were also the parallel incursions. But those who were opposing them held them alone, for they had taxes <note>or tributes</note> gathered, and the treaties were becoming no taxes, already ruling both their own and those who had come through the treaties to act for themselves, both of the alliance and the present things of the Athenians and hating those of the Lacedaemonians, and many to one another while absent, with no allies, as they were away on those things that were present and for the Lacedaemonians for whatever reason, and Xenares <note>a Spartan ephor</note> and these men, at the time of the tribute, wished most of all to defend the treaties, they make speeches; more people requesting that they know these things of the land most of all, and to act for me, the Argives having become toward the allies themselves, rather the Argives to make the Lacedaemonians allies; for in this way they would most of all dissolve the Athenians to the messages of the treaties having come
<margin>of the Lacedaemonians</margin>
for the Lacedaemonians, before the enmity of them themselves and to dissolve the treaties with the Argives as friends to themselves.

text:
<margin>Megara</margin>
To others, these matters seemed different. Those who were in the greatest danger for the city and wished to dissolve the alliance with their allies for this summer alone were also making parallel incursions. They alone held those who opposed them, for they had their own tributes, and the treaties were becoming nothing but tributes. They were already ruling their own affairs and, being opposed to the treaties that had been made, they sought to act for themselves regarding the alliance, especially since the Athenians were present and they hated the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>. Many things were said to one another in the absence of a single ally, as they were away from the current situation and from the Lacedaemonians. Xenares and Cleobulus <note>Ephors at Sparta who opposed the peace with Athens</note>, who were the overseers of the tribute, especially wanted to defend the treaties through words. They urged that it was best to recognize these matters of the land and for me to make the Argives <note>people of Argos</note> become allies to them, rather than having the Argives make the Lacedaemonians their allies. For in this way, they could best detach the Athenians from the treaties that had been reported.
<margin>of the Lacedaemonians</margin>
For they wished the Lacedaemonians, before their own enmity and the dissolution of the treaties, to make the Argives their friends.

<summary>This page discusses the political maneuvering between Sparta, Athens, and Argos during a period of unstable peace. Spartan officials Xenares and Cleobulus attempt to secure an alliance with Argos to undermine Athenian influence.</summary>
<keywords>Thucydides, Peloponnesian War, Megara, Lacedaemonians, Spartans, Athenians, Argives, Xenares, Cleobulus, diplomacy, alliances, treaties</keywords>

<margin>Megara</margin>
and other Helots, and as many as had deserted from Laconia, and they settled them in Cranii on Cephallenia. During this summer, there was peace and mutual visits. But in the following winter, because different ephors <note>Spartan magistrates</note> were in office, and not those under whom the treaties were made, and some of them were even opposed to the treaties, embassies arrived from the alliance. With Athenians, Boeotians, and Corinthians present, they spoke much to one another but reached no agreement. As they were departing for home, Cleobulus and Xenares, who were among the ephors and were most eager to dissolve the treaties, held private discussions with the Boeotians and Corinthians. They advised them to pursue this course: the Boeotians should first become allies of the Argives, and then, together with the Boeotians, make the Argives allies of the Lacedaemonians. In this way, the Boeotians would be least compelled to enter into the Attic treaties. For the Lacedaemonians, before the enmity of the Athenians and the dissolution of the treaties, preferred to have the Argives as their friends.
<margin>of the Lacedaemonians</margin>

<summary>This passage describes the political maneuvering of Spartan ephors Cleobulus and Xenares, who sought to undermine the peace treaty with Athens by orchestrating a new alliance between the Boeotians and the Argives.</summary>

[context] Then Prohaeresius, like a war-horse summoned to the plain,
made a speech about the imperial gift, and cited Celeus and Triptolemus and how Demeter sojourned among men that she might bestow on them the gift of corn. With that famous narrative he combined the tale of the generosity of Constans, and very speedily he invested the occurrence with the splendour and dignity of ancient legend. Then, as he declaimed, his gestures became more lively, and he displayed all his sophistic art in handling the theme. The fact that he obtained the honour that he asked for shows what his eloquence must have been.
His wife came from Asia, from the city of Tralles, and her name was Amphiclea. They had two little girls, between whose ages there was only so much difference as the time necessary for their conception and birth. But no sooner had they reached that time of life when a child is a wholly lovely and charming thing, and made their father's heart tremble with joy, than they left their parents desolate, both within a few days; so that his grief almost shook Prohaeresius from the reflections that become a philosopher. However, the Muse of Milesius proved able to meet this crisis, and by composing lovely harmonies and expending all his gifts of charm and gaiety he recalled him to reason. When the Romans asked him to send them one of his own pupils, Prohaeresius sent forth Eusebius who was a native of Alexandria. He seemed to be peculiarly suited to Rome, because he knew how to flatter and fawn on the great; while in Athens he was regarded as a seditious person.
At the same time Prohaeresius wished to increase his own reputation
[context] by sending a man who had been initiated into the sharp practices of political oratory.

text:
<meta>This page continues the biography of the sophist Prohaeresius. Having secured the promise of a grain endowment for Athens from Emperor Constans, Prohaeresius now performs before the Praetorian Prefect Anatolius to finalize the grant, using his oratorical skills to elevate the political gift into a legendary event.</meta>

## PROHAERESIUS. 91.

In honor of this gift, he produced orations in which he introduced **Celeus** and **Triptolemus** and the arrival of **Demeter** <note>In Greek mythology, Demeter (goddess of agriculture) came to Eleusis near Athens and taught Celeus and his son Triptolemus the art of farming. By citing these figures, Prohaeresius frames the Emperor's gift of grain as a divine act of restoration.</note> regarding the gift of grain. By weaving the Emperor’s favor into these ancient narratives, he very quickly restored current events to their ancient grandeur. He seemed to dance along with his own words as he displayed his mastery of the theme; the very magnificence of his speech served as proof of his **Philotimia** <term>Philotimia: (Greek: φιλοτιμία) literally "love of honor." It refers to a noble ambition or the public display of excellence and generosity that wins a citizen high status.</term>. 

It happened that he took a wife from the city of **Tralles** <note>A prominent city in the Roman province of Asia, modern-day Turkey.</note> in Asia, and her name was **Amphicleia**. They had two daughters born so close together that the only difference in their ages was the time required for conception and birth. But just as they reached that age when a child is a truly beautiful and blessed thing, and had begun to stir their father’s soul with joy, <insert>161.</insert> within a few days both children died, leaving their parents behind. This suffering was so great that it nearly drove Prohaeresius out of his proper senses. 

However, the "Muse of Milesius" <note>This refers to Milesius, a pupil of Prohaeresius known for his rhythmic and charming style of speaking. He used his rhetorical talents to console his teacher and distract him from his grief.</note> proved sufficient to help him; by kindling the graces of harmony and playing much with **Aphrodite** <note>The goddess of love; here suggesting the comforts of beauty, art, or perhaps the renewed companionship of his wife.</note>, she called his reason back to him. 

When the Romans requested that he send a special associate to live among them, Prohaeresius sent **Eusebius**. Eusebius was from **Alexandria**, and he seemed particularly well-suited for the city of Rome, as he knew how to flatter and fawn upon those in power (though in **Athens** he had appeared to be a man of a more rebellious and factional nature). At the same time, Prohaeresius wished for a greater...

<summary>Prohaeresius uses mythological oratory to secure a grain grant for Athens, but soon suffers the tragic loss of both his young daughters. He eventually recovers his reason through the consolations of a friend and pupil, later sending his associate Eusebius to represent his school in Rome.</summary>
<keywords>Prohaeresius, Athens, grain endowment, Demeter, Celeus, Triptolemus, Philotimia, Tralles, Amphicleia, Milesius, Eusebius, Rome, bereavement</keywords>

text:
PROAERESIUS. 91

He presented speeches on the gift, bringing forward Celeus and Triptolemus and the arrival of Demeter for the gift of grain. By attaching the favor of the emperor to those narratives, he very quickly shifted the proceedings back to their ancient grandeur. He danced through his words, demonstrating his skill in the subject matter, and the proof of his speeches was his own ambition. A marriage befell him from Asia, from the city of the Trallians, and the woman’s name was Amphicleia. Two daughters were born to them, separated in age by only the time it takes for conception and birth. When they reached the age where a child is a beautiful and blessed thing, having stirred the father’s soul with joy, <insert>161.</insert> they both left their parents within a few days, so that the suffering nearly cast Proaeresius out of his own rational senses. But the Muse of Miletus sufficed for this, rekindling the harmonious graces, playing much with Aphrodite, and recalling his reason. When the Romans requested that he send them a personal associate, Proaeresius sent Eusebius, who was from Alexandria (it seemed he would otherwise fit the city, knowing how to flatter and fawn over those in power; yet he appeared seditious in Athens), and at the same time he wished for a greater

text:
# Proaeresius 91

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
He offered speeches in return for the gift, bringing forward the stories of Celeus and Triptolemus <note>figures from Eleusinian mythology associated with the origin of agriculture</note> and the arrival of Demeter <note>the goddess of the harvest</note> in connection with the gift of grain. By attaching the Emperor's favor to those ancient narratives, he very quickly elevated the current events to their ancient grandeur. He danced through his words, demonstrating his mastery of the subject matter, and the proof of his eloquence was his own ambition for excellence.

A marriage then occurred for him with a woman from the city of Tralles in Asia. Her name was Amphicleia. Two daughters were born to them, separated in age only by the time required for conception and birth. When they had reached an age that is a most beautiful and blessed thing in a child, stirring their father's soul with joy, <insert>161.</insert> both left their parents within a few days. The suffering was so great that it nearly drove Proaeresius out of his proper senses. However, the Muse of Milesius <note>referring to the sophist Milesius of Smyrna</note> was sufficient to meet this grief, striking up the graces of harmony, playing much with Aphrodite, and calling back his reason.

When the Romans requested that he send them a private teacher, Proaeresius sent out Eusebius. He was from Alexandria. It seemed he would fit that city well in other ways, as he knew how to flatter and fawn upon those in power, though in Athens he had appeared to be a man prone to factionalism. At the same time, Proaeresius wished for something greater

<summary>Proaeresius uses mythological oratory to thank the Emperor for grain supplies and later suffers the tragic loss of his two young daughters. He sends his student Eusebius of Alexandria to Rome to serve as a teacher.</summary>
<keywords>Proaeresius, Demeter, Triptolemus, Amphicleia, Eusebius of Alexandria, grief, Roman education, flattery</keywords>
