ἀσπίδα δαιδάλλουσα πολύχροον, ἧς ἐνὶ μέσσῳ
ἐν μὲν γαῖαν ἔπηξε περίδρομον, ἀμφὶ δὲ γαίῃ
οὐρανὸν ἐσφαίρωσε χορῷ κεχαραγμένον ἄστρων,
καὶ χθονὶ πόντον ἔτευξεν ὁμόζυγον· αἰθέριον δὲ
χρυσῷ μὲν φλογέων ἐποχημένον ἄντυγι δίφρων
Ἡέλιον ποίκιλλεν, ἀπ᾽ ἀργυρέου δὲ μετάλλου
λευκαίνων τροχόεσσαν ὅλην κύκλωσε Σελήνην·

μιτρώσας στεφανηδὸν ἕλιξ ποικίλλεται αἰθὴρ
ἑπτὰ περὶ ζώνῃσι, καὶ ἀξονίῳ παρὰ κύκλῳ

text:
<header>NONNI DIONYS.</header>
<warning>Large vertical stain on the left side of the page; text remains legible.</warning>

So that I may kill with a wise spear the remnants of the Indians;
for Bacchus sat there, near the fertile ridge of the Indian forest,
a citizen of the desert wilderness,
in the delay of war. And Ganges trembled with fear,
<margin>5</margin> pitying his own children; and upon the fate of those recently perished,
the whole city was shaken; and the streets resounded
with the mournful clatter of the lamenting women.
And fear and amazement and shame shook Deriades;
for he had already heard everything; and he was distressed
<margin>10</margin> looking with a sidelong eye because he had changed a divine form.
The black Hydaspes murmured with wine-like waves;
And there, rolling his own sluggish foot of the flowing river,
And having the gloomy mist of fire,
he sprinkled the yellow dew of the drunkenness that releases pains
<margin>15</margin> with sticky eyes. And with the drawing countenance,
wine-like drops were opened in his eyes;
and delighting with his feet, the old man danced, singing
of the reddening moisture of the evil-averting river.
And with his old hands, drawing the stream like clouds,
<margin>20</margin> he filled the sweet-smelling skins with purple drunkenness,
and he lit an altar to Zeus and to the wine-pouring Dionysus;
forgetting the late radiance of unaccustomed Phaethon,
and leaving the wine-drunk sheep on the shores, the youth
lapping the sweet water of the reddening river.
<margin>25</margin> A hunter, a companion of the mountain-dwelling Archeress <note>Diana/Artemis</note>,
bent his path into the city to the disobedient Deriades,
rejoicing in the sweet stream of the wine-erring river.
Already the vineyard-scent was running through the city,
and in the clear winds, it intoxicated the whole town,
<margin>30</margin> dancing around Lyaeus <note>Dionysus</note>, who brings the victory of the Indian-slaughter.
And the citizens were dwelling in the high towers,
fearing lest the guards of the high-crested city
might have girded the wall with ox-hides, and towards the hills...

<summary>Dionysus transforms the river Hydaspes into wine, causing confusion among the Indian inhabitants and signaling his impending victory.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysus, Hydaspes, wine, transformation, Ganges, Deriades</keywords>

Ὄφρα κατακτείνω νοερῷ δορὶ λείψανον Ἰνδῶν·
Ὡς ὁ μὲν Ἰνδῴοιο παρὰ ῥάχιν εὔβοτον ὕλης
Ἔζεε Βάκχος ὅμιλος ἐρημάδος ἀστὸς ἐρείκης,
Ἀμβολίῃ πολέμοιο· φόβῳ δ᾽ ἐλελίζετο Γάγγης,
<margin>5</margin>Οἰκτείρων ἑὰ τέκνα· νεοφθιμένων δ᾽ ἐπὶ πότμῳ
Πᾶσα πόλις δεδόνητο· φιλοθρήνων δὲ γυναικῶν
Πενθαλέοις πατάγοισιν ἐπεσμαράγησαν ἀγυιαί·
Δηριάδην δ᾽ ἐλέλιζε φόβος καὶ θάμβος καὶ αἰδώς·
Ἤδη γὰρ κλύε πάντα· τὸ δὲ πλέον ὄμματι λοξῷ
<margin>10</margin>Ἄχνυτο παπταίνων ὅτι θέσκελον εἶδος ἀμείψας.
Οἴνῳ κυματόεντι μέλας κελάρυζεν Ὑδάσπης·
Καί θι καὶ εὐῤῥέεος ἑὸν πόδα νωθρὸν ἐλίσσων·
Καὶ πυρὸς ἀχλυόεσσαν ἔχων ἀλαωπὸν ὁμίχλην
Ξανθινῷ λυσιπόνοιο μέθης ἐῤῥαίνεν ἐέρσην
<margin>15</margin>Ὄμμασι κολλητῆσιν· ἀρυομένῳ δὲ προσώπῳ
Οἰνωπὰς ῥαθάμιγγας ἀνῴχθησαν ὀπωπαί·
Τερπμένους δὲ πόδεσσι, γέρων ἐχόρευε λιγαίνων
Ἰκμάδα φοινίσσουσαν ἀλεξικάκου ποταμοῖο·
Χερσὶ δ᾽ ἡγηλαίῃσι ῥέον νεφεληδὸν ἀφύσσων,
<margin>20</margin>Πορφυρέης ἔπλησε μέθης εὐώδεας ἀσκούς,
Καὶ Διῒ βωμὸν ἅνψε καὶ οἰνοχύτῳ Διονύσῳ·
Ληθήσας Φαέθοντος ἀήθεος ὄψιμον αἴγλην,
Καὶ κώας οἰνωθέντας ἐπ᾽ ἤϊσι κοῦρος ἐάσας,
Λαρὸν ὕδωρ λάπτοντας ἐρευθομένῳ ποταμοῖο·
<margin>25</margin>Θηρητὴρ ὁμόφοιτος ὀρειάδος Ἰοχεαίρης,
Εἰς πόλιν ἴχνος ἔκαμψεν ἀπειθέϊ Δηριαδῆϊ·
Ἀγάλλον γλυκὺ χεῦμα μεθυσφαλίος ποταμοῖο·
Ἤδη οἱ ἀμπελόεσσα δι᾽ ἄστεος ἔτρεχεν ὀδμή,
Καὶ λιγυροῖς ἀνέμοισιν ὅλας ἐμέθυσεν ἀγυιάς·
<margin>30</margin>Νικίῳ ἱδροφόνοιο περισκαίρουσα Λυαίῳ·
Πύργοις τ᾽ ἠλιβάτοισιν ἐναυλίζοντο πολῖται·
Δειδιότες μὴ τεῖχος ἐμιτρώσαντο βοείαις
Ἄστεος ὑψιλόφοιο φυλάκιοι, ἔς τ᾽ ἐπὶ κολώνας

NONNI DIONYS.
<warning>Large vertical stain on the left side of the page; text remains legible.</warning>

So that I may slay with a mental spear the remnant of the Indians.
Thus Bacchus, a citizen of the desert heath, sat beside the fertile ridge of the Indian forest,
Delaying the war. Fear shook the Ganges,
<margin>5</margin> Pitying his own children. The whole city was stirred
At the fate of the newly dead. The streets resounded
With the mournful clatter of women who love to lament.
Fear, astonishment, and shame shook Deriades.
For he already heard everything, and more so with a sidelong glance
<margin>10</margin> He grieved, gazing at how he had changed his divine form.
The dark Hydaspes gurgled with wine like a wave,
And even there, rolling his sluggish foot in the well-flowing stream,
And holding the misty haze of fire,
He sprinkled the dew of the toil-releasing intoxication with a golden hue
<margin>15</margin> Upon his fixed eyes. And as he drew from it, his face
Opened its wine-colored eyes.
Delighting with his feet, the old man danced, singing aloud
Of the reddening moisture of the evil-averting river.
With guiding hands, drawing it in clouds,
<margin>20</margin> He filled fragrant skins with purple intoxication,
And lit an altar to Zeus and to the wine-pouring Dionysus.
He forgot the late-appearing radiance of the unaccustomed Phaethon,
And the youth, having left the wine-soaked fleeces upon the banks,
Drinking the delicious water of the reddening river.
<margin>25</margin> The hunter, companion of the mountain-dwelling Archeress <note>Artemis</note>,
Turned his steps into the city to the disobedient Deriades,
Boasting of the sweet stream of the intoxicating river.
Already the scent of vines ran through the city,
And with shrill winds it intoxicated the whole of the streets,
<margin>30</margin> Dancing around the sweat-shedding Lyaeus <note>Dionysus</note> with victory.
The citizens dwelt in the high towers,
Fearing lest the guards of the high-crested city
Should gird the wall with ox-hides, and up to the hills

<summary>This passage describes the transformation of the river Hydaspes into wine by Dionysus, the subsequent intoxication of the landscape and the people, and the growing fear of the Indian king Deriades as the divine influence of Bacchus spreads through the city.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysus, Bacchus, Deriades, Hydaspes, Ganges, intoxication, transformation, Indian war</keywords>

NONNI DIONYS.
<warning>Large vertical stain on the left side of the page; text remains legible.</warning>

So that I may slay with a mental spear the remnant of the Indians.
Thus Bacchus, a citizen of the desert heath, sat beside the fertile ridge of the Indian forest,
Delaying the war. Fear shook the Ganges,
<margin>5</margin> Pitying his own children. The whole city was stirred
At the fate of the newly dead. The streets resounded
With the mournful clatter of women who love to lament.
Fear, astonishment, and shame shook Deriades.
For he already heard everything, and more so with a sidelong glance
<margin>10</margin> He grieved, gazing at how he had changed his divine form.
The dark Hydaspes gurgled with wine like a wave,
And even there, rolling his sluggish foot in the well-flowing stream,
And holding the misty haze of fire,
He sprinkled the dew of the toil-releasing intoxication with a golden hue
<margin>15</margin> Upon his fixed eyes. And as he drew from it, his face
Opened its wine-colored eyes.
Delighting with his feet, the old man danced, singing aloud
Of the reddening moisture of the evil-averting river.
With guiding hands, drawing it in clouds,
<margin>20</margin> He filled fragrant skins with purple intoxication,
And lit an altar to Zeus and to the wine-pouring Dionysus.
He forgot the late-appearing radiance of the unaccustomed Phaethon,
And the youth, having left the wine-soaked fleeces upon the banks,
Drinking the delicious water of the reddening river.
<margin>25</margin> The hunter, companion of the mountain-dwelling Archeress <note>Artemis</note>,
Turned his steps into the city to the disobedient Deriades,
Boasting of the sweet stream of the intoxicating river.
Already the scent of vines ran through the city,
And with shrill winds it intoxicated the whole of the streets,
<margin>30</margin> Dancing around the sweat-shedding Lyaeus <note>Dionysus</note> with victory.
The citizens dwelt in the high towers,
Fearing lest the guards of the high-crested city
Should gird the wall with ox-hides, and up to the hills

# NONNUS’S DIONYSIACA

...so that I may slay the remnant of the Indians with a mental spear.
While the Bacchic host, now citizens of the desert heather, seethed along the ridge of the fertile Indian forest, delaying the war; the Ganges trembled with fear,
<margin>5</margin>pitying its own children. At the fate of the newly dead, every city was shaken; the streets rang out with the mournful clatter of lamenting women. Fear, amazement, and shame shook Deriades <note>The Indian King and primary antagonist of Dionysus</note>; for he had already heard everything. But even more, with a sidelong glance,
<margin>10</margin>he was grieved to see that the river had changed its divine form.
The dark Hydaspes <note>A major river in ancient India, modern Jhelum</note> gurgled with surging wine; and there, dragging his sluggish foot through the fair-flowing stream, and having a sightless, misty gloom of fire, he <note>referring to a local inhabitant or perhaps the river god himself</note> sprinkled the yellow dew of pain-releasing intoxication
<margin>15</margin>upon his closed eyes. With a face drawing in the liquid, his eyes were opened by the wine-colored drops. Delighted in his feet, the old man danced, singing of the reddening moisture of the evil-averting river. With guiding hands, drawing the cloud-like flow,
<margin>20</margin>he filled fragrant skins with the purple intoxication, and lit an altar to Zeus and to Dionysus, the pourer of wine. Forgetting the late-shining, unfamiliar brightness of Phaethon <note>The sun-god, or here referring to the previous scorching heat</note>, and leaving the wine-soaked fleeces upon the banks, the youth left behind those who were lapping the sweet water of the reddening river.
<margin>25</margin>A hunter, the companion of mountain-roaming Artemis <term>Iocheaira</term> <gloss>the Archeress</gloss>, turned his steps toward the city to the disobedient Deriades, exulting in the sweet stream of the wine-staggering river. Already the scent of the vine was running through the city, and with clear winds it intoxicated all the streets,
<margin>30</margin>skipping about with the victory of <term>Lyaeus</term> <gloss>Dionysus the Deliverer</gloss>, the slayer of sweat. The citizens took shelter in the towering turrets, fearing lest the guardians of the high-crested city had girded the walls with ox-hides, and up onto the hills...

<meta>catchword: Exulting</meta>

<summary>The river Hydaspes is miraculously transformed into wine, causing the Indian people to marvel and feast while King Deriades is struck with fear. The scent of the vine fills the city as the Bacchic influence spreads through the landscape.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysus, Hydaspes, Deriades, wine transformation, Indian War, Bacchic revelry, Ganges</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] And at nightfall they came to the island of Philyra, where Cronos, son of Uranus, what time in Olympus he reigned over the Titans, and
Zeus was yet being nurtured in a Cretan cave by the Curetes of Ida, lay beside Philyra, when he had deceived Rhea; and the goddess found them in the midst of their dalliance; and Cronos leapt up from the couch with a rush in the form of a steed with flowing mane, but Ocean’s daughter, Philyra, in shame left the spot and those haunts, and came to the long Pelasgian ridges, where by her union with the transfigured deity she brought forth huge Cheiron, half like a horse, half like a god.
Thence they sailed on, past the Macrones and the far-stretching land of the Becheiri and the overweening Sapeires, and after them the Byzeres; for ever forward they clave their way, quickly borne by the gentle breeze. And lo, as they sped on, a deep gulf of the sea was opened,
[context] and lo, the steep crags of the Caucasian mountains rose up, where, with his limbs bound upon the hard rocks by galling fetters of bronze, Prometheus fed with his liver an eagle that ever rushed back to its prey.

text:
<header>APOLLONIUS OF RHODES</header>
<meta>Continuity: Following the Argonauts' journey past the land of the Macrones and the Bechirians.</meta>

Zeus was still being raised among the Idaean <term>Curetes</term> <gloss>mythological guardians of the infant Zeus</gloss>, and, deceiving <term>Rhea</term> <gloss>mother of the gods</gloss>, he lay with her. The goddess caught them in the bed between them. He sprang up from the bed <margin>1240</margin>
and rushed forth, appearing like a thick-maned horse.
She, in her shame, left those places and those haunts,
the Oceanid <term>Philyra</term> <gloss>a nymph, daughter of Oceanus</gloss>, and went to the long mountains of the <term>Pelasgians</term>,
where she bore the monstrous <term>Chiron</term> <gloss>the wise centaur</gloss>, in that shared union,
being in one part like a horse, and in another like a god. <margin>1245</margin>
From there, they passed by the <term>Macrones</term> and the boundless land of the <term>Bechirians</term>,
and they went past the overbearing <term>Sapires</term>,
and in addition to these, the <term>Byzeres</term>. For they were always cutting
their path easily, carried along by a gentle wind.
And now, to those sailing, the inner bay of the sea <margin>1250</margin>
began to appear.

---

*Jupiter, while he was still being educated among the Idaean Curetes, deceived Rhea and acquiesced. But the goddess caught them in the midst of their union. There, having been aroused, he rushed forth, resembling in form a thick-maned horse. But, having left those places and homes out of shame, Philyra, the daughter of Oceanus, migrated to the high mountains of the Pelasgians, where she brought forth from that mutual embrace the monstrous Chiron, similar to a horse in one part of himself and to a god in another. Thence they skirted the Macrones and the wide region of the Bechirians, and the truculent Sapires, and besides these, the Byzeres. For they were proceeding further and further, swiftly carried by a modest wind. Immediately, the gulf of the Pontus <note>original: "Ponti se sinus"</note> presents itself to those arriving.*

---

<gloss>1</gloss> As for "thick-maned," it means having a mane; from "mane." Just as from "dew" comes "dewy," and from "honor" comes "honored." <gloss>2</gloss> It has been spoken of previously regarding the Macrones, the Bechirians, and the Sapires. <gloss>3</gloss> By saying, "the inner bay of the sea began to appear," he showed that the Colchian land is in the inner bay of the sea.

<summary>The Argonauts continue their journey past various tribes, as the narrator recounts the mythological birth of Chiron from Cronus and Philyra, ultimately reaching the bay of the Pontus.</summary>
<keywords>Argonautica, Apollonius Rhodius, Zeus, Rhea, Philyra, Chiron, Macrones, Pontus</keywords>

Zeus was still being raised among the Idaean Curetes <note>The Curetes were attendants of the infant Zeus on Mount Ida who hid him from his father Cronus.</note>, Cronus lay with Philyra, having deceived Rhea. But the goddess <note>Rhea</note> caught them in the act of their union. Then Cronus, leaping up from the bed, rushed away in the form of a long-maned horse. But Philyra, the daughter of Oceanus, leaving that place and her former haunts out of shame, came to the high Pelasgian mountains. There she gave birth to the monstrous Chiron from that shared bed, a creature who was part horse and part god.

From there the Argonauts sailed past the Macrones and the vast land of the Bechiri, and the arrogant Sapires, and the Byzeres after them. For they were continually cutting their way forward swiftly, carried along by a gentle wind. And as they traveled, the innermost recess of the sea <note>The Black Sea</note> began to appear.

---

<gloss>1</gloss> The word <term>chaiteeis</term> <gloss>long-maned</gloss> means having a mane; it is derived from <term>chaite</term> <gloss>mane</gloss>. Just as from <term>erse</term> <gloss>dew</gloss> comes <term>erseeis</term> <gloss>dewy</gloss>, and from <term>time</term> <gloss>honor</gloss> comes <term>timeeis</term> <gloss>honored</gloss>. <gloss>2</gloss> Concerning the Macrones, Bechiri, and Sapires, these have been discussed previously. <gloss>3</gloss> By saying "the innermost recess of the sea began to appear," the author shows that the land of Colchis is located at the very end of the sea.

reference.text:
[context] And even now the yellow banks by the sea are
red with the blood of the Typhonian battle. O Hermes, glorious in counsel, thee especially do fishermen worship.
Therefore invoking thee with the gods who aid their hunt I pursue the glorious song of their chase.
First of all the fisher should have body and limbs both swift and strong, neither over fat nor lacking in flesh. For often he must fight with mighty fish in landing them—which have exceeding strength so long as they circle and wheel in the arms of their mother sea. And lightly he must leap from a rock ; and, when the toil of the sea is at its height, he must swiftly travel a long way and dive into the deepest depths and abide amongst the waves and remain labouring at such works as men upon the sea toil at with enduring heart. Cunning of wit too and wise
should the fisher be, since many and various are the devices that fishes contrive, when they chance upon unthought-of snares. Daring also should he be and dauntless and temperate and he must not love satiety
of sleep but must be keen of sight, wakeful of heart and open-eyed. He must bear well the wintry weather and the thirsty season of Sirius
; he must be fond of labour and must love the sea. So shall he be successful in his fishing and dear to Hermes.
In the autumn season fishing is best in the evening and when the morning-star rises. In winter the fisher should set out with the spreading rays of the sun. In bloomy spring the whole day is prosperous in all manner of fishing, what time all fishes
[context] are drawn to haunt the coasts near the land by the travail of birth and the thirst of desire.

<note>Decorative initial letter Γ</note>For they are full of many devices, and they are quick to perceive when they encounter unexpected snares. The <term>phlemys</term> <gloss>a type of fish, likely a species of bass or similar</gloss> is particularly clever, guileless, and prudent. It does not love the surfeit of sleep, but is sharp in its spirit and in its eyes. It endures winter twice over, and the harsher seasons, and loves the labors and the sea. For thus lives the brave and friendly [creature] of Hermes. The hunting is most fitting in the seasons of autumn, when the morning star rises. In winter, as it scatters along with the rays of the sun, it is captured, and all day long in the burgeoning spring, by manifold nets, it is raised when the season is full.

text:
ON FISHING, PAGE 30

<note>A decorative initial letter Γ (Gamma) begins the text.</note>

Hermes of the deep counsels, you whom the fishers honor above all others. Therefore, calling upon you alongside the gods of the headlands, I go forth to seek celestial glory.

Observe the body of the fisherman, and his land, and his swiftness, and his strength. Let him lack nothing, neither in flesh nor in spirit, for necessity often compels him to struggle against fish being hauled up by the hooks, those which possess overweening strength, until they are twisted and tossed in the embrace of their mother, the salt sea. Let his skin be such that he may leap across and spring back with ease, and let his hands be hardened by the labor of the deep. Let him quickly discern the long path, and dive into the deepest parts, and remain among the swells, as if he were performing tasks upon the land, for the man who possesses a steadfast heart must labor twice as hard in the sea.

The fisherman must be cunning and intelligent in his soul. For fish are very numerous and devise many shifting tricks when they encounter unexpected snares. He must be especially vigilant, alert, and prudent. He must not love the satiety of sleep, but must keep his heart sharp and his eyes wide open. He must endure both winter and the shivering cold of the season, and he must love his labors and love the sea. For thus he lives as a friend to strength and to Hermes.

The hunt is most fitting in the seasons of autumn, when the morning star rises. In winter, he must go forth as the rays of the sun scatter, and throughout the day in the flourishing spring, he must strive with all manner of nets when the time is right.

<summary>This passage outlines the physical and mental requirements for a fisherman, emphasizing the need for strength, vigilance, and a deep connection to the sea and the god Hermes.</summary>

text:
ON FISHING, PAGE 30

<note>A decorative initial letter Γ (Gamma) begins the text.</note>

Hermes of the deep counsels, you whom the fishers honor above all others. Therefore, calling upon you alongside the gods of the headlands, I go forth to seek celestial glory.

Observe the body of the fisherman, and his land, and his swiftness, and his strength. Let him lack nothing, neither in flesh nor in spirit, for necessity often compels him to struggle against fish being hauled up by the hooks, those which possess overweening strength, until they are twisted and tossed in the embrace of their mother, the salt sea. Let his skin be such that he may leap across and spring back with ease, and let his hands be hardened by the labor of the deep. Let him quickly discern the long path, and dive into the deepest parts, and remain among the swells, as if he were performing tasks upon the land, for the man who possesses a steadfast heart must labor twice as hard in the sea.

The fisherman must be cunning and intelligent in his soul. For fish are very numerous and devise many shifting tricks when they encounter unexpected snares. He must be especially vigilant, alert, and prudent. He must not love the satiety of sleep, but must keep his heart sharp and his eyes wide open. He must endure both winter and the shivering cold of the season, and he must love his labors and love the sea. For thus he lives as a friend to strength and to Hermes.

The hunt is most fitting in the seasons of autumn, when the morning star rises. In winter, he must go forth as the rays of the sun scatter, and throughout the day in the flourishing spring, he must strive with all manner of nets when the time is right.

<summary>This passage outlines the physical and mental requirements for a fisherman, emphasizing the need for strength, vigilance, and a deep connection to the sea and the god Hermes.</summary>
<keywords>fishing, Hermes, endurance, maritime labor, ancient techniques, Oppian</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: the poet addresses the gods of the sea and the skills required for the hunt.</meta>

...men are stirred by the rushing storm. Among them, they especially honor you,
O Hermes of famous counsel <note>original: "Ἑρμεία κλυτόβουλε"</note>. For this reason, I come to you with the gods who dwell on the heights, seeking the fame of your clever arts.

<note>A small decorative initial letter G marks the beginning of the instructional passage.</note>

First, let the fisherman be well-shaped in body, both lean and tall, swift and strong, neither lacking in fat nor burdened with excessive flesh. For it is often necessary for him to struggle against powerful fish being hauled in by force, which possess immense strength as long as they are tossed and whirled in the arms of their mother, the sea. He should be able to leap across and spring up easily, and his hand should be quick to endure the labor of the deep. He must swiftly recognize the long path of the water, dive into the deepest parts, and remain among the swells, performing his tasks as if on dry land, laboring in the sea with a steadfast heart.

The soul of the fisherman must be versatile and intelligent. For fish devise many and varied schemes when they encounter unexpected snares. He must be especially patient, silent, and temperate. Let him not be a lover of excessive sleep, but keep a sharp heart and watchful eyes. Furthermore, he should endure both the winter and the freezing season of the dog-star <note>the heat of midsummer</note>, being a lover of toil and a lover of the sea. For in this way, he will be strong and a friend to Hermes.

The morning hunt is best in the seasons of late summer and when the morning star <note>original: "ἑωσφόρος"</note> rises. In winter, one should set out when the rays of the sun are spreading, but in the blooming spring, the entire day is favorable for all kinds of catches.

<summary>Oppian describes the physical and mental qualities of an ideal fisherman, emphasizing strength, endurance, and intelligence. He also provides guidance on the best times of day and seasons for successful fishing.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes, fisherman qualities, physical fitness, patience, seasonal fishing, ancient Greek poetry, Halieutica</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] All these Hephaestus' cunning hands had wrought
For Hercules; and these to Poeas' son, Most near of friends and dear, he gave to bear.
So glorying in those arms he smote the foe. But Paris at the last to meet him sprang Fearlessly, bearing in his hands his bow And deadly arrows--but his latest day Now met himself. A flying shaft he sped Forth from the string, which sang as leapt the dart, Which flew not vainly: yet the very mark It missed, for Philoctetes swerved aside A hair-breadth, and it smote above the breast Cleodorus war-renowned, and cleft a path Clear through his shoulder; for he had not now The buckler broad which wont to fence from death Its bearer, but was falling back from fight, Being shieldless; for Polydamas' massy lance Had cleft the shoulder-belt whereby his targe Hung, and he gave back therefore, fighting still With stubborn spear. But now the arrow of death Fell on him, as from ambush leaping forth. For so Fate willed, I trow, to bring dread doom On noble-hearted Lernus' scion, born Of Amphiale, in Rhodes the fertile land.
But soon as Poeas' battle-eager son Marked him by Paris' deadly arrow slain, Swiftly he strained his bow, shouting aloud: "Dog! I will give thee death, will speed thee down To the Unseen Land, who darest to brave me! And so shall they have rest, who travail now For thy vile sake. Destruction shall have end When thou art dead, the author of our bane."
Then to his breast he drew the plaited cord. The great bow arched, the merciless shaft was aimed Straight, and the terrible point a little peered Above the bow,
[context] in that constraining grip.

text:
<meta>This page continues from the description of the legendary gear of Heracles. The narrative shifts from the physical description of the armor to the battlefield, where Philoctetes (the son of Poeas) uses these weapons against the Trojans, specifically engaging in a fatal duel with Paris.</meta>

-># BOOK 10 <-

->**THE DUEL OF PHILOCTETES AND PARIS**<-

...to mighty Heracles <note>original: "ὀβρίμῳ ἡρακλῆϊ" (obrimō Hēraklēï). This refers back to the armor and bow described on the previous page, which originally belonged to the hero Heracles.</note>. And he gave them to the son of Poeas <note>Philoctetes, the famous archer of the Greeks. He inherited Heracles' bow because he was the only one with the courage to light Heracles' funeral pyre.</note> to wear; for he was a very close and like-minded friend to him. But he, exulting in the armor, was subduing the ranks of the enemy. At last, Paris rushed against him, daringly wielding mournful arrows in his hands along with his curved bow. For indeed, his final day was approaching him in silence.

<margin>210.</margin> Paris loosed a shaft from the bowstring; and it whizzed as the arrow sped forth. It did not fly in vain from his hands, but it missed the man himself by just a hair as he dodged. Instead, it struck the glorious Cleodorus; the arrow hit a little above the breast and drove through even to the shoulder. For he did not have a broad shield, a lack that brought him a dismal death. But as he was exposed <note>original: "γυμνὸς" (gymnos). In a military context, this means "unprotected" or "without a shield," rather than completely unclothed.</note>, he began to retreat. For Polydamas <note>A prominent Trojan hero and advisor to Hector.</note> had struck the shield from his shoulders earlier, having severed the strap with a heavy ox-goad; and so Cleodorus was retreating, though he continued to fight with a sharp spear.

<margin>220.</margin> But a mournful arrow fell upon him, darting from another direction; for even so the deity <note>original: "δαίμων" (daimon). A reference to the impersonal force of Fate or a divine power steering the course of the war.</note> wished to bring terrible death upon the noble son of Lernus, whom the sea-girt island of Rhodes bore in its fertile land. So when Paris had subdued him with the mournful missile, then the mighty son of blameless Poeas, in his fury, drawing his swift bow against him, shouted aloud: "You dog! I shall surely bring you slaughter and a destructive fate, since you now dare to face me in battle! And all those who are suffering in this dismal war because of you shall find relief; 

<margin>230.</margin> for soon there will be an end to their destruction when you die here, since you have been a plague to them." Having spoken thus, he drew the well-twisted bowstring back to his chest; the horn of the bow <note>Ancient bows were often "composite," made of wood, sinew, and the horns of animals like the ibex, which gave the bow its spring and power.</note> was curved into a circle, and the pitiless arrow was aimed; the point of the arrow projected far beyond the bow...

iiii

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>ΤΟ ΔΕΚΑΤΟΝ.</header>
<sig>iiii</sig>

ὀβρίμῳ ἡρακλῆϊ. ὃ δ' ὤπασε παιδὶ φορῆναι
Ποίαντος· μάλα γάρ οἱ ὁμόφρονος φίλος ἦεν.
αὐτὰρ ὃ κυδιόων ἐν τεύχεσι, δάμνατο λαούς.
ὀψὲ δέ οἱ μετόρουσε Πάρις στονόεντας ὀϊστοὺς
νωμῶν ἐν χείρεσσι μετὰ γναμπτοῖο βιοῖο
θαρσαλέως. τῷ γάρ ῥα σιωπήεν ὕστατον ἦμαρ.
<margin>210.</margin> ἧκε δ' ἀπὸ νευρῆφι βέλος· ἥ δ' ἰάχησεν,
ἰῷ ἐπεσσυμένοιο· ὃ δ' οὐχ ἅλιον φύγε χειρῶν,
ἀλλ' αὐτοῦ μὲν ἅμαρτεν ἀλευομένοιο μάλα τυτθόν.
καί ῥ' ἔβαλεν Κλεόδωρον ἀγακλυτόν· ὃς ῥ' ἐόντα
βαιὸν ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο, διήλασε δ' ἄχρις ἐς ὦμον.
οὐ γάρ ἔχεν σάκος εὐρύ, τό, οἱ λυγρὸν ἔχεν ὄλεθρον.
ἀλλ' ὅτε γυμνὸς ἐὼν, ἀνεχάζετο. τῷ γάρ ἀπ' ὤμων
Πουλυδάμας ἀπάραξε σάκος, τελαμῶνα δαΐξας
βουπλήγι στιβαρῷ· ὃ δ' ἐχάζατο μαρνάμενός περ
αἰχμῇ ἀνικρῇ· στονόης δέ οἱ ἔμπεσεν ἰὸς
<margin>220.</margin> ἄλλοθεν ἀΐξας· ὣς γάρ νύ περ ἤθελε δαίμων
θήσειν αἰνὸν ὄλεθρον ἐϋφρονος ἠδ' ἐπὶ Λέρνῳ,
ὅν τέκετ' ἀμφιάλη ῥοδίων ἐν πίονι γαίῃ.
τόν δ' ὣς οὖν ἐδάμασσε Πάρις στονόεντι βελέμνῳ,
δὴ τότε δὴ Ποίαντος ἀμύμονος ὄβριμος υἱὸς
ἐμμεμαὼς, θοὰ τόξα τιταίνων οἱ, μέγ' ἀΰτει·
ὦ κύον, ὡς σοὶ ἔγωγε φόνον, καὶ κῆρ' ἀΐδηλον
δώσω, ἐπεί νύ μοι ἄντα λιλαίεαι ἰσοφαρίζειν·
καί κεν ἀναπλάσουσιν, ὅσσοι σέθεν εἵνεκα λυγρῷ
τείροντ' ἐν πολέμῳ· τάχα γὰρ λύσις ἔσσετ' ὀλέθρου
<margin>230.</margin> ἐνθάδε σεῖο θανόντος, ἐπεὶ σφίσι πῆμα τέτυξαι.
ὣς εἰπὼν, νευρὴν ἐΰστροφον ἀγχόθι μαζῷ
ἕρυσσε· κυκλώθη δὲ κέρας, καὶ ἀμείλιχος ἰὸς
ἰθύνθη· τόξου δὲ λίην ὑπέρεχεν ἀκωκή

text:
### BOOK TEN

<sig>iiii</sig>

to mighty Hercules. He <note>Hercules</note> gave them to the son of Poeas <note>Philoctetes</note> to carry, for he was the friend of a like-minded man. But he, exulting in his armor, was subduing the ranks of men. At last Paris rushed toward him, wielding mournful arrows in his hands with his curved bow, acting boldly; for the silent final day of his life was standing over him.
<margin>210.</margin> He released a shaft from the string, and it hissed as it rushed forth with the arrow. It did not fly in vain from his hands, yet it missed the man himself as he avoided it by a very small margin. Instead, it struck the glorious Cleodorus; hitting him just above the breast, it drove all the way through to the shoulder. For he did not have a wide shield, which might have kept away his dismal destruction. Rather, being exposed, he was drawing back; for Polydamas had struck the shield from his shoulders, severing the strap with a heavy ox-goad. He was retreating even as he fought with his sharp spear, but the groaning arrow fell upon him,
<margin>220.</margin> darting from another direction. For so the divinity <note>the personification of fate or a specific god</note> wished to bring dread destruction upon the kind-hearted man and upon Lernus, whom the sea-girt land of the Rhodians bore in its rich soil. When Paris had thus overcome him with the mournful missile, then the mighty son of noble Poeas <note>Philoctetes</note>, raging and stretching his swift bow against him, shouted aloud: "O dog, truly I shall give you slaughter and invisible death, since you now desire to match yourself against me. And all those who are worn down in dismal war because of you shall breathe again; for soon there will be a release from ruin once you have died here, since you have become a bane to them."
<margin>230.</margin> So he spoke, and drew the well-twisted string close to his breast. The horn bow was curved into a circle, and the pitiless arrow was aimed; the point of the arrow extended far beyond the bow.

<summary>Philoctetes and Paris engage in a deadly archery duel during the Trojan War. Paris kills Cleodorus after the latter loses his shield, prompting Philoctetes to vow Paris's imminent death as the cause of the war's suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Philoctetes, Paris, Cleodorus, Polydamas, Trojan War, archery, Hercules, fate, Rhodes</keywords>

text:
BOOK TEN.
<sig>iiii</sig>

to mighty Heracles. He granted it to the son of Poeas to carry, for he was a very close companion to him. He, exulting in the armor, subdued the people. But late in the day, Paris rushed toward him, wielding groaning arrows in his hands along with his curved bow, boldly. For his final day was meeting him.
<margin>210.</margin> He let fly a shaft from the string; it hissed as the arrow sped on. It did not fly from his hands in vain, but missed the man himself, who had dodged it by a very small margin. It struck Cleodorus, famous though he was, just above the breast, and drove through as far as the shoulder. For he did not have his broad shield, which brought him miserable destruction. But he, being unprotected, retreated. For Polydamas had struck the shield from his shoulders, having severed the strap with a sturdy ox-goad. He retreated, though he was fighting with a painful spear-point; and a groaning arrow struck him,
<margin>220.</margin> having darted from elsewhere. For so, perhaps, a god wished to bring terrible destruction upon the son of the noble Lernus, whom he bore in the fertile land of the Rhodians. When Paris had thus subdued him with a groaning missile, then indeed the mighty son of blameless Poeas, eager for battle, stretching his swift bow against him, shouted loudly:
"O dog, I shall give you slaughter and unseen doom, since you desire to match yourself against me. And those who are worn down in the miserable war because of you shall breathe again; for soon there shall be a release from destruction
<margin>230.</margin> here, once you are dead, since you have been a bane to them."
Having spoken thus, he drew the well-twisted string near his breast; the horn was bent into a circle, and the pitiless arrow was aimed; and the bow always held the point above.

<summary>This passage from Book Ten of the Posthomerica describes the battlefield actions of Philoctetes, the son of Poeas, as he engages in combat against Paris and the Trojans, ultimately threatening Paris with death to end the suffering of the Greeks.</summary>
<keywords>Philoctetes, Paris, Trojan War, Heracles' bow, Cleodorus, Polydamas, epic combat</keywords>

reference.text:
[context] Ere long they came to the lofty dwelling of the son of Peleus for which the Myrmidons had cut pine and which they had built for their king; when they had built it
they thatched it with coarse tussock-grass which they had mown out on the plain, and all round it they made a large courtyard, which was fenced with stakes set close together. The gate was barred with a single bolt of pine which it took three men to force into its place, and three to draw back so as to open the gate, but Achilles could draw it by himself. Mercury opened the gate for the old man, and brought in the treasure that he was taking with him for the son of Peleus. Then he sprang from the chariot on to the ground and said, “Sir, it is I, immortal Mercury, that am come with you, for my father sent me to escort you. I will now leave you, and will not enter into the presence of Achilles, for it might anger him that a god should befriend mortal men thus openly. Go you within, and embrace the knees of the son of Peleus: beseech him by his father, his lovely mother, and his son; thus you may move him.”
With these words Mercury went back to high Olympus. Priam sprang from his chariot to the ground, leaving Idaeus where he was, in charge of the mules and horses. The old man went straight into the house where Achilles, loved of the gods, was sitting. There he found him with his men seated at a distance from him: only two, the hero Automedon, and Alcimus of the race of Mars, were busy in attendance about his person, for he had but just done
[context] eating and drinking, and the table was still there.

text:
<header>Iliad Ω.</header>

...Lashed with cut reeds.
And they made a great courtyard for the lord
With dense stakes, and the door was held by a single bolt
Of fir. Three Achaeans would usually bolt it,
And three would undo the great key of the gates
Of the others; but Achilles would undo it alone.
Then Hermes the Bringer of Luck opened it for the old man.
He led in the glorious gifts for the swift-footed son of Peleus.
From the chariot he stepped onto the ground and spoke:

"Old man, I have come as an immortal god,
Hermes. For my father sent me as a guide to you.
But I will return, nor will I look upon the face of Achilles;
It would be unseemly
For an immortal god to show such favor to mortals openly.
But you, go in, and clasp the knees of Peleus’ son.
Entreat him by his father, and his fair-haired mother,
And his child, that you may stir his spirit."

So having spoken, he departed to high Olympus,
Hermes. But Priam leaped from the chariot to the earth.
He left Idaeus there, who remained holding back
The horses and mules, and the old man went straight to the house.
There sat Achilles, dear to Zeus. He found him himself.
His companions were sitting apart, and two alone
The hero Automedon and the warlike Almus,
Were busying themselves near him; and he had just finished his meal.

They thatched the roof with downy meadow-grass <note>original: "Λαχνάντ’ ὀρέφον λαιμώνοδαν"</note> which they had mown.
And around it they, the warriors, built a great courtyard for their lord
With thick-set stakes; the door was held by a single bar
Of fir-wood. It took three Achaeans to drive it home,
And three to open the great bolt of the doors—
Three of the other men—but Achilles could drive it home even alone.
Then Hermes, the bringer of luck, opened the gate for the old man.
He brought in the glorious gifts for the swift-footed son of Peleus.
He stepped down from the chariot to the ground and spoke:

"O old man, truly I have come here as an immortal god,
Hermes; for my father sent me to be your guide.
But now I shall go back, and I will not go before the eyes
Of Achilles; for it would be a cause of indignation
For an immortal god to be thus openly entertained by mortals.
But you, go inside and clasp the knees of the son of Peleus.
Entreat him by his father, and his fair-haired mother,
And by his child, so that you may move his heart."

<margin>
Mercury reveals himself to Priam. <note>original: "Mercurius Priamo spindicat."</note>
</margin>

Having spoken thus, Hermes departed for high Olympus.
Priam leaped from the chariot to the ground.
He left Idaeus there; he remained behind, holding
The horses and the mules. The old man went straight into the house
Where Achilles, beloved of Zeus, used to sit. He found him
Inside; his companions sat apart from him, while only two,
The hero Automedon and Alkimos, a branch of Ares,
Were busy attending him; he had just ceased from eating.

reference.text:
And like some vagrant menial he slunk about begging his living, his head rough and dirty; and he spoke bitterly of the royal house of the Atreidae—as though he were really opposed to those chiefs!
Would, oh! would he had perished, as was his due, before he set foot on Phrygia’s soil!
Whether it was really Odysseus or not, I am afraid;
for Hector will blame us sentinels.
What can he allege?
He will suspect.
What have we done? Why are you afraid?
They got past us—
Well, who?
The ones who came this night to the Phrygian army.
Oh, oh! Cruel stroke of fate. Woe, woe!
Hush! be silent all, crouch low; for perhaps there comes someone into the snare.
Oh, oh! dire mishap to the Thracians.
It is one of the allies who is groaning.
Oh, oh! woe to me and to you, O king of Thrace, how cursed the sight of Troy to you!
what an end to your life!
Who are you? One of the allies? Night’s gloom has dulled these eyes and I cannot clearly recognize you.
Where can I find some Trojan chief? Where does Hector
take his rest under arms? To which of the captains of the army am I to tell my tale? What sufferings ours! what dark deeds someone has wrought on us and gone his way, when he had wound up a ball of sorrow manifest to every Thracian!

cause.diagnosis: The print is sharp but set in early Greek type full of ligatures, and the OCR misread roughly one word in three (δυσοίζων as "Δυσσέων", δύστηνος as "Δύσσωνος", περᾶσαι as "πυρᾶσαι", διόπων as "διοτῶν", πένθος τολυπεύσας as "πυγθ’ πολυπονύσας"); the translator then turned each garbled word into a plausible one (two false Odysseuses, a fire, two kings), so nearly all lost meaning starts in the OCR.

causes.ocr_has: ἡμι τίς λαίσκων; Ημι. Δυσσέων.
causes.english_says: Semi. Who is calling? Semi. Odysseus.
causes.note: δυσοίζων (δ-ligature + οίζων) read as a capitalised non-word, which the translator took for Odysseus.

causes.image_reads: καθ’ ἡμᾶς περᾶσαι
causes.ocr_has: καθ’ ἡμᾶς πυρᾶσαι
causes.english_says: To set fire among us
causes.note: The ερ ligature was read as υρ; "to have passed by us" became fire.

causes.image_reads: ἰώ. δύστηνος ἐγὼ, σύ τ’ ἄναξ Θρῃκῶν. ὦ στυγνοτάτην Τροίαν ἐσιδὼν
causes.ocr_has: ἰώ. Δύσσωνος ἐγὼ, σύ τ’ ἄναξ Θρηκῶν. ὦ συγνοτάτω Τροίαν ἐσιδὼν
causes.english_says: Oh, alas. I am of Odysseus, and you, king of the Thracians. O most wretched one, having looked upon Troy
causes.note: δύστηνος (στ and ην ligatures) became "Δύσσωνος" and a second false Odysseus; στυγνοτάτην (of Troy) lost its case and was attached to the king.

causes.image_reads: τίνι σημήνω διόπων στρατιᾶς;
causes.ocr_has: τίνι σημήνω διοτῶν στρατιᾶς;
causes.english_says: To whom do I signal the army of the two kings?
causes.note: διόπων ("of the commanders", π printed as ϖ) misread as διοτῶν; "two kings" is the translator's guess.

causes.image_reads: δράσας ἀφανῆ, φροῦδος, φανερὸν Θρῃξὶν πένθος τολυπεύσας

causes.english_says: has made us disappear, gone, clearly the Thracian army suffering much

causes.image_reads: Βίον δ’ ἐπαιτῶν, εἷρπ’ ἀγύρτης τις λάτρις, ψαφαρόχρουν κάρα πουλυπίνητ’ ἔχων

text:
<header>EURIPIDES</header>

And I ask for my livelihood, like some wandering servant,
having a rough head, with a miserable garment.
And much he
struck the royal house of the Atreidae with evil words,
appearing as an enemy to the commanders.
May he perish, may he perish utterly,
before he sets foot in the land of the Phrygians.
Semi. But fear of Odysseus, or not, holds me.
For Hector will blame us, the guards.
Semi. Who is calling? Semi. Odysseus.
Semi. What are you doing? Why are you trembling?
Semi. To set fire among us. Semi. Which of the men
Semi. These who came by night to the Phrygian army.
Oh, alas. The heavy fate of the spirit. Alas, alas.
Semi. Behold. Silence, everyone.
Semi. Are you afraid? For perhaps someone is coming into the net.
Oh, alas, heavy misfortune of the Thracian allies.
Semi. Who is listening?
Oh, alas. I am of Odysseus, and you, king of the Thracians.
O most wretched one, having looked upon Troy,
what end of life has taken you?
Chor. Who are you among the allies? In the night
my eyes are dim, and I do not know you at all.
Oh, where are the Trojan guards?
Where is Hector
who sleeps under the shield?
To whom do I signal the army of the two kings?
What we have suffered. What someone
has made us disappear, gone, clearly
the Thracian army suffering much.

ἡμι ἆτ’ ἐν Ὀδυσσέως, εἴτε μὴ, φόβω μ’ ἔχει.

οἰκ ἰώ. δαίμονος τύχα βαρεῖα. φεῦ, φεῦ.
ἡμι ἔα. σίγα πᾶς.
ἡμι ὕβει; ἴσως γὰρ εἰς βόλον τις ἔρχεται.
οἰκ ὦ συμφορὰ βαρεῖα Θρηκῶν συμμάχων.
ἡμι τίς ὁ κλύων;

χο τίς εἶ ποτ’ ἀνδρῶν συμμάχων; κατ’ εὐφρόνην
ἀμβλῶπες αὐγαὶ, κ’ οὐ σε γινώσκω γ’ ὅλως.

ποῦ λῆθ’ Εκτωρ
ὃν ὑπασπίδιον κοῖτον ἰαύει;
τίνι σημήνω διοτῶν στρατιᾶς;
οἷα πεπόνθαμεν. οἷα τις ἡμᾶς
ἀρασας ἀφανῆ, φροῦδος, φανερὸν
Θρηκὶν πυγθ’ πολυπονύσας.

reasons.j1: Source OCR of an early Greek typeface is corrupt in many lines; [served] gets the plain lines right (Hector will blame the guards; those who came by night to the Phrygian army; heavy misfortune of the Thracian allies; dim eyes at night) but fills the corrupt ones with guesses that twice put Odysseus into the dialogue ('Δυσσέων', 'Δύσσωνος') and turns 'got past us' into 'set fire', 'captains' into 'two kings'.
reasons.j2: Source OCR is badly garbled; [served] keeps the line layout and gets the plain lines right (Hector will blame the guards; those who came by night to the Phrygian army; heavy misfortune of the Thracian allies; dim eyes at night; where does Hector sleep under shield) but fills the garbled ones with plausible content, twice introducing 'Odysseus' as a speaker's answer or identity, plus 'set fire among us' for 'got past us' and a first-person opening for the third-person beggar.

text:
EURIPIDES

I beg for my life, a wandering beggar and servant,
bearing a dry-skinned head, <note>referring to the appearance of age or hardship</note> worn down.
And many things against the
royal house of the Atreidae, he spoke ill,
as if an enemy to the generals.
May he perish, may he perish utterly,
before he sets foot upon the land of the Phrygians.
I say, is it Odysseus, or not? Fear holds me.
For Hector will blame us, the guards.
I say, who is calling? I say, Odysseus.
I say, what are you doing? Why are you afraid?
I say, to set fire among us. I say, which of the men
I say, have come into the Phrygian camp by night?
Alas, woe. The heavy fortune of a spirit. Woe, woe.
I say, hush. Be silent, everyone.
I say, are you insolent? For perhaps someone is walking into a trap.
Alas, the heavy calamity of the Thracian allies.
I say, who is listening?
Alas, woe. I am Odysseus, and you are the king of the Thracians.
O you who saw Troy most clearly,
what kind of end of life has taken you?
Chorus: Who are you among the allied men? In the night
the rays are dim, and I do not recognize you at all.
Alas, where is the <term>aulaktos</term> <gloss>furrowed/cultivated</gloss> Trojan mold?
Where lies Hector,
who sleeps in his bed beneath his shield?
To whom shall I signal the army of the gods?
What we have suffered. How someone
has destroyed us, unseen, gone, manifest
to the Thracians, <unclear>a great labor</unclear>.

<meta>This page contains a portion of the tragedy Rhesus, traditionally attributed to Euripides. The scene depicts the confusion and alarm in the Trojan camp following a night raid by Odysseus and Diomedes.</meta>

# EURIPIDES

I beg for my life, like some wandering, gathering servant,
having a dusty-colored head and <unclear>λυπινκτ’</unclear> <note>The OCR reading here is likely a corruption of a Greek term for "miserable" or "shabby".</note>.
And many things
he cast evilly against the royal house of the Atreidae <note>The sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus</note>,
supposedly as an enemy to the generals.
May he perish, may he perish utterly,
before setting foot upon the land of the Phrygians <note>Trojans</note>.
Whether he is among us in the guise of Odysseus or not, fear holds me.
For Hector will blame us guards.
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Who is shouting? <term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Odysseus.
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: What are you doing? Why do you fear?
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: To set a watch by us. <term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Which of the men?
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: These men came by night into the Phrygian army.
<term>Oik</term> <gloss>Charioteer/House-servant</gloss>: Oh, alas! Heavy is the fortune of the divinity. Alas, alas.
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Ha! Everyone be silent.
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Do you hear? For perhaps someone is coming into the snare.
<term>Oik</term> <gloss>Charioteer</gloss>: O heavy misfortune of the Thracian allies!
<term>Hemi</term> <gloss>Semi-chorus</gloss>: Who is the one crying out?
<term>Oik</term> <gloss>Charioteer</gloss>: Oh, alas! I am a miserable man, and you too, lord of the Thracians.
O you who saw Troy with such ill-omen,
what an end of life has seized you?
<term>Cho</term> <gloss>Chorus</gloss>: Who of the allied men are you? In the darkness of night
my eyes are dimmed, and I do not recognize you at all.
<term>Oik</term> <gloss>Charioteer</gloss>: Where can I find some prince of the Trojans?
Where does Hector sleep
taking his rest under his shield?
To whom of the leaders of the army shall I report
what things we have suffered? What things someone
has done to us, striking us unseen, and is gone, having brought
manifest and much-toiled pain upon the Thracians.

<summary>The Thracian charioteer laments the slaughter of King Rhesus and his men during a night raid on the Trojan camp. The Chorus of guards reacts with confusion and alarm as they realize an enemy has infiltrated their lines.</summary>

text:
EURIPIDES

Begging for his living, he crept about as a mendicant servant,
with a dusty head and matted hair.
And often he spoke ill of the royal
hearth of the Atreidae, pretending to be an enemy to the commanders.
May he perish, may he perish justly,
before setting foot upon the land of the Phrygians.
<note>Speaker 1</note> Whether it is Odysseus or not, fear possesses me.
For Hector will blame us, the guards.
<note>Speaker 2</note> Who is shouting? <note>Speaker 1</note> I am. I am anxious.
<note>Speaker 2</note> What are you doing? Why are you afraid?
<note>Speaker 1</note> That someone might pass by us. <note>Speaker 2</note> Which of the men?
<note>Speaker 1</note> Those who came this night into the Phrygian camp.
<note>Speaker 3</note> Oh, woe. The heavy fortune of a spirit. Alas, alas.
<note>Speaker 1</note> Hush. Be silent, everyone.
<note>Speaker 2</note> Be insolent. For perhaps someone is coming into the net.
<note>Speaker 3</note> Oh, the heavy calamity of the Thracian allies.
<note>Speaker 1</note> Who is the one lamenting?
<note>Speaker 3</note> Oh, wretched am I, and you, O king of the Thracians.
O you who looked upon most hateful Troy,
what an end of life has seized you?
<note>Chorus</note> Who are you among the allied men? In the night
the rays are dim, and I do not know you at all.
<note>Speaker 3</note> Where might I find one of the Trojan lords?
Where indeed does Hector
sleep his rest beneath his shield?
To whom shall I signal the destruction of the army?
What we have suffered. What someone has done to us,
invisible, gone, having spun
a manifest grief for the Thracians.

[context] All this they tell us: but I have ever suspected them
of having convenient lapses of memory, and omitting the worst part for very shame. For myself, I shall have no such scruple. All that I have heard, or can reasonably infer, of the evils of dependence, I shall place before you. For either, friend, my penetration is at fault, or you have long had a hankering for this profession.
Yes, I have seen it from the first, whenever the conversation has fallen on this subject of salaried intellects. ‘Happy men!’ some enthusiast has cried. ‘The élite of Rome are their friends. They dine sumptuously, and call for no reckoning. They are lodged splendidly, and travel comfortably—nay, luxuriously — with cushions at their backs, and as often as not a fine pair of creams in front of them. And, as if this were not enough, the friendship they enjoy and the handsome treatment they receive is made good to them with a substantial salary. They sow not, they plough not; yet all things grow for their use.’ How I have seen you prick up your ears at such words as these! How wide your mouth has opened to the bait!
Now I will have a clear conscience in this matter. I will not be told hereafter that I saw you swallowing this palpable bait, and never stirred a finger to snatch it from you, and show you the hook while there was yet time; that I watched you nibbling, saw the hook well in and the fish hauled up, and then stood by shedding useless tears, A grave charge, indeed, were I to leave it in your power to bring it; such neglect would admit of no palliation, You shall therefore hear the whole truth. Now, in leisurely fashion, from without, not hereafter from within, shall you examine this weel from which no fish escapes. You shall take in hand this hook of subtle barb. You shall try the prongs of this eel-spear against your inflated cheek;
[context] and if you decide that they are not sharp, that they would be easily evaded, that a wound from them would be no great matter, that they are deficient in power and grasp—then write me among those who have cowardice to thank for their empty bellies; and for yourself, take heart of grace, and swoop upon your prey, and cormorant-wise, if you will, swallow all at a gulp.

text:
<meta>This page continues Lucian’s introduction to his treatise. He is addressing his friend Timocles, warning him about the seductive lure of taking a paid position in the household of a wealthy Roman aristocrat. Lucian uses vivid fishing metaphors to describe the hidden dangers of such a "comfortable" life.</meta>

...to hide their misfortunes and were willing to forget them entirely. But I, by putting those accounts together along with whatever else I can find from common discourse regarding such associations, will not hesitate, my dear Timocles, to go through everything with you. Indeed, I think I have noticed for a long time now that you are setting your sights on this kind of life.

3. First of all, whenever the talk happened to fall upon such matters, and someone present praised this kind of salaried service <margin>654</margin>—calling those men "thrice-blessed" who, in addition to having the best of the Romans as their friends, dine on luxurious meals for which they pay no share <note>original: "ἀσύμβολα" (asymbola). In Greek social life, an "asymbolon" meal was one where a guest did not have to contribute a "symbolon" or portion of the cost, a rare privilege for those not of independent means.</note>, live in beautiful houses, and travel abroad with every ease and pleasure, perhaps reclining in a carriage drawn by white horses—they would say that the salary they receive for their friendship and for the benefits they enjoy is no small thing. To such men, they claimed, everything simply grows "without sowing or plowing" <note>This is a reference to Homer's description of the land of the Cyclopes in the *Odyssey*, where nature provides food without any human labor.</note>.

Whenever you heard these and similar things, I saw <margin>655</margin> how you gaped at them, and how you offered your mouth wide open to the bait. Therefore, so that my own conduct may be blameless in the future, and so you cannot say that we saw you swallowing such a large hook along with the shrimp <note>The "shrimp" or "prawn" (karidos) refers to the small, tasty bait used to hide a large, lethal hook.</note> and yet did not stop you, nor pull you away before it went down your throat, nor warn you beforehand—instead of just standing by and weeping as we watched you being dragged away by force once the hook was already stuck and pulled tight—so that you may never have cause to say these things (which would be quite reasonable and difficult for us to answer if we had not warned you), hear the whole story from the beginning. 

Examine the net itself and the inescapable wicker-traps <note>term: "κύρτος" (kyrtos) — a bell-shaped trap made of wicker used by ancient fishermen; once a fish entered, the narrow neck made it impossible to swim back out.</note> from the outside at your leisure, rather than from deep within the interior. Take the curve of the hook into your hands, along with the backward-pointing barb <margin>656</margin> and the sharp points of the trident, and consider how they might feel against a jaw puffed up with pride...

<summary>Lucian warns Timocles against the lure of taking a paid position in a Roman household, comparing the perceived luxuries to a fisherman's bait that hides a painful hook.</summary>
<keywords>Timocles, Roman patronage, salaried service, fishing metaphors, luxury, social criticism</keywords>

text:
to hide them and to be willingly forgetful of them. But I, for my part, will not hesitate to go through all these things for you, my good Timocles, as well as any others that I find, by putting the argument together, to be inherent in such associations. For I think I have long since noticed that you are plotting to enter this life. 3. And first of all, when the discussion turned to such matters, and then one of those present praised such a salary, calling those thrice-blessed who, besides having the best of the Romans as friends, and dining on luxurious, contribution-free dinners, and living in a fine house, and traveling with every ease and pleasure in a white carriage, if it so happens, while reclining at full length, also receive no small salary for their friendship and for the benefits they receive—for truly, for such people, everything grows unsown and unplowed—whenever you heard these things and the like, I saw how you gaped at them and kept your mouth wide open for the bait. Therefore, so that my own conduct may be blameless in the future, and so that you may not be able to say that, seeing you swallowing such a large hook along with the bait, we did not intervene, nor pull it away before it fell into your throat, nor give you warning, but instead waited until you were being dragged out and hooked, and stood by weeping when it was too late to be of any use—so that you may never say these things, which are very reasonable if they are said, and inescapable for us, as we do not act unjustly by not giving prior warning, listen from the beginning to everything. Examine the net itself and the inescapable nature of the fish-traps from the outside, at your leisure, and not from within the depths. And take the curved hook, and the backward turn of the barb, and the points of the trident into your hands, and <unclear>examine them</unclear> against your swollen jaw.

<summary>Lucian warns Timocles against the deceptive allure of seeking a life of luxury and patronage among the Roman elite, using the metaphor of a fisherman's trap to illustrate the hidden dangers of such a path.</summary>

them. But as for me, by putting together those points and any others I find in the argument that belong to such associations, I will not hesitate, my dear Timocles, to recount them all to you. For I think I have long since noticed that you are setting your sights on this way of life. 3. And first of all, whenever the conversation turned to such matters, and then someone present praised this kind of hired service <note>original: "misthophora"</note>, saying that those men are thrice-blessed who, besides having the best of the Romans as friends and eating sumptuous dinners without paying a contribution <note>original: "asymbola"</note>, living in a fine house and traveling with every ease and pleasure on a pair of white horses, perhaps, lounging back at their ease, also receive no small salary for their friendship and for the benefits they enjoy—for absolutely everything grows for such people without sowing or plowing—whenever you heard these and similar things, I saw how you gaped at them and held your mouth wide open for the bait. So, in order that our side may be blameless in the future, and that you may not be able to say that we saw you swallowing such a large hook along with the shrimp and did not stop you, nor pulled it away before it went down your throat, nor warned you beforehand, but instead waited until you were being hauled out with it already stuck fast, watching you being dragged and led by force when it was of no use for us to stand by and weep; so that you may never say these things—which would be quite reasonable if said, and impossible for us to escape, as if we were not doing wrong by not warning you—listen to everything from the beginning. Examine the net itself and the inescapable nature of the weels <note>a type of wicker fish-trap</note> from the outside at your leisure, rather than from the inside at the very bottom. Take into your hands the curve of the hook, the backward turn of its barb, and the points of the trident, and consider them in relation to your puffed-out jaw

reference.text:
[context] There was Ptolemy in his sister’s arms, the son of Lysimachus plotting against his father, Seleucus’s son Antiochus making signs to his step-mother Stratonice, Alexander of Pherae being murdered by his wife, Antigonus corrupting his daughter-inlaw, the son of Attalus putting the poison in his cup;
Arsaces was in the act of slaying his mistress, while the eunuch Arbaces drew his sword upon him; the guards were dragging Spatinus the Mede out from the banquet by the foot, with the lump on his brow from the golden cup. Similar sights were to be seen in the palaces of Libya and Scythia and Thrace—adulteries, murders, treasons, robberies, perjuries, suspicions, and monstrous betrayals.
Such was the entertainment afforded me by royalty; private life was much more amusing; for I could make that out too. I saw Hermodorus the Epicurean perjuring himself for £40, Agathocles the Stoic suing a pupil for his fees, lawyer Clinias stealing a bowl from the temple of Asclepius, and Herophilus the cynic sleeping in a brothel. Not to mention the multitude of burglars, litigants, usurers, duns; oh, it was a fine representative show!
I must say, Menippus, I should have liked the details here too; it all seems to have been very much to your taste.
I could not go through the whole of it, even to please you; to take it in with the eyes kept one busy. But the main divisions were very much what Homer gives from the shield of Achilles: here junketings and marriages, there courts and councils, in another compartment a sacrifice, and hard by a mourning. If I glanced at Getica, I would see the Getae at war; at Scythia, there were the Scythians wandering about on their waggons; half a turn in another direction gave me Egyptians at the plough, or Phoenicians chaffering, Cilician pirates, Spartan flagellants, Athenians at law.
All this was simultaneous, you understand; and you must try to conceive what a queer jumble it all made. It was as if aman were to collect a number of choristers, or rather of choruses
, and then tell each individual to disregard the others and start a strain of his own; if each did his best, went his own way, and tried to drown his neighbour, can you imagine what the musical effect would be?
A very ridiculous confusion.
Well, friend, such are the earthly dancers; the life of man is just such a discordant performance; not only are the voices jangled, but the steps are not uniform, the motions not concerted, the objects not agreed upon—until the impresario dismisses them one by one from the stage, with a ‘not wanted.’ Then they are all alike, and quiet enough, confounding no longer their undisciplined rival strains. But as long as the show lasts in its marvellous diversity, there is plenty of food for
laughter in its vagaries.
The people who most amused me, however, were those
[context] who dispute about boundaries, or pride themselves on cultivating the plain of Sicyon, or holding the Oenoé side of Marathon, or a thousand acres at Acharnae.

<margin>disposed theories</margin>
<margin>prostitution</margin>
<margin>inactivity</margin>
<margin>nocturnal</margin>
<margin>except that he speaks of the green <note>or fresh/raw</note> in accordance with right reason</margin>
<margin>erotically</margin>
<margin>except that he varies in relation to right reason, one must attend to the theater</margin>

They truly bring no small amount; and the whole is entirely from parts of the sword, a trumpet; and shields are like hoplites, as if escorting a rhapsode, as it seemed good to him with his feet, not in a golden rhythm, but they are made similar to these rhythms because they are many, or even beyond being revered, for I remember them rhapsodizing with tin <note>or perhaps "cheap metal"</note>, helping the feast, as they say. And just as when someone is under the influence of those who cause forgetfulness of the rhythms and the cutting of the tin; for I think such is the occupation of these things, some of them to process, and for the speeches themselves, when interpreted, one draws the hand toward the <unclear>curion</unclear>, a drachma of the feast, just as your rhythm falls into weak things, of learning, and by being divided; and the orator himself is a witness, weak and the rhythm being corrupted, this one which he says is from a low-lying sleeper; for why should I speak of the <unclear>amous</unclear> who <unclear>tachoruchountas</unclear> those who are only for blood; the fingers that are stretched out; for in general, poetic and of every speaker, to know forgetfulness; and indeed as these things, and others which one might use, for thus having happened upon Tartarus, to begin; all things as if through my own, I do not say it is impossible; how that this was the work of the goddess being cut, the matter of such a claim; and as many things as equal the part, his own in return, for it is able to be equal and excessive, and I bring it from weakness to have fallen in; and just as a part sacrificed, for the rhythms, just as I said, that the dishonored one, as another, removes; fighting just as they were, because I am able to, in this way; wandering upon the Amazons, it was one thing to behold, that our rhythms are others; the <unclear>aumatos</unclear> just as thus desiring, and merchants of the palm tree it was; and that it removed as a rhythm, yet it is as another; <unclear>raios</unclear> was an obscurity of these, under the more we use rhythm; as <unclear>rasoi</unclear> <unclear>idi</unclear> <unclear>opmou</unclear> forms, as having seen each in order, it was as the self, it was as to clarify, <unclear>memos</unclear> the <unclear>mous</unclear> dancing; <unclear>mamon</unclear> but for many choruses; there will be the <unclear>propas</unclear> <unclear>ase</unclear> of those handed down to each, the sun as it was released, feasting indeed in rhythms, he says, of my <unclear>morous</unclear> of a deer, and the sun of the rhapsode; and to the most rhythms of the great fame; being eager then in rhythm toward the <unclear>diossaimois</unclear> of the other; just as in all rhythms; thick and slippery; in which he sings, such a thing I say, as those dancing in few for themselves, as <unclear>amarmonas</unclear>, as of the man, as living; I swear as of rhythm, in rhythms we harmonize the figures, as in rhythms, as in rhythms; and these are not even rhythmized, as until <unclear>amauton</unclear>, as of <unclear>aphomou</unclear> in choruses having molded, as in rhythms, as in rhythms, as <unclear>amarmon</unclear>, this door, all things similar in rhythm, in rhythms, as until another for us; and to test the unshaken, as in rhythm, in rhythms, as in rhythms, as in rhythms, as in rhythms, as of the theater attending in rhythms, as in rhythms, as in rhythms; <unclear>mamon</unclear> but to the <unclear>epidamois</unclear>

κασιτέροις λιμοῦ ῥαψῳδοῦντας φορβούσας ἐπικουλοῦντας ὡς φασι τῆς
ἑορτῆς ὥσπερ δὲ ὅταν ᾖ τις ὑπὸ τῶν οἱ λήθην τῶν ῥυθμῶν καὶ ταμεῖν

οὐτῶν· πομπεύειν ἑτέραν καὶ γὰρ αὐτὰς τὰς ῥήσεις ἑρμηνευομένας τὸ μὲν

περιπεσοῦ τοῦ μαθεῖν τῇ δὲ διαζομένου· μάρτυρα δὲ τὸν ῥήτορα ἑαυτοῦ
ἀσθενῆ καὶ διαφθείρεσθαι ῥυθμὸν τοῦδε λυσιτελῆ ὃν φησὶν ἐκ χαμαιζήλου

λαλοῦντος λήθην ἴσασθαι· καὶ μὲν ὡς ταῦτα δὲ μὲν καὶ ἄλλας ἃ χρῆσθαι μὲν ἐοῖτε
γὰρ οὕτω τυχούσαν τάρταρον ἥλισοι παρ' ἄρχεσθαι· πάντα μὲν ὡς δι' ἐμῶν

θεᾶς τὸ πρᾶγμα τὸν τοιαῦτα φαιμῆς· ὅσα δὲ ἰσοῖ τὸ μέρος τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀντιδὲ

ὅτι ἐμᾶς τὰς ῥυθμοὺς ἑτέραι· τοὺς αὖματους ὥσπερ οὕτως ἐπιθυμοῦ
καὶ φοίνικος ἐμπόρους ἦν· καὶ ὅτι μὲν ἐξήρησεν ὡς ῥυθμὸν ὅμως ἐστὶν ὡς ἄλλο
ῥαῖος δὲ ἴαν ἦν ἀσάφειαν τούτων ὑπὸ τὸ μᾶλλον ῥυθμὸν χρῶμεν· ὡς ῥασοι

And they truly bring no small amount; and the whole body <note>original: "oulomeles"</note> is part of the sword, the whole is a trumpet; shields and heavy infantry, just like a rhapsode <gloss>a performer of epic poetry</gloss> acting as a bodyguard, wherever it seemed fit to him with his feet, not in a golden rhythm, but they are made like these rhythms because they remember more than even worshipping themselves with tin, rhapsodizing, feeding, and shouting as they say of the festival. Just as when someone is under the influence of those who have forgotten the rhythms and the cutting of the tin; for I think such a pastime is like these things. To process in another way, for even the speeches themselves being interpreted, on the one hand, draw a drachma <gloss>a silver coin</gloss> of the festival toward a youthful hand, just as your rhythm falls among the weak for the sake of learning, while he is being girded. He takes the orator as his own weak witness, and the rhythm of this man is corrupted, which he says sleeps on the ground. For why should I speak of our men who dig quickly for the sake of blood alone? The fingers that are stretched out like yours; for they know how to heal the forgetfulness of every poetic and speaking thing. And while these things are so, and there are others which you might use, for having happened upon Tartarus <gloss>the deep abyss of the underworld</gloss> in this way, they begin there. I do not say that everything through me is impossible; so that these things were the work of a goddess being cut, the matter of such a report. As much as the part equals its own, it is able to be equal and very much so, and I bear it because of falling into weakness. Just as a part sacrificed, for I would say of the rhythms that the dishonored part moves away as something else. Those who are at war, just as they were, I marvel at him who is thus. Wandering among the Amazons, it was another thing to look upon, because our rhythms are different; those who are bloodless, just as you desire, and there were merchants of Phoenicia. And because he took it out as a rhythm, it is nonetheless like another, and it was a clear thing, we use the rhythm more because of the lack of clarity in these things. As if one had seen the forms of each in order, as if to make clear the parts of my dances. A breast for many dances; the signs of things handed down to each will be clear, the sun as it has been released, celebrating with rhythms, he says, the fates of a deer and the sun of a rhapsode. And I speak of the one with the most rhythms of great fame; being eager, therefore, in rhythm toward the sons of Zeus and the others. Just as with all rhythms, thick and slippery; where he sings such a thing, I say, as those who dance for themselves in small numbers as if they were harmonious, as if they were living men. I swear by the rhythm, we harmonize with rhythms in the gestures, as with rhythms, as with rhythms. And these things are not even rhythmic as far as making myself like the dances, having molded them as with rhythms, as with rhythms, as if harmonious. This heart is all similar to rhythm, to rhythms, as far as another is for us. And it is unshakeable to refute, as with rhythm, with rhythms, as with rhythms, as with rhythms, as with rhythms, cutting back on the rhythms of the theater, as with rhythms, as with rhythms, as with rhythms. A breast for the people.

<summary>This page discusses the technical application of rhythm and movement in theatrical performances, comparing the dancer's discipline to military formation and rhapsodic recitation. The marginal notes provide a moralizing commentary, warning against the erotic and irrational influences of the theater.</summary>
<keywords>rhythm, dance, theater, rhapsode, gestures, harmony, morality, festival</keywords>

Elsewhere, I saw Arsaces murdering his wife, and the eunuch Arbaces drawing his sword against Arsaces. Spatinus the Mede was being dragged out of the banquet by the guards, his brow crushed by a golden cup. Similar things to these were to be seen in Libya, and among the Scythians and Thracians in their royal palaces: men committing adultery, murdering, plotting, plundering, perjuring themselves, living in fear, being betrayed by their own kin. Such was the spectacle the kings provided for me. The affairs of private citizens were much more ridiculous. For I saw them too: Hermodorus the Epicurean perjuring himself for a thousand drachmae; Agathocles the Stoic litigating against his student over a fee; Cleinias the orator stealing a bowl from the Asclepieion; and Herophilus the Cynic sleeping in a brothel. Why should I even mention the others who were breaking into houses, litigating, lending money, or demanding payment? The sight was altogether varied and of every kind. "Indeed, Menippus, these things were well worth telling, for it seems they provided you with no small delight." "To go through everything in order, my friend, is impossible, since even to see them was a task. However, the main points of the events appeared as Homer describes those on the shield: for in one place there were feasts and weddings, elsewhere courts and assemblies; in another part someone was sacrificing, while in the neighborhood another appeared mourning. And whenever I looked toward the land of the Getae, I would see the Getae at war; when I turned to the Scythians, I could see them wandering on their wagons. Tilting my eye slightly to the other side, I watched the Egyptians farming, the Phoenician trading, the Cilician plundering, the Spartan being whipped, and the Athenian litigating. Since all these things were happening at the same time, it is time for you to imagine what this mixture <note>original: "κυκεών" <gloss>a potion made of wine, honey, barley-meal, and water; since he says life is composed of many things, he calls it a mixture</gloss></note> looked like. It is as if someone were to bring forward many dancers, or rather many choruses, and then order each of the singers to abandon the harmony and sing his own song. With each one striving for honor, finishing his own part, and eager to surpass his neighbor in loudness, do you imagine, by Zeus, what kind of song that would be?" "Altogether ridiculous and confused, Menippus." "And yet, my friend, all those who dance upon the earth are like that, and human life is composed of such disharmony. They not only utter discordant sounds, but they also move with dissimilar postures and perform opposite actions, and they devise nothing in common, until the <term>choregos</term> <gloss>chorus-leader/producer</gloss> drives each of them from the stage, saying they are no longer needed. From then on, they are all alike and silent, no longer singing that mixed and disorderly song. But in that very varied and multi-formed theater, everything that was happening was surely ridiculous, especially regarding those

<margin>A <term>kykeon</term> <gloss>mixture</gloss> is a drink composed of wine, honey, barley-meal, and water; since he says life is composed of many things, for this reason he called it a mixture.</margin>

<summary>Menippus describes the chaotic and contradictory nature of human life, comparing the world to a theater where everyone acts in discordance until death removes them from the stage.</summary>
<keywords>Menippus, human life, discordance, theater, death, choregos, kykeon</keywords>

reference.edition_note: Jowett (3rd ed. 1892) translates a pre-Burnet text; page is Burnet OCT 1902; no material differences in this span. Jowett reorders the 571c-d sentence, so the clause 'parted company with all shame and sense' (page start) sits inside the incest/parricide clause.
reference.coverage_note: full main text; apparatus criticus not covered. Page ends mid-word 'δοκοῦ-' (572b5): 'even in good men' straddles the page break.
reference.text:
[context] I mean those which are awake when the reasoning and human and ruling power is asleep; then the wild beast within us, gorged with meat or drink, starts up and having shaken off sleep, goes forth to satisfy his desires;
and there is no conceivable folly or crime—not excepting incest or any other unnatural union, or parricide, or the eating of forbidden food—which at such a time, when he has parted company with all shame and sense, a man may not be ready to commit.
Most true, he said.
But when a man’s pulse is healthy and temperate, and when before going to sleep he has awakened his rational powers, and fed them on noble thoughts and enquiries, collecting himself in meditation; after having first indulged his appetites neither too much nor too little, but just enough to lay them to sleep, and prevent them and their enjoyments and pains from interfering with the higher principle—which he leaves in the solitude of pure abstraction, free to contemplate and aspire to the knowledge of the unknown, whether in past, present, or future: when again he has allayed the passionate element, if he has a quarrel against any one—I say, when, after pacifying the two irrational principles, he rouses up the third, which is reason, before he takes his rest, then, as you know, he attains truth most nearly, and is least likely to be the sport of fantastic and lawless visions.
I quite agree.
