text:
...shame and prudence. It does not hesitate to attempt intercourse with a mother, as it fancies, or with anyone else, whether man, god, or beast, nor to commit any kind of murder, nor to refrain from any kind of food. In a word, it lacks no manner of folly or shamelessness."

"You speak most truly," he said.

"But when someone is in a healthy and temperate state regarding himself, and goes to sleep after awakening his rational part and nourishing it with fine words and reflections, attaining a state of inner contemplation; and has neither starved nor overfilled the appetitive part, so that it may sleep and cause no disturbance to the best part, whether by joy or sorrow, but leaves it alone, pure, to investigate and reach out for some perception of things unknown—things that have been, are, or are yet to come—and likewise has calmed the spirited part, falling asleep without having given way to anger; when he has thus quieted the two parts and stirred the third, in which wisdom resides—you know that he reaches the truth most effectively, and at such times the visions of his dreams are least likely to be unlawful."

"I entirely agree," he said, "that it is so."

"We have been led to speak of this at some length, but what we wish to know is this: that there is indeed a certain terrible, savage, and lawless kind of desire in everyone, even in those who seem to be moderate, but this becomes evident in sleep. If you think I speak well and you agree, observe this."

"I do agree."

"Then recall the democratic man we described."

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: describing the lawless desires that emerge when the rational part of the soul is asleep</meta>

released from all shame and prudence. For it does not shrink from attempting to lie with a mother, as it supposes, nor with any other <margin>d</margin> man, god, or beast. It does not hesitate to commit any foul murder, nor does it abstain from any food. In a single word <note>original: "ἑνὶ λόγῳ"</note>, it lacks nothing in terms of folly or shamelessness.

You speak most truly, he said.

But I suppose when a man is healthy and self-controlled in himself, and goes to sleep having awakened his rational part <note>the <term>logistikon</term> <gloss>rational or calculating part of the soul</gloss></note> and feasted it on noble words and inquiries, reaching a state of inner reflection; and when he has neither starved nor overfed the appetitive part <margin>e</margin> <note>the <term>epithymetikon</term> <gloss>desiring part of the soul</gloss></note>, so that it may fall asleep and not disturb the best part with its joy or its grief, but allows that best part to remain alone <margin>572</margin> and pure by itself, to consider and reach out to perceive something it does not know, whether of things past, present, or future; and likewise, when he has calmed the spirited part <note>the <term>thymoeides</term> <gloss>the part of the soul associated with anger, honor, and courage</gloss></note> and does not go to sleep with his spirit stirred up in anger against anyone, but has quieted <margin>5</margin> these two parts and aroused the third part in which wisdom resides, and so takes his rest—you know that in such a state he most grasps the truth, and the lawless visions of his dreams are then least likely to appear. <margin>b</margin>

I entirely agree, he said.

We have been led to speak of these things at greater length than necessary. What we want to recognize is this: that a certain terrible, wild, and lawless form of desire exists in everyone, even in those of us who seem <margin>5</margin> entirely moderate. This becomes manifest in our sleep. Consider then if I seem to be saying anything of substance and if you agree.

I do agree.

Remember then what we said the democratic man <note>the man whose soul is governed by the equality of all desires, both necessary and unnecessary</note> was like. <margin>10</margin>

---

reference.text:
[context] Again, the 'now' which seems to bound the past and the future-
does it always remain one and the same or is it always other and other? It is hard to say. (1) If it is always different and different, and if none of the parts in time which are other and other are simultaneous (unless the one contains and the other is contained, as the shorter time is by the longer), and if the 'now' which is not, but formerly was, must have ceased-to-be at some time, the 'nows' too cannot be simultaneous with one another, but the prior 'now' must always have ceased-to-be. But the prior 'now' cannot have ceased-to-be in itself (since it then existed); yet it cannot have ceased-to-be in another 'now'. For we may lay it down that one 'now' cannot be next to another, any more than point to point. If then it did not cease-to-be in the next 'now' but in another, it would exist simultaneously with the innumerable 'nows' between the two-which is impossible. Yes, but (2) neither is it possible for the 'now' to remain always the same. No determinate divisible thing has a single termination, whether it is continuously extended in one or in more than one dimension: but the 'now' is a termination, and it is possible to cut off a determinate time. Further, if coincidence in time (i.e. being neither prior nor posterior) means to be 'in one and the same "now"', then, if both what is before and what is after are in this same 'now', things which happened ten thousand years ago would be simultaneous with what has happened to-day, and nothing would be before or after anything else. This may serve as a statement of the difficulties about the attributes of time. As to what time is or what is its nature, the traditional accounts give us as little light as the preliminary problems which we have worked through. Some assert that it is (1) the movement of the whole, others that it is (2) the sphere itself. (1) Yet part, too, of the revolution is a time, but it certainly is not a revolution: for what is taken is part of a revolution, not a revolution.
Besides,
[context] if there were more heavens than one, the movement of any of them equally would be time, so that there would be many times at the same time.

text:
# Δ, 10. 218ᵃ 10 — 218ᵇ 3.

[Aristotle considers whether the "now"] remains the same or is constantly changing. For if it is always different and different, and no part of time is distinct from another part except that which contains it, and that which is contained—just as the lesser time is contained by the greater—then the "now" which is not but was previously must have perished at some time. Consequently, the "nows" will not be simultaneous with each other, but the earlier one must have perished. It is not possible for it to have perished within itself, because it existed then, nor is it possible for the earlier "now" to have perished in another "now." For it is impossible for "nows" to be adjacent to one another, just as a point cannot be adjacent to a point <note>meaning that discrete time-units cannot touch without an interval, because time is continuous</note>. If, therefore, it has not perished in the next one but in another, it would exist simultaneously in the intermediate "nows" which are infinite; but this is impossible. 

However, it is also not possible for it to remain the same. For no finite divisible thing has a single limit, whether it is continuous in one dimension or more; but the "now" is a limit, and it is possible to take a finite time. Furthermore, if "being at the same time" means being in the same "now," and neither before nor after, then if the things that occurred a myriad years ago and those occurring today are in the same "now," things would be simultaneous, and nothing would be earlier or later than anything else. 

Let this be enough regarding the puzzles of the properties of time. Regarding what time is and what its nature is, it remains unclear from traditional accounts and from the subjects we have already discussed. For some say it is the movement of the whole, while others say it is the sphere itself <note>referring to celestial rotation</note>. Yet even a part of the rotation is a time, but it is not a rotation; for the part taken is a part of the rotation, but it is not the rotation itself.

<note>Critical apparatus:
10 "or changing" — some read "or always changing" (Torstrik).
14 "that" — some read "that which" (Simplicius).
18 "is" — some read "let it be".
19 "point" — some manuscripts read "a point" (Simplicius).
26 "and in the" — Bonitz suggests removing this or changing it to "and in one".
28 "a year" — some read "for a year". "having occurred" — some read "that will occur" (Simplicius). "to those occurring" — some manuscripts read "to those having occurred" (Bekker, Simplicius).</note>

text:
Δ, 10. 218ᵃ 10 — 218ᵇ 3.

It is not easy to see whether the <term>nyn</term> <gloss>the "now" or present moment</gloss> always remains one and the same, or if it is always different. For if it is always different, and no part of time is different from another part at the same time, unless it contains it, while the other is contained—just as a lesser time is contained by a greater one—and if the <term>nyn</term> that is not, but was previously, must have perished at some time, then the <term>nyn</term>s will not exist together with one another, and the previous one must necessarily have perished. Now, it is not possible for it to have perished in itself, because it existed at that time; nor is it possible for the previous <term>nyn</term> to have perished in another <term>nyn</term>. For it is impossible for <term>nyn</term>s to be contiguous to one another, just as a point is to a point. If, therefore, it did not perish in the next one, but in another, it would exist at the same time in the infinite <term>nyn</term>s between them; but this is impossible. Furthermore, it is not possible for the same <term>nyn</term> to remain always. For no finite divisible thing has a single limit, whether it is continuous in one direction or in more; but the <term>nyn</term> is a limit, and it is possible to take a finite time. Furthermore, if to be at the same time in terms of time, and to be neither before nor after, is to be in the same <term>nyn</term>, and if both the before and the after are in this <term>nyn</term>, then things that happened ten thousand years ago would be at the same time as things happening today, and nothing would be before or after anything else. Let these points, then, be the difficulties raised regarding its properties. As for what time is and what its nature is, it remains unclear, both from what has been handed down and from what we have discussed previously. For some say it is the motion of the whole, while others say it is the sphere itself. And yet, a part of the revolution is also a certain time, but it is not a revolution; for what is taken is a part of a revolution, but not a revolution. Furthermore,

text:
Δ, 10. 218ᵃ 10 — 218ᵇ 3.

It is not easy to see whether the <term>nyn</term> <gloss>the "now" or present moment</gloss> always remains one and the same, or if it is always different. For if it is always different, and no part of time is different from another part at the same time, unless it contains it, while the other is contained—just as a lesser time is contained by a greater one—and if the <term>nyn</term> that is not, but was previously, must have perished at some time, then the <term>nyn</term>s will not exist together with one another, and the previous one must necessarily have perished. Now, it is not possible for it to have perished in itself, because it existed at that time; nor is it possible for the previous <term>nyn</term> to have perished in another <term>nyn</term>. For it is impossible for <term>nyn</term>s to be contiguous to one another, just as a point is to a point. If, therefore, it did not perish in the next one, but in another, it would exist at the same time in the infinite <term>nyn</term>s between them; but this is impossible. Furthermore, it is not possible for the same <term>nyn</term> to remain always. For no finite divisible thing has a single limit, whether it is continuous in one direction or in more; but the <term>nyn</term> is a limit, and it is possible to take a finite time. Furthermore, if to be at the same time in terms of time, and to be neither before nor after, is to be in the same <term>nyn</term>, and if both the before and the after are in this <term>nyn</term>, then things that happened ten thousand years ago would be at the same time as things happening today, and nothing would be before or after anything else. Let these points, then, be the difficulties raised regarding its properties. As for what time is and what its nature is, it remains unclear, both from what has been handed down and from what we have discussed previously. For some say it is the motion of the whole, while others say it is the sphere itself. And yet, a part of the revolution is also a certain time, but it is not a revolution; for what is taken is a part of a revolution, but not a revolution. Furthermore,

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: whether the "now"</meta> remains always one and the same or is always different, is not easy to see. For if it is always different and different, and if no two parts of time exist simultaneously unless one contains and the other is contained <note>as a shorter time is contained by a longer one</note>, and if the "now" which is not currently existing but was formerly existing must have ceased to exist at some point, then the "nows" cannot exist simultaneously with one another, and the prior "now" must always have ceased to exist. Now, it is not possible for it to have ceased to exist while it was itself existing <note>because it was then in being</note>, and it is not possible for the prior "now" to have ceased to exist in another "now." For it is impossible for "nows" to be next to one another, just as it is impossible for a point to be next to a point. If, therefore, it did not cease to exist in the very next "now" but in another one, it would have to exist simultaneously with the infinite "nows" that lie between them; but this is impossible. Furthermore, it is not possible for the same "now" to remain always the same. For no finite divisible thing has only one limit, whether it is continuous in one dimension or in more; but the "now" is a limit, and it is possible to take a finite period of time. Moreover, if to be "simultaneous" in time and neither prior nor posterior means to be in the same and in the <note>one</note> "now," then if both prior and posterior events were in this present "now," things that happened ten thousand years ago would be simultaneous with what is happening today, and nothing would be either prior or posterior to anything else. Let these be the difficulties raised concerning the attributes of time. As for what time is and what its nature is, this is equally unclear from the traditions handed down to us and from the discussions we have just gone through. For some say that time is the motion of the whole universe, while others say it is the sphere itself. Yet even a part of the revolution is a certain time, but it is certainly not a revolution; for what is taken is a part of a revolution, but not a revolution. Furthermore,

<summary>Aristotle examines the paradoxes of the "now," arguing that it can neither be always the same nor always different, and begins reviewing previous definitions of time.</summary>

reference.text:
[context] Wherefore,
even to this day in prayer for an abundant inundation - - - - - - - - - And they depict THREE WATERPOTS, or HEAVEN AND EARTH GUSHING FORTH WITH WATER, because they make a waterpot like a heart having a tongue,—like a heart, because in their opinion the heart is the ruling member of the body, as the Nile is the ruler of Egypt, and like [a heart with?] a tongue, because it is always in a state of humidity, and they call it the producer of existence. And they depict three waterpots, and neither more nor less, because according to them there is a triple cause of the inundation. And they depict one for the Egyptian soil, as being of itself productive of water; and another for the ocean, for at the period of the inundation, water flows up from it into Egypt; and the third to symbolise the rains which prevail in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the rising of the Nile. Now that Egypt generates the water, we may deduce from this, that in the rest of the earth the inundations of the rivers take place in the winter,
[context] and are caused by frequent rains; but the country of the Egyptians alone, inasmuch as it is situated in the middle of the habitable world, like that part of the eye, which is called the pupil, of itself causes the rising of the Nile in summer.

text:
<header>Hieroglyphica.</header>
<sig>D 4</sig>

in the beginning with an abundance of moisture.

<margin></margin>
<note>The marginal notes contain fragments of commentary regarding the heart and tongue in Egyptian symbolism.</note>
</margin>

Regarding the divine water vessel, or the sky and earth pouring forth water, they liken the vessel to a heart possessing a tongue. A heart, because for them it is the governing principle of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt; and a tongue, because it is always in moisture, and they call it the mother of the good. They also depict two water vessels, neither more nor less, because the action of the rising is twofold. One they assign to the land of Egypt, since Egypt is by itself generative of water. The other they assign to the ocean, for from it water arrives in Egypt at the time of the rising. They attribute grain to the rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the Nile’s rising. That Egypt generates its own water can be learned from this: in the rest of the world, river floods occur in the winter.

<summary>The symbolism of the heart and tongue as representations of the Nile's generative power is explained, alongside the theory of the river's dual source and the seasonal nature of its flooding.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Egypt, heart, tongue, flooding, Ethiopia, hydrology</keywords>

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...at the beginning of winter due to an excess of moisture.</meta>

<margin>By the abundance of water in it, they use the heart and tongue of Egypt.</margin>
A divine water-jar <note>original: "Θεία δ’ ὑδρεία"</note>, or one that causes water to gush forth to heaven and earth, is depicted by likening the water-vessel to a heart that possesses a tongue. It is likened to a heart because, among the Egyptians, the heart is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of Egypt. It is likened to a tongue because the tongue always exists in moisture and they call it the producer of what is good. There are two water-jars, neither more nor less, because the process of the Nile's rising is twofold. They assign one jar to the land of Egypt, since Egypt is capable of generating water by itself. They assign the other to the Ocean, for water also comes from the Ocean into Egypt at the time of the inundation. They also attribute the rising to the rains that occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the season of the Nile's overflow. That Egypt itself generates the water can be understood from this: in the rest of the world's climates, the flooding of rivers is completed in the winter.

<summary>This page explains the hieroglyphic symbolism of the water-jar as a representation of the Nile's inundation, comparing the river's governance of Egypt to the heart's governance of the body. It discusses the Egyptian belief in the dual sources of the Nile's flood from both the local land and the southern rains of Ethiopia.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Egypt, heart, tongue, water-jar, inundation, Ethiopia, anatomy, symbolism, hydrology</keywords>

text:
Hieroglyphica.

<sig>D 4</sig>

up to the present, according to a prayer for an abundance of moisture.

<margin>Perhaps some signs are missing here. They use a heart with a tongue in Egypt.</margin>
To represent three water jars, or heaven and earth pouring forth water, they depict the water jar as a heart possessing a tongue. They use the heart because, among them, it is the governing part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the ruler of the Egyptian land. They use the tongue because, being always in moisture, they call it the generator of existence. They use three water jars, neither more nor fewer, because the process of the rising <note>referring to the annual flooding of the Nile</note> is, according to them, threefold. They assign one to the Egyptian land, since it is by its own nature generative of water. Another they assign to the ocean, for water comes from there into Egypt during the time of the rising. A third they assign to the rains, which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the time of the Nile's rising. That Egypt generates water can be understood from this: in the rest of the world's climate, river floods occur during the winter,

<summary>This page explains the symbolic use of the heart and tongue in Egyptian hieroglyphs to represent the Nile as the governing, life-giving force of Egypt, and details the three-part nature of the Nile's annual flood.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Egypt, Ethiopia, heart, tongue, flooding, water jars, symbolism</keywords>

reference.located: Enneads II.5.5 (end, from 'ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὸ ψεῦδος') + II.6.1 (to 'ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐ συμπληροῦσα') = MacKenna 1921 pp. 202-204
reference.edition_note: MacKenna translated from Volkmann's Teubner text; the page is a medieval MS (fol. 80) whose readings may differ; MacKenna is free and adds bracketed glosses
reference.coverage_note: full main text; the red rubric title is represented by MacKenna's tractate title 'Quality and Form-Idea' (Greek title differs: περὶ οὐσίας ἢ περὶ ποιότητος); marginal notes not covered
reference.text:
[context] for, note, in the case of things whose Being is a falsity,
to take away the falsity is to take away what Being they have, and if we introduce actualisation into things whose Being and Essence is Potentiality, we destroy the foundation of their nature since their Being is Potentiality.
If Matter is to be kept as the unchanging substratum, we must keep it as Matter : that means — does it not ? — that we must define it as a Potentiality and nothing more — or refute these considerations.
Quality and Form-Idea
Are not Being and Reality (to 6n and he oiisia) distinct ; must we not envisage Being as the substance stripped of all else, while Reality is this same thing, Being, accompanied by the others — Movement, Rest, Identity, Difference — so that these are the specific constituents of Reality ?
The universal fabric, then, is Reality in which Being, Movement, and so on are separate constituents.
Now Movement has Being (not essentially but) as an accident and therefore should have Reality as an accident ; or is it something serving to the completion of Reality ?
No : Movement is a Reality ; everything in the Supreme is a Reality.
Why, then, does not Reality reside, equally, in this sphere ?
In the Supreme there is Reality because all things are one ; ours is the sphere of images whose separation produces grades of difference. Thus in the spermatic unity all the human members are present undistinguishably ; there is no separation of head and hand : their distinct existence begins in the life here, whose content is image, not Authentic Existence.
And are the distinct Qualities in the Authentic Realm to be explained in the same way ? Are they differing Realities centred in one Reality or gathered round Being — differences which constitute Realities distinct from each other within the common fact of Reality ?
This is sound enough ; but it does not apply to all the qualities of this sphere, some of which, no doubt, are differentiations of Reality — such as the quality of two-footedness or four-footedness — but others are not such differentiations of Reality and, because they are not so, must be called qualities and nothing more.
On the other hand, one and the same thing may be sometimes a differentiation of Reality and sometimes not — a differentiation when it
is a constitutive element, and no differentiation in some other thing, where it is not a constitutive element but an accidental.

If you take away being from those things of which it was, the power <term>dynamis</term> <gloss>potentiality</gloss> does not exist, but rather [you must] also have the essence, for as much as it was of those things, you have destroyed their simple substance. It is not necessary, if it was potentiality, that it must not destroy matter, for matter itself was what it was. It is necessary, therefore, to speak of power as not just not being, in order that they may stand in the things that have been spoken of, [which] must be examined.

<note>A red decorative initial letter 'P' marks the start of the section.</note>

It is easy and later. And there are those things which we note of another, for see, the name is of another, movement simply, these things of another as not being otherwise? Because I do not know, because each of those things, because one. And it is of that. Because it was called, according to accident. Is it then according to accident? Insofar as it is an accident. Insofar as it was the essence itself and the things upon it, as many as were of—how then and in the same? And that one [is] of all, but also from elsewhere, as those things having been said are in agreement. Insofar as each is of all. And insofar as it is apart, and without a head, it is separated in another way. For where it was in another way. Let us consider those things which are toward the substances, concerning the difference of beings, as many as, because therefore, the differences making that which is toward each other, altogether insofar as many. Insofar as also a certain quality. But passing by, to the one making, of which the differences were, as of as many as also being others. The differences were, [but] it itself only, why are they called? And what of its difference becomes insofar as those, and difference not having it in another way.

<summary>The author examines the role of potentiality in defining substance and the nature of differences and accidents in the context of intelligible beings.</summary>

text:
<margin>
<unclear>the thing itself and the other, the same and other, the same and other, the same and other, the same and other, the same and other</unclear>
</margin>

If you remove being from the things of which it was, the potentiality does not exist, but it also possesses the essence, for as many things as it was of, you have destroyed their simple substance. It is not necessary, therefore, if it was a potentiality, that one must not destroy the matter, the matter itself which it was. One must therefore speak of potentiality as not being, only so that it may be examined in relation to the things mentioned.

<note>A red decorative initial letter P.</note>

Easy and later. And there are things which we note of others, for see the name of that which is motion to another simply, and these things are of another so as not to be otherwise? Because I do not know, because each of those things, because it is one. And it is of that. Because it was called, according to accident. Is it then according to accident? Insofar as it is an accident, then. Insofar as it was the essence itself and the things upon it, as many as were, how then also in the same. And that thing of all things, but also from elsewhere in other ways, because as has been said, they are very much in agreement. Insofar as each of all things. And insofar as it is apart, and without a head, it is separated in another way. Is it then insofar as it was in another way? Let us consider those things which are in relation to substances, concerning the differences of beings, as many as there are, because therefore, the differences making the relation to one another, entirely insofar as they are. Insofar as they are and what kind. But passing by, to the one making them, the differences were, as of those things which are also other beings. But the differences were, it itself only, what is said. And what is the difference of it becomes insofar as those, and the difference not having it otherwise.

<summary>This passage explores the ontological relationship between potentiality, essence, and substance, questioning how accidents and differences define the nature of being.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, metaphysics, substance, potentiality, essence, difference, accident</keywords>

ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὸ ὂν ἀπὸ τῶν, ὧν ἦν, οὐκ ἔστιν ἡ δύναμις, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἔχειν, ὅσα γὰρ ὧν ἦν, ἀπολώλεκας αὐτῶν τὴν ὑπόστασιν τὴν ἁπλῆν. οὐ δὴ ἀναγκαῖον, εἰ δύναμιν ἦν, ἁπλᾶ δεῖν οὐ λεθροῦν τὴν ὕλην τὴν, ὕλην αὐτὴν δὴ τὴν ἦν. δεῖ ἄρα δύναμιν ὡς οὐκ οὖσαν λέγειν μόνον, ἵνα ὑπόστηνται τοῖς ῥηθεῖσι ἐξεταστέον.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Red decorative initial letter P</image-desc>
Ραδὸν καὶ ὕστερον. Καὶ δ' ἐστὶν ἃ σημειώμεθα ὧν ἄλλῳ, ἰδὲ γὰρ ὄνομα ὧν ἄλλῳ κίνησις ἁπλῶς, αἱ ταῦτα δ' ἑτέρου ὡς οὐκ εἶναι ἑτέρως; ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα, ὅτι ἕκαστον δ' ἐκείνων, ὅτι ἕν. δ' ἐκείνης τ' ἐστὶν. ὅτι ἦν κεκλημένων, κατὰ συμβεβηκός. ἆρα δ' ἆρα τῇ συμβεβηκώς; ᾗ συμβεβηκὼς μὲν ἆρα. ᾗ ἦν αὐτὴ ἡ οὐσία καὶ τὰ ἐπ' αὐτῇ, ὅσα ὧν πῶς οὖν καὶ ἐν ταὐτῷ. κἀκεῖνο δὲ πάντων ὧν ἀλλὰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλοθεν ὧν ἀλλῶς, ὅτι ὡς ειρημένων ὧν μαλ' ὁμονοοῦτα. ᾗ ἕκαστον πάντων. Καὶ ᾗ χωρὶς ὧν, καὶ χωρὶς κεφαλὴν ὧν δὲ, χωρίζεται ἄλλῃ. ἆρα ᾗ γὰρ ἦν ἄλλῃ. Τὰ ὅσα πρὸς τὰ σκεψώμεθα οὐσίας, διαφορᾶς περὶ ὄντων ὅσας, ὅτι οὖν, διαφορᾶς δὲ ποιοῦσαι τὸ πρὸς ἄλληλα, ὅλως ᾗ ὅσα. ᾗ ᾗ καὶ ποῖον. ἀλλὰ παριὼν τῇ δὲ ποιοῦντι ὧν αἱ μὲν διαφοραὶ ἦσαν, ὡς δ' ὅσων καὶ ἕτερα ὄντων. αἱ δὲ διαφοραὶ ἦσαν, αὐτὸ δ' μόνον ποῖ ὅτι λέγονται. Καὶ τὶ δ' αὐτῆς διαφορὰ γίνεται ᾗ ἐκείνων, καὶ διαφορὰ ἄλλως οὐκ ἔχουσα.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

If you take away being from the things in which it was present, the potentiality no longer exists, but one must also possess the <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence or substance</gloss>. For as many things as it was present in, you have destroyed their simple <term>hypostasis</term> <gloss>underlying reality or subsistence</gloss>. It is not necessary, then, if it was potentiality, for simple things to fail to escape <term>hyle</term> <gloss>matter</gloss>, that very matter which it was. One must therefore speak of potentiality only as non-being, so that the things mentioned may be examined in their subsistence.

<note>A small red decorative initial letter P marks the beginning of a new section or paragraph.</note>

Prior and posterior. And there are things which we note as belonging to another; for see, the name of those things in another is simply motion, and are these things of another so as not to be otherwise? Because I do not know that each of those things is one. For it belongs to that which was called so by <term>symbebekos</term> <gloss>accident or incidental property</gloss>. Is it then by accident? Insofar as it is accidental. Insofar as it was the essence itself and the things upon it, how then are they also in the same? And that too of all things, but also from elsewhere in another way, because as it has been said, they are very much in harmony. Insofar as each is of all. And insofar as they are apart, and apart from the head, they are separated elsewhere. Is it then because it was elsewhere? Let us consider how many things pertain to the essences and differences concerning beings, because the differences produce the relation to one another, entirely in the way they are. In what way and of what quality. But passing by the one who produces them, the differences were present as if they were of as many things as are also different. The differences were present, but it is only said in what way it becomes a difference of itself in relation to those things, and a difference not having any other state.

text:
If you remove their falsehood, what substance did they have? And for those that possess being and substance in potentiality, by introducing actuality, you have destroyed the cause of their subsistence, because their being was in potentiality. If, therefore, it is necessary to keep matter indestructible, one must keep it as matter. It is necessary, then, as it seems, to speak of it only as being in potentiality, so that it may be what it is. Or, these arguments must be refuted.

### Plotinus, Enneads, Second: On Substance or Quality
<margin>16</margin>

<note>A red decorative initial letter A begins the text.</note>

Are being and substance different? Is being that which is stripped of other things, while substance is being together with other things, such as motion, rest, sameness, and difference, and are these the elements of that substance? Is the whole, then, substance, while each of those things is, one being, another motion, another something else? Motion, then, is being by accident. But is substance also by accident, or is it that which completes substance? Or are substance itself and all things there also substance? How, then, is it not so here? Or is it because there all things are one, while here, since the images are divided, one thing is separate from another? It is as in the seed, where all things are together, and each thing is all things, and there is no hand without a head, whereas here, they are separated from one another, for they are images and not true. Shall we say, then, that the qualities there are substances, being differences concerning substance, or concerning being, and that they make differences between substances in relation to one another, and in relation to substance as a whole? Or is this not absurd? But concerning the qualities here, some are differences of substances, such as two-footed and four-footed, while others, not being differences, are called qualities only. And yet, the same thing becomes a completing difference in one case, and not a difference in another, where it does not complete.

<summary>This passage explores the ontological distinction between being and substance, examining how potentiality and actuality relate to the nature of matter and the role of qualities as either essential differences or mere accidents.</summary>

If you take being away from the things to which it belonged, there is no potentiality, nor yet any having of substance; for of all the things to which it belonged, you have destroyed their simple subsistence. It is surely not necessary, if it was potentiality, that the simple things should destroy matter, that very matter which it was. One must therefore speak of potentiality only as of what is not, so that it may stand under what has been said. This must be examined.

<note>A small decorative initial letter in red ink opens the next section.</note>

<unclear>Ραδὸν</unclear> and afterwards. And there are things that we mark as belonging to something else. For consider: a name of things that are in another, movement taken simply; and do these belong to another in such a way that they cannot be otherwise? That I do not know: that each of those is one, and is of that. That it was among things so called, by accident. Is it then by way of the accidental? In so far as it is accidental, then. In so far as it was the substance itself and the things that rest upon it, as many as there are, how then are they also in the same thing? And that too belongs to all things, yet it also comes from elsewhere and in another way, since it agrees closely with what has been said. In so far as each belongs to all. And in so far as it is apart, and apart as a head, it is separated in another way. For is it so in so far as it was in another way? Let us examine all that bears on substance: how many differences there are among beings, and that the differences produce the relation of things to one another, wholly, in so far as they are so many. In what way, and of what quality. But passing on to that which produces them, to which the differences belonged, as belonging to so many beings that are also other. The differences existed, but it alone, in what respect they are said. And what difference of it arises in so far as it is of those, and a difference that has no other mode.

# CHRY SIPPVS. LIB. VII.

<sig>Nu iij</sig>

Regarding the small speech to Stagoras, two; regarding speeches against propinations, and regarding those at rest to Onetor, two; regarding the covered <note>a reference to the "Sorites" or "Veiled" paradox</note> to Aristobulus, two; regarding the latent to Athenades, two. 

**Eighth composition.** Regarding the useful to Menecrates, eight; regarding speeches which consist of the infinite and defined, to Pasylus, two; regarding the useful speech to Epicrates, one. 

**Ninth construction.** Regarding sophisms to Heraclitus and Pollis, two; regarding ambiguous dialectical speeches to Dioscorides, five; against the art of Arcesilaus to Sphaerus, one. 

**Tenth construction.** Against custom to Metrodorus, six; regarding custom to Gorgippides, seven. 

Logical things which are outside the aforementioned four differences, and which contain logical questions sparingly, not connected and reduced into a body: the numbered questions are thirty-nine. All volumes of the logical part together are three hundred and eleven. 

**Ethical reason**, regarding the emendation of moral notions, first order.

text:
CHRY SIPPUS. BOOK VII.

<column-break/>

On the argument concerning the "little" <note>referring to the Sorites paradox, or the "heap" argument</note>, to Stagoras, 2 books. On arguments concerning assumptions, to Onetor, 2 books. On the "covered" <note>the Veiled Man paradox</note>, to Aristobulus, 2 books. On the "hidden," to Athenadas, 1 book. Eighth collection: On the "worthless," to Menecrates, 8 books. On arguments from the infinite and the definite, to Pasylus, 2 books. On the fact that it is through one's own reason, to Epicrates, 1 book. Ninth collection: On sophisms, to Heraclides and Pollis, 2 books. On difficult dialectical arguments, to Dioscorides, 5 books. Against Arcesilaus, a method, to Sphaerus, 1 book. Tenth collection: 27 books. On "nothings," to Metrodorus, 16 books. On habit, to Dionysius, 7 books. Of the logical part, on the four differences that are external, 6 books, and on declarative and non-corporeal statements, 7 books. On logical inquiries, 6 books. These are all the volumes of the logical part, 311. On ethical discourse, on the correction of moral concepts, first collection.

<column-break/>

On the little argument, to Stagoras, two: on arguments against assumptions, and on those that are quiescent, to Onetor, two: on the covered, to Aristobulus, two: on the latent, to Athenadas, two. Eighth composition: on the useful, to Menecrates, eight: on arguments that consist of the infinite and the definite, to Pasylus, two: on the little argument, to Epicrates, one. Ninth construction: on sophisms, to Heraclides and Pollis, two: on ambiguous dialectical arguments, to Dioscorides, five. Against the art of Arcesilaus, to Sphaerus, one. Tenth construction: 27 books. Against custom, to Metrodorus, six: on custom, to Gorgippides, seven. Logical works which are outside the aforementioned four differences, and contain logical questions sporadically, not connected and reduced into a body: the questions numbered 39.
There are in total 311 volumes of the logical part.
Of the ethical reason, which concerns the emendation of moral notions, the first order.

text:
<meta>continues from previous page: the bibliography of Chrysippus</meta>

<column-break/>

On the Little-by-Little Argument <note>original: "peri tēs para mikron logou"; likely referring to the Sorites or "heap" paradox</note>, addressed to Stagoras, two books. On arguments regarding assumptions and on the Quiescent <note>original: "hēsychazontōn"; referring to the "quietist" strategy of stopping an argument before a paradox is reached</note>, addressed to Onetor, two books. On the Veiled Argument <note>original: "peri tou enkekalymmenou"</note>, addressed to Aristobulus, two books. On the Hidden Man <note>original: "peri tou dialanthanontos"</note>, addressed to Athenadas, one book.

Eighth collection: On the Nobody Argument <note>original: "peri tou outidanou"</note>, addressed to Menecrates, eight books. On arguments from the infinite and the definite, addressed to Pasylus, two books. On the argument that proceeds through its own form, addressed to Epicrates, one book.

Ninth collection: On Sophisms <note>original: "peri tōn erismatōn"</note>, addressed to Heraclides and Pollis, two books. On insoluble dialectical arguments, addressed to Dioscorides, five books. Against the Method of Arcesilaus <note>Arcesilaus was a skeptical philosopher of the Academy</note>, addressed to Sphaerus, one book.

Tenth collection: twenty-seven books. On the "Nothings" <note>original: "peri mēdenōn"</note>, addressed to Metrodorus, sixteen books. On Common Usage <note>original: "peri synētheias"</note>, addressed to Dionysius, seven books.

Logic works outside the four main divisions, six books; and on propositions and incorporeals, seven books. On logical inquiries, six books. All these logic volumes together total three hundred and eleven.

Ethical discourse: On the correction of ethical concepts, first collection.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text provided in the second column of the original page.</note>

On the very small speech, to Stagoras, two books. On speeches against assumptions, and on those who are silent, to Onetor, two books. On the covered <note>the Veiled Argument</note>, to Aristobulus, two books. On the hidden, to Athenadas, two books.

Eighth composition: On the useful <note>The Latin "vtili" here likely misreads the Greek "outidanou" (Nobody)</note>, to Menecrates, eight books. On speeches consisting of the infinite and the definite, to Pasylus, two books. On the speech <note>to Epicrates</note>, one book.

Ninth construction: On sophisms, to Heraclides and Pollis, two books. On ambiguous dialectical speeches, to Dioscorides, five books. Against the art of Arcesilaus, to Sphaerus, one book.

Tenth construction: Against custom, to Metrodorus, six books. On custom, to Gorgippides, seven books.

Logic works which are outside the four aforementioned differences, and contain scattered logical questions, not connected or reduced into a single body: thirty-nine questions enumerated.

All the volumes of the logical part together are three hundred and eleven.

Of the Ethical reasoning, which pertains to the correction of moral notions, the first order.

reference.text:
[context] After, therefore, we have added a few observations more, in order to show that the unperverted conceptions of the multitude accord with a right opinion respecting the Gods,
we shall conclude this book. Those poets, therefore, who are wise, though but in a small degree, say, What man so credulous and void of mind, What man so ignorant, as to think the Gods In fiery bile and fleshless bones rejoice, For hungry dogs a nutriment not fit; Or that such offerers they will e'er reward? But another poet says, My offerings to the Gods from cakes alone And frankincense shall be; for not to friends But deities my sacrifice I make.
Apollo also, when he orders men to sacrifice according to paternal institutes, appears to refer every thing to ancient custom. But the ancient custom of sacrificing was, as we have before shown, with cakes and fruits. Hence also, sacrifices were called θυσιαι thusiai, and θυηλαι thuelai, and θυμελαι thumelai, and αυτο το θυειν auto to thuein, i.e. the act of sacrificing, signified the same thing as του θυμιαν ton thumian, i.e. to offer incense, and which is now called by us, επιθυειν epithuein, i.e. to
sacrifice something more. For what we now call θυειν thuein, i.e. to sacrifice, the ancients denominated ερδειν erdein, i.e. to perform or make. They perfect hecatombs of bulls, or goats, Made to Apollo.
But those who introduced costliness into sacrifices, were ignorant that, in conjunction with this, they also introduced a swarm of evils, viz., superstition, luxury, an opinion that a divine nature may be corrupted by gifts, and that a compensation may be made by sacrifices for injustice. Or whence do some make an oblation of three animals with gilded horns, but others of hecatombs? And whence did Olympias, the mother of Alexander [the Great,] sacrifice a thousand of each species of animals, unless sumptuousness had at length proceeded to superstition? But when the young man was informed that the Gods rejoiced in magnificent sacrifices, and, as they say, in solemn banquets of oxen and other animals, how, though he was willing to act wisely, was it possible that he could? How also, when he conceived that these sacrifices were acceptable to the Gods,
[context] was it possible he should not fancy that he was permitted to act unjustly, when he might exonerate himself from erroneous conduct through sacrifices?

text:
<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Porphyry's second book, moving from historical examples of extreme behavior to a philosophical argument about the nature of true sacrifice and the corruption of piety through extravagance.</meta>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE II.<-

...supposition, we shall bring the book to a close. At any rate, even those poets who are wise for a short time say:

> Who is so foolish and so utterly slack
> Among men as to believe the gods—
> In bare bones and smoldering gall,
> Which even hungry dogs would not eat—
> Rejoice in such first-fruits and receive this as their prize?

And another says:

> Barley cakes, frankincense, sacrificial cakes; these I shall buy.
> For I am not sacrificing to my friends, but to the gods
> at this time.

<margin>59</margin> Since Apollo also advises sacrificing "according to ancestral custom"—that is, according to the habit of our fathers—he seems to be leading us back to the ancient custom. And the ancient custom was through sacrificial cakes and fruits, as we have demonstrated. Hence, they were called *thusiai* <note>sacrifices</note>, *thuēlai* <note>sacrificial offerings</note>, and *thumelai* <note>altars for incense</note>, and the word "to sacrifice" <term>thuein <note>originally meaning to burn or fumigate</note></term> itself was linked to "to burn incense" <term>thumian</term> and to what we now call "to offer a sacrifice" <term>epithuein</term>. For what we now call "sacrificing" <term>thuein</term>, they used to call "performing" <term>erdein <note>literally "to do" or "to work," used in religious contexts for performing a rite</note></term>.

> And they offered <note>original: *erdon*</note> to Apollo perfect hecatombs <note>literally a "hundred-ox sacrifice," but used for any large-scale offering</note>
> of bulls and goats.

<margin>60</margin> But those who introduced extravagance into sacrifices are unaware how they introduced a swarm of evils along with it: superstition, luxury, and the idea that one can bribe the divine and heal injustice through sacrifices. Otherwise, from where did some get the practice of sacrificing "triplets with gilded horns" <note>a rare and expensive ritual involving three animals</note>, and others hecatombs, and why did Olympias, the mother of Alexander, sacrifice a thousand of everything, once extravagance had led the way toward superstition? When a young man learns that the gods rejoice in extravagance and, as they say, in the feasts of oxen and other animals, when would he ever choose to be temperate <note>original: *sōphronēseien*</note>? And how, believing that he offers things pleasing to the gods...

<summary>Porphyry argues that true sacrifice should return to the ancient, simple offerings of fruits and incense, asserting that animal sacrifice and extravagance lead to superstition and moral corruption.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, sacrifice, Apollo, Olympias, superstition, piety, etymology, temperance, animal sacrifice, ancient custom</keywords>

DE ABSTINENTIA II.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...by this assumption, we shall bring the book to a close. For even those poets who are moderately temperate say:</meta>

> Who among men is so foolish and utterly lax,
> so credulous, as to hope that the gods
> take pleasure in fleshless bones and burning bile,
> things not even edible to starving dogs,
> and that they receive this as an offering?

And another says:

> Sacrificial cakes, frankincense, and flatbreads; these I shall buy.
> For I am not sacrificing to friends, but to the gods
> at this time.

<margin>59</margin> Since Apollo also advises sacrificing according to ancestral custom, which is to say according to the habit of the fathers, he seems to lead us back to the ancient custom. And the ancient custom was through cakes and fruits, as we have demonstrated. Hence, sacrifices <term>thysiai</term> <gloss>sacrifices</gloss>, offerings <term>thyelai</term> <gloss>offerings</gloss>, and altars <term>thymelai</term> <gloss>altars</gloss> were so named, and the very act of sacrificing <term>thyein</term> <gloss>to sacrifice</gloss> was connected to the act of burning incense <term>thymian</term> <gloss>to burn incense</gloss> and to what we now call offering upon the altar <term>epithyein</term> <gloss>to offer upon</gloss>. For what we now call sacrificing, they called performing <term>erdein</term> <gloss>to perform/do</gloss>.

> And they performed for Apollo perfect hecatombs
> of bulls and goats.

<margin>60</margin> Those who introduced extravagance into sacrifices are ignorant of how, along with it, they introduced a swarm of evils: superstition, luxury, and the assumption that one can bribe the divine and heal injustice with sacrifices. For whence did some bring gold-horned triple-offerings, others hecatombs, and Olympias, the mother of Alexander, sacrifice a thousand of everything, if not from extravagance leading them toward superstition? DE ABSTINENTIA II.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...by this assumption, we shall bring the book to a close. For even those poets who are moderately temperate say:</meta>

> Who among men is so foolish and utterly lax,
> so credulous, as to hope that the gods
> take pleasure in fleshless bones and burning bile,
> things not even edible to starving dogs,
> and that they receive this as an offering?

And another says:

> Sacrificial cakes, frankincense, and flatbreads; these I shall buy.
> For I am not sacrificing to friends, but to the gods
> at this time.

<margin>59</margin> Since Apollo also advises sacrificing according to ancestral custom, which is to say according to the habit of the fathers, he seems to lead us back to the ancient custom. And the ancient custom was through cakes and fruits, as we have demonstrated. Hence, sacrifices <term>thysiai</term> <gloss>sacrifices</gloss>, offerings <term>thyelai</term> <gloss>offerings</gloss>, and altars <term>thymelai</term> <gloss>altars</gloss> were so named, and the very act of sacrificing <term>thyein</term> <gloss>to sacrifice</gloss> was connected to the act of burning incense <term>thymian</term> <gloss>to burn incense</gloss> and to what we now call offering upon the altar <term>epithyein</term> <gloss>to offer upon</gloss>. For what we now call sacrificing, they called performing <term>erdein</term> <gloss>to perform/do</gloss>.

> And they performed for Apollo perfect hecatombs
> of bulls and goats.

<margin>60</margin> Those who introduced extravagance into sacrifices are ignorant of how, along with it, they introduced a swarm of evils: superstition, luxury, and the assumption that one can bribe the divine and heal injustice with sacrifices. For whence did some bring gold-horned triple-offerings, others hecatombs, and Olympias, the mother of Alexander, sacrifice a thousand of everything, if not from extravagance leading them toward superstition? And when a young man learns that the gods delight in extravagance and, as they say, in the feasts of oxen and other animals, when would he willingly be temperate? And how, believing that he is offering pleasing sacrifices to the

<summary>Porphyry argues that ancient, simple sacrifices of fruits and cakes were the original custom, while modern, extravagant animal sacrifices are the result of superstition and moral corruption.</summary>

> Who among men is so foolish, so utterly slack
> and gullible, as to hope that the gods
> rejoice in offerings of fleshless bones and burnt gall,
> which are not even edible for hungry dogs,
> and that they receive this as their due reward?

And another says:

> Barley-groats, frankincense, and sacrificial cakes: these I will buy.
> For I do not sacrifice to friends, but to the gods
> at this time.

<margin>59</margin> Since even Apollo, when advising that one should sacrifice according to ancestral customs <note>original: "kata ta patria"</note>, meaning according to the habit of the forefathers, seems to lead us back to the ancient custom. As we have demonstrated, that ancient custom consisted of sacrificial cakes and fruits. This is why the terms <term>thysiai</term> <gloss>sacrifices</gloss>, <term>thyēlai</term> <gloss>offerings</gloss>, and <term>thymelai</term> <gloss>altars</gloss> were used; the word for sacrificing itself <note>original: "thyein"</note> was connected to the act of fumigating with incense <note>original: "thymian"</note> and to what we now call "offering upon" <note>original: "epithyein"</note>. For what we now call "to sacrifice" <note>original: "thyein"</note>, they used to call "to perform" <note>original: "erdein"</note>.

> They performed <note>original: "erdon"</note> for Apollo perfect hecatombs
> of bulls and goats.

<margin>60</margin> Those who introduced extravagance into sacrifices are unaware that they simultaneously introduced a swarm of evils: superstition, luxury, and the notion that the divine can be bribed or that injustice can be healed through sacrifices. Otherwise, why would some offer three-animal sacrifices with gilded horns, and others hecatombs <note>sacrifices of one hundred cattle</note>? Why did Olympias, the mother of Alexander, sacrifice a thousand of every kind at once, since extravagance leads directly to superstition? reference.text:
Spirit pervading [body] by means of veins and arteries and blood, bestows upon the living creature motion, and as it were doth bear it in a way. For this cause some do think the soul is blood, in that they do mistake its nature, not knowing that [at death] it is iteh spirit that must first withdraw into the soul, whereon the blood congeals and veins and arteries are emptied, and then the living creature <or life> is withdrawn; and this is body's death.
Now from one Source all things depend; while Source [dependeth] from the One and Only [One]. Source is, moreover, moved to become Source again; whereas the One standeth perpetually and is not moved. Three then are they: "God, the Father and the Good", Cosmos and man. God doth contain Cosmos; Cosmos [containeth] man. Cosmos is e'er God's Son, man as it were Cosmos' child.
Not that, however, God ignoreth man; nay, right well doth He know him, and willeth to be known. This is the sole salvation for a man - God's Gnosis. This is the Way Up to the Mount. By Him alone the soul becometh good, not whiles is good, whiles evil, but [good] out of necessity.
Tat: What dost thou mean, Thrice-greatest one? Hermes: Behold an infant's soul, my son, that is not yet cut off, because its body is still small and not as yet come unto its full bulk. Tat: How? Hermes: A thing of beauty altogether is [such a soul] to see, not yet befouled by body's passions, still all but hanging from the Cosmic Soul! But when the body grows in bulk and draweth down the soul into its mass,
[context] then doth the soul cut off itself and bring upon itself forgetfulness, and no more shareth in the Beautiful and the Good.

For this reason, some have thought the soul to be blood, being mistaken about its nature, not knowing that first the <term>pneuma</term> <gloss>spirit or breath</gloss> must withdraw into the soul. Then the blood congeals, the veins and the arteries are emptied, and then the living being perishes. This is the death of the body.

All things depend on one beginning, and the beginning comes from the One and Only. The beginning is moved so that it may again become a beginning, but the One alone stands still and is not moved. There are, then, these three: God the Father and the Good, the Cosmos, and Man. God contains the Cosmos, and the Cosmos contains Man. The Cosmos becomes the son of God, and Man becomes the offspring of the Cosmos.

For God is not ignorant of Man, but knows him fully and wishes to be known by him. This alone is salvation for Man: the <term>gnosis</term> <gloss>divine knowledge or direct experience</gloss> of God. This is the ascent to Olympus <note>the dwelling of the gods, representing the highest spiritual realm</note>. By this alone a soul becomes good; a soul is never good by nature, but becomes so by necessity.

How can you say this, O Thrice-Greatest?

Behold the soul of a child, my son, which has not yet accepted its own separation, its body being still small and not yet fully grown to its full mass.

[context] Bezeleel also will be summoned up, being thought worthy of the same honours.
For him, also, God calls up for the preparation of the sacred furniture and for the care of the sacred works. (27) But he receives only the second honour of this summons, and the all-wise Moses shall have the first place assigned to him. For the former fashions shadows only, like painters do, in which it is not right to form any living thing. For the very name Bezeleel is interpreted to mean, "working in shadows." But Moses does not make shadows, but the task is assigned to him of forming the archetypal natures of things themselves. And in other places, also, the great Cause of all things is accustomed to reveal his secrets to some in a more conspicuous and visible manner, as if in the pure light of the sun, and to others more sparely, as though in the shade. VII. (28) Having therefore gone through all the larger plants in the universe, let us see in what manner the all-wise God made the trees which exist in the smaller world, that is to say, in man. In the first place, then, taking our body as if it were a field of deep soil, he created the external senses to be in it as so many channels. (29) And after that, he arranged the place of each separate one of them, as if it had been a fruit-bearing and most useful tree, assigning the sense of hearing to the ear, that of sight to the eyes, that of smell to the nostrils, and each of the other senses and faculties to their kindred and appropriate organs. And the divine man bears his testimony to this account of mine, speaking thus in his Psalms, "He that planted the ear, doth he not hear? and he that made the eyes, shall he not See?"
(30) Moreover, all the different powers which run down as far as the legs and hands, and all the other parts of the body, whether internal or external, are all those of an unimportant kind. (31) But those which are better and more perfect he has rooted in the more central portion; that which is pre-eminently able to bring forth fruit, the dominant portion of the man. These faculties are perception, comprehension, felicity of conjecture, study, memory, habit, disposition, the various species of art, the firmness of knowledge of different things, the apprehension of the speculations of universal virtue in such a way as is never forgotten. Now, no mortal is competent to plant any one of these things himself. But of all of them together there is one architect, the uncreated God, who has not only made them originally, but who also makes them for and implants them in every individual man that is born. VIII. (32) Now the account of the planting of Paradise is consistent with what has been already said. For it is stated, "God planted a Paradise in Eden, towards the east; and there is placed the man whom he has Made."
Now, to think that it is here meant that God planted vines, or olive trees, or apple trees, or pomegranates, or any trees of such kinds, is mere incurable folly. (33) For why should he have done so? any one may ask. Was it that he might have a pleasant abode to spend his time in? Even the whole world could not be considered a dwelling sufficient for God, the governor of the universe. Would it not appear to be deficient in innumerable other things, so that it could never be looked upon as a place worthily suited to the reception
[context] of the great King?

<header>PHILO JUDAEUS, BOOK</header>

Beseleel also, being deemed worthy of the second honor, shall be called up. For God also calls him up for the construction and care of the sacred works. But while he holds the second place in this calling, Moses, the wisest, shall hold the first. For the former fashions shadows, like painters, who are not permitted to create anything living. For Beseleel is interpreted as "working in shadows." But Moses was allotted to represent not shadows, but the archetypal natures of the things themselves, which he was assigned to fashion; and otherwise, the Supreme Cause is accustomed to show His things more clearly and manifestly to some, as if in pure sunlight, and to others more obscurely, as if in shadow. 

Now, after we have discussed the larger plants of the world, let us see how the wisest Creator, God, founded certain trees in man, the lesser world. First, in our body, as if in good soil, He prepared furrows for the senses; into these He placed each one as if it were a mild and useful tree: hearing in the ears, sight in the eyes, smell in the nostrils, and the others in their own proper places. The prophetic seer bears witness to this opinion of mine, speaking thus in his hymns: "He who plants the ear, does He not hear? He who fashions the eyes, does He not see?" Furthermore, all the other faculties that extend to the legs, hands, and other parts of the body, both internal and external, are noble seedlings. But those that bring forth the most excellent and perfect fruits are more deeply rooted in the ruling faculty, by which man is governed. These are: thought, perception, conjecture, meditation, memory, habit, disposition, the manifold forms of the arts, the firm grasp of sciences, and the indelible acquisition of the theorems of all virtue. No mortal man knows how to plant any of these. But there is one Unbegotten Craftsman of all things, who has not only created them once, but also plants these trees daily for each of those being born. 

The planting of that Paradise, of which it is said, "God planted a Paradise in Eden toward the east, and placed there the man whom He had fashioned," is consistent with our discourse. If this is understood to be about vines, olive trees, apple trees, pomegranate trees, and similar trees, it would be a great and incurable folly. For one could ask, for what purpose was it made? Was it for a pleasant dwelling? Then is not the whole world a more suitable dwelling for God the King? Are there not many other things...

Beseleel quoque secundo honore dignatus furfum vocabitur. Nam & hunc furfum Deus evocat, ad fabricam & curam sacrorum operum. Verùm hic secundas hujus evocationis partes, Moses verò sapientissimus primas feret. Nam ille umbras fingit, sicut pictores, quibus non est fas animatum quicquam condere. Beseleel enim in umbris faciens interpretatur. At Moses non umbras, sed naturas archetypas earum rerum, quas fingendas fortitus est, & alioquin etiam summus ille autor, aliis clarius manifeste & fluisque tanquam in sole puro: aliis obscurius, tanquam in umbra, solet res suas ostendere. Nunc postquam disseruimus de grandioribus mundi plantis, videamus, quomodo & in homine, minore mundo, sapientissimus opifex Deus arbores quasdam condidit. Primùm in corpore nostro, quasi bono agro, sensuum scrobes praeparavit: in quas unumquemque tanquam mitem utilemque arborem indidit, auditum in aures, visum in oculos, in nares odoratum, & suis quoque locis caeteros. Attestatur autem huic meae sententiae fatidicus vates, qui in suis hymnis sic loquitur: Qui plantat aurem non audit? qui fingit oculos non inspiciet? Quin & aliae, quae usque crura manusque ac caeteras corporis partes externas internasque pertinent, facultates omnes sunt generosae plantulae; sed quae praestantissimos perfectissimosque fructus afferunt, penitius insitae sunt in vim qua homo regitur. Sunt autem hae: cogitatio, perceptio, conjectura, meditatio, memoria, habitus, dispositio, artium species multifariae, scientiae confirmatae, virtutis totius contemplationum conceptus indelebilis. Horum nihil ullus homo plantare scit: sed univerforum unus ingenitus est artifex, qui non solum creavit ea semel, sed & singula plantat quotidie. Huic nostro sermoni adstipulatur etiam paradisi illius plantatio, de quo dicitur: Plantavit Deus Paradisum in Edem contra orientem, & collocavit ibi hominem, quem finxerat. First, in our body, as in good soil, he prepared the furrows of the senses, into which he placed each one as a mild and useful tree: hearing in the ears, sight in the eyes, smell in the nostrils, and the others in their own places as well. The prophetic seer bears witness to this opinion of mine, who speaks thus in his hymns: "He who plants the ear, does he not hear? He who fashions the eyes, shall he not look?" These are: thought, perception, conjecture, meditation, memory, habit, disposition, the multifarious species of arts, confirmed sciences, and the indelible concept of the contemplations of all virtue. No man knows how to plant any of these, but the one unbegotten craftsman of all things is he who not only created them once, but also plants each one daily. Beseleel quoque secundo honore dignatus furfum vocabitur. Nam & hunc furfum Deus evocat, ad fabricam & curam sacrorum operum. Verùm hic secundas hujus evocationis partes, Moses verò sapientissimus primas feret. Nam ille umbras fingit, sicut pictores, quibus non est fas animatum quicquam condere. Beseleel enim in umbris faciens interpretatur. At Moses non umbras, sed naturas archetypas earum rerum, quas fingendas fortitus est, & alioquin etiam summus ille autor, aliis clarius manifeste & fluisque tanquam in sole puro: aliis obscurius, tanquam in umbra, solet res suas ostendere. Nunc postquam disseruimus de grandioribus mundi plantis, videamus, quomodo & in homine, minore mundo, sapientissimus opifex Deus arbores quasdam condidit. Primùm in corpore nostro, quasi bono agro, sensuum scrobes praeparavit: in quas unumquemque tanquam mitem utilemque arborem indidit, auditum in aures, visum in oculos, in nares odoratum, & suis quoque locis caeteros. Attestatur autem huic meae sententiae fatidicus vates, qui in suis hymnis sic loquitur: Qui plantat aurem non audit? qui fingit oculos non inspiciet? Quin & aliae, quae usque crura manusque ac caeteras corporis partes externas internasque pertinent, facultates omnes sunt generosae plantulae; sed quae praestantissimos perfectissimosque fructus afferunt, penitius insitae sunt in vim qua homo regitur. Sunt autem hae: cogitatio, perceptio, conjectura, meditatio, memoria, habitus, dispositio, artium species multifariae, scientiae confirmatae, virtutis totius contemplationum conceptus indelebilis. Horum nihil ullus homo plantare scit: sed univerforum unus ingenitus est artifex, qui non solum creavit ea semel, sed & singula plantat quotidie. Huic nostro sermoni adstipulatur etiam paradisi illius plantatio, de quo dicitur: Plantavit Deus Paradisum in Edem contra orientem, & collocavit ibi hominem, quem finxerat. Beseleel quoque secundo honore dignatus furfum vocabitur. Nam & hunc furfum Deus evocat, ad fabricam & curam sacrorum operum. Verùm hic secundas hujus evocationis partes, Moses verò sapientissimus primas feret. Nam ille umbras fingit, sicut pictores, quibus non est fas animatum quicquam condere. Beseleel enim in umbris faciens interpretatur. At Moses non umbras, sed naturas archetypas earum rerum, quas fingendas fortitus est, & alioquin etiam summus ille autor, aliis clarius manifeste & fluisque tanquam in sole puro: aliis obscurius, tanquam in umbra, solet res suas ostendere. Nunc postquam disseruimus de grandioribus mundi plantis, videamus, quomodo & in homine, minore mundo, sapientissimus opifex Deus arbores quasdam condidit. Primùm in corpore nostro, quasi bono agro, sensuum scrobes praeparavit: in quas unumquemque tanquam mitem utilemque arborem indidit, auditum in aures, visum in oculos, in nares odoratum, & suis quoque locis caeteros. Attestatur autem huic meae sententiae fatidicus vates, qui in suis hymnis sic loquitur: Qui plantat aurem non audit? qui fingit oculos non inspiciet? Quin & aliae, quae usque crura manusque ac caeteras corporis partes externas internasque pertinent, facultates omnes sunt generosae plantulae; sed quae praestantissimos perfectissimosque fructus afferunt, penitius insitae sunt in vim qua homo regitur. Sunt autem hae: cogitatio, perceptio, conjectura, meditatio, memoria, habitus, dispositio, artium species multifariae, scientiae confirmatae, virtutis totius contemplationum conceptus indelebilis. Horum nihil ullus homo plantare scit: sed univerforum unus ingenitus est artifex, qui non solum creavit ea semel, sed & singula plantat quotidie. Huic nostro sermoni adstipulatur etiam paradisi illius plantatio, de quo dicitur: Plantavit Deus Paradisum in Edem contra orientem, & collocavit ibi hominem, quem finxerat. Id si accipiatur de vitibus, & olearum, malorum, punicarum, similiumque arboribus, magna & incurabilis stultitia fuerit; quaeri enim posset, in quem usum factus fit: An propter amoenam habitationem ergo totus mundus non est aptius Deo Regi habitaculum? annon & aliae multae res sunt ad excipiendum

<column-break/>

Α Βεσελεήλ. ᾗ γὰρ τοῦτον ἀνακαλεῖ ὁ Θεὸς πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἱερῶν κατασκευὴν τε καὶ ἐπιμέλειαν ἔργων, ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν τὰ δευτερεῖα δ’ ἀνακλήσεως, Μωϋσῆς δὲ ὁ πάνσοφος οἴσεται τὰ πρωτεῖα. ἐκεῖνος γὰρ τὰς σκιάς πλάττει, καθάπερ οἱ ζωγραφοῦντες, οἷς θέμις οὐδὲν ἔμψυχον δημιουργῆσαι· Βεσελεὴλ γὰρ ἐν σκιαῖς ποιῶν ἑρμηνεύεται· Μωϋσῆς δὲ οὐ σκιάς, ἀλλὰ τὰς ἀρχετύπους Φύσεις αὐτὰς τῶν πραγμάτων ἔλαχεν ἀνατυποῦν· ἄλλως τε ἢ τὸ ἄϊτιον, οἷς μὲν τηλαυγέστερον κ’ ἀριδηλότερον, ὡς ἂν ἐν ἡλίῳ καθαρῷ· οἷς δὲ ἀμυδρότερον, ὡς ἂν ἐν σκιά τὰ οἰκεῖα ἄμωθεν ἐπιδεικνυσθαι. διεξεληλυθότες ἐπὶ τῶν ὁλοχερεστέρων ἐν κόσμῳ Φυτῶν, ἴδωμεν ὃν τρόπον καὶ τὰ ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ βραχεῖ κόσμῳ δένδρα ὁ πάνσοφος ἐδημιούργει Θεός. αὐτίκα τοίνυν ὥσπερ βαθύγειον χωρίον σῶμα τὸ ἡμέτερον λαβών, δεξάμενος αὐτῷ τὰς αἰσθήσεις ὑπεργάζετο· κἄπειθ’ ὅσα Φυτὸν ἥμερον καὶ ὠφελιμώτατον ἑκάστην αὐτῶν ἐνετίθει, ἀκοὴν μὲν εἰς τοὺς, ὄψιν δὲ εἰς ὄμματα, καὶ εἰς μυκτήρας ὅσφρησιν, καὶ τὰς ἄλλας εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα καὶ συγγενῆ χωρία. μαρτυρεῖ δὲ μὲν τῷ λόγῳ ὁ θεσπέσιος ἀνήρ, ἐν ὕμνοις λέγων ὧδε, ὁ Φυτεύων ὃν ἐκ ἀκούει; ὁ πλάσσων ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐκ βλέψει; καὶ τὰς διηκούσας μέντοι μέχρι σκελῶν τε καὶ χειρῶν καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν τοῦ σώματος μερῶν, ὅσα ἐντὸς τε καὶ ἐκτὸς, δυνάμεις ἁπάσας, εὐγενῆ μοχεύματα εἶναι συμβέβηκε· τὰ δὲ ἀμείνω καὶ τελειότερα τῷ μεσαϊτάτῳ καρπαφορεῖν δυναμένῳ διαφερόντως ἡγεμονικῷ, ὡς ἐρρέρρις· ταῦτα δὲ εἰσι, νόησις, κατάληψις, εὐσοχία, μελέτη, μνῆμαι, ἕξις, διάθεσις, τεχνῶν ἰδέαι πολύτροποι, βεβαιότης ἐπιστημῶν, τῶν ἀρετῆς ἁπάσης θεωρημάτων ἀληθ’ ἀνάληψις. τῶν ὧδ’ ἐδεὶς θνητὸς ἱκανὸς Φυτουργῆσαι· πάντων δὲ ἀθρόων εἷς ἀγέννητος τεχνίτης, ὃ πεποιηκὼς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ποιῶν καθ’ ἕκαστον τῶν γεννωμένων τὰ Φυτὰ ταῦτα. τοῖς εἰρημένοις ἐσὶν ἀκόλουθος καὶ ἡ τῷ παραδείσῳ Φυτουργία. λέγεται γὰρ, ΕΦύτευσεν ὁ Θεὸς παράδεισον ἐν Εδέμ κ’ ἀνατολάς, κ’ ἔθετο ἐκεῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ὃν ἔπλασε. τὸ μὲν οὖν ἀμπέλους, κ’ ἐλαϊῶν, ἢ μηλέων, ἢ ῥοιῶν, ἢ τῶν ὧδ’ ἀπλησίων δένδρα οἴεσθαι, πολλὴ κ’ δυσθεράπευτος ἡ εὐήθεια. τίνος γὰρ ἕνεκεν, κ’ ἐποιεὶς ἄν· ἵνα ἐνδιατήσεις εὐαγωγὲς ἔχῃς; ὁ γὰρ κόσμος ἅπας αὐταρκέστατον ἐνδιαίτημα ἂν νομισθείη Θεῷ τῷ πανηγεμόνι ἢ ἔχει μυρίων καὶ ἄλλων δόξαν ἂν ὑστερίζειν, ὡς πρὸς ὑποδοχήν

# THE BOOK OF PHILO JUDAEUS

Bezalel <note>original: "Beseleel"</note> also, having been deemed worthy of the second honor, shall be called upward. For God calls him upward as well, for the construction and care of the sacred works. However, he shall hold the second rank of this calling, while Moses the all-wise shall bear the first. For the former fashions shadows, like painters, for whom it is not permitted to create anything living. Indeed, Bezalel is interpreted as "working in shadows." But Moses was allotted to model not shadows, but the archetypal natures of the things themselves. Moreover, the Supreme Author is accustomed to show his works to some more clearly and manifest, as if in pure sunlight, and to others more obscurely, as if in a shadow. Now, after we have discussed the larger plants of the world, let us see how in man, the lesser world <note>the microcosm</note>, the all-wise artisan God planted certain trees. First, in our body, as if in a good field, he prepared the trenches of the senses; into which he placed each one like a mild and useful tree: hearing in the ears, sight in the eyes, smell in the nostrils, and the others in their proper places. The divinely inspired prophet <note>the Psalmist</note> bears witness to this opinion of mine, speaking thus in his hymns: "He who plants the ear, does he not hear? He who fashions the eyes, will he not see?" Furthermore, all the faculties that extend to the legs and hands and the other external and internal parts of the body are noble little plants; but those which bear the most excellent and perfect fruits are more deeply implanted in the power by which man is ruled <note>the "hegemonikon" or ruling faculty of the soul</note>. These are: thought, perception, conjecture, meditation, memory, habit, disposition, the manifold forms of the arts, confirmed sciences, and the indelible grasp of the contemplations of all virtue. No mortal man knows how to plant any of these; but there is one unbegotten artisan of all things, who not only created them once, but plants each of them daily. The planting of that paradise also agrees with our discourse, of which it is said: "God planted a Paradise in Eden toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had fashioned." If this were taken to mean vines, and olives, apples, pomegranates, and similar trees, it would be a great and incurable folly; for it might be asked, for what use was it made? Was it for a pleasant habitation? Is not the whole world a more fitting dwelling for God the King? Are there not many other things to receive

<column-break/>

Bezalel. For God calls him also to the preparation and care of the sacred works, but he shall receive the second prize of the calling, while Moses the all-wise shall carry off the first. For that one fashions shadows, just like those who paint, for whom it is not lawful to create anything with a soul; for Bezalel is interpreted as "making in shadows." But Moses was allotted to model not shadows, but the archetypal natures themselves of the things. Otherwise, the First Cause is accustomed to display his own works from above, to some more clearly and brightly, as if in pure sun; to others more dimly, as if in a shadow. Having gone through the more general plants in the world, let us see in what manner the all-wise God fashioned the trees in man, the small world. Immediately, therefore, taking our body like a region of deep soil, he prepared the senses within it; and then he placed each of them as a cultivated and most useful plant, hearing into the ears, sight into the eyes, and smell into the nostrils, and the others into their proper and kindred places. The divine man <note>the Psalmist</note> bears witness to this word, saying thus in his hymns: "He who plants the ear, does he not hear? He who fashions eyes, does he not look?" And indeed, all the powers reaching as far as the legs and hands and the other parts of the body, both those within and without, happen to be noble grafts; but the better and more perfect ones he rooted in the most central part, the ruling faculty <term>hegemonikon</term> <gloss>the governing part of the soul</gloss>, which is uniquely able to bear fruit. These are: thought, apprehension, sagacity, practice, memories, habit, disposition, the many-turned forms of the arts, the stability of the sciences, and the true grasping of the contemplations of all virtue. No mortal is sufficient to plant these; but there is one unbegotten craftsman of all of them together, who has not only made them once, but makes these plants in each of those being born. The planting of the paradise is also consistent with what has been said. For it is said: "God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had fashioned." To think then that this means vines, or olives, or apples, or pomegranates, or trees similar to these, is a great and incurable silliness. For for what reason would he have made it? So that he might have a comfortable place to spend time? For the whole world would be considered a most self-sufficient dwelling for God the all-ruler, or would it be thought to fall short of ten thousand other things in terms of reception

<summary>Philo provides an allegorical interpretation of Bezalel and Moses, contrasting the fashioning of shadows with archetypal realities. He argues that the Garden of Eden represents the planting of human senses and intellectual faculties by God within the soul.</summary>
