text:
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of knowledge, moving from general understanding to the specific disciplines of the mathematical sciences.</meta>

...and knowledge. The task of the natural philosopher <note>original: "φυσικοῦ" (physikos) - one who studies the 'physis' or nature of things</note> is to learn what the nature of the universe truly is; how the world is like a living being; what place he holds within that world; and how the sun provides providence for the whole. These, and all other things that follow from what has been said, already go beyond one's private concerns. 

The task of the mathematician, however, is to understand the form and nature of sensible things, and the character of the motion and revolution that follows them. This is the study we call "theory."

<margin>**Arithmetic**</margin> **This subject, then,** is taken up for the sake of the sharpest intellect, as Plato says <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, where arithmetic is described as waking up the mind to seek truth</note>, which remains constant in the same way, and for the sake of those who strive for precision in perception. This part of mathematics dealing with numbers exists not merely for the sake of craft or practical science, but for its own sake. Indeed, almost all that labor and the necessary release from our distress <gloss>is</gloss> directed toward the knowledge of true being. It produces a greater reverence than any practical social need. 

<margin>**Geometry**</margin> <insert>**And before this, geometry too**</insert> deals with <unclear>existing</unclear> magnitude, and is like a kind of knowledge of the good. For when one is trained in mathematical study alongside virtue, so as to look upon truth, it is not like tasting honey, but is something healthy and pure.

<margin>**Astronomy**</margin> **And indeed, we shall make use of geometry.** For after such a collection of principles, <margin>**we say**</margin> the study of astronomy follows by analogy, holding the third rank. **It is useful** for the fourth branch of learning and for those who seek an advantage. For it reveals the heavenly bodies, their motion, and the cycles of months, years, days, and hours. From these we shall seek our own path and the Creator of all things. For having learned from these <unclear>beings</unclear>, it is as if we were taught by a theater of the elements. 

**And after these things,** <margin>**Music**</margin> again, not as mere ornaments, but the same principles applied to things heard, though not senselessly. For just as the eyes are the organs for all practical work (of power), so is hearing for the study of harmonies. And just as astronomy leads the mind back to true beings from things seen, and brings us toward true essence, so also the harmony of voice and hearing leads us from things heard to the same principles of straight lines <note>likely referring to the mathematical ratios of string lengths</note>; these things we shall study afterward. This is so that these things are not merely crafted for the sake of the physical world, for that in itself, being concerned with sensation, is worth no account.

<summary>This page outlines the curriculum of the Quadrivium (Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy, and Music), explaining how these mathematical sciences lead the soul from the physical world to the contemplation of divine truth and the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>natural philosophy, mathematics, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, Plato, Quadrivium, cosmology, education</keywords>

text:
and knowledge. It is the task of the natural philosopher to learn what the nature of the whole is, what kind of living being the cosmos is, what place it holds within the universe, how the sun provides for all things, and all other matters that follow from these. Having already passed beyond these familiar topics, the task of the mathematician is to understand the form and nature of sensible things and the motion and movement that follow them. We call this study theory, and we also speak of <margin>**arithmetic**^a</margin> <note>original: "ἀριθμητική"</note>. **This, therefore**, is adopted for the sharpest intellect of Plato, which is likewise disposed, and for the sake of precision in sensory perception. The part of mathematics concerned with numbers is not for the sake of craft or science for utility alone. Rather, almost all that labor, which ought to be our happy release, <gloss>is</gloss> for the sake of the knowledge of essence. It creates greater caution <margin>**geometry**^a</margin> <note>original: "γεωμετρία"</note> for every need of social requirements. <insert>**And before this, geometry**</insert> from quantity <unclear>being</unclear>, and as one of those who have knowledge of good things. For when someone is trained in mathematical study with virtue, as if to see the truth, it is not equal to honey, but healthy and unpolluted. <margin>**astronomy**^a</margin> <note>original: "ἀστρονομία"</note> **And indeed we shall use geometry.** For after such a selection, <margin>**we say**^a</margin> <note>original: "λέγομεν"</note> that astronomy is analogous, holding the third rank. **It is useful** for the fourth discipline, and they have the advantage. For the bodies of the heavens, both in their movement and in themselves, and the manifestation of months, cycles, days, and certain hours, from which we shall seek the path of the individual and the creator of all things. For having learned from these <unclear>beings</unclear>, as if from a theater and elements. **And after these** <margin>**music**^a</margin> <note>original: "μουσική"</note> again, not as ornaments, but the same things of what is heard, foolishly. For just as eyes are for every task (of power), so hearing is for the harmonies. And just as astronomy leads the mind back to beings from visible things, and brings them to essence, so too does harmonics, being of voice and hearing, from audible things, lead us to learn the same things of straight lines. So that we may not craft these things after the world, it itself and the matters concerning sensation are worthy of no account.

<summary>This page outlines the four disciplines of the quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music), describing their roles in elevating the intellect from sensory perception toward the knowledge of essence and the divine creator.</summary>
<keywords>natural philosophy, mathematics, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, Plato, quadrivium, essence, sensory perception</keywords>

The task of the natural philosopher <note>original: "physikos"</note> is to learn what the nature of the universe is, and that the world is like a living being, and what place he holds within the world. He also studies how the sun provides for all things, and all other matters that follow from these points, going beyond the limits of one's own private concerns. The task of the mathematician is to study the form and nature of sensible things and the character of their subsequent motion and travel. We call this study and theory <margin>arithmetic</margin> arithmetic. **This subject**, then, is taken up for the sake of the sharpest intellect, according to Plato, which remains always the same, and for the sake of those who strive for precision in perception. The part dealing with numbers is a portion of mathematics, existing not merely for the sake of utility in art or science, but rather because almost all that labor and necessary release from our misfortunes <gloss>is</gloss> directed toward the knowledge of essence. It creates a greater reverence <margin>geometry</margin> for every need of social relations. <insert>And before this is geometry</insert> which proceeds from quantity <unclear>being</unclear>, and is like a kind of knowledge of good things. For when someone is trained in mathematical study alongside virtue, so as to see the truth, it is not like honey, but is healthy and pure. <margin>astronomy</margin> **And indeed we shall make use of geometry.** For after such a selection, <margin>we say</margin> the study of astronomy is analogous, holding the third rank. **It is useful** for the fourth branch of learning and for those who excel. For it reveals the heavenly bodies, their motion and the motion of the heavens themselves, and the cycles of months, circles, days, and hours. From these we shall seek our own path and the Creator of all things. For having learned from these the things that <unclear>exist</unclear>, it is as if we were in a theater of elements. **And after these** <margin>music</margin> again, let there be no mere ornaments, but the same principles applied to things heard, though not senselessly. For just as the eyes are for every practical work of power, so is hearing for the harmonies. And just as astronomy leads the mind back toward the things that exist from the things seen, and brings it toward essence, so also the science of harmony, being of voice and hearing, leads from the things heard to the same principles of straight lines, which we shall study afterward. This is so that these things are not crafted merely for the sake of the physical world, for such things concern only perception and are worth no account.

<summary>This page outlines the curriculum of the Quadrivium, explaining how arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music lead the soul from sensory perception to the knowledge of divine essence and the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>Quadrivium, Plato, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, natural philosophy, essence, Creator, harmony</keywords>

Againe, the SOUL hath motion of it ſelfe; but a number is undoubtedly unmoveable. Againe, a number remaining one and the ſame in nature, is able to alter no quality that belongeth unto numbers: But, the Soul remaining one and the ſame in ſubſtance, doth change his qualities, altering from ignorance to knowledge, and from vice to vertue; therefore (all theſe particulars conſidered) the SOVL is not a number. Theſe were the ancient Philoſophers opinions concerning the SOUL. But Eunomius defined it to be a SVBSTANCE void of body, and created in the body, agreeing therein both with Plato and Ariſtotle. For, he took theſe words, a ſubſtance void of body, out of Plato; and theſe, created in the body, from Ariſtotle: not conſidering (though hee was otherwiſe very quick witted) that he endeavours to knit thoſe things into One which can by no meanes be united together. For, every thing that is engendred both bodily and in time, is corruptible and mortall. To this the doctrine and judgement of Moſes is agreeable. For, in deſcribing the Creation of things ſubject unto ſenſe, hee did not therein deliver in expreſſe words, that the nature of things intelligible were then made. But, ſome (though otherſome are not of their opinion) inſiſting upon conjectures, are of that minde. Now if any man ſuppoſe that the SOUL was made after the body; becauſe it was put into the body, after the ſame was faſhioned, he erreth wide from the truth. For, neither doth Moſes ſay, that the SOUL was at the ſame time created when it was brought into the body, neither doth any reaſon perſwade thereunto. Eunomius therefore, might aſwell have ſaid that the Soul is mortall, as doth Ariſtotle, and the Stoicks, as affirme it is engendred in the body. For, if he will ſay the ſoul is an incorporeall Eſſence;
[context] hee ſhould have refuſed to ſay that, it was created in the body; leſt hee give men occaſion to thinke the ſoule mortall, and utterly void of Reaſon.

text:
<meta>This page continues Nemesius’s refutation of the Pythagorean and Xenocratean definition of the soul as a "self-moving number." On the previous page, he began arguing that the soul's mobility distinguishes it from the nature of mathematical numbers.</meta>

# ON THE NATURE OF MAN

...is mobile. But number is, by definition, immobile. Furthermore, while a number remains one and the same in its nature, it cannot change any quality that exists within numbers <note>Nemesius means that the mathematical properties of a specific number, like 'three' or 'four,' are fixed and immutable.</note>. But the soul, while remaining one and the same in its **substance** <term>substance</term> <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia). In Greek philosophy, this refers to the fundamental being or "stuff" that makes something what it is.</note>, can change its qualities, shifting from ignorance to knowledge and from vice to virtue. Therefore, the soul is not a number. Such, then, are the doctrines of the ancients concerning the soul.

However, **Eunomius** <note>Eunomius of Cyzicus (d. 393 AD) was a prominent leader of the "Anomoean" Arians. Nemesius critiques him here for attempting to blend incompatible philosophical schools.</note> defined the soul as an **incorporeal substance** <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "ἀσώματον" (asomaton). Literally "without a body." This is a key Platonic descriptor for the soul.</note> created within the body, attempting to harmonize **Plato** and **Aristotle** at the same time. He took the idea of an "incorporeal substance" from Plato, but the idea of it being "created within the body" from the teaching of Aristotle. He did not realize, despite his sharp mind, that he was attempting to bring together things that are fundamentally incompatible. For everything that has a beginning that is both bodily and temporal is necessarily corruptible and mortal.

The writings of **Moses** <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis. Early Christian philosophers like Nemesius frequently sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with the "Mosaic" account of creation.</note> also harmonize with these points. For in describing the creation of sensible things <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, he did not explicitly state that the nature of **intelligible** <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "νοητῶν" (noēton). Refers to things grasped by the mind or intellect rather than the senses, such as souls or divine truths.</note> things came into being at that same moment. Some people hold this opinion by conjecture, but not everyone agrees with them. 

If anyone should think that because the soul was "breathed into" the body after it was formed, the soul itself must have been created after the body, they miss the truth. For Moses does not say the soul was created at the exact moment it was placed into the body, nor is such a view consistent with reason. Therefore, a thinker must either call the soul mortal—as did **Aristotle**, who said it comes to be within the body, and as did the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy that believed the soul was a physical "breath" (pneuma) that eventually dissipated.</note>—or, if calling it an incorporeal substance...

He argues that if the soul is created simultaneously with the body, it must be mortal, a view he rejects by appealing to both reason and the Book of Genesis.</summary>
<keywords>soul, substance, incorporeal, Eunomius, Plato, Aristotle, Moses, Stoics, immortality, creation</keywords>

text:
ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

is mobile. But number is definitively immobile. Furthermore, while number remains one and the same in its nature, it cannot alter any quality that arises within numbers. The soul, however, while remaining one and the same in its essence, alters its qualities, shifting from ignorance to knowledge and from vice to virtue. Therefore, the soul is not a number. Such, then, are the doctrines of the ancients concerning the soul. Eunomius defined the soul as an incorporeal essence created within a body, agreeing simultaneously with Plato and Aristotle. For he took the idea of an incorporeal essence from Plato, and the idea of being created within a body from the teaching of Aristotle. He did not realize, despite being sharp-witted, that he was attempting to bring together incompatible things. For everything that has a bodily and temporal origin is perishable and mortal. The words of Moses also harmonize with this; for in describing the origin of sensible things, he did not explicitly state that the nature of intelligible things came into being at the same time. But some people conjecture this and hold it as an opinion, though not everyone agrees with them. If anyone thinks that because the soul was inserted after the formation of the body, it came into existence after the body, he misses the truth. For Moses does not say that it was created at the moment it was inserted into the body, nor does it stand to reason that this is the case. is subject to movement. But number is, by its definition, without movement. Further, number, remaining one and the same in nature, cannot change any of the qualities that arise in numbers. But the soul, while remaining one and the same in its substance, does change its qualities, passing over from ignorance to knowledge and from vice to virtue. The soul, therefore, is not a number. Such, then, are the doctrines of the ancients concerning the soul. Eunomius <note>the fourth-century Arian theologian, bishop of Cyzicus</note>, however, defined the soul as an incorporeal substance created in a body, agreeing at once with Plato and with Aristotle. For the phrase "incorporeal substance" he took from Plato, and the phrase "created in a body" from the teaching of Aristotle. He did not perceive, sharp as he was, that he is trying to bring together into one things that cannot be reconciled. For everything that has a bodily origin, and at the same time an origin in time, is perishable and mortal. The words of Moses also agree with this. For in describing the coming into being of the things perceived by the senses, he did not expressly say that the nature of the things grasped by the mind also came to exist within that same creation. [context] As the lamp burns it will become empty, and if we pour in water through the cup, it will pass into the vessel A B, and the oil will ascend and fill up the deficiency in the lamp,
until it reaches the lamp-nozzle. When the oil has sunk again, we must do the same, repeating it till the supply is expended. If it is required to remove the vessel A B, the oil being retained in the lamp, there must be a valve or tap in the pipes C D, E F, close to the vessel A B, with keys near the lamp, so that when the keys are turned, the oil in the lamp, and that in the tubes, shall be confined. Thus the vessel may be removed from the lamp, and, whenever it is desired, we may bring them together again, and open the keys. It is better that the pipe E F should lead to the handle of the lamp, and C D a little behind it, having the cup which communicates with it, and through which water will be poured in, placed above; so that the oil will flow from the handle at the same time that the water is poured into the cup.

until the oil reaches the wick. Then again, if the oil settles, we will do the same thing, until the oil is consumed. And if it is necessary to remove the vessel $ΑΒ$ while oil is still left in the lamp, there will be ground-pipe joints <term>smerismatia</term> <gloss>lapping/ground airtight joints</gloss> in the tubes $ΓΔ$ and $ΕΖ$ near vessel $ΑΒ$, and keys <note>stopcocks</note> near the lamp, so that when they are turned, the oil in the lamp and the oil in the tubes is contained, and thus it will be removable. And when we wish, after they are replaced, we will open the keys. It is better to lead the $ΕΖ$ small tube into the handle of the lamp, and to have the $ΓΔ$ tube behind the handle, slightly higher, with a small cup-like attachment on top, perforated for it, through which the water will be poured, so that upon the pouring of water, the oil flows from the handle.

until the oil reaches the wick. Then, if the oil level drops again, we shall perform the same action, until the oil is consumed. Then, if the oil level drops again, this same action must be performed, until the oil is consumed. reference.text:
[context] If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point straight lines be drawn through to the circle, one of which is through the centre and the others are drawn at random, then, of the straight lines which fall on the concave circumference,
that through the centre is greatest, while of the rest the nearer to that through the centre is always greater than the more remote, but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference, that between the point and the diameter is least, while of the rest the nearer to the least is always less than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall on the circle from the point, one on each side of the least.
Let ABC be a circle, and let a point D be taken outside ABC; let there be drawn through from it straight lines DA, DE, DF, DC, and let DA be through the centre; I say that, of the straight lines falling on the concave circumference AEFC, the straight line DA through the centre is greatest, while DE is greater than DF and DF than DC.; but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference HLKG, the straight line DG between the point and the diameter AG is least;
[context] and the nearer to the least DG is always less than the more remote, namely DK than DL, and DL than DH.

text:
<meta>This page continues the formal statement and begins the proof of Proposition 8 in Book III. It describes the properties of lines drawn from a point outside a circle to the circle's circumference.</meta>

# BOOK III OF THE ELEMENTS

...is the one through the center. Of the others, the one nearer to the line through the center is always greater than the more remote. Of the straight lines falling toward the convex circumference <note>The "convex" side is the outer surface of the circle facing the point.</note>, the least is the one between the point and the diameter. ### Proposition 8

Let there be a circle <term>ABC</term>, and let some point <term>D</term> be taken outside of <term>ABC</term>, and from it let certain straight lines be drawn, <term>DA</term>, <term>DE</term>, <term>DF</term>, and <term>DC</term>, and let <term>DA</term> be through the center. I say that, of the straight lines falling toward the concave circumference <term>AEFC</term>, the greatest is <term>DA</term>, which passes through the center, and <term>DE</term> is greater than <term>DF</term>, and <term>DF</term> is greater than <term>DC</term>; but of the straight lines falling toward the convex circumference <term>THLK</term>, the least is <term>DH</term>, which is between the point and the diameter <term>AH</term>, and always <note>the text continues to describe the relationship of lines to the convex arc</note>

<column-break/>

<note>
The following section contains the critical apparatus, which notes variations in the ancient manuscripts labeled P, B, F, V, and p.
1. "is" becomes "will be" in manuscript B. After "center," manuscript P adds: "and the least is the one falling between the point and the diameter."
2. "nearer" and "more remote" show minor spelling variations between manuscripts P and p.
3. "is" shows various grammatical endings across manuscripts P, F, V, and B.
4. The phrase "the least... diameter" is in the margin of manuscript P and omitted in others.
8. "equal" is omitted in manuscript p; manuscript B specifies "equal straight lines."
12. "certain" is expanded to "certain lines toward the circle" in several later manuscripts.
The editor Augustus noted that he adjusted the word order of the proposition according to his own judgment.
</note>

[context] The geometric proportion has a peculiar property shared by none
of the rest, that the differences of the terms are in the same ratio to
each other as the terms to those adjacent to them, the greater to the less, and vice versa. Still another property is that the greater terms have as a difference, with respect to the lesser, the lesser terms themselves, and similarly difference differs from difference, by the smaller difference itself, if the terms are set forth in the double ratio; in the triple ratio both terms and differences will have as a difference twice the next smaller, in the quadruple ratio thrice, in the quintuple four times, and so on.
Geometric proportions come about not only among the multiples, but also among all the superparticular, superpartient, and mixed forms, and the peculiar property of this proportion in all cases is preserved, that in the continued proportions the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the mean, but in disjunct proportions, or those with a greater number of terms, even if they are not continued, but with an even number of terms, that the product of the extremes equals that of the means.
As an illustration of the fact that in all the relations, all kinds of multiples, superparticulars, superpartients, and mixed ratios the peculiar property of this proportion is preserved, let that suffice and be sufhcient for us wherein we fashioned, beginning with equality,
[context] by the three rules all the kinds of inequality out of one another, when they were In both direct and reverse order; for each act of fashioning and each series set forth is a geometric proportion with all the aforesaid properties as well as a fourth, namely, that they keep the same ratio in both the greater and the smaller terms.

text:
<meta>This page continues the analysis of geometric proportions, specifically focusing on the mathematical properties of the "differences" between terms and the fundamental rule of the product of the extremes.</meta>

## NICOMACHUS OF GERASA

among the remaining properties, is that the differences between the terms exist in the same **ratio** <term>logos|The relationship between two numbers</term> to one another as the terms themselves have toward their neighbors—the larger to the smaller, and inversely, as the inverse. Furthermore, another property <margin>5</margin> is that the larger terms have a difference toward the smaller terms that is equal to the smaller terms themselves <note>For example, in the sequence 2, 4, 8, the difference between 4 and 2 is 2 (the smaller term)</note>, and in the same way, the difference between those differences differs from the smaller difference by that same smaller difference. This occurs when the terms are set out in a **double ratio** <term>diplasios logos|A 2:1 ratio, like 2, 4, 8</term>. However, in a **triple ratio** <term>triplasios logos|A 3:1 ratio, like 3, 9, 27</term>, the differences between the terms will be twice the smaller term under them; <margin>10</margin> in a quadruple ratio, three times; and in a quintuple ratio, four times; and this continues infinitely.

<margin>4</margin> Geometric proportions do not only occur among "multiple" types of ratios, but also among all "superparticular" types <term>epimorios|A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus one part of it, like 3:2 or 4:3</term>, "superpartient" types <term>epimeres|A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus several parts of it, like 5:3</term>, and "mixed" types. The exceptional property <margin>15</margin> of this specific **mean** <term>mesotes|The middle term or the relationship that links the terms together</term> is preserved in all of them: in "connected" proportions <term>synemmenon|A continuous sequence like a:b = b:c</term>, the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the middle term; while in "disjoint" proportions <term>diazeuxei|A sequence where the pairs are separate, like a:b = c:d</term>, even if they are not connected but consist of an even number of terms, the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means.

<margin>20</margin> <margin>5</margin> To demonstrate that this unique property of geometric proportion is preserved in all relations—multiple, superparticular, superpartient, and mixed—it will be sufficient and satisfactory for us to use that method in which we build these proportions starting from **equality** <note>Nicomachus refers to a standard ancient method of generating complex ratios by starting with a series of equal numbers (like 1, 1, 1) and applying specific transformations</note>...

NICOMACHUS OF GERASA

of the others, that the differences of the terms are in the same ratio to one another as the terms themselves are to their consecutive terms, the greater to the lesser, and conversely as the converse. Furthermore, there is another property: the greater terms have a difference in relation to the lesser terms, and these lesser terms themselves, in the same way, have a difference in relation to the difference, differing by a double ratio when the terms are set out; but in a triple ratio, the terms and the differences will have twice the value of the term below them, and in a quadruple ratio three times, and in a quintuple ratio four times, and this continues indefinitely. Geometric proportions occur not only in multiple ratios, but also in all <term>epimoric</term> <gloss>superparticular</gloss> forms, and in <term>epimeres</term> <gloss>superpartient</gloss> forms, and in mixed forms. The exceptional property of this mean is preserved in all of them: for connected terms, the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the mean, and for those in disjunction or in more terms, even if they are not connected but are evenly arranged, the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means.

Let that which was formed from equality be sufficient and enough for us as an example that the property of this proportion is preserved in all relations, whether multiple of every kind, or <term>epimoric</term> <gloss>superparticular</gloss> of every kind, or <term>epimeres</term> <gloss>superpartient</gloss> of every kind, or mixed of every kind.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
of the remaining <note>properties</note>, is that the differences between the terms are in the same ratio to one another as the terms themselves are to those adjacent to them, the greater to the lesser, and conversely as the converse. Furthermore, there is another property: <margin>5</margin> the greater terms have as their difference to the lesser terms the lesser terms themselves; and in the same manner, difference compared to difference differs by that same lesser term. This occurs when the terms are set out in a <term>double</term> <gloss>duple or 2:1</gloss> ratio. In a <term>triple</term> <gloss>triple or 3:1</gloss> ratio, the <margin>10</margin> terms and the differences will have a difference twice that of the term below it; in a quadruple ratio, three times; and in a quintuple ratio, four times; and so on indefinitely.

<margin>4</margin> Geometric proportions arise not only in <term>multiple</term> <gloss>pollaplasios</gloss> ratios, but also in all forms of <term>superparticular</term> <gloss>epimorios, such as 3:2 or 4:3</gloss>, <term>superpartient</term> <gloss>epimeres</gloss>, and <term>mixed</term> <gloss>miktos</gloss> ratios. The exceptional property <margin>15</margin> of this <term>mean</term> <gloss>mesotes</gloss> is preserved in all of them: in <term>continuous</term> <gloss>synemmenon</gloss> proportions, the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the mean; in <term>disjunct</term> <gloss>diazeuxis</gloss> proportions, or those with more terms, even if they are not continuous but are of an even number, the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means.

<margin>20</margin> <margin>5</margin> Let this be a sufficient and self-evident example for us that the property of this proportion is preserved in all relations: in all kinds of multiples, all kinds of superparticulars, all kinds of superpartients, and all kinds of mixed ratios. It is that <note>example</note> in which we formed <note>the ratios</note> starting from equality.

<summary>Nicomachus explains the unique properties of geometric proportions, specifically how the ratios of differences mirror the ratios of the terms themselves across various mathematical relations. He defines the rule that the product of the extremes equals the square of the mean in continuous proportions or the product of the means in disjunct ones.</summary>

[context] And it will be better also that he should
get some gentle emetics. The sore is to be treated with dressings for fresh wounds, which permit of allusions, or with the leaves of camomile, or with the applications for fractured bones of the head, but nothing very cold must be applied. The first (most distant?) joints are least dangerous, but those still higher, are more so. Reduction should be made the same day, or the next, but by no means on the third or fourth, for it is on the fourth day that exacerbations especially attack. In those cases, then, where immediate reduction cannot be accomplished, we must wait until after the aforesaid days; for whatever you reduce within ten days, may be expected to induce spasm. But if the spasm supervene on its being reduced, the joint should be quickly displaced, and bathed frequently with warm water, and the whole body should be kept in a warm, soft, and easy condition, and more especially about the joints, for the whole body should rather be in a bent than in an extended state. Moreover, it is to be expected, that the articular extremities of the bones of the fingers will for this generally happens, if even the least degree of inflammation take place, so that if it were not that the physician would be exposed to censure, owing to the ignorance of the common people, no reduction should be made at all. The reduction of the bones of joints which have protruded through the skin, is attended with the dangers which have been described.
When the articular bones of the fingers are fairly chopped off, these cases are mostly unattended with danger, unless deliquium come on in consequence of the injury, and ordinary treatment will be sufficient to such sores. But when resection is made, not at the articulations, but at some other point in the bones,
[context] these cases also are free from danger, and are still more easily cured than the others;

with some light medicine. And one must treat the ulcer either with bloody <note>remedies designed for wounds</note> dressings that are soaked, or with <term>polyophthalmia</term> <gloss>a plant with many buds/leaves</gloss>, or with those things with which fractured bones in the head are treated. 6 And one must not apply anything very cold. The first joints <note>fingers/toes</note> are therefore the least dangerous. 7 But those still higher are more dangerous. One must replace them on the same day or the day after. 8 On the third or fourth day, least of all. For being on the fourth day, they indicate the greatest possibility of relapses. 9 Therefore, for those in whom the replacement does not happen immediately, one must exceed these mentioned days. 10 Whoever replaces them within ten days, everything is within control. 11 If, however, a convulsion should befall one who has been replaced, one must quickly dislocate the joint. And soak it as often as possible with warm [substances], and keep the whole body warm, oily, and soft, especially around the joints. 12 The whole body should be bent rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints of the fingers which are being replaced will be prone to abscess. For most things happen this way, if even any inflammation should arise. 13 So that, if the doctor were not going to be blamed due to the ignorance of the common people, there would be no need to replace them at all. Therefore, bones protruding around the joints are dangerous if replaced, as has been said.

### LXXIX.
As many things as are cut off completely at the joints of the fingers, these for the most part are harmless, unless one is harmed by fainting during the very wounding. 2 And ordinary treatment will suffice for such ulcers. Moreover, even those that are not at the joints, but at another...

The first joints are therefore the least dangerous. 7 But the higher ones are more dangerous. It is necessary to replace them on the same day or the day after: 8 On the third or fourth day, least of all. For on the fourth day they are accustomed to recrudesce <note>flare up</note> the most. 9 In those, however, for whom they have not been replaced immediately, one must pass beyond these mentioned days. For whatever has been replaced within ten days, all of that is contained. 10 If, however, a convulsion approaches a replaced bone, one must quickly eject the joint. And soak it as often as possible with warm [liquids], and treat the whole body, and especially around the joints, warmly and gently and softly. 11 Verily, the whole body ought to be bent rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints around the fingers which are replaced will abscess. For it usually happens in this way, if even any inflammation underlies it. 12 Wherefore, if a doctor were not to fear accusation on account of the ignorance of the masses, it would be necessary to replace none at all. And in this manner, bones protruding around the joints are dangerous if they are replaced, as it has been said.

One must treat the wound either with bloody moistening applications, or with polyophthalmos <note>original: "πολυοφθαλμοῖσιν"; a plant used for healing</note>, or with those things used to treat fractured bones in the head. 6 One must not apply anything very cold. The first joints are the least dangerous, 7 but those further up are more dangerous. One must reset them on the same day or the next day; 8 on the third or fourth day, it is least advisable. For on the fourth day, they are most prone to relapse. 9 Therefore, for those in whom the resetting does not occur immediately, one must wait until after these mentioned days. 10 Whatever is reset within ten days is entirely manageable. 10 If, however, a convulsion occurs after the bone has been reset, one must quickly dislocate the joint again, moisten it with warm applications as often as possible, and keep the whole body warm, lubricated, and soft, especially around the joints. 11 The whole body should be kept flexed rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints of the fingers being reset will form abscesses. For this happens in most cases if any inflammation at all is present. 12 Thus, if the physician were not to be blamed due to the ignorance of the common people, there would be no need to reset them at all. The bones protruding at the joints are as dangerous to reset as has been stated.</meta>

### LXXIX.
Whatever is completely severed at the joints of the fingers is for the most part harmless, unless someone is harmed by fainting during the injury itself. 2 A simple treatment is sufficient for such wounds. But also those that are not at the joints, but at another

<column-break/>

use some light application. The first joints are therefore the least dangerous; 7 but those higher up are more dangerous. One must reset them on the same day or the day after; 8 on the third or fourth day, it is least advisable. For on the fourth day, they are most prone to relapse. 9 For those in whom they have not been reset immediately, one must wait until after the mentioned days. For whatever is reset within ten days is entirely manageable. 10 If, however, a convulsion occurs after the bone has been reset, one must quickly dislocate the joint, moisten it with warm applications as often as possible, and keep the whole body, and especially the areas around the joints, warm, supple, and soft. 11 The whole body should be kept flexed rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints of the fingers being reset will form abscesses. For this happens in most cases if any inflammation at all is present. 12 Therefore, if the physician were not to be blamed due to the ignorance of the common people, there would be no need to reset them at all. And in this manner, bones protruding at the joints are dangerous if they are reset, as has been stated.

<meta>continues from previous page: the discussion regarding the treatment of compound fractures and dislocations where the bone protrudes through the skin.</meta>

# ON THE JOINTS

<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
<note>The Greek text and Latin translation provided here discuss the risks of resetting bones in compound dislocations.</note>

...purge the upper gut with some light medicine. The wound itself must be treated either with applications for fresh wounds <note>original: "enaimoisi" / "cruentis emplastris"</note>, or with the leaves of the <term>polyophthalmos</term> <gloss>many-eyed plant, likely a species of potentilla or houseleek</gloss>, or with those remedies used for treating fractured bones in the head. $^6$ One must also apply nothing very cold. Now, the joints of the fingers are the least dangerous; $^7$ but those higher up are more dangerous. One should reset the bone on the same day or the next; $^8$ but least of all on the third or fourth day. For on the fourth day, the wounds are most prone to exacerbations <note>original: "paligkotiesi" / "recrudescere"</note>. $^9$ In those cases where the bone is not reset immediately, one should wait until these aforementioned days have passed. $^{10}$ Whatever is reset within ten days can be successfully held in place. $^{10}$ If, however, a convulsion <note>original: "spasmos"</note> occurs after the bone has been reset, the joint must be displaced again immediately. One should apply warm fomentations as often as possible, and keep the whole body warm, oiled, and soft, especially around the joints. $^{11}$ The whole body should be kept in a flexed rather than an extended position. One must expect, however, that the joints of the fingers which are reset will eventually slough off <note>original: "apostatika" / "abscessuros"</note>. For this happens in most cases if any degree of inflammation occurs. $^{12}$ Indeed, if it were not for the risk of the physician being blamed due to the ignorance of the common people, there would be no need to reset such bones at all. Thus, bones protruding at the joints are as dangerous when reset as has been described.

### LXXIX.
Those parts which are completely cut off at the joints of the fingers are for the most part harmless, unless someone should be harmed by fainting at the very moment of the injury. $^2$ Ordinary treatment will suffice for such wounds. But also those parts not at the joints, but along some other

<column-break/>

part of the bone <note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text provided above, offering a parallel translation of the same surgical instructions.</note>

...use some light remedy. It is necessary to treat the wound either with bloody plasters which are moistened, or by applying the leaves of <term>polyophthalmos</term> or <term>buphthalmos</term> <gloss>ox-eye plant</gloss>, or those things with which bones in the head are treated. $^6$ Apply nothing very cold. Therefore, the first joints are the least dangerous; $^7$ the higher ones are more dangerous. It is necessary to replace them on the same day or the day after. $^8$ On the third and fourth day least of all. For on the fourth day they are most accustomed to grow worse. $^9$ For those in whom they have not been replaced immediately, it is necessary to pass over the said days. For whatever has been replaced within ten days, all that is retained. $^{10}$ If indeed a convulsion should follow the replacement of the bone, it is necessary to eject the joint immediately, and to moisten it with warm applications as often as possible, and to treat the whole body, and especially around the joints, warmly, gently, and softly. $^{11}$ Truly, the whole body should be inclined rather than stretched out. It must be expected, however, that the joints around the fingers which are replaced will fall away. For it generally happens so, if any inflammation at all is present. $^{12}$ Wherefore, if it were not for the ignorance of the common people, and the physician fearing accusation, it would not be necessary to replace them at all. And in this manner, bones protruding outward around the joints are dangerous if they are replaced, just as was said.

### LXXIX.
Whatever parts are entirely cut away around the joints of the fingers, these are mostly harmless, unless someone is injured by a fainting fit during the wounding itself. $^2$ And common treatment suffices for such ulcers. But also those which are not around the joints, but near...

<summary>Hippocrates discusses the dangers of resetting compound dislocations, noting that finger joints are safest while higher joints are riskier. He warns that inflammation or convulsions may require re-displacing the bone to save the patient's life.</summary>

**3** Some boil a little of the wine, let it cool, and taste it; whatever is found in the taste, they believe the rest of the wine will be the same. The sampling for the taste must be taken from the middle of the vessel. **4** Others take the sign from the jar stoppers; having uncovered the jar, they taste the moisture on the stoppers and determine how the wine will be. A wine-like taste signifies that the wine is excellent, but a watery one is not safe. **5** Some test it from the taste of the wine itself; if the wine is astringent from the start, it signifies safety, but if it is flat, the opposite. **6** It is possible to test the wine also from the "flower" <note>the film that forms on the surface of wine</note> that sits and floats upon it. If a purplish, wide, and soft flower forms, the wine is safer. If the flower is slimy, it is not good. A black or yellow flower floating on the wine indicates the wine is weak; white indicates it is stable. A flower gathered into the shape of spiderwebs signifies that it will turn to vinegar soon. **7** Again, if you see a snake entwined in the vine during the grape harvest, expect the wine to turn to vinegar. **8** If, at the time of treading the wine or putting it into the jars, the grape juice is thick and sticky (this you will test by touch), the wine will be more stable.

the quality of the vintage, and they judge what the wine will be like. **3** Some people boil a small amount of the wine, and after cooling it, they taste it; whatever quality is found in the tasting, they believe the rest of the wine will be of that same sort. It is necessary, however, for the sample for tasting to be taken from the middle of the vessel. **4** Others take their indication from the lids of the vessels; for when the jar <term>pithos</term> <gloss>a large earthenware storage jar</gloss> is uncovered, they taste the moisture on the lids, and from this they judge what the wine will be like. If the taste is wine-like, it signifies the wine is of the best quality; if it is watery, it is not stable. **5** Some also judge from the taste of the wine itself; for if the wine is harsh <note>original: "austēros", meaning dry or astringent</note> from the beginning, it signifies stability; but if it is flabby <note>original: "chaunos", meaning porous, spongy, or lacking structure</note>, the opposite is true. **6** It is also possible to test the wine from the flower <term>anthos</term> <gloss>a film of yeast or mold that forms on the surface</gloss> lying upon and floating on top of it. For if a purple-colored flower develops that is broad and soft, the wine is more stable; but if the flower is slimy, it is not good. A black or yellow flower floating on the wine indicates the wine is weak; but a white one indicates it is durable. reference.text:
PLUTARCH’S SYMPOSIACS.
BOOK I.
Some, my dear Sossius Senecio, imagine that this sentence, μισέω μνάμονα συμπόταν, was principally designed against the stewards of a feast, who are usually troublesome and press liquor too much upon the guests. For the Dorians in Sicily (as I am informed) called the steward μνάμονα, a remembrancer. Others think that this proverb admonisheth the guests to forget every thing that is spoken or done in company; and agreeably to this, the ancients used to consecrate forgetfulness with a ferula to Bacchus, thereby intimating that we should either not remember any irregularity committed in mirth and company, or apply a gentle and childish correction to the faults. But because you are of opinion that to forget absurdities is indeed (as Euripides says) a piece of wisdom, but to deliver over to oblivion all sort of discourse that merry meetings do usually produce is not only repugnant to that endearing quality that most allow to an entertainment, but against the known practice of the greatest philosophers (for Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, Speusippus, Epicurus,
[context] Prytanis, Hieronymus, Dion the Academic, have thought it a worthy and noble employment to deliver down to us those discourses they had at table), and since it is your pleasure that I should gather up the chiefest of those scattered topics which both at Rome and Greece amidst our cups and feasting we have disputed on, in obedience to your commands I have sent three books, each containing ten problems; and the rest shall quickly follow, if these find good acceptance and do not seem altogether foolish and impertinent.

# CONVIVIAL QUESTIONS
## BOOK IX.

### BOOK ONE.

->PROLOGUE.<-

1. The saying,
> “I hate a guest who remembers,”

O Sosius Senecio, some say was spoken regarding the inspectors <note>original: "ἐπιστάθμους", the officials who monitored the conduct of a symposium</note>, who were quite boorish and ill-mannered while drinking; for the Dorians in Sicily, it seems, called the inspector a <term>mnāmōn</term> <gloss>remembrancer</gloss>. Others think the proverb is intended to bring oblivion to what is said and done over drink. For this reason, our ancestral traditions dedicate both forgetfulness and the fennel-rod <note>symbolizing the light discipline of the god</note> to the god <note>Dionysus</note>, as if one should either remember nothing of the errors committed in wine, or that they deserve only the lightest and most childish admonition. Since it also seems to you that forgetfulness of things out of place is truly wise, according to Euripides, yet to forget entirely the events of a drinking party does not merely conflict with the friendly nature of the table, but also has the most famous philosophers bearing witness against it: Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, and Speusippus, and Epicurus...

## BOOK IX

### BOOK ONE

->PREFACE<-

1. The saying "I hate a guest who remembers" <note>original: "μισέω μνάμονα συμπόταν"</note>, O Sossius Senecio, some say was spoken regarding those who are billeted in one's house, as they are quite boorish and ill-mannered while drinking; for the Dorians in Sicily, it seems, called a person billeted upon them a "rememberer." Others think the proverb brings about an amnesty for what is said and done during a drinking party. # TABLE TALK PROBLEMS

## BOOK IX

### BOOK ONE

->PREFACE<-

1. The saying "I hate a guest who remembers" <note>original: "μισέω μνάμονα συμπόταν"</note>, O Sossius Senecio, some say was spoken regarding those who are billeted in one's house, as they are quite boorish and ill-mannered while drinking; for the Dorians in Sicily, it seems, called a person billeted upon them a "rememberer." Others think the proverb brings about an amnesty for what is said and done during a drinking party. For this reason, ancestral traditions consecrate both forgetfulness and the fennel-stalk <note>a symbol of Dionysus</note> to the god, implying that one should either remember nothing of the offenses committed in wine, or that they require only a very light and childish admonition. Since it also seems to you that forgetfulness of absurdities is, in truth, wise according to Euripides, yet to be entirely forgetful of what happens in wine conflicts not only with what is called the "friend-making" nature of the table, but also has the most distinguished philosophers testifying against it—Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, and Speusippus, Epi-

# TABLE-TALK QUESTIONS

## NINE BOOKS

### BOOK ONE

->PREFACE<-

1. The saying
> "I hate a drinking companion with a memory"

O Sossius Senecio <note>Quintus Sosius Senecio was a Roman consul and a close friend of Plutarch to whom many of his works are dedicated.</note>, some say this was spoken in reference to the overseers of the feast <note>original: "epistathmoi"</note>, who are generally vulgar and ill-bred while drinking. It seems the Dorians in Sicily used to call the overseer a <term>mnamon</term> <gloss>one who remembers or records</gloss>. Others, however, think the proverb suggests that a veil of forgetfulness should be drawn over what is said and done over wine. For this reason, our ancestral traditions dedicate both <term>lethe</term> <gloss>forgetfulness</gloss> and the <term>narthex</term> <gloss>the giant fennel stalk carried by followers of Dionysus</gloss> to the god. This implies either that one should remember nothing of the errors committed under the influence of wine, or that such errors require only a very light and playful correction. But since you also believe that forgetfulness of unpleasant things is truly wise, as Euripides says, yet to completely forget everything that happens over wine not only conflicts with what is called the table's love of beauty, but also has the most esteemed philosophers as witnesses against it: Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, Speusippus, Epi-

[context] And it would really be a shameful and miserable thing, that
the pilot should choose his mariners, and the master of a ship the pilot, Who well can rule the helm, and in good guise Hoist up the sails, when winds begin to rise, and that an architect should make choice of such servants and workmen as will not prejudice his work, but take pains in the best manner to forward it; but that a statesman—who, as Pindar has it, The best of artists and chief workman is Of equity and justice— should not presently choose himself like-affected friends and ministers, and such as might co-inspire into him a love of honesty; but that one or other should be always unjustly and violently bending him to other uses. For then he would seem to differ in nothing from a carpenter or mason who, through ignorance or want of experience, uses such squares, rules, and levels as will certainly make his work to be awry. Since friends are the living and intelligent instruments of statesmen, who ought to be so far from bearing them company in their slips and transgressions, that they must be careful they do not, even unknown to them, commit a fault. And this it was, that disgraced Solon and brought him into disrepute amongst his citizens; for he, having an intention to ease men’s debts and to bring in that which was called at Athens the Seisachtheia (for that was the name given by way of extenuation to the cancelling of debts), communicated this design to some of his friends, who thereupon did a most unjust act; for having got this inkling, they borrowed abundance of money, and the law being a little after brought to light, they appeared to have purchased stately houses, and great store of land with the wealth they had borrowed; and Solon, who was himself injured, was accused to have been a partaker of their injustice. Agesilaus also was most feeble and mean-spirited in what concerned the suits of his friends, being like the horse Pegasus in Euripides, Who, frighted, bowed his back, more than his rider would, so that, being more ready to help them in their misfortunes than was requisite, he seemed to be privy to their injustices. For he saved Phoebidas, who was accused for having without commission surprised the castle of Thebes, called Cadmea, saying that such enterprises were to be attempted without expecting any orders. And when Sphodrias was brought to trial for an unlawful and heinous act, having made an incursion into Attica at such time as the Athenians were allies and confederates of the Spartans, he procured him to be acquitted, being softened by the amorous entreaties of his son. There is also recorded a short epistle of his to a certain prince, written in these words: If Nicias is innocent, discharge him; if he is guilty, discharge him for my sake; but however it is, discharge him. But Phocion (on the contrary) would not so much as appear in behalf of his son-in-law Charicles, when he was accused for having taken money of Harpalus; but having said, Only for acts of justice have I made you my son-in-law,—went his way. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not by admonitions or requests dissuade his brother from being a tyrant, confederated with his destroyers. For a magistrate ought not to be a friend even to the altar (or till he comes to the point of being forsworn), as Pericles sometime said, but no farther than is agreeable to all law, justice, and the utility of the state; any of which being neglected brings a great and public damage, as did the not executing of justice on Sphodrias and Phoebidas, who did not a little contribute to the engaging of Sparta in the Leuctrian war. Otherwise, reason of state is so far from necessitating one to show himself severe on every peccadillo of his friends, that it even permits him, when he has secured the principal affairs of the public, to assist them, stand by them, and labor for them. There are, moreover, certain favors that may be done without envy, as is the helping a friend to obtain an office, or rather the putting into his hands some honorable commission or some laudable embassy, such as for the congratulating or honoring some prince or the making a league of amity and alliance with some state. But if there be some difficult but withal illustrious and great action to be performed, having first taken it upon himself, he may afterwards assume a friend to his assistance, as did Diomedes, whom Homer makes to speak in this manner: Since a companion you will have me take, How can I think a better choice to make, Than the divine Ulysses? And Ulysses again as kindly attributes to him the praise of the achievement, saying: These stately steeds, whose country you demand, Nestor, were hither brought from Thracian land, Whose king, with twelve of his best friends, lies dead, All slain by th’ hand of warlike Diomed. For this sort of concession no less adorns the praiser than the praised; but self-conceitedness, as Plato says, dwells with solitude. He ought moreover to associate his friends in those good and kind offices which are done by him, bidding those whom he has benefited to love them and give them thanks, as having been the procurers and counsellors of his favors to them. But he must reject the dishonest and unreasonable request of his friends, yet not churlishly but mildly, teaching and showing them that they are not beseeming their virtue and honor. Never was any man better at this than Epaminondas, who, having denied to deliver out of prison a certain victualler, when requested by Pelopidas, and yet a little after dismissing him at the desire of his miss, said to his friend, These, O Pelopidas, are favors fit for wenches to receive, and not for generals. Cato on the other side acted morosely and insolently, when Catulus the censor, his most intimate and familiar friend, interceded with him for one of those against whom he, being quaestor, had entered process, saying: It would be a shame if you, who ought to reform young men for us, should be thrust out by our servants. For he might, though in effect refusing the requested favor, have yet forborne that severity and bitterness of speech; so that his doing what was displeasing to his friend might have seemed not to have proceeded from his own inclination, but to have been a necessity imposed upon him by law and justice. There are also in the administration of the state methods, not dishonorable, of assisting our poorer friends in the making of their fortune. Thus did Themistocles, who, seeing after a battle one of those which lay dead in the field adorned with chains of gold and jewels, did himself pass by him; but turning back to a friend of his, said, Do you take these spoils, for you are not yet come to be Themistocles. For even the affairs themselves do frequently afford a statesman such opportunities of benefiting his friends; for every man is not a Menemachus. To one therefore give the patronage of a cause, both just and beneficial; to another recommend some rich man, who stands in need of management and protection; and help a third to be employed in some public work, or to some gainful and profitable farm. Epaminondas bade a friend of his go to a certain rich man, and ask him for a talent by the command of Epaminondas, and when he to whom the message was sent came to enquire the reason of it; Because, said Epaminondas, he is a very honest man and poor; but you, by converting much of the city’s wealth to your own use, are become rich. And Xenophon reports, that Agesilaus delighted in enriching his friends, himself making no account of money. Now since, as Simonides says, all larks must have a crest, and every eminent office in a commonweal brings enmities and dissensions, it is not a little convenient for a statesman to be forewarned also of his comportment in these rencounters. Many therefore commend Themistocles and Aristides, who, when they were to go forth on an embassy or to command together the army, laid down their enmity at the confines of the city, taking it up again after their return. Some again are highly pleased with the action of Cretinas the Magnesian. He, having for his rival in the government one Hermias, a man not powerful and rich, but ambitious and high-spirited, when the Mithridatic war came on, seeing the city in danger, desired Hermias either to take the government upon himself and manage the affairs whilst he retired, or, if he would have him take the command of the army, to depart himself immediately, lest they should through their ambitious contention destroy the city. The proposal pleased Hermias, who, saying that Cretinas was a better soldier than himself, did with his wife and children quit the city. Cretinas then escorted him as he went forth, furnishing him out of his own estate with all such things as are more useful to those that fly from home than to those that are besieged; and excellently defending the city, unexpectedly preserved it, being at the point to be destroyed. For if it is generous and proceeding from a magnanimous spirit to cry out, I love my children, but my country more, why should it not be readier for every one of them to say, I hate this man, and desire to do him a diskindness, but the love of my country has greater power over me? For not to condescend to be reconciled to an enemy for those very causes for which we ought to abandon even a friend, is even to extremity savage and brutish.
[context] But far better did Phocion and Cato, who grounded not any enmity at all on their political differences, but being fierce and obstinate only in their public contests not to recede from any thing they judged convenient for the state, did in their private affairs use those very persons friendly and courteously from whom they differed in the other.

text:
<header>POLITICS</header>

<margin>for different purposes <note>original: ἄλλον ἄλλην .H.</note></margin> the pilot, and the shipowner the pilot; for one understands the stern, the other the prow, and they apply their skills to the rigging or the drum. Just as the architect has assistants and craftsmen who do not ruin his work but work together to complete it properly, the statesman is a master craftsman of sorts and a creator of power and justice. He will not immediately choose friends who are identical to himself, or servants and co-purchasers for the sake of goodness, but rather [he chooses] one for one need and another for another, because [of the pressure of those who] act against him unjustly and violently. For he said that it makes no difference to a builder or carpenter whether a person is inexperienced and uses rulers and levels incorrectly, as this would cause the work to become distorted. Friends are indeed the living and thinking instruments of political men; and one should not join them when they overstep, but rather pay attention so that they do not commit errors even through ignorance.
<margin>friends <note>original: φίλοι .H.</note></margin> This is what concerned Solon regarding his friends. For when he knew that he had taken the debts to lighten them by the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>, and the promise was to introduce a cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends. The latter, however, acted wickedly and took advantage; for they preemptively borrowed much silver, and after a short time, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased bright houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon bore the blame for being a co-conspirator. Through ignorance of his friends' ambitions, he himself became the weakest and most humble of them, like the Pegasus of Euripides, retreating and yielding more than he wished. By assisting in their misfortunes more than he should have, he seemed to be complicit in their injustices. For to save a man who is being punished—like pushing a fire that is rolling along—is to invite the commands that come with it. By nature, such men err greatly, and he bore the shame of his actions, as if eating the bitter fruit of hunger. He cast himself into dishonor while protecting his allies, and he managed to get them released out of an erotic devotion. Being softened by one, he feared writing a letter to a certain ruler on his behalf. Nicias, if he does not act unjustly, he is not unjust, and if he acts unjustly, he is still not [necessarily] unjust; but Phocion did not even join his son-in-law, who was involved in a lawsuit regarding stolen goods, but saying "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," he walked away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not persuade his brother to stop his tyranny through teaching and entreaty, joined those who executed him. For it is not the goal to be a friend "up to the altar" <note>a Greek proverb meaning to support a friend only insofar as it does not violate religious duty</note>, as Pericles once said, but up to the limit of law, justice, and the common good. He who is overlooked brings great damage to the public, as [Antiphon] said regarding not giving justice to Strophios or Phoebidas; for these were the very people who plunged the Lacedaemonian city into war. Since it is a heavy thing to trample on the moderate errors of friends, the political argument does not force one to do so, but rather, by placing the greatest public matters in a secure position, one should assist friends from one’s own resources, and stand by them, and work with them. There are also these graces [to offer]: to assist a friend in obtaining an office; or rather, to entrust him with an administration, a reputation, or a humane embassy—such as one having the honors of a leader, or a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and harmony. For this trust is correct, and their action is clear and great, provided it is done first for oneself, and then by sending the friend, like Diomedes: "If you command me to choose a companion, how could I forget noble Odysseus?" And he in turn likewise gave him equal praise for his own deeds. "There are other noble arrivals whom you might urge, of the Thracians, whom noble Diomedes met, and killed twelve of their leaders, all best." For

<header>PRECEPTS</header>

this yielding toward friends does not at all adorn the one who praises those who praise him. But obstinacy, says Plato, is the neighbor of solitude. Furthermore, alongside these graces of humanity, one should also contribute non-friendship; for one should not command that those who are not present be praised or loved, as one has been the cause and contributor to their status. One should put aside base or absurd requests, not bitterly, but teaching and comforting them gently, that such things are not worthy of their virtue or reputation. Epaminondas did this best: arriving to Menexenus, to whom Pelopidas had left a guard to free him from the virtue of his deeds, and not long after having left those things, he said he was taking the needs of Pelopidas as if for treasuries or generals. But someone who is heavy and obstinate—since Catulus the censor, who was a friend, sought from him a treasury that was being managed by him—said, "It is shameful, you, who should be correcting us young men, to be expelled by our own servants." For by refusing the need quickly with anger, one removes the heaviness and bitterness from the word, as one who does not offer the pain willingly, but necessarily, because of the law and justice. There are also ways in politics that are not ignoble regarding the finances of friends in need, such as Themistocles, who after the battle saw a dead man wearing golden bracelets and a necklace; he himself passed by, but turning to a friend, he said, "Pick these up, for you have not become Themistocles." For affairs often grant this to the statesman regarding friends; for they are not all warriors, and if one is not in need, one can help in other ways regarding justice, and for those who are bound to him, he provides care and protection, and to another, cooperation in a contract, or a contribution of aid. Epaminondas, when a friend approached him, commanded him to ask for a talent, as if his slave had commanded it. When the person who was asked came and inquired, he said first, "Because this man is good, he is poor; but you are wealthy, having embezzled much from the city." And Xenophon says that most men admire their friends who are superior to money. Since one must become a "bulwark" to all, and every political life bears some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate that the politician knows this. Many praise the way Themistocles and Aristides would put aside their enmity whenever they were sent on an embassy or military command, and then take it up again. And how Cretinus was extraordinarily pleasing to the Magnesian! Who, while engaging in politics with his opponent—not with a blow, but with a soul that was ambitious and brilliant—when the war saw the city in danger due to the beard of Mithridates, he ordered the one who had taken the power to manage affairs while he himself stepped aside. "If he wishes to be the general, I shall depart so that we do not destroy the city by being ambitious against each other." The challenge pleased the army, and having decided that it was more warlike for him to be a woman, he withdrew with his children and wife. For Cretinus sent him off, having given him his own money, which was more useful to those fleeing or besieged, and he saved the city from being destroyed by a command that had come from nowhere, unexpectedly. For if noble and wise men do not disappear, "I love my friends, but I love my fatherland even more." For not wishing to be dissolved into enmity, for the sake of which one must sacrifice a friend, is terribly savage and beastlike.

<summary>This section focuses on the proper political conduct of statesmen regarding the selection of friends, the management of debts and public funds, and the necessity of prioritizing the state over personal ambition or personal loyalties.</summary>

<header>POLITICAL PRECEPTS</header>

<margin>one for one purpose, another for another</margin> a pilot, and the shipowner for the pilot; for one knows how to stretch the stern-cable, and the other the prow, or how to work the capstan. To the architect, he assigns assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work, but will work together to complete it perfectly. The statesman, as a master craftsman of certain tools and instruments, and as a creator of power and justice, will not immediately choose friends who are merely like-minded, or servants and those who join him for the sake of what is noble, but rather one for one purpose and another for another, according to our need. <note>The text here discusses the necessity of assigning roles based on utility rather than mere personal affinity.</note> For he said it makes no difference whether a builder or carpenter uses corners, rules, and levels with inexperience and error, by which the work is destined to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking tools of political men. And one must not agree with them when they transgress, but must take care that they do not commit errors even out of ignorance.

<margin>friends</margin> This is what moved Solon and <unclear>Sila</unclear> regarding their friends. For when he had taken on the task of lightening the debts and the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking-off of burdens</gloss>, and the promise was to introduce a cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends. But they, having acted unjustly, took advantage; for they had borrowed a large amount of money beforehand, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they appeared to have purchased brilliant houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was blamed as a conspirator. Being ignorant of the ambitions of his friends, he himself became the weakest and most humble of them, like the Pegasus of Euripides, cowering and yielding more than he wished. And by helping them in their misfortunes more than was necessary, he seemed to be complicit in their injustices. For he who saves a man from a fire that is rolling toward him, and takes the commands given to him, is very much at fault for such things. And he was vehement in what he did, and <unclear>ate the penalty</unclear> in his thirst. For he cast into dishonor those who were guarding and allied with him, and he managed to have them released <unclear>in an amorous manner</unclear>. Softened by the <unclear>foot</unclear>, and writing a letter to a certain ruler, he feared for Nicias; if he does not act unjustly, he is a fool, and if he acts unjustly, he is a fool, but in any case, he is a fool. But Phocion did not even join his son-in-law, Chares, who had a lawsuit regarding stolen goods, but saying, "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," he went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when his brother would not desist from tyranny despite his teaching and entreaties, cooperated with those who killed him. For one should not be a friend "up to the altar" <note>A common Greek proverb meaning to support a friend only as far as piety and justice allow.</note> by not swearing false oaths, as Pericles once said, but up to the point of every law, justice, and benefit. He who is overlooked brings great harm to the community, as <unclear>Antipheron</unclear> <unclear>did not pay the penalty</unclear> <unclear>nor</unclear> <unclear>Phoebidas</unclear>. For these men, in no small way, caused the Lacedaemonian war. Since it is burdensome for the statesman to trample upon the moderate sins of his friends, reason does not compel it, but rather, by placing the greatest of public matters in a safe position, he helps his friends from his own surplus, and stands by them and works with them. There are also these favors: to assist a friend in obtaining an office, or rather to entrust him with some administration, a reputation, or a philanthropic embassy, such as one holding the honors of a leader, or a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and harmony. For this trust is correct, and a manifest and great deed of theirs <unclear>is</unclear> in this, first for themselves, then by sending the friend, as Diomedes said: "If you command me to choose a companion, how could I forget the godlike Odysseus?" And he, in turn, gave him equal praise in his own home. "There are aged newcomers whom you urge, Thracian, of whom <unclear>good</unclear> Diomedes killed twelve, all the best, beside their companions." For this
