yielding to friends does not decorate the praised any less than those who praise. But stubbornness, says Plato, is a companion of solitude. Furthermore, with the beautiful favors of philanthropy, one should also contribute those that are not friendly; for he does not command one to praise or love those who are not present, as having been the cause and contributor at the same time, but to put aside base or absurd demands, not bitterly, but gently teaching and comforting, as if they were not worthy of their virtue or glory. For Epaminondas did this best, when he came to Menexenus, whom Pelopidas had released from prison, and not long after releasing them, he said he was taking <unclear>the needs</unclear> of Pelopidas to the treasurers or generals as was fitting. But he who is heavy and stubborn, since Cato the Censor, being a friend, in matters where he most sought to be a treasurer of those things managed by him, said, "It is shameful, you who ought to be disciplining us young men, to be cast out by our own servants." For by refusing the need sharply, he removed the harshness and bitterness from the speech, so as not to bring the painful thing willingly, but necessarily, because of the law and justice. There are also, regarding money, not ignoble agreements for the statesman to make with friends in need, such as Themistocles, who, after the battle, seeing a dead man wearing gold and a necklace, passed by himself, but turning to a friend, said, "Take these, for you have not become Themistocles." For affairs often give this to the statesman regarding his friends, for not all are <unclear>fighting alone</unclear>, if they are not in need of helping one another for the sake of justice, but for the one who is <unclear>with them</unclear>, he cares for him and gives him <unclear>a position</unclear>, and to another, a partnership in some contract, or a gift of benefit. Epaminondas, when a friend approached him, ordered him to ask for a talent, as if his slave had ordered it. But when the one asked came and inquired, he said first: "Because this man is good, he is poor; but you are wealthy, having stolen much from the city." And Xenophon says that one should admire friends who are better than money. Since it is necessary for all <unclear>natures</clear> and <unclear>Simonides</unclear> to become a <unclear>crest</unclear>, and every political life brings some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate for the statesman to know this. Many, therefore, praise Themistocles and Aristides, who would put aside their enmity at the boundary whenever they were sent on an embassy or a command, and then take it up again. And the case of Cretinus and the Magnesian is wonderfully pleasing; he who was involved in politics with the <unclear>accuser</unclear>, not with malice, but with a soul that was ambitious and brilliant, when the war of Mithridates saw the city in danger, he ordered the <unclear>one seeking</unclear> to take the authority and use the affairs, himself stepping aside. If he wishes to be the general, he himself should depart out of the way, so that by not being ambitious toward each other, they might destroy the city. The challenge pleased the <unclear>Bemeia</unclear>, and having a nature more warlike than himself, he withdrew with his children and wife. For Cretinus sent him off, giving him of his own money, which was more useful to those fleeing or besieged, and he preserved the city from the generalship which had come to it unexpectedly. For if they are noble and wise, they will not destroy the great, "Dear children, but I love my city more," how is it not more ready to say to each one, "I am in the middle of my life and I wish to persuade <unclear>badly</unclear>, but I love my fatherland more." For not wishing to be reconciled to enmity, for the sake of which one must abandon a friend, is terribly savage and beastly. <unclear>For</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the proper conduct of a statesman toward his friends, emphasizing that political utility, justice, and the welfare of the city must take precedence over personal loyalty or private gain.</summary>

<header>POLITICAL PRECEPTS</header>

<margin>one for one purpose, another for another</margin> a pilot, and the shipowner for the pilot; for one knows how to stretch the stern-cable, and the other the prow, or how to work the capstan. To the architect, he assigns assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work, but will work together to complete it perfectly. The statesman, as a master craftsman of certain tools and instruments, and as a creator of power and justice, will not immediately choose friends who are merely like-minded, or servants and those who join him for the sake of what is noble, but rather one for one purpose and another for another, according to our need. <note>The text here discusses the necessity of assigning roles based on utility rather than mere personal affinity.</note> For he said it makes no difference whether a builder or carpenter uses corners, rules, and levels with inexperience and error, by which the work is destined to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking tools of political men. And one must not agree with them when they transgress, but must take care that they do not commit errors even out of ignorance.

<margin>friends</margin> This is what moved Solon and <unclear>Sila</unclear> regarding their friends. For when he had taken on the task of lightening the debts and the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking-off of burdens</gloss>, and the promise was to introduce a cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends. But they, having acted unjustly, took advantage; for they had borrowed a large amount of money beforehand, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they appeared to have purchased brilliant houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was blamed as a conspirator. Being ignorant of the ambitions of his friends, he himself became the weakest and most humble of them, like the Pegasus of Euripides, cowering and yielding more than he wished. And by helping them in their misfortunes more than was necessary, he seemed to be complicit in their injustices. For he who saves a man from a fire that is rolling toward him, and takes the commands given to him, is very much at fault for such things. And he was vehement in what he did, and <unclear>ate the penalty</unclear> in his thirst. For he cast into dishonor those who were guarding and allied with him, and he managed to have them released <unclear>in an amorous manner</unclear>. Softened by the <unclear>foot</unclear>, and writing a letter to a certain ruler, he feared for Nicias; if he does not act unjustly, he is a fool, and if he acts unjustly, he is a fool, but in any case, he is a fool. But Phocion did not even join his son-in-law, Chares, who had a lawsuit regarding stolen goods, but saying, "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," he went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when his brother would not desist from tyranny despite his teaching and entreaties, cooperated with those who killed him. For one should not be a friend "up to the altar" <note>A common Greek proverb meaning to support a friend only as far as piety and justice allow.</note> by not swearing false oaths, as Pericles once said, but up to the point of every law, justice, and benefit. He who is overlooked brings great harm to the community, as <unclear>Antipheron</unclear> <unclear>did not pay the penalty</unclear> <unclear>nor</unclear> <unclear>Phoebidas</unclear>. For these men, in no small way, caused the Lacedaemonian war. Since it is burdensome for the statesman to trample upon the moderate sins of his friends, reason does not compel it, but rather, by placing the greatest of public matters in a safe position, he helps his friends from his own surplus, and stands by them and works with them. There are also these favors: to assist a friend in obtaining an office, or rather to entrust him with some administration, a reputation, or a philanthropic embassy, such as one holding the honors of a leader, or a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and harmony. For this trust is correct, and a manifest and great deed of theirs <unclear>is</unclear> in this, first for themselves, then by sending the friend, as Diomedes said: "If you command me to choose a companion, how could I forget the godlike Odysseus?" And he, in turn, gave him equal praise in his own home. "There are aged newcomers whom you urge, Thracian, of whom <unclear>good</unclear> Diomedes killed twelve, all the best, beside their companions." For this

<header>PRECEPTS</header>

yielding to friends does not decorate the praised any less than those who praise. But stubbornness, says Plato, is a companion of solitude. Furthermore, with the beautiful favors of philanthropy, one should also contribute those that are not friendly; for he does not command one to praise or love those who are not present, as having been the cause and contributor at the same time, but to put aside base or absurd demands, not bitterly, but gently teaching and comforting, as if they were not worthy of their virtue or glory. For Epaminondas did this best, when he came to Menexenus, whom Pelopidas had released from prison, and not long after releasing them, he said he was taking <unclear>the needs</unclear> of Pelopidas to the treasurers or generals as was fitting. But he who is heavy and stubborn, since Cato the Censor, being a friend, in matters where he most sought to be a treasurer of those things managed by him, said, "It is shameful, you who ought to be disciplining us young men, to be cast out by our own servants." For by refusing the need sharply, he removed the harshness and bitterness from the speech, so as not to bring the painful thing willingly, but necessarily, because of the law and justice. There are also, regarding money, not ignoble agreements for the statesman to make with friends in need, such as Themistocles, who, after the battle, seeing a dead man wearing gold and a necklace, passed by himself, but turning to a friend, said, "Take these, for you have not become Themistocles." For affairs often give this to the statesman regarding his friends, for not all are <unclear>fighting alone</unclear>, if they are not in need of helping one another for the sake of justice, but for the one who is <unclear>with them</unclear>, he cares for him and gives him <unclear>a position</unclear>, and to another, a partnership in some contract, or a gift of benefit. Epaminondas, when a friend approached him, ordered him to ask for a talent, as if his slave had ordered it. But when the one asked came and inquired, he said first: "Because this man is good, he is poor; but you are wealthy, having stolen much from the city." And Xenophon says that one should admire friends who are better than money. Since it is necessary for all <unclear>natures</clear> and <unclear>Simonides</unclear> to become a <unclear>crest</unclear>, and every political life brings some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate for the statesman to know this. Many, therefore, praise Themistocles and Aristides, who would put aside their enmity at the boundary whenever they were sent on an embassy or a command, and then take it up again. And the case of Cretinus and the Magnesian is wonderfully pleasing; he who was involved in politics with the <unclear>accuser</unclear>, not with malice, but with a soul that was ambitious and brilliant, when the war of Mithridates saw the city in danger, he ordered the <unclear>one seeking</unclear> to take the authority and use the affairs, himself stepping aside. If he wishes to be the general, he himself should depart out of the way, so that by not being ambitious toward each other, they might destroy the city. The challenge pleased the <unclear>Bemeia</unclear>, and having a nature more warlike than himself, he withdrew with his children and wife. For Cretinus sent him off, giving him of his own money, which was more useful to those fleeing or besieged, and he preserved the city from the generalship which had come to it unexpectedly. For if they are noble and wise, they will not destroy the great, "Dear children, but I love my city more," how is it not more ready to say to each one, "I am in the middle of my life and I wish to persuade <unclear>badly</unclear>, but I love my fatherland more." For not wishing to be reconciled to enmity, for the sake of which one must abandon a friend, is terribly savage and beastly. <unclear>For</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the proper conduct of a statesman toward his friends, emphasizing that political utility, justice, and the welfare of the city must take precedence over personal loyalty or private gain.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page: Plutarch is discussing the selection of associates in political life.</meta>

<margin>One for one task, another for another.</margin> A pilot needs a helmsman, and a ship-owner needs a pilot; for one knows how to tighten the stern-cable and the other how to manage the prow or work the capstan. Likewise, an architect requires assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work but will labor alongside him to complete it. So too the statesman, as a master-craftsman and a creator of power and justice, will not immediately choose friends who merely share his passions, but rather assistants and those who will strive with him toward what is noble. We must choose different men for different needs, rather than those who would act unjustly or violently. For he said it makes no difference whether a builder or a carpenter uses corners, rulers, and plumb-lines with ignorance and error, by which the work is bound to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking tools of statesmen. One must not join them in their transgressions, but rather take care that they do not commit errors even through ignorance.

<margin>Friends.</margin> This is what moved and distressed Solon regarding his friends. For when he intended to lighten the debts and introduce the <term>Seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>, and his plan was to bring in a cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends. But they committed an injustice: they anticipated the law by borrowing a great deal of silver, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased splendid houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was blamed for participating in this scheme, though he was actually a victim of it. Being ignorant of his friends' eagerness, he became the weakest and most humble of men, just like Euripides' Pegasus, who cowered more than he wished to yield. By helping them in their misfortunes more than was proper, he seemed to be a partner in their injustices. For even those who save someone lying in a ditch might be pushed by the rolling fire. 

When Phocion's son-in-law, Charicles, was on trial regarding the money from Harpalus, Phocion did not join him in court, but said: I made you my son-in-law only for what is just; and he went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny by teaching and entreating him, joined those who put him to death. For a man should be a friend only as far as the altar <note>meaning: as far as his religious and moral oaths allow</note>, as Pericles once said, not joining in perjury, but remaining a friend only as far as law, justice, and the public good allow. If this is overlooked, it brings great harm to the community, as when they failed to punish Sphodrias or Phoebidas; for these men, by their actions, brought war upon Sparta. 

While the statesman should not be harsh in attacking the moderate failings of his friends, he should, after securing the most important public interests, use his surplus influence to help his friends, stand by them, and labor with them. These are favors that do not provoke envy: helping a friend toward an office, or rather handing over some administration to him, or an honorable embassy that carries the prestige of a leader, or a mission to a city for the sake of friendship and concord. For this is a proper trust, and a visible and great deed for them. First, he should manage his own affairs, then go on an embassy with a friend, as Diomedes did: If you indeed bid me choose a companion myself, how then could I forget godlike Odysseus? And Odysseus in turn gave him equal praise. There are also those who, like Diomedes, slew twelve of the best Thracians among their comrades. For

<header>PRECEPTS OF STATECRAFT</header>

this yielding to friends does not less adorn the one praised than those who praise him. But stubbornness, as Plato says, is the companion of solitude. Furthermore, one should combine these noble favors of kindness with those that are less pleasant; he should not bid them to praise or love those who are not present as if they were the causes and tokens of success, but rather set aside mean or absurd demands—not bitterly, but by gently teaching and comforting them, showing that such things are not worthy of their virtue or reputation. 

Epaminondas acted best in this regard: when he refused to release a certain prisoner at the request of Pelopidas, but released him shortly after when a common girl asked for him, he said that such favors were for girls to receive, but for Pelopidas to receive treasurerships or generalships. And Cato the Censor acted with weight and dignity when his friend Catulus, who was then Censor, sought to intervene for someone being audited by him as treasurer; Cato said: It is a shame that you, who ought to be disciplining us young men, are being driven out by our own subordinates. For by refusing the request with spirit, he removed the abruptness and bitterness from his words, so that the pain did not seem to come from his own will but from the necessity of law and justice. 

There are also ways for friends to profit from political life that are not ignoble. For instance, after the battle, Themistocles saw a corpse wearing gold bracelets and a necklace; he passed by himself, but turning to a friend, he said: Pick these up, for you have not become a Themistocles. For circumstances often give the statesman such opportunities for his friends; for not all men are of a single mold. If one is not able to help in a matter of justice, he may assist a friend by giving him charge of a contract or a partnership in some public work, or by providing the benefit of a loan. 

When a friend came to Epaminondas asking for a talent of silver, he ordered him to ask a certain wealthy man for it, saying that Epaminondas ordered it. When the man who was asked came to inquire why, Epaminondas said: Because this man is honest but poor, while you are rich from having embezzled much from the city. And Xenophon says that it is a great thing to be able to benefit friends while remaining superior to money. 

Since every position of leadership and every public career brings certain enmities and differences, it is especially necessary for the statesman to know how to handle this. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides because they would lay aside their enmity at the border whenever they went out on an embassy or a military command, and then take it up again afterward. Some are also exceedingly pleased by the conduct of Cretinus of Magnesia. He was a political rival of Hermias, a man of ambitious and brilliant spirit. When the war with Mithridates broke out and he saw the city in danger, he proposed that Hermias take over the command and manage affairs while he himself withdrew; or, if Hermias wished him to lead, that Hermias should step aside so they would not destroy the city by competing with one another. The challenge pleased Hermias, and saying that Cretinus was the better soldier, he withdrew with his wife and children. Cretinus then escorted him out, giving him money from his own funds, as it was more useful to those in exile than to those under siege; thus he unexpectedly saved the city which had come to the brink of ruin. 

For if noble and wise men say: I love my children, but I love my country more, why should it not be even readier for each of them to say: I hate this man and wish to best him, but I love my country more? For to be unwilling to settle an enmity for the sake of things for which one ought to give up even a friend is a terribly savage and bestial trait. But...

<header>POLITICS</header>

<margin>one to another</margin> a pilot, and the shipowner to the pilot; knowing how to handle the rudder well at the stern, and the yardarm well when the wind rises. Just as an architect chooses assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work, but will work together with him in the best way, so the statesman, being a master craftsman according to Pindar, and a creator of good order and justice, will not immediately choose friends who are like-minded, and servants who are enthusiastic with him for the good, but rather those who are suited to the specific need at hand, lest they bend him unjustly and violently. For he will appear no different from a builder or carpenter who, through inexperience and error, uses squares, rules, and levels that would cause the work to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking instruments of political men. And one must not slide along with them when they transgress, but must take care that they do not commit errors even out of ignorance. 

This is what disgraced Solon and brought him into disrepute with the citizens. For when he conceived the idea of lightening the burden of debts and the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>—which was a euphemism for introducing a cancellation of debts—he shared this with his friends. But they did a most unjust thing; they borrowed a great deal of money beforehand, and a short time later, when the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased brilliant houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was accused of being a partner in the injustice, though he had been wronged. 

Agesilaus, regarding the requests of his friends, became weak and humble himself, like the Pegasus of Euripides, <margin>he would wish</margin> cowering, yielding more than he would wish. And by helping them in their misfortunes more readily than he should have, he seemed to make himself complicit in their injustices. For he saved Phoebidas, who was on trial for seizing the Cadmea without orders, saying that such things should be done spontaneously. And he also saved Sphodrias, who was fleeing trial for an illegal and terrible act; for he had invaded Attica while they were friends and allies. He managed to get him acquitted, softened by the amorous pleas of the boy, and a letter of his to a certain potentate is still circulated, saying: "If Nicias is not guilty, acquit him; if he is guilty, acquit him for my sake; but in any case, acquit him." 

But Phocion would not even join his son-in-law Charillus, who was on trial regarding the Harpalus affair, but saying, "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," he walked away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny through teaching and entreaty, cooperated with those who killed him. For one must not be a friend "up to the altar" in order not to perjure oneself, as Pericles once said, but up to the point of law, justice, and the common good. When this is overlooked, it leads to great and common harm, just as the failure to punish Sphodrias and Phoebidas led to the ruin of Sparta in the Leuctrian War. 

Since the statesman is not forced by reason to be harsh in dealing with the moderate mistakes of friends, he may even provide for their safety by using the surplus of public affairs to help his friends, and to stand by and work with them. There are also favors that are not subject to reproach, such as helping a friend toward an office, or entrusting him with a glorious administration or a humane embassy, such as one holding the honors of a leader, or an interview with a city on behalf of friendship and harmony. If there is a difficult, prominent, and great task, he should assign it to himself first, and then choose his friend as an associate, as Diomedes did: "If you command me to choose a companion myself, how then could I forget the godlike Odysseus?" And he in turn returns the praise in a fitting manner: "Old man, you ask about these horses, which are new arrivals, Thracian; the good Diomedes killed their master, and twelve companions, all the best." For this yielding to friends adorns the praisers no less than those who are praised. 

<column-break/>

<header>PRECEPTS</header>

And stubbornness, says Plato, is the companion of solitude. Furthermore, one must make friends partners in noble and humane favors, and command those who have been well-treated to praise and love them, as they have been both the cause and the advisors. But one must brush aside base and absurd demands, not bitterly, but by teaching and comforting them gently, <margin>base</margin> as they are not worthy of their virtue and reputation. 

Epaminondas was the best of men; when he refused Pelopidas's request to release a pimp from prison, and shortly after released him when his mistress asked, he said, "Such favors, Pelopidas, are fitting for mistresses, not for generals." Cato, however, was harsh and stubborn; when Catulus the censor, who was one of his closest friends and acquaintances, asked for the release of one of those being judged by him while he was treasurer, he said, "It is shameful, you who ought to be disciplining us young men, to be cast out by our own servants." For he could have refused the favor by deed, and removed the harshness and bitterness from his words, so as not to appear to be inflicting the pain of the act willingly, but necessarily, because of the law and justice. 

There are also ways in politics to help friends in need of money that are not ignoble. For example, Themistocles, after the battle, seeing a dead man wearing gold necklaces and bracelets, passed by himself, but turning to his friend, said, "Take these, for you have not become Themistocles." For circumstances often give the statesman the opportunity to help his friends; for not everyone is a Menemachus. To one, entrust a paid advocacy on behalf of justice; to another, introduce a wealthy man in need of care and protection; to another, assist in some contract or lease that has profit. Epaminondas, when a friend approached a certain rich man, told him to ask for a talent, as if he himself had ordered it to be given. When the one asked came and inquired about the reason, he said, "Because this man is good, but poor; and you are rich, having stolen much from the city." And Xenophon says that Agesilaus took pride in enriching his friends while he himself was superior to wealth. 

Since, according to Simonides, every lark must have a crest, and every state brings some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate for the statesman to have considered these matters as well. Most people praise Themistocles and Aristides for laying aside their enmity at the borders whenever they went out on an embassy or a military command, and then taking it up again. To some, the conduct of Cretinas the Magnesian is also exceedingly pleasing. For while he was in political opposition to Hermeias, a man who was not powerful but ambitious and brilliant in spirit, when the Mithridatic War gripped the city and he saw it in danger, he ordered Hermeias to take over the leadership and manage affairs while he himself withdrew. If he wishes to be the general, he should go out of the way, lest by being ambitious toward each other, they destroy the city. The proposal pleased Hermeias, and saying that Cretinas was more warlike than himself, he withdrew with his children and wife. Cretinas sent him off, contributing from his own funds whatever was more useful for those in exile or under siege, and by managing the city in the best way, he saved it when it had come to nothing and was expected to be lost. For if it is noble and of great spirit to exclaim, "I love my children, but I love my fatherland more," how is it not more readily said by each one, "I hate so-and-so and I wish to do him harm, but I love my fatherland more"? For not wanting to be reconciled with an enemy, for whose sake one must abandon a friend, is terribly savage and beastly. Not, however...

<summary>Plutarch discusses the proper conduct of a statesman toward his friends, emphasizing that political duty and the common good must take precedence over personal loyalty, illustrated by historical examples of leaders like Solon, Agesilaus, and Epaminondas.</summary>

reference.text:
[context] There are some who without reservation assert that Osiris is the Sun and is called the Dog-star (Sirius) by the Greeks
even if among the Egyptians the addition of the article has created some ambiguity in regard to the name; and there are those who declare that Isis is none other than the Moon; for this reason it is said that the statues of Isis that bear horns are imitations of the crescent moon, and in her dark garments are shown the concealments and the obscurations in which she in her yearning pursues the Sun. For this reason also they call upon the Moon in love affairs,
and Eudoxus asserts that Isis is a deity who presides over love affairs. These people may lay claim to a certain plausibility, but no one should listen for a moment to those who make Typhon to be the Sun.
But now let us take up again the proper subject of our discussion.
Isis is, in fact, the female principle of Nature, and is receptive of every form of generation, in accord with which she is called by Plato the gentle nurse and the all-receptive, and by most people has been called by countless names, since,
[context] because of the force of Reason, she turns herself to this thing or that and is receptive of all manner of shapes and forms.

For this reason, they call upon the Moon for erotic matters, and Eudoxus says that Isis presides over erotic matters. And in these, in one way or another, there is a share of plausibility; but those who make the Sun into Typhon are not even worth hearing. But let us again take up our proper discourse.

53. For Isis is the feminine aspect of Nature, and is receptive of all generation, in accordance with which she is called Nurse and All-Receiving by Plato, and by the many <gloss>1</gloss> Myrionymos [Ten-thousand-named] because she receives all things [into herself]

PLUTARCH ON

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the intention of the article has made the name ambiguous</meta> they declare Isis to be none other than the Moon, and that some of her statues are horned as imitations of the crescent, while those dressed in black <gloss>8</gloss> signify the concealments and shadows in which she pursues the sun out of longing. For this reason, they invoke the Moon for matters of love, and Eudoxus says that Isis presides over love. And these accounts <gloss>9</gloss> have, in some way or another, a share of plausibility; but as for those who make Typhon the Sun, it is not even worth listening to them. But let us return again to our own argument.

53. For Isis is the female principle of Nature, and receptive of all generation, in which capacity she is called the Nurse and the All-Receptive by Plato, and by the many <gloss>1</gloss> she is called Myrionymos <gloss>the Myriad-Named</gloss>, because she is <column-break/>

<margin>
In the Greek manner of dialect, Osiris is the many-eyed one; reasonably so, for by casting his rays everywhere, he sees all land and sea as if with many eyes. Some of the ancient mythologists among the Greeks call Osiris Dionysus, and by a similar name, Sirius. Isis, when translated, means "ancient," the name having been applied to the Moon, etc.
</margin>

<margin>
<gloss>8</gloss> signify the concealments] Scribe, TO SIGNIFY. *Markland*.

<gloss>9</gloss> in some way or another] Scribe, SOMEHOW. Thus below on page 140, "and Plato somehow calls the myth of things..." *Markland*.

<gloss>1</gloss> is called Myrionymos] Consult *Apuleius, Metamorphoses, book XI, page 362*, where you may read various things recited from the *Names of Isis*: "For the gods are captured by the variety of their titles."
</margin>

<summary>Plutarch discusses the identification of Isis with the Moon and her role in love, while dismissing the identification of Typhon with the Sun. He then introduces Isis as the female principle of Nature, known as the All-Receptive and the Myriad-Named.</summary>
<keywords>Isis, Osiris, Moon, Nature, Plato, Myrionymos, Typhon, Sun</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...among the Egyptians, the addition of the article has caused the name to be misunderstood</meta> while they declare that Isis is none other than the Moon. For this reason, some of her statues are made with horns as imitations of the crescent moon, and by her black-robed garments <gloss>8</gloss> they signify the occultations and the overshadowings in which she pursues the Sun, longing for him. Therefore, they also call upon the Moon in matters of love, and Eudoxus says that Isis presides over love affairs. These arguments indeed possess some degree of plausibility; but as for those who make Typhon to be the Sun, they are not even worth listening to. But let us resume our own proper discourse.

53. For Isis is the female principle of Nature, and she is receptive to every form of generation, in which respect she is called Nurse and All-receiving by Plato, and by the many she is called <term>Myrionymos</term> <gloss>She of the Ten Thousand Names</gloss>, because she is transformed by...

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
...into the Greek manner of speech, Osiris is "many-eyed"; and reasonably so, for by casting his rays everywhere, he sees the whole land and sea as if with many eyes. Some of the ancient mythologists among the Greeks address Osiris as Dionysus, and as Sirius by a similar name. They say that Isis, when translated, means "ancient," the name having been given to the Moon, etc.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
<gloss>8</gloss> they signify the occultations] The scribe wrote <term>emphainesthai</term> <gloss>to be shown</gloss>. Note by Markland.

<gloss>9</gloss> in some other way] The scribe wrote <term>amosgepos</term> <gloss>somehow or other</gloss>. Likewise below on page 140: "he also invites the myth of Plato, which somehow or other <note>original: amosgepos</note> touches on the facts." Note by Markland.

<gloss>1</gloss> called She of the Ten Thousand Names] Consult Apuleius, Metamorphoses, Book 11, page 362, where you may read various names recited from the Names of Isis: "For the Gods are won over by a variety of titles."
</margin>

<summary>Plutarch discusses the identification of Isis with the Moon and her role as the receptive female principle of Nature, comparing her to Plato's concept of the universal receptacle. Marginal notes provide philological corrections and references to Apuleius regarding the many names of the goddess.</summary>
